Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 1:

(p-63)﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾. The exegetes (mufassirun) differed concerning it in eight opinions (aqawil, sing. qawl, "sayings"):

The first: it is one of the names of the Qur'an, like al-Furqan and al-Dhikr. This is the view of Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj.

The second: it is one of the names of the surahs. This is the view of Zayd ibn Aslam.

The third: it is the Greatest Name of God (ism Allah al-a'zam). This is the view of al-Suddi and al-Sha'bi. (p-64)

The fourth: it is an oath that God, exalted is He, swore by, and it is one of His names. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and 'Ikrimah.

The fifth: they are disjoined letters (huruf muqatta'ah) drawn from names and verbs. The alif is from "ana" (I), the lam from "Allah," and the mim from "a'lamu" (I know). So the meaning is: "I am God, the Knowing." This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and a similar view is reported from Ibn 'Abbas as well.

The sixth: they are letters, each of which contains different meanings. The alif is a key whose name is Allah, the lam is a key whose name is Latif, and the mim is a key whose name is Majid. The alif is the blessings (ala') of God, the mim is His glory (majd), the alif is a year, the lam is thirty years, and the mim is forty years: terms (ajal, pl. ajal) that God has mentioned.

The seventh: they are letters from the abjad reckoning (hisab al-jummal), on the basis of what came in a report from al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas and Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab passed by the Messenger of God ﷺ while he was reciting the Opening of the Book and Surah al-Baqarah: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim. That is the Book, there is no doubt in it﴾. So he came to his brother Huyayy ibn Akhtab with some men of the Jews to the Messenger of God ﷺ, and they said: 'O Muhammad, did you not tell us that you recite, in what God has sent down to you: ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾ ﴿That (p-65) is the Book﴾?' The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'Yes.' They said: 'Did Jibril bring them to you from God?' He said: 'Yes.' They said: 'God sent prophets before you, and we do not know that the term of the reign of any of them was specified for a prophet other than you, nor the lifespan of his community.' Then Huyayy ibn Akhtab turned to those who were with him and said to them: 'The alif is one, the lam is thirty, and the mim is forty; these are seventy-one years.' Then he turned to the Messenger of God ﷺ and said: 'O Muhammad, is there anything beyond this?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'What?' He said: '(Alif-Lam-Mim-Sad)'. He said: 'This is heavier and longer: the alif is one, the lam is thirty, the mim is forty, and the sad is ninety; these are one hundred and sixty-one years. Is there anything beyond this, O Muhammad?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'What?' He said: '(Alif-Lam-Ra)'. He said: 'This is heavier and longer: the alif is one, the lam is thirty, and the ra is two hundred; these are two hundred and thirty-one years. Is there anything beyond this, O Muhammad?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'What?' He said: '(Alif-Lam-Mim-Ra)'. He said: 'This is heavier and longer: the alif is one, the lam is thirty, the mim is forty, and the ra is two hundred; these are two hundred and seventy-one years.'

Then he said: 'Your affair has become confused for us, to the point that we do not know whether you were given little or much.' Then they rose from him. Abu Yasir said to his brother Huyayy ibn Akhtab and to those of the rabbis with him: 'What do you know? Perhaps all of this has been gathered for Muhammad: seventy-one, and one hundred and sixty-one, and two hundred and thirty-one, and two hundred and seventy-one. That makes seven hundred and thirty-four years.' They said: 'His affair has become confused for us!'" They claim that these verses were revealed concerning them: ﴿He it is who has sent down to you the Book, in which there are clear verses, they are the mother of the Book, and others are ambiguous﴾.

The eighth: they are letters of the alphabet (huruf hija') by which God, exalted is He, informed the Arabs when He challenged them with the Qur'an, that it is composed of the letters of speech, these same letters from which their speech is built, so that their inability to produce its like would be more decisive as proof against them, since it did not go outside their speech.

As for the letters of abjad, their speech is not built upon them, nor are they its root. The people of knowledge have differed concerning them in four opinions: (p-66)

The first: they are the six days in which God, exalted is He, created the world. This is the view of al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim.

The second: they are the names of the kings of Madyan. This is the view of al-Sha'bi, and the saying of one of the poets of Madyan is evidence for that. Their poet said:

Ala ya Shu'ayb qad nataqta maqalatan / sababta biha 'Amran wa Hayya Bani 'Amr
Muluk Bani Huttay wa Hawwaz minhum / wa Sa'faṣ asl lil-makarim wal-fakhr
Hum sabbahu ahl al-Hijaz bi-ghaaratin / kamithli shu'a'i al-shamsi aw matla'i al-fajr

(Oh Shu'ayb, you have spoken a word / by which you reviled 'Amr and the living clan of the sons of 'Amr. / The kings of the sons of Huttay and Hawwaz are among them, / and Sa'faṣ is the root of nobility and pride. / They attacked the people of the Hijaz with a raid / like the rays of the sun or the rising of dawn.)

The third: what Maymun ibn Mihran related from Ibn 'Abbas, that Abu Jad has a wondrous tale: (Aba) — Adam refused obedience; (Jadda) — he persisted in eating from the tree; as for (Hawwaz), Adam descended and fell from the sky to the earth; as for (Huṭṭī), his sin was removed (huttat khatī'atuhu); as for (Kalamun), he ate from the tree, and was granted forgiveness through repentance; as for (Sa'faṣ), Adam disobeyed and was expelled from bliss to hardship; as for (Qarashat), he acknowledged the sin and was spared punishment.

The fourth: they are letters from the names of God, exalted is He. This was related by Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah, from his father, from the Prophet ﷺ. (p-67)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 2:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is the Book﴾. There are three interpretations of this:

The first: it means the Torah and the Gospel, so that it is a report about something past.

The second: it means what was revealed of the Qur'an before this, at Makkah and Madinah. This is the view of al-Asamm.

The third: it means this Book. That demonstrative may be used to point to something present, even though it is originally designed to point to something absent. Khufaf ibn Nudbah said:

"I say to him while the spear bends its shaft: Consider Khufaf, for I am that one (dhalika)."

As for those who held the first interpretation, that what is meant is the Torah and the Gospel, they differed about who is addressed by it, on two views:

One of them: the one addressed is the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: that Book which I mentioned in the Torah and the Gospel is the one I have sent down to you, O Muhammad.

The second view: the one addressed are the Jews and the Christians, and the sense is: that which I promised you is this Book which I sent down to Muhammad, upon him and his family be peace.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿there is no doubt in it﴾. There are two interpretations of this:

One of them: that doubt (rayb) is suspicion (shakk). This is the saying of Ibn Abbas, and from it is the saying of Abdullah ibn al-Zib'ara:

"There is no doubt in the truth, O Umaymah; doubt is only what the ignorant one says."

The second interpretation: that rayb means accusation (tuhmah). From it is the saying of Jamil:

"Buthaynah said: O Jamil, you have made me doubtful (arbtani). I said: Both of us, O Buthayn, are suspect (murib)."

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿a guidance for the God-conscious﴾. It means guidance from misguidance.

Regarding the God-conscious (al-muttaqun), there are three interpretations: (p-68)

The first: they are those who refrain from what God has forbidden them and fulfill what He has obligated upon them. This is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri.

The second: they are those who fear God's punishment and hope for His mercy. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The third: they are those who guard against shirk and are free of hypocrisy. This is weak, because a person may be like that and still be a sinner; the text specified the God-conscious, though it is guidance for all people, because they are the ones who believed and affirmed what it contains.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 3:

﴿Those who believe in the unseen﴾. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who believe in the unseen﴾. Regarding it there are two interpretations. The first: they affirm the unseen (yuṣaddiqūna bil-ghayb). This is the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: they fear the unseen (yakhshawna bil-ghayb). This is the statement of al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas.

Regarding the origin of faith (īmān) there are three opinions. The first: its origin is tasdīq (affirmation, confirmation), and from it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and you are not a believer (muʾmin) to us﴾, meaning, not one who affirms (muṣaddiq) us.

The second: its origin is amān (security), so the believer (al-muʾmin) secures his soul from the punishment of God, and God is the Giver of security (al-Muʾmin) to His allies from His punishment. (p-69)

The third: its origin is ṭumaʾnīna (tranquillity), so one who affirms a report is called muʾmin, because he is tranquil (muṭmaʾinn).

Regarding faith (al-īmān) there are three sayings. The first: faith is avoiding the major sins (kabāʾir).

The second: every single obligation (farīḍa) is a part of faith.

The third: every act of obedience is faith.

Regarding the unseen (al-ghayb) there are three interpretations. The first: what has come from God, and this is the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: it is the Qurʾan, and this is the statement of Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh.

The third: belief in Paradise and Hell, resurrection and rising (al-baʿth wal-nushūr).

﴿And they establish the prayer (ṣalāh), and from what We have provided them they spend﴾. Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they establish the prayer﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: they perform it with its obligatory parts (furūḍ).

The second: it is the completion of the bowing (rukūʿ), prostration (sujūd), recitation, and humility (khushūʿ) within it, and this is the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas.

It has been disputed why the performance of the prayer was called "establishing" it on this view, on two sayings. The first: from straightening (taqwīm) a thing, from their saying "qāma bil-amr" when he perfected it and guarded it.

The second: that the performance of the prayer was called "establishing" it because of the standing (qiyām) in it; therefore it is said: "the prayer has been established (qad qāmat al-ṣalāh)."

Regarding His saying: ﴿and from what We have provided them they spend﴾ there are three interpretations. The first: giving zakāh seeking reward for it, and this is the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas. (p-70)

The second: a man's expenditure on his family, and this is the statement of Ibn Masʿūd.

The third: voluntary spending in what brings one closer to God, exalted is He, and this is the statement of al-Ḍaḥḥāk. The origin of infāq (spending) is ikhrāj (bringing out), and from it it is said: "nafaqat al-dābba" when its spirit (rūḥ) came out.

The exegetes differed concerning who these two verses were revealed about, on three sayings. The first: they were revealed concerning the believers of the Arabs alone and not others, because He said after this: ﴿and those who believe in what has been sent down to you and what was sent down before you﴾, meaning by it the People of the Book, and this is the statement of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: that they, together with the two verses after four verses, were revealed concerning the believers among the People of the Book, because He mentioned them in some of them.

The third: that the first four verses of the surah were revealed concerning all the believers. Ibn Abī Najīḥ narrated from Mujāhid who said: ("Four verses of Surat al-Baqara were revealed describing the believers, two verses describing the disbelievers, and thirteen concerning the hypocrites.")

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 4:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And those who believe in what has been revealed to you﴾ and what follows it.

As for His saying: ﴿And those who believe in what has been revealed to you﴾, it means the Qur'an. ﴿And what was revealed before you﴾ means the Torah and the Gospel and what preceded them of the books of the prophets, in contrast to what the Jews and the Christians did, in believing in some of them and not all of them.

﴿And in the Hereafter they are certain﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations: (p-71)

The first: it means the Abode of the Hereafter.

The second: it means the Hereafter's creation (the resurrection). As for its being named the "Hereafter abode," there are two views. The first: because it comes later than the first abode (this world). The second: because it comes later than creation, just as this world was named (al-dunya, "the nearer") for its nearness to creation.

And His saying: ﴿they are certain﴾, that is, they know. Knowledge was called certainty (yaqin) because it arises from an evidence through which it becomes certain.

Al-Mawardi, in al-Nukat wa al-Uyun, on surah 2, verse 5:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They are upon guidance from their Lord﴾, meaning: (clear proof and right direction). ﴿And they are the successful ones﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first is that they are the victorious, the happy ones. From this is the verse of Labid:

؎ If anyone who attains success could attain it, it would be attained by the one who plays with spears.

The second is that they are those for whom good is decreed, because al-falh (success) in their speech means cutting (qat'), and it is for this reason that a farmer is called fallah (ploughman), since he cleaves the earth. The poet has said:

؎ Indeed you know, O son of Umm Sahsah, that iron is split (yufhalu) only by iron.

Scholars differed about who is meant by them, in three ways. The first: the believers among the Arabs who have faith in the unseen, and the believers in what was sent down to Muhammad, and to those before him among the other prophets, from non-Arabs.

The second: they are the believers among the Arabs alone.

The third: they are all the believers.

The Qur'anic phrase: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, it is the same for them﴾. The root meaning of kufr (disbelief) among the Arabs is covering over. From it is His saying, ﴿The farmers were pleased by its growth﴾, meaning the tillers, because they cover the seed in the earth. Labid said:

*In a night whose clouds covered over the stars.*

... ... ...

That is, it covered them. Thus the one who disbelieves in Allah, the Exalted, is named by this, because he covers over the blessings of Allah by denying them.

As for shirk (associating partners with Allah), it carries the ruling of kufr, and its root lies in associating others in worship.

Scholars differed about who is meant by this, and there are three views:

The first: they are the Jews who lived around Madinah. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, who used to name them individually.

The second: they are all the polytheist People of the Book. This is the choice of al-Tabari.

The third: the verse was revealed concerning the leaders of the factions. This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

"His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah has set a seal upon their hearts﴾. The khatm (seal) is the ṭabʿ (stamping, imprinting), and from it comes khatm al-kitab (sealing a book). In this there are four interpretations.

The first, which is the saying of Mujahid: the heart is like the palm of the hand. When the servant commits a sin, it is folded up like a finger; when he sins a second time, a second finger is folded, until all of it is folded up and then it is stamped with a stamp.

The second: it is a mark (simah) that serves as a sign upon them, by which the angels recognize them from among the believers.

The third: it is a report from Allah the Exalted about their disbelief and their turning away from hearing the truth to which they were called, likened to something that has been blocked and sealed, so that no good enters it.

The fourth: it is a testimony from Allah the Exalted concerning their hearts, that they do not comprehend the reminder and do not accept the truth, and concerning their hearing, that they do not listen to it. And the ghishawah (covering) is their blindness to the truth.

The heart was named qalb (heart) because of its qalab (turning, fluctuation) with thoughts, and it has been said:

"The heart was only named for its turning,
and opinion turns, and man is in stages."

And the ghishawah is the all-encompassing covering."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 8–9:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They seek to deceive Allah and those who believe, but they deceive none except themselves﴾. He means: the hypocrites (al-munafiqun) seek to deceive the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers, by showing from faith the opposite of what they conceal of disbelief, because the origin of khada'a (deception) is concealment, and from it comes makhda' al-bayt (the inner chamber of the house), in which one hides. Allah made their deception of His Messenger a deception of Himself, because he called them with His message.

﴿But they deceive none except themselves﴾: [the deception returns] with its harm upon them.

﴿And they do not perceive﴾: means they do not notice (yafṭunūn). From this comes the name of the poet (al-sha'ir), because he perceives what others do not perceive, and from it comes their saying: "Would that I knew" (layta shi'ri).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 8–9:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They seek to deceive Allah and those who believe, but they deceive none except themselves﴾. He means: the hypocrites (al-munafiqun) seek to deceive the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers, by showing from faith the opposite of what they conceal of disbelief, because the origin of khada'a (deception) is concealment, and from it comes makhda' al-bayt (the inner chamber of the house), in which one hides. Allah made their deception of His Messenger a deception of Himself, because he called them with His message.

﴿But they deceive none except themselves﴾: [the deception returns] with its harm upon them.

﴿And they do not perceive﴾: means they do not notice (yafṭunūn). From this comes the name of the poet (al-sha'ir), because he perceives what others do not perceive, and from it comes their saying: "Would that I knew" (layta shi'ri).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 10:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿In their hearts is a disease﴾ — regarding this there are three interpretations: (p-74)

The first: doubt (shakk). This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: hypocrisy (nifaq). This is the statement of Muqatil, and from it is the verse of the poet:

"I flatter people out of shame, though I see their chests seething against me with their sicknesses."

The third: that the disease is grief (ghamm) at the rise of the Prophet's (ﷺ) affair over his enemies. The root of "marad" (disease) is weakness, as one says, "marrada fi al-qawl" (he weakened the statement) when he made it weak.

﴿So Allah increased them in disease﴾ — regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: it is an invocation against them with this.

The second: it is an report from Allah, exalted is He, about the increase in their disease upon the descent of the obligations (fara'id) and the prescribed punishments (hudud).

﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾ — meaning: "painful" (mu'lim).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 11–12:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Do not cause corruption on the earth"﴾, there are three interpretations concerning it. The first: it is disbelief (kufr).

The second: doing what Allah has forbidden and neglecting what He has commanded to be preserved.

The third: that it is backing the disbelievers (mumalaʾah al-kuffar).

All three of these are corruption on the earth, because corruption (fasad) is deviating from uprightness (istiqamah) to its opposite.

Scholars differed regarding who is meant by this saying, in two ways. The first: it was revealed concerning a people who were not present at that time but would come later; this is the view of Sulayman.

The second: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites (munafiqun) who were present; this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid. (p-75)

﴿They say, "We are only reformers"﴾. There are four interpretations concerning it. The first: they thought that backing the disbelievers was beneficial for them, but it was not as they thought, because if the disbelievers were to gain the upper hand over them, they would not spare them; therefore He said: ﴿Unquestionably, they are the corrupters, but they do not perceive﴾. The second: they denied, by this, that they had done what they had been forbidden, namely backing the disbelievers, and said: "We are only reformers in avoiding what we have been forbidden."

The third: its meaning is that our backing of the disbelievers is only intended as reconciliation between them and the believers; this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The fourth: they meant that backing the disbelievers is reform and guidance, and not corruption; this is the view of Mujahid.

If it is said: how is their hypocrisy valid alongside their striving (mujahadah) with this saying? There are two answers. The first: they made this saying by allusion, and spoke of it indirectly without explicit declaration.

The second: they said it secretly to those Muslims with whom they were alone, and did not declare it openly, so they remained upon their hypocrisy.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 13:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Believe as the people have believed"﴾, meaning the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), ﴿they say, "Shall we believe as the fools have believed?"﴾ There are two interpretations regarding this. One: they meant by "the fools" the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ). The second: they intended the believers among the People of the Book.

As for al-Sufaha' (fools), it is the plural of safih (foolish, ignorant person). The root meaning of safah is lightness (khiffah), derived from their saying: "a thawb safih" (a sheer garment), when it is thin in weave. Thus the lightness of forbearance (ḥilm) was called safah. Al-Samaw'al said:

"We fear that our forbearances may become light (tasfah),
so that we are made to sink in lowliness for ages along with the lowly."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 14–15:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when they go apart to their devils﴾. Regarding "their devils" there are two views. The first is that they are the Jews, who command them to deny (the truth), and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second is that they are their leaders in disbelief, and this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud.

Regarding His saying ﴿to their devils﴾ there are three aspects. The first: its meaning is "with their devils," so "ila" (to) is placed in the position of "ma'a" (with), as the Exalted said: ﴿Who are my helpers to Allah?﴾ [Al 'Imran: 52], meaning "with Allah."

The second, which is the view of some of the Basran grammarians: it is said "khalawtu ila fulan" when you make him your goal in your need. "Khalawtu bihi" (I was alone with him) carries two meanings: the first is this (the sense of going to him for a need).

The other is mockery and ridicule of him. In this case His saying ﴿And when they go apart to their devils﴾ is more eloquent, and it is used in its literal sense.

The third, which is the view of some of the Kufan grammarians: its meaning is "when they turn back to their devils," so His saying "ila" is used in a place where the sentence is not correct without it.

As for "al-Shaytan" (the devil), there are three opinions regarding its derivation. The first: it is on the pattern "fay'al" from "shatana," meaning "to be distant," from which comes the saying "nawan shatun" (a distant goal/distant dwelling), meaning distant; and "shatanat daruhu," meaning his house became distant. He was named "shaytan" either because of his distance from good or because of the distance of his path in evil. According to this, the "nun" is original.

The second opinion: it is derived from "shata yashitu," meaning "halaka yahlaku" (to perish), as the poet said:

... ... ... ∗∗∗ and the champion has perished upon our spears

That is, he perishes. According to this, the "nun" is extra.

The decisive opinion: it is "fa'lan" from "al-shaytu," which is burning, as if he was named after what his state will come to.

﴿They say: Indeed we are with you﴾, meaning in what you are upon of denial and enmity, ﴿We are only mocking﴾, meaning we are ridiculing with what we show of affirmation and agreement.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾. In it there are five aspects. The first: its meaning is that He punishes them for their mockery, so He named the recompense by the name of what it is recompense for, as the Exalted said: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾, and the recompense is not transgression. 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

Ala la yajhalan ahadun 'alayna ∗∗∗ fanajhal fawqa jahli al-jahilina

The second: its meaning is that He repays them with the recompense of those who mock.

The second, which is the view of some of the Basran grammarians: it is said "khalawtu ila fulan" when you make him your goal in your need. "Khalawtu bihi" (I was alone with him) carries two meanings: the first is this (the sense of going to him for a need).

The other is mockery and ridicule of him. In this case His saying ﴿And when they go apart to their devils﴾ is more eloquent, and it is used in its literal sense.

... ... ... ∗∗∗ and the champion has perished upon our spears

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 16:

His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Those are the ones who have bought misguidance in exchange for guidance, so their commerce has not profited⦆. Al-dalala (misguidance) is disbelief (kufr), and al-huda (guidance) is faith (iman).

Regarding His words ﴿they have bought misguidance﴾ there are three interpretations. The first is that it is in its literal sense of buying, as though they bought disbelief in exchange for faith.

The second is that it means they preferred disbelief over faith, and so it was expressed with the word "buying," because buying happens in what the buyer prefers. Then, either it is in the sense of an actual exchange-transaction, since the hypocrites had not believed in the first place, so they could not have sold their faith.

The third is that it means they took disbelief and left faith. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud.

﴿So their commerce has not profited, and they were not guided﴾ has three interpretations. The first: "and they were not guided" in buying misguidance.

The second: "and they were not guided" to the commerce into which the believers were guided.

The third: since a merchant may not make a profit yet still be guided in his trade, God negated both matters from them, profit and being guided, as an intensification of their blame.

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿Their likeness is like that of one who kindled a fire﴾. Al-mathal, with a vowel on the first letter or with the letter sukun-ed, is used for proverbial examples (amthal madrubah), while al-mithl, with sukun, is used for a thing that resembles another.

His saying, ﴿like that of one who kindled a fire﴾, has two interpretations:

The first: He meant "like that of one who lit (awqada)," and the sin (in istawqada) is an extra particle in the speech. This is the view of al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash).

The second: He meant "one who sought from another a fire for light (istawqada min ghayrihi naran li-l-diya')." Fire (al-nar) is derived from light (al-nur).

﴿When it illuminated what was around him﴾. It is said: dza'at fi nafsiha (it shone in itself) and adza'at ma hawlaha (it lit up what was around it). Abu al-Tammah said:

Their noble lineages and their faces lit up for them
The darkness of the night, until the piercer strung the pearl.

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿God took away their light﴾. It has two interpretations:

The first: the light of the one who kindled the fire, because it carries the sense of a plural. This is the view of al-Akhfash.

The second: the light of the hypocrites, because the parable is struck concerning them. This is the view of the majority (al-jumhur, i.e., the majority of scholars).

Regarding the going away of their light, there are two interpretations:

The first, which is the view of al-Asamm: God took away their light in the Hereafter, until that became a mark by which they are recognised.

The second: it refers to the light they displayed to the Prophet ﷺ from their hearts through Islam.

Regarding His saying: ﴿and left them in darkness, they do not see﴾, there are two views:

The first: its meaning is that He did not bring them light by which they could see.

The second: that He did not bring them out of it, as one says, "I left him in the house," when you did not bring him out of it. It is as if what they were in of darkness after light was worse in condition, because whoever has the fire extinguished from him until he is in darkness is less able to see than the one who has never ceased to be in darkness. This is a parable which God, Exalted is He, struck for the hypocrites.

Regarding what they were in of light and what they were placed in of darkness, there are two views:

The first: their light was their entry into Islam after their disbelief, and the darkness was their leaving it through their hypocrisy.

The second: the light returns to the hypocrites by their entry into the body of the Muslims, and the darkness is its removal from them in the Hereafter. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Qatada.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Deaf, dumb, blind, so they will not return﴾. This is the plural of asamm (deaf), abkam (mute), and a'ma (blind). The root of deafness (al-samam) is blockage. It is said: qanah samma' (a hollow-less reed), when it is not hollow, and sammamta al-qarurah (I stopped up the bottle) when you sealed it. So the asamm is one whose ear-openings are blocked.

As for al-bakam (muteness), there are four sayings:

The first: it is a defect in the tongue, with which one cannot rely on the points of articulation of the letters.

The second: it is one born mute.

The third: it is one whose heart has been stripped, who neither comprehends anything nor understands it.

The fourth: it is one who combines muteness and loss of understanding.

The meaning of the statement is that they are deaf to hearing the truth, mute from speaking it, and blind to seeing it. This is narrated by Qatada. ﴿So they will not return﴾, meaning to Islam.

(p-81) Allah's saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Or like a downpour from the sky, in which are darkness, thunder and lightning﴾. There are two ta'wil (interpretations, meaning the explanation of what a word signifies) of al-sayyib (the downpour):

The first is that it is the rain. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud.

The second is that it is the cloud. 'Alqama ibn 'Abada said:

؎ As if a cloud has rained upon them, whose thunderbolts are a crawling for their birds ∗∗∗ So do not equalize between me and Mughammir ∗∗∗ Watered by the morning clouds when they pour

(p-82)

As for al-ra'd (thunder), there are three views. The first is that it is an angel who drives the rain forward, just as a shepherd calls to his flock, so the sound was named ra'd after that angel. This is the view of al-Khalil.

The second is that it is a wind that strikes beneath the cloud and so pours forth that sound. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The third is that it is the sound of the collision of bodies.

As for al-barq (lightning), there are three views. The first is that it is the striking of the angel, who is the thunder, upon the cloud with a mikhraq (a rod or hammer) of iron. This is the view of 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.

The second is that it is his striking with a whip of light. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The third is that it is what sparks from the collision of bodies.

As-sawa'iq is the plural of sa'iqa (thunderbolt), which is an intense sound of thunder accompanied by a piece of fire that burns whatever it reaches.

Regarding the comparison (tashbih al-mathal) in this verse, there are several sayings. The first is that it is a parable for the Qur'an: the rain sent down from the sky is likened to the Qur'an; the darkness in it to the trials in the Qur'an; the thunder in it to the admonition in the Qur'an; the lightning in it to the clarity in the Qur'an; and the thunderbolts in it to the deferred threat and the call to jihad in the immediate. This meaning is reported from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second is that it is a parable for what they fear of the threat of the Hereafter because of their doubt regarding their religion. The lightning in it is likened to the display of Islam, by which their blood, marriages and inheritances are protected; and the thunderbolts in it to the deterrents of Islam with punishment in the immediate and the deferred.

The third is that He struck the downpour as a parable for the outward faith of the hypocrite. The darkness in it is likened to his hardness, the lightning in it to the light of his faith, and the thunderbolts in it to the destruction of his hypocrisy.

(p-83)

Allah's saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿The lightning nearly snatches away their sight﴾. Its meaning: it takes it away swiftly.

﴿Every time it lights up for them, they walk in it, and when it grows dark over them, they stand still﴾. This is a parable which Allah, Exalted is He, struck for the hypocrites, and there are two ta'wil for it. The first: its meaning is that whenever the truth shines for them, they follow it, and when it grows dark for them through desire, they abandon it.

The second: its meaning is that whenever they gain and obtain some good from Islam, they follow the Muslims, and when it grows dark for them and they obtain no good, they hold back from jihad.

Allah's saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Had Allah willed, He would have taken away their hearing and their sight﴾. Here the intended meaning is the plural, even though the wording is singular.

Just as the poet said:

؎ Eat in half your belly, and you will live, for your time is a lean time

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 21–22:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿So do not set up rivals (andad) to God﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations (ta'wilat):

First: the andad are the equals (akfa'), and this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud.

Second: they are the likenesses (ashbah), and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

Third: they are the opposites (adhdad), and this is the view of al-Mufaddal. (p-84)

﴿While you know﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations:

First: the meaning is "while you know that God created you," and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah.

Second: its meaning is "while you know that He has no equal (nidd) and no opposite (didd)," and this is the view of Mujahid.

Third: its meaning is "while you understand (ta'qilun)," so He expressed intellect (al-'aql) by knowledge ('ilm).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 23–24:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And if you are in doubt about what We have sent down upon Our servant﴾ means: in the Qur'an. "Upon Our servant" means Muhammad ﷺ. The word ʿabd (servant) is derived from ta'abbud (worship), which is tadhallul (humbling oneself). The owned slave is called ʿabd, among those who possess intellect, because of his humbling himself before his master.

﴿Then produce a surah like it﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: "like it" means like it from the Qur'an. This is the saying of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: produce a surah like Muhammad ﷺ from among mankind, because Muhammad is a human being like them.

﴿And call your witnesses﴾. In this there are three interpretations. The first: it means your helpers. This is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: your gods, because they used to believe that these would bear witness for them. This is the saying of al-Farra'.

The third: people who would bear witness for you. This is the saying of Mujahid.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿So guard yourselves against the Fire whose fuel is men and stones﴾. Al-waqud (with a fatha) is the firewood, and al-wuqud (with a damma) is the blazing. The stones are of black sulfur. In this there are two sayings: (p-85)

The first: they will be tormented in it with stones along with the fire, whose fuel is men. This is the saying of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: the stones are fuel for the Fire along with men, mentioned to magnify the Fire, as if it burns the stones along with its burning of people.

Regarding His saying: ﴿It has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾, there are two sayings. The first: although it has been prepared for the disbelievers, it is also prepared for others besides them among those deserving punishment, other than the disbelievers. It is one Fire, and only their punishment within it varies.

The second: this Fire is prepared specifically for the disbelievers, and for others among those deserving punishment there is a fire other than it.

The word ʿabd (servant) is derived from ta'abbud (worship), which is tadhallul (humbling oneself). The owned slave is called ʿabd, among those who possess intellect, because of his humbling himself before his master.

﴿Then produce a surah like it﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: "like it" means like it from the Qur'an. This is the saying of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: produce a surah like Muhammad ﷺ from among mankind, because Muhammad is a human being like them.

﴿And call your witnesses﴾. In this there are three interpretations. The first: it means your helpers. This is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: your gods, because they used to believe that these would bear witness for them. This is the saying of al-Farra'.

The third: people who would bear witness for you. This is the saying of Mujahid.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿So guard yourselves against the Fire whose fuel is men and stones﴾. Al-waqud (with a fatha) is the firewood, and al-wuqud (with a damma) is the blazing. The stones are of black sulfur. In this there are two sayings: (p-85)

The first: they will be tormented in it with stones along with the fire, whose fuel is men. This is the saying of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: the stones are fuel for the Fire along with men, mentioned to magnify the Fire, as if it burns the stones along with its burning of people.

Regarding His saying: ﴿It has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾, there are two sayings. The first: although it has been prepared for the disbelievers, it is also prepared for others besides them among those deserving punishment, other than the disbelievers. It is one Fire, and only their punishment within it varies.

The second: this Fire is prepared specifically for the disbelievers, and for others among those deserving punishment there is a fire other than it.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 25:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And give good tidings to those who believe and do righteous deeds, that for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow.﴾ "Bashshir" (give good tidings) is derived from al-bisharah (good news), or it is news that comes to you with what gladdens. It was said: it may be used for what gladdens and what grieves. However, its use for what gladdens became so frequent that it was diverted from what grieves. It is derived from al-bashrah, which is the outer surface of the skin, because it changes upon the first news that arrives to it.

Al-jannat (gardens) is the plural of jannah, which is an orchard with trees. It is called jannah because the trees within it cover it (yasturuhu). Al-Mufaddal said: the jannah is every orchard in which there are date palms, even if there is no other tree in it. If there is a vine in it, it is firdaws, whether or not there are other trees than the vine. (p-86)

﴿beneath which rivers flow⁠﴾ means beneath the trees. It was said: the rivers of Paradise flow without a trench.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Whenever they are provided with a provision of its fruit, they say: "This is what we were provided with before."﴾ By His saying ﴿they were provided with a provision of its fruit﴾ is meant: from the fruits of its trees.

﴿They say: "This is what we were provided with before"﴾ has two interpretations. The first: its meaning is that what we have been provided with from the fruits of Paradise is like what we were provided with from the fruits of this world. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: when the fruits of Paradise are picked from its trees, something like them is substituted in their place; so when they see what has been substituted after what was picked, it becomes confused for them, and they say: "This is what we were provided with before." This is the view of Abu 'Ubayd and Yahya ibn Abi Kathir.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And they are given it in resemblance⁠﴾ has four interpretations. The first: the meaning of resemblance is that all of it is excellent, some of it resembling the rest, and it is not like the fruits of this world, which do not resemble one another because some of them are excellent and some are not. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj.

The second: the resemblance is in colour but not in taste, so the fruits of Paradise are in the colours of the fruits of this world, even though they differ in taste. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Mas'ud and al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

The third: the resemblance is in names but not in colours or tastes, so the fruits of Paradise do not resemble any of the fruits of this world in colour or taste. This is the view of Ibn al-Ash'ari, and it is "not anything" (laysa bi-shay'). (p-87)

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And for them therein are spouses purified⁠﴾ — purified in bodies, in morals and in actions; so they do not menstruate, do not give birth, and do not go to defecate or urinate. This is the view of all the people of tafsir.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on surah 2, verses 26–27:

God Most High says: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike an example, [even of] a mosquito or what is above it.﴾ Regarding His words ﴿is not ashamed﴾ (*la yastahyi*), there are three interpretations. The first is that its meaning is "does not leave off." The second is [He intends] "does not fear." The third is "does not refrain," and this is the view of al-Mufaddal.

The root of *istihya'* (shame, modesty) is withdrawing from something and refraining from it out of fear of falling into what is ugly.

The *ba'udah* (mosquito) is among the small kinds of *baqq* (bedbugs). It was named *ba'udah* because it is like a part of a *baqqah* due to its smallness.

Regarding His words ﴿what [is] a mosquito﴾ (*ma ba'udatan*), there are three possibilities. The first is that *ma* means *alladhi* (that which), and its implied sense is "that which is a mosquito." The second is that its meaning is "from a mosquito up to what is above it." The third is that *ma* is an extra, redundant particle (*silah za'idah*), as al-Nabigha said:

"She said, 'Would that this dove of ours were to our dove, and half of it is lost.'"

Regarding His words ﴿or what is above it﴾ (*fa-ma fawqaha*), there are two interpretations. The first is "or what is above it in size," and this is the view of Qatadah and Ibn Jurayj. The second is "or what is above it in smallness," because the intended point is smallness.

Regarding the example, there are three views. The first is that it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, since He had struck two examples for them, mentioned earlier: ﴿Their example is that of one who kindled a fire﴾ and His words ﴿or like a rainstorm from the sky﴾. The hypocrites said, "Allah is too exalted to strike these examples." So Allah Most High revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike an example, [even of] a mosquito or what is above it.﴾ This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas.

The second is that this is an independent example which Allah Most High struck for this world and its people: the mosquito lives as long as it is hungry, and when it is satiated it dies. Likewise is the case of the people of this world: when they are filled with the world, Allah Most High seizes them at that moment. This is the view of al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

The third is that when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned the spider and the fly in His Book and struck them as examples, the people of misguidance said, "What is the matter with the spider and the fly that they are mentioned?" So Allah Most High revealed this verse. This is the view of Qatadah. The interpretation of al-Rabi' is the best, and the first is closer [to the context].

God, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿He leads many astray thereby, and He guides many thereby.﴾ Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first is that its meaning is: [they are led astray] by denying His examples, which He struck for them, [and] many [are led astray]; and [they are guided] by affirming them, and many [are guided].

The second is that He tested them with His examples; some people went astray, so He made that a misguidance for them, and some people were guided, so He made it a guidance for them.

The third is that it is a report about those who went astray and those who were guided.

God, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Those who break the covenant of Allah after its ratification﴾

As for *naqd* (breaking), it is the opposite of *ibram* (confirming/making firm). Regarding *'ahd* (covenant), there are two views. The first is "a charge/injunction (*wasiyyah*)." The second is "a binding pledge (*mawthiq*)."

The *mithaq* (ratified pledge) is that by which a firm bond is established.

Regarding what His covenant and ratified pledge comprise, there are four views:

The first is that the covenant is Allah's charge to His creation and His command to them of what He has commanded them to do of obedience, and His prohibition to them of what He has forbidden them of disobedience, in His Books and through the tongues of His messengers. Breaking it is abandoning acting upon it.

The second is that His covenant is what He placed in their minds of the proof concerning His oneness and the truthfulness of His messengers, through the miracles that indicate their truthfulness.

The third is that His covenant is what He sent down to the People of the Book [concerning] the description of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the emphatic charge to follow him. That is the covenant they broke by denying it, after they had given Allah, Most High, the pledge from themselves, that they would make it clear to the people and not conceal it. So He informed, Glorified is He, that they cast it behind their backs and sold it for a small price.

The fourth is that the covenant He took from them when He brought them forth from the loins of Adam, which He described in His words, Most High: ﴿And [mention] when your Lord took from the Children of Adam, from their loins, their descendants, and made them testify concerning themselves, [saying], "Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes, we testify."﴾ [al-A'raf: 172].

Regarding the pronoun in ﴿His ratified pledge﴾, there are two views. The first is that it is a pronoun referring to the name of Allah, and its implied sense is: "after the ratified pledge of Allah." The second is that it is a pronoun referring to the covenant, and its implied sense is: "after the ratified pledge of the covenant."

Regarding who is intended by this address from Allah Most High, there are three views. The first is the hypocrites. The second is the People of the Book. The third is all the disbelievers.

God, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And they sever what Allah has commanded to be joined﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations:

The first is that what Allah Most High commanded to be joined is His Messenger, and they severed him through denial and disobedience. This is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri.

The second is that it is the womb and kinship ties. This is the view of Qatadah.

The third is that it is general, covering everything Allah Most High has commanded to be joined.

God, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿And they cause corruption on the earth.﴾ Regarding their causing corruption on the earth, there are two views. The first is that it is their calling people to disbelief. The second is that it is their terrifying travellers on the roads and their cutting off the highway.

Regarding His words ﴿Those are the losers﴾, there are two views. The first is that *khusran* (loss) is deficiency, and from this is Jarir's saying:

"Indeed Salit is in loss; indeed they are the children of a people made into slaves."

He means by *khasar* (loss) that which diminishes their shares and their nobility.

The second is that *khusran* here means ruin, and its meaning is: "Those are the ones who are ruined."

Some have said: Every loss that Allah Most High attributes to non-Muslims means disbelief, and what He attributes to Muslims means sin.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 28:

His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah, when you were dead and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die and then bring you to life again?﴾ Regarding His statement ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah﴾ there are two opinions. The first: it is in the form of rebuke (tawbikh).

The second: it is in the form of wonder (ta'ajjub), and its implied meaning is: "Marvel at them, how they disbelieve!" (p-91)

Regarding His statement ﴿and you were dead and He gave you life, then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you to life again﴾ there are six interpretations (ta'wilat):

The first: ﴿and you were dead﴾ meaning you were not anything; ﴿and He gave you life﴾ meaning He created you; ﴿then He will cause you to die﴾ at the end of your terms; ﴿then He will bring you to life again﴾ on the Day of Resurrection. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: that His statement ﴿and you were dead﴾ means in the graves; ﴿and He gave you life﴾ for questioning; ﴿then He will cause you to die﴾ in your graves after your questioning; then He will bring you to life again at the blowing of the Trumpet for the rising. This is because the reality of death is only what comes after life. This is the saying of Abu Salih.

The third: that His statement ﴿and you were dead﴾ means in the loins of your fathers; ﴿and He gave you life﴾ meaning He brought you out from the wombs of your mothers; ﴿then He will cause you to die﴾ with the death that is unavoidable; ﴿then He will bring you to life again﴾ for the resurrection on the Day of Resurrection. This is the saying of Qatadah.

The fourth: that His statement ﴿and you were dead﴾ means: when Allah, Mighty and Majestic, took the covenant from Adam and his offspring, He gave them life in his loins, endowed them with intellect, and took the covenant from them; then He caused them to die after taking the covenant from them; then He gave them life and brought them out from their mothers' wombs. This is the meaning of His, Exalted is He, statement: ﴿He creates you in the wombs of your mothers, creation after creation﴾ [al-Zumar: 6]. So His statement ﴿and you were dead﴾ means after the taking of the covenant; ﴿and He gave you life﴾ by creating you in the wombs of your mothers and then bringing you out alive; ﴿then He will cause you to die﴾ after your terms in this world have ended; ﴿then He will bring you to life again﴾ by the rising for the resurrection on the Day of Resurrection. [This is] the saying of Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: that the first death is the separation of the man's sperm-drop from his body into the womb of the woman, so it is dead from the moment of its separation from his body until He breathes the spirit into it; then He gives it life by breathing the spirit into it, making it a complete human; then He causes it to die the second death by taking the spirit from it; so it is dead until the Day when the Trumpet is blown, and He returns its spirit into its body, and it returns alive for the resurrection. That makes two deaths and two lives.

The sixth: that His statement ﴿and you were dead﴾ means unremembered and with obliterated traces; ﴿and He gave you life﴾ by becoming prominent and remembered; ﴿then He will cause you to die﴾ at the end of your terms; ﴿then He will bring you to life again﴾ for the resurrection. Whoever held this interpretation cited the verse of Abu Bujayla al-Sa'di: (p-92)

"You gave life to my remembrance, and I was not obscure, but some remembrance is more striking than other remembrance."

Regarding His statement ﴿then to Him you will be returned﴾ there are two interpretations: The first: to the place where Allah alone judges between you.

The second: to the recompense for deeds.

The words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿Then He turned to the heaven﴾. Concerning it there are six opinions.

The first: the meaning of His words ﴿He turned to the heaven﴾ is: He turned toward it. This is the view of al-Farra' (al-Farra').

The second: its meaning is: He intended it, and aimed at creating it.

The third: that the action of Allah turned toward the heaven. This is the view of al-Mufaddal.

The fourth: its meaning is: then His command and His workmanship, by which He made things, turned toward the heaven. This is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri.

The fifth: its meaning is: then the heaven was made to level (istawat) by it.

The sixth: that istiwa', ascent and elevation (al-'uluww) are the meaning. Among those who said this is al-Rabi' ibn Anas. Then those who hold this interpretation differed concerning who it is that rose to the heaven and was above it, into two views. The first: that it is its Creator and Originator. The second: that it is the smoke, which Allah made into the heaven for the earth.

And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed I am making upon the earth a khalifah" (﴿وَإذْ قالَ رَبُّكَ لِلْمَلائِكَةِ إنِّي جاعِلٌ في الأرْضِ خَلِيفَةً﴾). Regarding His words (idh, "when"), there are two aspects. The first is that it is a superfluous connective (ṣilah zā'idah, a particle added without changing the meaning), and the sense of the sentence is: "Your Lord said to the angels." This is the view of Abu 'Ubaydah, who cited the verse of al-Aswad ibn Ya'fur:

"Then when that happens, there is no avoiding its mention, and time follows good with corruption."

The second aspect is that idh is a word of fixed form (kalimah maqsurah), not a superfluous connective. The interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil) have two views on it. The first is that when God, exalted is He, reminded His creation of His blessings upon them through what He created for them on the earth, He reminded them of His blessings upon their father Adam: ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, "Indeed I am making upon the earth a khalifah"﴾. This is the view of al-Mufaddal.

The second is that God, exalted is He, mentioned the beginning of creation, as if He had said: "And He began your creation. ﴿And when your Lord said to the angels, 'Indeed I am making upon the earth a khalifah'﴾." This is among the omitted elements that the context indicates, as al-Namir ibn Tawlab said:

"Indeed, whoever fears death, death will surely overtake him wherever he goes."

He means: wherever he goes.

As for al-mala'ikah (the angels), it is the plural of malak, which is derived from risalah (message). It is said: alikni ilayha, meaning "send me to her." Al-Hudhali said:

"Send me, and the best of messengers is the one who knows the news of distant places best."

And al-alūk is the message, as Labid ibn Rabi'ah said:

"And a youth whom his mother sent with a message, and we gave what he asked."

The message was called alūk because it is chewed in the mouth (tu'lak fi al-fam), and the horse ya'lukū the bit (ya'lukuhu), meaning it chews the iron with its mouth.

The angels are the best of living beings and the most intelligent of creation, except that they do not eat, drink, marry, or reproduce. They are the messengers of God; they do not disobey Him in anything small or great. They have subtle bodies and are not seen unless God strengthens our sight to see them.

As for His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed I am making upon the earth a khalifah﴾, there is a difference over the meaning of jā'il ("making") in two respects. The first is that it means "creating" (khāliq). The second is that it means "making" (jā'il), because the true meaning of jaʿl is doing something in a certain attribute, while the true meaning of ihdath (bringing into existence) is producing a thing after it did not exist.

It is said that al-ard (the earth) is Makkah. Ibn Sabit narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The earth was spread out (duhiyat) from Makkah," and for this reason it was called Umm al-Qura (the Mother of Towns). He said: the graves of Nuh, Hud, Salih, and Shu'ayb are between Zamzam, the Corner, and the Station.

As for al-khalifah, it is one who stands in place of another, from the saying: "Fulan khalafa fulanan" (so-and-so succeeded so-and-so). Al-khalaf, with the lam vowelled, refers to the righteous, and al-khalf, with the lam sukūn, refers to the wicked. In the Revelation: ﴿Then there succeeded them a generation who neglected prayer﴾ [Maryam: 59]. In a hadith: "This knowledge is carried by the trustworthy of every generation (khalaf)."

Regarding the khilafah (succession) of Adam and his offspring, there are three views:

The first is that the jinn were on the earth, but they corrupted in it and shed blood, so they were destroyed, and Adam and his offspring were placed in their stead. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second is that He meant a people among the offspring of Adam, some of whom succeed others, who succeed their father Adam in establishing the truth and cultivating the earth. This is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri.

The third is that He meant: "I am making upon the earth a khalifah who will succeed Me in judging among My creation," and that is Adam and whoever stands in his place from his offspring. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿They said: "Will You place upon it one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood?"﴾ This is the answer of the angels when He informed them that He is making upon the earth a khalifah. There is a difference over (p. 96)

their answer, whether it is in the form of a question or in the form of an affirmation, on two views. The first is that they said it as a question and inquiry when He said to them, "Indeed I am making upon the earth a khalifah," so they said: "O our Lord, inform us: will You place upon it one who will cause corruption therein and shed blood?" He replied: "Indeed I know what you do not know," and He did not inform them.

The second is that it is an affirmation, even though the alif takes the form of a question, as Jarir said:

"Are you not the best of those who rode mounts, and the most generous of all people in the giving of wine?"

On this view, there are two views regarding their answer. The first is that they said it by conjecture and assumption, because they had seen the jinn before them corrupting the earth and shedding blood, so they imagined that if He appointed a successor, He would appoint upon the earth one who would cause corruption and shed blood.

Regarding their saying this, there are two aspects. The first is that they said it to magnify their act, meaning: how could they cause corruption therein and shed blood, when You have bestowed blessings upon them and made them successors therein? He said: "Indeed I know what you do not know."

The second is that they said it in wonder at His appointing them as successors, meaning: how can You appoint them upon the earth when You know that they will cause corruption therein and shed blood? He said: ﴿"Indeed I know what you do not know"﴾.

His words: ﴿and shed blood﴾. As-safk is pouring out blood specifically, not water or other liquids. As-safh is similar, but it is used for any liquid in the sense of wasting it. For this reason they called fornication (zina) sifah, because it wastes its water in it.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿"While we glorify You with Your praise and sanctify You"﴾. Tasbih in their speech means declaring God free of imperfection in a manner of magnification. From this is the saying of A'sha Banu Tha'labah:

"I said when his boasting came to me: 'Glory be to the one who is free from the wicked 'Alqamah!'"

Meaning: a disavowal of 'Alqamah.

It is not permissible to glorify anyone other than God, even if he is free from imperfection, because tasbih has become a term in religion for the highest degree of magnification, which none deserves except God, exalted is He.

Regarding the intended meaning of their saying: ﴿"while we glorify You with Your praise"﴾, there are four views. The first is that it means "we pray to You." In the Revelation: ﴿Had he not been of those who glorify (al-musabbihin)﴾ [al-Saffat: 143], meaning of those who pray. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud.

The second is that it means "we magnify You." This is the view of Mujahid.

The third is that it is the well-known tasbih. This is the view of al-Mufaddal, who cited the verse of Jarir:

"May God disfigure the faces of Taghlib, whenever the pilgrims glorify and proclaim the talbiyah."

As for His words: ﴿"and sanctify You"﴾, the root of taqdis is purification. From this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the sacred land (al-ard al-muqaddasah)﴾, meaning the purified. The poet said:

"They seized him by the shin and the sinew, as the boys tore the garment of the one who was purified."

Meaning: the purified one.

Regarding the intended meaning of their saying: ﴿"and sanctify You"﴾, there are three views. The first is that it means prayer. The second is purifying Him from defects. The third is the well-known taqdis.

Regarding His words, exalted is He: ﴿He said: "Indeed I know what you do not know"﴾, there are three views. The first is that He meant what Iblis concealed of arrogance and disobedience in what they were commanded, namely prostrating to Adam. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud.

(p. 98) The second is those among the offspring of Adam, the prophets and messengers, who set things right on the earth and do not corrupt. This is the view of Qatadah.

The third is what He alone knows of the management of the public good.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And He taught Adam the names, all of them﴾. Regarding his being named Adam, there are two opinions. The first is that he was named Adam because he was created from the surface of the earth (adim al-ard), and its surface is its apparent face. This is the view of Ibn Abbas. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari narrated that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah the Exalted created Adam from a handful He took from all of the earth, so the children of Adam came according to the earth's variety: some are red, some black, some white, some easy-going, some wicked, and some good." (p-99)

The second is that it is derived from al-udma (adma), which means complexion (lawn).

Regarding the names that Allah the Exalted taught Adam, there are three opinions. The first: they are the names of the angels. The second: they are the names of his offspring. The third: they are the names of all things. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and Mujahid.

Then, concerning this, there are two aspects. The first: the teaching was limited to the name without its meaning. The second: He taught him the names and their meanings, since there is no benefit in knowing names without meanings, so the meanings are the intended thing and the names are indicators of them.

If the first aspect is adopted, that the teaching was limited to the wording of the names without their meanings, then there are two views. The first: He taught them to him in the language he used to speak. The second: He taught him all languages, and Adam taught them to his offspring. When they dispersed, each people spoke with a tongue they found easy and became accustomed to, and then they forgot the others, and time lengthened. Some people claimed that they woke up one morning, each of them speaking a language they had forgotten all others in a single night. Such a thing is impossible in common practice.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Then He presented them to the angels﴾. Regarding what He presented to them, there are two opinions. The first: He presented to them the names without the named things. The second: He presented to them the named things themselves.

In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is "and He presented them" (wa 'aradahunna), and in the reading of Ubayy it is "and He presented it" (wa 'aradaha). So the more correct view is that the presentation was directed at the named things. (p-100)

Then, regarding the time of their presentation, there are two opinions. The first: He presented them after He had created them. The second: He formed them in the hearts of the angels, then presented them before their creation.

﴿He said, "Tell Me the names of these, if you are truthful"﴾. The meaning of anbi'uni ("tell Me") is "inform Me," derived from al-inba' (informing). Regarding inba', there are two opinions. The more apparent of them: it is informing, and naba' is news, and the Prophet (nabi, with hamza) is derived from this. The second: inba' is notifying, and it is used for informing only figuratively.

His saying: ﴿the names of these﴾ means the names that He taught Adam.

Regarding His saying: ﴿if you are truthful﴾, there are six opinions. The first: "if you are truthful that I do not create a creation except that you would be more knowledgeable than it," because it occurred to their souls that they were more knowledgeable than others. The second: "if you are truthful in what you claimed, that My successors will cause corruption on the earth." The third: "if you are truthful that if I appoint you as successors on it, you will glorify Me and sanctify Me, and if I appoint others as successors on it, they will disobey Me." The fourth: "if you are truthful in what occurred to your souls, that I do not create a creation except that you would be better than it." The fifth: the meaning of His saying "if you are truthful" is "if you are knowing." The sixth: its meaning is simply "if you are truthful."

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Indeed, You are the All-Knowing, the All-Wise﴾. Al-'Alim (the All-Knowing) is the one who knows without being taught. Regarding al-Hakim (the All-Wise), there are three opinions. The first: He is the one who makes His actions firm (al-muhkim li-af'alihi). The second: He is the one who prevents corruption, and from this the bit of a bridle is called hakama, because it prevents the horse from running fiercely. Jarir said:

"O Banu Hanifa, restrain your foolish ones; I fear that you will be angered by me."

That is, restrain them.

The third: He is the one who is correct about the truth, and from this the judge is called hakim, because he reaches the truth in his judgment. This is the view of Abu al-Abbas al-Mubarrad.

وقوله عز وجل: ﴿وَإِذْ قُلْنَا لِلْمَلَائِكَةِ اسْجُدُوا لِآدَمَ فَسَجَدُوا إِلَّا إِبْلِيسَ أَبَى وَاسْتَكْبَرَ﴾. اختلف أهل التأويل (أهل التفسير والتأويل) في أمره الملائكة بالسجود لآدم، على قولين: أحدهما: أنه أمرهم بالسجود له تكرمةً وتعظيمًا لشأنه. (p. 102)

والثاني: أنه جعله قبلةً لهم، فأمرهم بالسجود إلى قبلتهم، وفيه ضربٌ من التعظيم.

وأصل السجود الخضوع والتطامن (الانخفاض والتذلل)، قال الشاعر:

بِجَمْعٍ تَضِلُّ البَلْقُ فِي حُجُرَاتِهِ ... تَرَى الأَكَمَ فِيهِ سُجَّدًا لِلْحَوَافِرِ

وسمّى سجودَ الصلاة سجودًا، لما فيه من الخضوع والتطامن، فسجدت الملائكة لآدم طاعةً لأمر الله تعالى، إلا إبليس أبى أن يسجد له حسدًا واستكبارًا.

واختلفوا في إبليس: هل كان من الملائكة أم لا؟ على قولين: أحدهما: أنه كان من الملائكة، وهذا قول ابن عباس، وابن مسعود، وابن المسيب، وابن جريج، لأنه استثناء منهم، فدلّ على دخوله فيهم.

والثاني: أنه ليس من الملائكة، وإنما هو أبو الجن، كما أن آدم أبو الإنس، وهذا قول الحسن وقتادة وابن زيد. ولا يمتنع جواز الاستثناء من غير جنسه، كما قال تعالى: ﴿مَا لَهُمْ بِهِ مِنْ عِلْمٍ إِلَّا اتِّبَاعَ الظَّنِّ﴾ [النساء: 157]، وهذا استثناءٌ منقطع (استثناء ليس من جنس المستثنى منه).

واختُلف في تسميته بإبليس على قولين: أحدهما: أنه اسمٌ أعجميّ (غير عربي) وليس بمشتقّ.

والثاني: أنه اسم اشتقاق، اشتُقّ من الإبلاس، وهو اليأس من الخير، ومنه قوله تعالى: ﴿فَإِذَا هُمْ مُبْلِسُونَ﴾ [الأنعام: 44]، أي: آيسون من الخير. وقال العجّاج:

يَا صَاحِ هَلْ تَعْرِفُ رَسْمًا مُكْرَسًا ∗∗∗ قَالَ نَعَمْ أَعْرِفُهُ وَأَبْلَسَا

فأما من ذهب إلى أن إبليس كان من الملائكة، فاختلفوا في قوله تعالى: (p. 103)

﴿إِلَّا إِبْلِيسَ كَانَ مِنَ الْجِنِّ﴾ [الكهف: 50]، لِمَ سمّاه الله تعالى بهذا الاسم؟ على أربعة أقاويل: أحدها: أنهم حيٌّ من الملائكة يُسمَّون جنًّا، كانوا من أشدّ الملائكة اجتهادًا، وهذا قول ابن عباس.

والثاني: أنه جُعل من الجن، لأنه من خُزّان الجنة، فاشتُقّ اسمه منها، وهذا قول ابن مسعود.

والثالث: أنه سُمّي بذلك لأنه جَنّ عن طاعة ربه، وهذا قول ابن زيد.

والرابع: أن الجِنّ لكل ما اجتنّ فلم يظهر، حتى إنهم سمّوا الملائكة جنًّا لاستتارهم، وهذا قول أبي إسحاق، وأنشد قول أعشى بني ثعلبة:

لَوْ كَانَ حَيٌّ خَالِدًا أَوْ مُعَمَّرًا ∗∗∗ لَكَانَ سُلَيْمَانُ البَرِيَّ مِنَ الدَّهْرِ
بَرَاهُ إِلَهِي وَاصْطَفَاهُ عِبَادَهُ ∗∗∗ وَمَلَّكَهُ مَا بَيْنَ نُوبَا إِلَى مِصْرِ
وَسَخَّرَ مِنْ جِنِّ المَلائِكِ تِسْعَةً ∗∗∗ قِيَامًا لَدَيْهِ يَعْمَلُونَ بِلَا أَجْرِ

فسمّى الملائكةَ جنًّا لاستتارهم.

وفي قوله تعالى: ﴿وَكَانَ مِنَ الْكَافِرِينَ﴾ ثلاثة أقاويل: أحدها: أنه قد كان قبله قومٌ كفّارٌ، كان إبليس منهم.

والثاني: أن معناه: وصار من الكافرين.

والثالث: وهو قول الحسن: أنه كان من الكافرين، وليس قبله كافرٌ، كما كان من الجن وليس قبله جنٌّ، وكما تقول: كان آدمُ من الإنس، وليس قبله إنسيٌّ.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on surah 2, verses 35–36:**

His saying, may He be glorified and exalted: ﴿And We said, "O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden"﴾. God, exalted is He, created Hawwa' (Eve) from Adam's left rib after He had cast sleep upon him. For this reason it was said of the woman: "a rib, crooked."

She was called *imra'ah* (woman) because she was created from *al-mar'* (the man). As for her name Hawwa', there are two opinions. The first is that she was so named because she was created from a living being (*hayy*). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud. The second is that she was so named because she is the mother of every living being (*hayy*).

The exegetes differed over the time at which Hawwa' was created, in two opinions. The first is that Adam was made to enter the Garden alone, and when he felt lonely, Hawwa' was created from his rib after his entry into the Garden. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud. The second is that she was created from his rib before he entered the Garden, and then the two of them were made to enter the Garden together, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We said, "O Adam, dwell, you and your wife, in the Garden"﴾. This is the view of Abu Ishaq.

They also differed concerning the Garden in which they were made to dwell, in two opinions. The first is that it is the Garden of Eternity (*Jannat al-Khuld*). The second is that it is a garden which God prepared for them. And God knows best.

His saying, may He be glorified and exalted: ﴿And eat from it freely, wherever you wish﴾. Concerning *raghadan* (freely) there are three interpretations (p-105):

The first is that it means a pleasant life. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, and from it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*"While a man is seen by you, living comfortably, secure from calamities, in a life of plenty."*

The second is that it means a wide, abundant life. This is the view of Abu 'Ubaydah.

The third is that it means lawful provision for which there is no reckoning. This is the view of Mujahid.

His saying, may He be glorified and exalted: ﴿But do not approach this tree﴾. The exegetes differed over the tree from which they were forbidden, in four opinions:

The first is that it is wheat. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second is that it is the vine. This is the view of al-Suddi and Ja'dah ibn Hubayrah.

The third is that it is the fig. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj, who relates it from some of the Companions.

The fourth is that it is the Tree of Eternity, from which the angels eat.

Concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and you would be among the wrongdoers﴾, there are two opinions. The first is: among the transgressors, in eating what was not permitted to you both. The second is: among those who wronged themselves by your eating.

They differed concerning Adam's disobedience in eating from the tree, in what manner it occurred from him, in four opinions:

The first is that he ate from it while forgetful of the prohibition, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We had already taken a covenant from Adam before, but he forgot﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115]. The proponent of this view holds that prophets are obliged to be more watchful and alert than others, because of the abundance of their knowledge and the loftiness of their ranks. Therefore his preoccupation that made him neglect remembering the prohibition was a form of negligence, through which he became disobedient.

The second opinion is that he ate from it while intoxicated, and so he was held accountable for what he did while intoxicated, even though he did not intend it, just as he would be held accountable for it had he been sober. This is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.

The third opinion is that he ate from it deliberately and knowingly of the prohibition, and he interpreted His saying: ﴿And We had already taken a covenant from Adam before, but he forgot﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115] to mean that he slipped, so that the intention was in an act of disobedience for which he deserves blame (p-106).

The fourth opinion is that he ate from it by way of interpretation (*ta'wil*), and so became disobedient by neglecting the evidence, because it is not permissible for prophets to commit major sins. This is also based on His saying, exalted is He, concerning Iblis: ﴿So he brought them down by deception﴾ [al-A'raf: 22], which refers to the interpretation that he turned them towards.

Those who held this view differed concerning the interpretation by which they deemed eating permissible, in three opinions. The first is that it was an interpretation by way of exhortation to abstain (*tanzih*), not of prohibition (*tahrim*). The second is that the prohibition was against that particular tree and not its kind, so that if he ate from another tree of the same kind he would not have disobeyed. The third is that the interpretation was what God, exalted is He, related of Iblis in His saying: ﴿Your Lord has forbidden you this tree only lest you become angels or become of the eternal﴾ [al-A'raf: 20].

His saying, may He be glorified and exalted: ﴿So Satan caused them to slip from it, and removed them from that in which they had been﴾. Hamzah alone read *fa-azālahumā* (he removed them), meaning he moved them away, from your saying "I moved from the place" (*zult 'ani al-makan*), when you withdrew from it. The rest read ﴿*fa-azallahumā*﴾ with the shadda, meaning he caused them to slip (*istazallahumā*) from *al-zalal*, which is error. It was called *zalal* because it is a departure from the truth; likewise *al-zallah* (slip) is a departure from the truth, and its root meaning is departure.

The Satan who caused them to slip is Iblis.

The exegetes differed over whether he reached them, so that he addressed them directly with speech and spoke to them face to face, or not. 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, Wahb ibn Munabbih, and most of the exegetes said that he did reach them, and they cited His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he swore to them, "Indeed, I am to you among the sincere advisors"﴾ [al-A'raf: 21]. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: he did not reach them; rather he merely placed desire in their souls and whispered to them without being seen, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then Satan whispered to them﴾ [al-A'raf: 20]. The first view is more apparent and more well known.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He removed them from that in which they had been﴾ means: Iblis was the cause of their expulsion, because he invited them to that which necessitated their expulsion.

His saying, may He be glorified and exalted: ﴿And We said, "Go down, some of you to others an enemy"﴾. *Al-hubut* with a damma on the *ha'* means descent, and with a fatha on it means the place of descent. Al-Mufaddal said: *al-hubut* means departure from a town, and it also means entering it; thus it is among the words with opposite meanings (*al-adhdad*). Since *al-hubut* originally means descent, entering a town in order to settle in it is a descent into it, and so it became *hubut*.

They differed concerning those addressed by the command to descend, in three opinions. The first is that they are Adam, Hawwa', Iblis, and the serpent. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. The second is that they are Adam and his offspring, and Iblis and his offspring. This is the view of Mujahid. The third is that they are Adam, Hawwa', and the one who whispered (Iblis).

It was called *'aduww* because of transgressing the limit in harming one's companion. From it comes *al-'adw* with the foot, for passing beyond in walking. This statement is an informing them of enmity and a warning to them, not a command, because God, exalted is He, does not command enmity.

They differed concerning those of whom it was said: ﴿some of you to others an enemy﴾, in two opinions. The first is that they are those who were told "descend," in accordance with what we mentioned of the differences among the exegetes concerning it. The second is that they are the children of Adam and the children of Iblis. This is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri.

His saying, may He be glorified and exalted: ﴿And for you on the earth is a dwelling place﴾. There are two interpretations concerning it. The first is that *al-mustaqarr* on the earth is the place of their residence upon it, based on His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He made for you the earth a resting place﴾ [Ghafir: 64]. This is the view of Abu al-'Aliyah. The second is that it is the place of their graves within it. This is the view of al-Suddi.

From it is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so provide for them﴾ [al-Ahzab: 49], meaning give them what they may benefit from. The poet said:

*"And every delight that you have from a beloved, for which you are beloved, or with which you amuse yourself, is provision."*

The first is: until death. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi. The second is: until the Hour is established. This is the view of Mujahid. The third is: until a term. This is the view of al-Rabi'.

The second is that she was so named because she is the mother of every living being (*hayy*).
