Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 37–39:

His statement, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He turned to him in forgiveness﴾. As for (al-kalam, speech), it is derived from "impact" (al-ta'thir), because it has an impact on the soul through the meanings it indicates; for this reason a wound is called kalm (kalm, wound) because of its impact on the body. The word (al-lafz, utterance) is derived from your saying: "I lafaztu the thing," when you expel it from your heart.

Scholars differed concerning the words which Adam received from his Lord, into three opinions. The first: His saying: ﴿Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves, and if You do not forgive us and have mercy upon us, we will surely be among the losers﴾ [al-A'raf: 23]. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd.

The second: the saying of Adam: "O Allah, there is no deity except You; glory be to You and praise. My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me, for You are the best of forgivers. O Allah, there is no deity except You; glory be to You and praise. I have wronged myself, so accept my repentance, for You are the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful." This is the view of Mujahid.

The third: that Adam said to his Lord when he disobeyed Him: "My Lord, what do You think if I repent and make amends?" And his Lord said: "Indeed, I will return you to the Garden." And these were the words which he received from his Lord. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

His statement, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿and He turned to him in forgiveness﴾, that is, He accepted his repentance. Repentance (al-tawbah) is return. So, from the servant, it is his returning from sin by regret over it and abandoning it; and from Allah, exalted is He, toward His servant, it is a return to him to what he had been upon. (p-110)

If it is said: Why did He say ﴿and He turned to him﴾ and not "and He turned to them both," since the repentance was directed to both of them? It is answered: There are two responses to this. The first: when He mentioned Adam alone with His words ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words﴾, He mentioned after it the acceptance of his repentance, and did not mention the repentance of Eve, although her repentance was also accepted, because her mention had not preceded.

The second: that when the action of two is one in meaning, it is permissible to mention one of them while the meaning applies to both, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when they saw a trade or amusement, they dispersed toward it﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 11], and as He, exalted and majestic, said: ﴿And Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62].

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, He is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful﴾, that is, the Greatly Accepting of repentance. He followed it with mercy, so that Allah, exalted is He, would not leave His servants devoid of His blessings.

Al-Hasan said: Allah, exalted is He, did not create Adam except for the earth, so had he not disobeyed, he would have come forth in a state other than that. Others said: It is permissible that He created him for the earth if he disobeyed, and for other than it if he did not disobey.

Allah, exalted is He, did not bring Adam out of the Garden and cause him to descend to the earth as a punishment, for two reasons. The first: that his sin was minor. The second: that he was sent down after his repentance was accepted.

He was sent down for one of two reasons: either as discipline, or as an intensification of the trial.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 40–41:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you﴾. Isra'il is Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Isra" in Hebrew means "servant" ('abd), and "Il" is Allah, so his name was 'Abd Allah (Servant of God). (p-111)

His saying: ﴿Remember My blessing﴾. Dhikr (remembrance, mention) is a shared term (ism mushtarak). Remembrance by the heart is the opposite of forgetfulness; remembrance by the tongue is the opposite of silence; and dhikr also means honour (sharaf). Al-Kisa'i said: what is by the heart is pronounced with a dammah on the dhal (dhukr). Others said: they are two dialects, dhikr and dhukr, and their meaning is one.

The intended meaning of the verse is remembrance by the heart, and its sense is: do not be heedless of My blessing which I bestowed upon you, and do not forget it.

Regarding the blessing He bestowed upon them there are two views. The first: the generality of His blessings which He bestowed upon His creation, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you should count the blessings of Allah, you could not enumerate them﴾ [an-Nahl: 18]. The second, which is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri, is that He meant the blessings upon their forefathers, when He saved them from the people of Pharaoh, made prophets among them, sent down the Scriptures upon them, caused water to gush for them from the stone, and sent down upon them manna and quails. Blessings upon the fathers are also blessings upon the sons, because they are honoured by the honour of their fathers.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And fulfil My covenant; I will fulfil your covenant﴾, there are two views. The first: fulfil My covenant which I took from you concerning the pledge that you believe in Me and affirm My messengers; I will fulfil your covenant concerning what I promised you of Paradise.

The second, said by 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas: fulfil what I commanded you; I will fulfil what I promised you.

In this there are three opinions. The first: confirming what is in the Torah concerning the oneness of Allah and obedience to Him. The second: confirming what is in the Torah, that it is from Allah. The third: confirming what is in the Torah concerning the mention of the Qur'an and the sending of Muhammad (ﷺ) as a prophet. (p-112)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not be the first to disbelieve in it﴾ has three opinions. The first: do not be the first of the People of the Book to disbelieve in the Qur'an; this is the view of Ibn Juraij. The second: do not be the first to disbelieve in Muhammad (ﷺ); this is the view of Abu al-'Aliyah. The third: do not be the first to disbelieve in what is in the Torah and the Gospel concerning the mention of Muhammad and the confirmation of the Qur'an.

The first: do not take a wage for it, and it is written among them in the earlier Book: "O son of Adam, teach freely as you were taught freely"; this is the view of Abu al-'Aliyah. The second: do not take a price for changing and altering it; this is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri. The third: do not take a small price for concealing what it contains of the mention of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the confirmation of the Qur'an; this is the view of al-Suddi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 40–41:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿O Children of Israel, remember My blessing which I bestowed upon you﴾. Isra'il is Ya'qub ibn Ishaq ibn Ibrahim. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Isra" in Hebrew means "servant" ('abd), and "Il" is Allah, so his name was 'Abd Allah (Servant of God). (p-111)

His saying: ﴿Remember My blessing﴾. Dhikr (remembrance, mention) is a shared term (ism mushtarak). Remembrance by the heart is the opposite of forgetfulness; remembrance by the tongue is the opposite of silence; and dhikr also means honour (sharaf). Al-Kisa'i said: what is by the heart is pronounced with a dammah on the dhal (dhukr). Others said: they are two dialects, dhikr and dhukr, and their meaning is one.

The intended meaning of the verse is remembrance by the heart, and its sense is: do not be heedless of My blessing which I bestowed upon you, and do not forget it.

Regarding the blessing He bestowed upon them there are two views. The first: the generality of His blessings which He bestowed upon His creation, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And if you should count the blessings of Allah, you could not enumerate them﴾ [an-Nahl: 18]. The second, which is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri, is that He meant the blessings upon their forefathers, when He saved them from the people of Pharaoh, made prophets among them, sent down the Scriptures upon them, caused water to gush for them from the stone, and sent down upon them manna and quails. Blessings upon the fathers are also blessings upon the sons, because they are honoured by the honour of their fathers.

The first: fulfil My covenant which I took from you concerning the pledge that you believe in Me and affirm My messengers; I will fulfil your covenant concerning what I promised you of Paradise.

The third: do not take a small price for concealing what it contains of the mention of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the confirmation of the Qur'an; this is the view of al-Suddi.

"The Exalted and Majestic said: ﴿And do not mix the truth with falsehood﴾. That is, do not confuse the truth with falsehood. Al-labs (confusion, mixing) is the mixing of matters. In this regard is His saying, ﴿And We would have confused them in what they confuse﴾ [al-An'am: 9]. Ibn 'Abbas said: its meaning is: 'We would have mixed up for them what they were mixing up.' From this is the saying of al-'Ajjaj:

Since they mixed the truth with accusation, they became rich and exchanged Zayd for me.

As for His saying, ﴿the truth with falsehood﴾, there are three interpretations concerning it. The first: the truth is truthfulness, the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: Judaism and Christianity are the falsehood, and Islam is the truth; this is the view of Mujahid.

The third: the truth is the Torah that was revealed to Musa, and the falsehood is what they wrote with their own hands. (p-113)

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and conceal the truth﴾, means Muhammad (ﷺ) and the recognition of his prophethood. ﴿while you know﴾ that he is in the books that are in your hands. This is the view of all of them.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And establish prayer and give zakah﴾. As for prayer, the discussion of it has already passed.

As for zakah: regarding the naming of the charity of wealth by it, there are two views. The first: it is derived from the increase and growth of wealth, and from this is their saying: "zakā al-zar'" (the crop grew) when it increased. It is also said: "zakā al-fard" (the single became even) when the addition of an extra made it an even number, until it became a pair, as the poet said:

They were odd or even, short of four, when they were not created, and the grandfathers of people were jostling.

Here khasa means odd (witr), and zakā means even (shaf'). And the rajiz said:

Neither its count was odd nor even, like the worst of the herbs, the tips of al-safa.

Al-safa: the thorns of al-buhma, and al-buhma: the long thorn, like al-sabla.

The second view: it is derived from purification. From this is His saying, ﴿Have you killed a pure soul?﴾ [al-Kahf: 74], meaning pure from sins.

Concerning what is purified, there are two views. The first: it is the purification of the wealth, so that by paying its due it becomes lawful; were it not for this, it would be impure.

The second: the purification of the soul of the one who gives zakah, as if the giver has purified himself from stinginess and miserliness.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and bow with those who bow﴾. Concerning it there are two views. The first: He intended the whole of the prayer, and expressed it by bowing, as a person says: "I finished my ruku'," meaning my prayer.

The second: He intended the bowing that is in the prayer, because there was no bowing in the prayer of the People of the Book, so He commanded them with what they did not do in their prayer.

Regarding the origin of ruku' (bowing), there are two views. The first: it is derived from lowering oneself and bending, and this is the view of al-Khalil and Ibn Zayd. Labid ibn Rabi'ah said:

I relate the accounts of the generations that passed, while I move slowly, as if, whenever I stand, I am bowing.

The second: it is derived from humiliation and submission, and this is the view of al-Asma'i and al-Mufaddal. Al-Adba' ibn Quray' al-Sa'di said:

Do not humiliate the weak, lest you one day bow, while time has raised you up.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 44:

His, may He be Exalted and Majestic, saying: ﴿Do you enjoin righteousness upon the people while you forget yourselves?﴾ Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: they used to command the people to obey Allah while they themselves disobeyed Him. This is the view of al-Suddi and Qatadah, because "al-birr" (righteousness) is sometimes used to express obedience. The poet said:

Oh Lord, indeed the family of Bakr are behind You,
the people are dutiful to You, while they commit sin against You.

That is, they obey You.

The second: they used to command the people to hold fast to the Book of their Lord while they abandoned it by denying what it contains of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The third: they used to command giving charity while they were stingy with it.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 45–47:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And seek help through patience and prayer﴾: (p-115)

As for patience (al-sabr): it is restraining the self from that which it craves. From it comes the patience of one afflicted by a calamity, that he restrains himself from wailing. Fasting is also called sabr because it restrains the self from food and drink, and for this reason the month of Ramadan is called the month of patience. And there is a hadith: "Kill the killer, and restrain the one who restrains (al-sabir)," and this refers to a man who held another man until a third person killed him; so the killer is ordered to be killed and the one who held him is confined.

Regarding the patience that is commanded, there are two views. The first: it is patience in obedience to Him and refraining from disobeying Him.

The second: it is fasting. The Prophet (ﷺ) "when a matter distressed him, would seek help through prayer and fasting." It is also narrated that "he saw Salman lying prone on his face, and said to him: 'Are you complaining of a cold?' He said: 'Stand and pray the prayer, and you will be healed.'"

As for His saying, ﴿And indeed it is a burden except for the humble (al-khashi'in)﴾, there are three views on it. The first: meaning, indeed prayer is heavy except upon the believers, because the pronoun returns to the feminine form of the word. (p-116)

The second: it means patience and prayer together; He intended both, though the pronoun returns to prayer because it is the nearest thing mentioned, as the poet said:

"Whoever has his tent in Medina tonight, then I and Qayyar there are strangers."

The third: indeed the answering (of the call) by Muhammad (ﷺ) is heavy except upon the humble.

Khushu' toward Allah is humility, and its counterpart is khudu' (submission). It is said that khudu' is in the body, while khushu' is in the voice and the gaze.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who suppose that they will meet their Lord﴾ has two interpretations. The first: they suppose they will meet their Lord with their sins, out of their apprehension of the sins they had committed. 

The second, which is the view of the majority: the supposing (zann) here means certainty (yaqin), as if He said: "those who are certain that they will meet their Lord." Similarly His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed I supposed that I would meet my reckoning﴾ means "I was certain." Abu Dawud said:

"Many a worry you relieved with a creditor, and hidden things you revealed by conjecture (zunun)."

﴿And that to Him they will return﴾ has three interpretations. The first: by "return" He meant death.

The second: that they will return by being resurrected in the Hereafter; this is the view of Abu al-Aliyah.

The third: they will return to Him, meaning no one possesses harm or benefit for them except Him, as they were at the beginning of creation.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 48:

His statement, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And guard yourselves against a Day when no soul will avail another soul in anything﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations (p-117):

The first: its meaning is "will not suffice (tughni)," as it is said: "The cow suffices (tajzi) for seven," meaning it is enough for them. This is the statement of al-Suddi.

The second: its meaning is "will not repay (taqdi)." From it is their saying: "May Allah repay (jaza) so-and-so on my behalf with good," meaning reward him. This is the statement of al-Mufaddal.

﴿Nor will intercession be accepted from it﴾. Al-Hasan said: its meaning is that no intercessor will come whose intercession would be accepted, due to his inability to do so. Others said: rather, its meaning is that the intercessor will not respond to the request to intercede on its behalf, and that even if he were asked to intercede, he would intercede.

His statement, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Nor will ransom be taken from it﴾. Al-'adl with a fatha on the ayn means ransom (fidya), and with a kasra on the ayn means an equivalent (mithl).

As for their saying: "Allah will not accept from him any ṣarf or ʿadl," there are four opinions regarding it. The first: that ṣarf means action (ʿamal), and ʿadl means ransom (fidya). This is the statement of al-Hasan al-Basri.

The second: that ṣarf means blood-money (diya), and ʿadl means a man in his place. This is the statement of al-Kalbi.

The third: that ṣarf means voluntary acts (taṭawwuʿ), and ʿadl means obligatory acts (fariḍa). This is the statement of al-Asmaʿi.

The fourth: that ṣarf means trickery (ḥīla), and ʿadl means ransom (fidya). This is the statement of Abu ʿUbayda.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 49–50:**

His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And [remember] when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh﴾. He means: from the people of Pharaoh. The *al* (family) of a man are those whose affairs return to him, either by lineage or by companionship. Scholars differ regarding *al* and *ahl* (people/household) on two views. The first is that they are the same. The second, which is the view of al-Kisa'i, is that one says *al al-rajul* (the family of a man) when his name is mentioned, but if he is referred to by a pronoun (kunaya), one says *ahluhu* (his people), not *aluhu*. Just as one says *ahl al-ilm* (people of knowledge) and *ahl al-Basrah* (people of Basra), but one does not say *al al-ilm* or *al al-Basrah*.

As for Pharaoh (Fir'awn): it is said that he is that very man. It is also said that it is the title of every king of the Amalekites, like Caesar for the Romans and Chosroes for the Persians. It is also said that the name of the Pharaoh of Moses was al-Walid ibn Mus'ab.

Regarding His statement, ﴿who afflicted you with the worst torment﴾, there are three interpretations. The first: its meaning is "they would appoint you (to it)," from the saying *sama-hu khutta khasf* (he imposed on him a humiliating condition), when he assigned it to him.

The second: they would compel you to hard labors.

The third: they would add to you beyond the worst torment. From this comes *musawamat al-bay'* (bargaining in sale), which is only that the seller increases the price above the cost and the buyer decreases it below. This is the view of al-Mufaddal.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿and they would spare your women﴾, means: they would keep them alive. It is a form of *istif'aal* (the tenth verb form, Form X) derived from *hayah* (life), because they would slaughter the males and let the females live.

As for the word *nisa'* (women), it is said that it applies to both young and old. It is also said that it applies only to adults, and that they called the young girls "women" in the sense that they are kept alive until they become women.

The sparing of the women was part of the worst torment because they would keep them for enslavement and service. Thus that enslavement itself was the worst torment, not the sparing.

Regarding His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿And in that was a great trial from your Lord﴾, there are two interpretations. The first: what they did to you, of the worst torment, the slaughter of your sons, and the sparing of your women, was a great hardship and a severe test. The second: that in saving you from the people of Pharaoh, who used to do this to you, there was a great blessing from your Lord. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi.

The original meaning of *bala'* (trial) is testing, whether by good or by evil, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya': 35], because testing may be by good just as it may be by evil. However, the more common usage for evil is *balawtuhu abluwhu balaa'*, and for good is *ablaytuhu ubliihi iblaa'*. From this is the verse of Zuhayr:

*"May Allah reward with good what the two of them did for you, so He tested them with the best of tests, the test that tries."*

Thus he combined the two usages.

His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And [remember] when We divided the sea for you﴾. Regarding it there are two interpretations. The first: "and when We separated the sea for you," because *al-farq* (division) is the separation between two things. He divided the sea into twelve paths. Their number was six hundred and twenty thousand, not counting those who were twenty years old for their youth or sixty for their age. Before Pharaoh was Haman with a thousand thousand, and seven hundred horses. This is His statement: ﴿Then Pharaoh sent heralds into the cities﴾ ﴿Indeed, these are but a small band﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 53–54]. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The second: its meaning is "and when We made a separation between you and the sea," that is, We distinguished you. The root of *al-farq* is distinguishing between two things, and a *firqah* (group) of people is a distinct company set apart from others.

The sea (*al-bahr*) was named *bahr* for its vastness and expanse. From it comes the saying *tabahhara fi al-ilm* (he became deep in knowledge) when he extended himself in it. And *al-bahirah* is a she-camel whose ear is split widely.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We saved you and drowned the people of Pharaoh﴾. He omitted the mention of Pharaoh, although he drowned with them, because it is known that he was included among them.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 49–50:**

His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And [remember] when We saved you from the people of Pharaoh﴾. He means: from the people of Pharaoh. The *al* (family) of a man are those whose affairs return to him, either by lineage or by companionship. Scholars differ regarding *al* and *ahl* (people/household) on two views. The first is that they are the same. The second, which is the view of al-Kisa'i, is that one says *al al-rajul* (the family of a man) when his name is mentioned, but if he is referred to by a pronoun (kunaya), one says *ahluhu* (his people), not *aluhu*. Just as one says *ahl al-ilm* (people of knowledge) and *ahl al-Basrah* (people of Basra), but one does not say *al al-ilm* or *al al-Basrah*.

As for Pharaoh (Fir'awn): it is said that he is that very man. It is also said that it is the title of every king of the Amalekites, like Caesar for the Romans and Chosroes for the Persians. It is also said that the name of the Pharaoh of Moses was al-Walid ibn Mus'ab.

Regarding His statement, ﴿who afflicted you with the worst torment﴾, there are three interpretations. The first: its meaning is "they would appoint you (to it)," from the saying *sama-hu khutta khasf* (he imposed on him a humiliating condition), when he assigned it to him.

The second: they would compel you to hard labors.

The third: they would add to you beyond the worst torment. From this comes *musawamat al-bay'* (bargaining in sale), which is only that the seller increases the price above the cost and the buyer decreases it below. This is the view of al-Mufaddal.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿and they would spare your women﴾, means: they would keep them alive. It is a form of *istif'aal* (the tenth verb form, Form X) derived from *hayah* (life), because they would slaughter the males and let the females live.

As for the word *nisa'* (women), it is said that it applies to both young and old. It is also said that it applies only to adults, and that they called the young girls "women" in the sense that they are kept alive until they become women.

The sparing of the women was part of the worst torment because they would keep them for enslavement and service. Thus that enslavement itself was the worst torment, not the sparing.

Regarding His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿And in that was a great trial from your Lord﴾, there are two interpretations. The first: what they did to you, of the worst torment, the slaughter of your sons, and the sparing of your women, was a great hardship and a severe test. The second: that in saving you from the people of Pharaoh, who used to do this to you, there was a great blessing from your Lord. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Suddi.

The original meaning of *bala'* (trial) is testing, whether by good or by evil, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya': 35], because testing may be by good just as it may be by evil. However, the more common usage for evil is *balawtuhu abluwhu balaa'*, and for good is *ablaytuhu ubliihi iblaa'*. From this is the verse of Zuhayr:

*"May Allah reward with good what the two of them did for you, so He tested them with the best of tests, the test that tries."*

Thus he combined the two usages.

His statement, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And [remember] when We divided the sea for you﴾. Regarding it there are two interpretations. The first: "and when We separated the sea for you," because *al-farq* (division) is the separation between two things. He divided the sea into twelve paths. Their number was six hundred and twenty thousand, not counting those who were twenty years old for their youth or sixty for their age. Before Pharaoh was Haman with a thousand thousand, and seven hundred horses. This is His statement: ﴿Then Pharaoh sent heralds into the cities﴾ ﴿Indeed, these are but a small band﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 53–54]. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The second: its meaning is "and when We made a separation between you and the sea," that is, We distinguished you. The root of *al-farq* is distinguishing between two things, and a *firqah* (group) of people is a distinct company set apart from others.

The sea (*al-bahr*) was named *bahr* for its vastness and expanse. From it comes the saying *tabahhara fi al-ilm* (he became deep in knowledge) when he extended himself in it. And *al-bahirah* is a she-camel whose ear is split widely.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We saved you and drowned the people of Pharaoh﴾. He omitted the mention of Pharaoh, although he drowned with them, because it is known that he was included among them.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿while you were looking on﴾. He means: at the parting of the sea, until they passed through it, and at its closing upon the people of Pharaoh, until they drowned in it.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 51–53:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿And when We appointed for Moses forty nights﴾: (p-120)

As for "Musa" (Moses), it is a name that combines two words in Coptic, which are: "ma" (water) and "shajar" (tree). So "Mu" is water, and "sa" is tree. He was named with this name that combines these two words because of what al-Suddi mentioned, that when his mother feared for him, she placed him in the ark and cast him into the river, as had been revealed to her. He was thrown among trees near the house of Pharaoh, and the maidservants of Asiya, the wife of Pharaoh, came out to bathe, and they found him. So he was named after the place.

Ibn Ishaq said: He is Musa son of 'Imran son of Yasjar son of Qahath son of Lawi son of Ya'qub (Israel) son of Ishaq son of Ibrahim.

And the Exalted's saying: ﴿forty nights﴾. Ibn al-Kalbi said: When Musa crossed the sea with the Children of Israel, the Children of Israel said to him: "Did you not promise us that you would bring us a Book from God, the Exalted?" So God promised him forty nights, and He promised them (the Children of Israel). Abu al-'Aliya said: They were the month of Dhu al-Qa'da and ten days of Dhu al-Hijja. Then He restricted the mention to the nights without the days, although the days were included with them, because the beginning of the months is the nights, so the days became subordinate to them.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿Then you took the calf after him﴾, meaning you took it as a god after Moses went out to the appointed time and appointed Harun (Aaron) over them.

The cause of that, as Ibn 'Abbas mentioned, is that the Samiri was from a people who worshipped cows, so love of that was in his soul after he had outwardly professed Islam. He had recognized Jibril, because when his mother feared that he would be slaughtered, she left him in a cave and closed it upon him, and Jibril used to come to him and nourish him with his fingers. When he saw him as he crossed the sea, he recognized him, so he took a handful from the trace of his horse. Ibn Mas'ud used to recite: "So I took a handful from the trace of the horse of the Messenger." The handful remained in his hand until Musa departed to his Lord and left Harun among the Children of Israel. Harun said to them: "You have borne burdens of the people's adornments," meaning goods and jewelry, "so purify yourselves from them, for they are impure." So he kindled a fire for them and commanded them to cast what was with them, and they did so. The Samiri came to the fire and said: "O Prophet of God, shall I cast what is in my hand?" He said: "Yes," while he (Harun) thought it was jewelry. So he cast it and said: "Be a calf, a body having a lowing sound."

They differed: Did it become a living animal of flesh and blood or not?

Al-Hasan said: It turned into a living animal of flesh and blood. Others said: It is not permissible, because that is among the signs of God, the Mighty and Majestic, which He does not manifest except as a miracle of a prophet. Rather, He placed in it openings through which the wind enters, so a sound like lowing arose from it.

Those who followed al-Hasan in his view argued against it on two grounds. The first: when he said, "This is your god and the god of Musa," he had already undermined for himself the claim that this was a miracle of the prophets, so it was possible that it occurred from him as a test.

The second: that this is not permissible in times other than those of prophets, but it is permissible in the times of prophets, because they make its falsehood manifest, and that happened in the time of two prophets.

They differed regarding naming it a calf. Abu al-'Aliya said: Because they hastened (ʿajilū) and took it as a god before Musa came to them. Others said: Rather it was named so because it became a calf, a body having a lowing sound.

Then they remained devoted to the calf, worshipping it. Harun had said to them earlier: "O my people, you are only being tested by it, and your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command." They said: "We will not cease to remain devoted to it until Musa returns to us."

The Exalted, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And when We gave Moses the Book and the Criterion﴾ [Ta-Ha: 90–91]: As for "idh" (when), it is a noun for past time, and "idha" is a noun for future time. And "al-Kitab" (the Book) is the Torah.

Regarding "al-Furqan" (the Criterion), there are four opinions. The first: al-Furqan is the Book itself, so He mentioned it by two names for emphasis; this is the view of al-Farra'.

The second: al-Furqan is what is in the Torah of distinction between truth and falsehood, so that would be a description of the Torah; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-'Aliya.

The third: al-Furqan is the victory by which God distinguished between Musa and Pharaoh, until He saved Musa and his people and drowned Pharaoh and his people; this is the view of Abu Zayd.

(p-122) The fourth: al-Furqan is the parting of the sea for the Children of Israel, until they crossed through it.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿So repent to your Creator﴾, meaning: return to obedience to your Creator. Al-bāri' (the Originator, the Creator) and al-barīyah (creation) are both from the same root. Al-barīyah is on the pattern fa'īlah in the sense of maf'ūlah (created), except that it is not hamzated.

The scholars differed about this designation, giving four opinions:

The first: it is derived from "bara'a Allāh al-khalq, yabra'uhum bar'an" (God originated creation, originating them).

The second: it is fa'īlah from al-bara', which is dust.

The third: it is derived from "bari'a al-shay' min al-shay'" (a thing was disassociated from another thing), meaning its separation from it. From this comes al-bara'ah min al-dīn (disavowal of the religion) because of one's separation from it, and "abra'ahu Allāh min al-maraḍ" (God cured him of the illness) when He removed it from him.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then kill yourselves﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: its meaning is that some of you should kill one another. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbās, Sa'īd ibn Jubayr, and Mujāhid.

The second: submit yourselves to being killed, and this was treated as equivalent to killing. This is the view of Abū Isḥāq.

The root meaning of qatl (killing) is the extinguishing of movement. From it comes "qataltu al-khamr bi-l-mā'" (I killed the wine with water) when you mix it, because you have extinguished its movement (its effervescence).

Killing was made a means of repentance because those who refrained from denouncing the worship of the calf refrained only out of fear of fighting and killing. Thus their repentance was made through the killing they had feared. This is what Ibn Juraij said.

Ibn 'Abbās said: Those who had bowed down to the calf sat down cross-legged, and those who had not bowed down to it stood up, took daggers, and darkness overtook them, so some of them began to kill others, until the darkness cleared away from seventy thousand slain in one hour of daytime. During that situation they were calling out: May God have mercy on a servant who endures patiently until God attains His pleasure. Mūsā and the Children of Israel grieved over that killing, so God, mighty and majestic, revealed to Mūsā: Do not grieve. As for those among you who were killed, they are alive with Me and are provided for; and as for those who remain, their repentance has been accepted. So he gave the Children of Israel this good news.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 55–56:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿حَتّى نَرى اللَّهَ جَهْرَةً﴾ ("until we see Allah plainly"). There are two interpretations of this. The first: openly (ʿalāniyah), and this is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: directly before the eyes (ʿiyānan), and this is the view of Qatadah.

The root of al-jahr (open, audible) is manifestness (al-ẓuhūr). From it comes al-jahr bi-l-qirāʾah (reciting aloud), which is only making it manifest, and al-mujāharah bi-l-maʿāṣī (openly flaunting sins) is displaying them openly.

﴿فَأخَذَتْكُمُ الصّاعِقَةُ﴾ ("Then the thunderbolt seized you"), meaning death, ﴿وَأنْتُمْ تَنْظُرُونَ﴾ ("while you were looking"), at what descended upon you of death.

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿ثُمَّ بَعَثْناكم مِن بَعْدِ مَوْتِكُمْ﴾ ("Then We raised you up after your death"), meaning those who died by the thunderbolt, and they are the seventy whom Moses chose to hear the converse of his Lord with him, after He had accepted the repentance of those who worshipped the calf.

Regarding His words, Exalted is He: ﴿ثُمَّ بَعَثْناكُمْ﴾ ("Then We raised you up"), there are two interpretations. The first: that it is their being brought back to life after their death, so that their appointed terms might be completed, and this is the view of Qatadah. The second: that after being revived, they asked to be raised up as prophets, so Allah raised them as prophets, and this is the view of al-Suddi.

The root of al-baʿth (raising up, sending) is dispatching (al-irsāl). It is also said that its root is rather: stirring a thing from its place.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 57:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And We shaded you with the clouds﴾: al-Ghamam (the clouds) is that which covers the sky, veiling it with clouds and dust-haze; everything that covers is ghamam. From this comes the expression ghumma al-hilal (the crescent was obscured), meaning the clouds covered it.

Regarding the ghamam with which Allah shaded them, there are two interpretations. The first: it is the cloud (al-sahaba), and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is that which brought the angels on the Day of Badr, similar to His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do they await anything but that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210]. This is the view of Mujahid.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And We sent down upon you al-Mann and al-Salwa﴾. Concerning it there are seven sayings. The first: al-Mann is what fell upon the trees, which the people would eat; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: al-Mann is a gum (samgha), and this is the view of Mujahid.

The third: al-Mann is a drink, which used to descend upon them, and they would drink it after mixing it with water; this is the view of al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

The fourth: al-Mann is honey, which used to descend upon them; this is the view of Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: al-Mann is thin bread (al-khubz al-ruqaq); this is the view of Wahb.

The sixth: it is ginger (al-zanjabil); this is the view of al-Suddi.

The seventh: it is terangbin (al-taranjabin; manna-like exudate).

Concerning al-Salwa there are two sayings. The first: it is the quail (al-sumani).

The second: it is a bird resembling the quail, which the south wind used to drive toward them; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. Its etymology is from al-salw (consolation), as if it consoles one from other things.

Ibn Jurayj said: If one of them took from the al-Mann and al-Salwa an excess beyond the food of one day, it would spoil, except on Friday; for when they took the food of two days, it would not spoil.

Concerning His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Eat of the good things which We have provided for you﴾, there are three interpretations (p-125):

The first: the delicious, pleasant things (al-shahiyyat al-ladhidha).

The second: it is the lawful (al-halal).

The third: it is the permissible (al-mubah).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 58–59:

His words, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿And when We said: Enter this town﴾. The commentators differed about it on three views. The first: it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), and this is the view of Qatada and al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

The second: it is a town near Bayt al-Maqdis, and this is the view of al-Suddi.

The third: it is Ariha (Jericho) near Bayt al-Maqdis, and this is the view of Ibn Zayd.

His words, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿And enter the gate prostrating﴾. The commentators differed about the gate on two views. The first: it is the Gate of Hittah, which is the eighth gate of Bayt al-Maqdis, and this is the view of Mujahid and al-Suddi.

The second: it is the gate of the town which they were commanded to enter.

Regarding His words ﴿prostrating﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: it means bowing (ruka'an), and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: its meaning is humbling themselves, submissive.

The root of prostration (sujud) is bending, out of glorification of the one prostrated to and submission. From it is the words of the poet:

؎ In a gathering in which the piebald horses lose their way in its crowded places, you see the hills in it prostrating before the hooves.

And Al-A'sha Qays said:

؎ He alternates between prayers to the king, at times prostrating and at times conversing.

Regarding His Exalted words ﴿And say: Hittah﴾ there are four interpretations. The first: it is the saying: There is no god but Allah, and this is the view of 'Ikrima.

The second: that Hittah means forgiveness, as if it were a command to seek forgiveness, and this is the narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: it is their saying: this command is true as it was said to you, and this is the narration of al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: its meaning is: remove our sins from us (hutta 'anna khatayaana), and this is the view of al-Hasan, Qatada and Ibn Zayd, and it is closest to the apparent wording.

His Exalted words ﴿We will forgive you your sins﴾: that is, We will show mercy to you and conceal them upon you, so We will not disgrace you with punishment for them.

Al-Khata' (error) is deviating from the intended aim. It is said: khati'a al-shay' khata'an, when he hit it without intending it, and akhta'a yukhti', when he intended it but did not hit it. So the first is khati'un (one who errs unintentionally) and the second is mukhti' (one who errs in intention).

The root of forgiveness (maghfirah) is covering and concealing; for this reason the iron helmet is called mighfar, because it covers the head and shields it. From it is the words of Aws ibn Hajar:

؎ I do not blame the cousin if he is at fault, and I overlook his ignorance if he is ignorant.

(p-127)

His Exalted words ﴿But those who did wrong substituted a saying other than that which had been told them﴾: meaning, they changed what they were commanded, both in speech and in action. They were commanded to enter the gate prostrating, but they entered crawling on their buttocks, and they were commanded to say: Hittah, but they said: Hintah fi sha'ir (wheat in barley), mocking at that.

﴿So We sent down upon those who did wrong a punishment from the sky﴾: Regarding ar-rijz there are three views. The first: it is the punishment, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada.

The second: it is the wrath, and this is the view of Abu al-'Aliya.

The third: it is the plague, which Allah sent upon them and destroyed them, and the children remained, and this is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 60:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when Moses asked for water for his people﴾. Its implied sense is: "And when Moses asked Us for water for his people." Al-istisqa' (asking for water) means seeking to be given water. The Arabs say saqaytuhu and asqaytuhu. It has been said that they are two forms (lughatan) with one meaning. It has also been said that rather, saqaytuhu means giving him a drink (saqy al-shafah, giving drink to the lips), while asqaytuhu means showing him where the water is (dalaltuhu 'ala al-ma').

﴿So We said: Strike the rock with your staff, and there gushed forth from it twelve springs﴾. There is an omission in the speech, and its implied sense is: "So he struck, and there gushed forth from it twelve springs."

Al-infijar (gushing forth) is splitting open (al-inshiqaq). Al-inbijas (bursting forth) is narrower than it, for it is first inbijas and then becomes infijar.

The word ayn (spring/eye) is among the homonymous terms (al-asma' al-mushtarakah). The ayn of water is likened to the ayn of a living creature, because water comes out of it, just as tears come out of the eye of a living creature. (p-128)

When Moses asked for water, he was commanded to strike with his staff a square rock of Tur (Mount Sinai) (min al-Tur), and there gushed forth from it twelve springs, three springs from each side.

﴿Every people had known their drinking place﴾. It means that for each tribe (sibt) among them there was a spring, which they had recognised and from which they drank no other. When they moved on, its water would cease, and it would be carried in a leather bag (al-juwaliq), and it was the size of a head.

﴿And do not commit abuse on the earth, causing corruption﴾. Regarding it there are two interpretations. The first: its meaning is "do not transgress" (la taghaw), and this is the saying of Ibn Zayd.

The second: its meaning is "do not strive on the earth, causing corruption," and this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas and Abu al-'Aliyah al-Riyahi.

Al-'ayth is the intensity of corruption, and from it is the verse of Ru'bah:

Wa'atha fina mustahill 'a'ith / musaddiq aw fajir munakith

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 61:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿wa-fumiha﴾ (and its garlic/wheat). Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first: it is wheat (al-hintah). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, and al-Suddi. Ibn 'Abbas, when someone asked him about al-fum and whether it meant wheat, recited the verse of Uhayhah ibn al-Julah:

؎ I was once the richest of people, a single person, who came to Madinah lacking the cultivation of fum (wheat).

The second: it is bread (al-khubz). This is the view of Mujahid, Ibn Zayd, and 'Ata'.

The third: it is garlic (al-thawm), spelled with the letter thā'. This is explicit in the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud, and it is the view of al-Rabi' ibn Anas and al-Kisa'i.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿ihbitu misran﴾ (go down to a city). The majority of reciters read it with tanwin, and some read it without tanwin; both are so. The recitation of Ibn Mas'ud is without the alif.

Concerning the city he meant, there are two views. The first: he meant any city, without specification, since what they asked for, of herbs, cucumbers and fum, is found only in cities. This is the view of Qatadah, al-Suddi, Mujahid, and Ibn Zayd.

The second: he meant the city of Pharaoh, from which they had come out. This is the view of al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliyah, and al-Rabi'.

Scholars differed about the derivation of misr (city). Some said it is derived from qat' (cutting off), because it is cut off by its settlement. Others said it is derived from separation between it and other places. 'Adi ibn Zayd said:

؎ And the maker of the sun a city, without doubt, that separates between the day and the night.

﴿And humiliation and poverty were stamped upon them, and they returned with anger from Allah. That was because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right. That was because they disobeyed and used to transgress.﴾

Concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and humiliation was stamped upon them﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: it is from dhillah and saghar (lowliness and abasement). The second: it means that He imposed the jizyah upon them. This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah.

Concerning (al-maskanah, poverty) there are two interpretations. The first: it is destitution (al-faqah), the view of Abu al-'Aliyah. The second: it is poverty (al-faqr), the view of al-Suddi.

Concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they returned with anger from Allah﴾ there are three interpretations. The first, which is the view of Abu al-'Abbas al-Mubarrad: the root of this is al-manzilah (station), and its meaning is that they were placed in the station of Allah's anger. It is related that a man brought another man to the Prophet ﷺ and said: "This is the killer of my brother." He said: "(Then he is baw' for him)," meaning that he is to be killed, so he takes his station. Layla al-Akhyaliyyah says:

؎ If the slain are baw' (equal), then you, a young man, have not killed the family of 'Awf ibn 'Amir.

The second, which is the view of Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj: the root of this is equalization (al-taswiyah), and its meaning is that they were made equal in anger from Allah. From this is what is related from 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who said: "Allah placed the spoils (al-anfal) in the hands of His Prophet ﷺ, and he divided them among them on baw' (equally)," meaning equally among them in the distribution.

The third, which is the view of al-Kisa'i: its meaning is that they returned with anger from Allah. He said: al-baw' is return, but it is only a return by something, either by evil or by good.

Concerning His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they used to kill the prophets without right﴾ there are two views. The first: Allah, mighty and majestic, allowed the disbelievers to be empowered over the killing of prophets only so that they might attain high ranks which they could not attain otherwise; this is not abandonment of them, as He does with believers among the people of His obedience.

The second, which is the view of al-Hasan: Allah, mighty and majestic, did not command a prophet to fight except that He gave him victory and he was not killed; rather, He left the disbelievers free to kill those prophets who were not commanded to fight.

(Al-anbiya') is the plural of (nabi), and the plural of (nabi) has also come as (nuba'), as al-'Abbas ibn Mirdas al-Sulami said, praising the Prophet ﷺ:

؎ O seal of the nuba' (prophets), you are indeed sent with truth, where God's guidance has guided you.

It is not hamzated in the reading of the majority, except Nafi', who read al-anbiya' and al-nabiyyin with hamz.

Concerning what the name "nabi" is derived from, there are three sayings. The first: it is derived from al-naba' (news), which is information, because he gives news of Allah, i.e., informs; and from this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has he not been informed of what is in the scriptures of Musa?﴾ [al-Najm: 36]. The second: the root of nabi is the path (al-tariq). Al-Qutami said:

؎ When we reached a nabi (path), and it became firm for us, its traces marked with the marks of weaving, clearly defined.

So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was called nabi, because he is the path to Him. The third: it is derived from al-nubuwwah (prophethood), because the station of the prophets is elevated.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 62:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾ means: they affirmed Muhammad ﷺ. ﴿And those who were Jews﴾ are the Jews (al-Yahud). Regarding their being named thus, there are three opinions. The first: they were ascribed to Yahudha (Judah), the eldest son of Ya'qub (Jacob), and the Arabs changed the dhal (ذ) to a dal (د), because when a foreign word is Arabized, it is altered from its original pronunciation. (p-132)

The second: it is derived from the saying of people: hada al-qawm yahudu hawdatan wa hiyadatan, meaning they repented. Zuhayr said:

Other than a campsite in which no fear came, nor any dread from a worshipper who has turned in repentance (mutahawwid).

He means a worshipper who repents, so they were named Yahud because of their repentance from worshipping the calf.

The third: they were named Yahud because of their saying: "Inna hudna ilayk" (indeed we have turned to You). This is the opinion of Ibn Jurayj.

As for ﴿and the Christians (al-Nasara)﴾, it is a plural, and its singular is (Nasrani). It was said that the singular is (Nasran) with the yā' dropped; this is the view of Sibawayh. Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad said: its singular is Nasri, but the first is the one in use.

Regarding their being named thus, there are three opinions. The first: they were named so after a village called (Nasirah), where ʿIsa (peace be upon him) used to dwell, so he was ascribed to it and called ʿIsa al-Nasiri; then his companions were ascribed to him and called al-Nasara. This is the opinion of Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah.

The second: they were named so because some of them supported one another (nusrah), as the poet said:

When I saw the Nabateans as helpers, I hitched up my garment from my knees.

I was for them, among the Nasara, a neighbour.

The third: they were named so because of His saying: ﴿Who are my helpers in the way of Allah?﴾

﴿And the Sabians (al-Sabi'in)﴾ is a plural, its singular being Sabi'. Its hamza has been disputed: the majority pronounced it with a hamza, except Nafi', who did not.

Regarding the source from which this name is derived, there are three opinions. The first: it is derived from rising and appearing, from the saying: sabaa nab al-ba'ir, meaning the camel's tooth emerged, and this is the view of al-Khalil.

The second: the sabi' is one who passes out of one thing into another, so the Sabians were named thus because they departed from Judaism and Christianity. This is the opinion of Ibn Zayd.

The third: it is derived from the saying: sabā yasbū, meaning he inclined toward a thing and loved it. This is the view of Nafi'; and for this reason he did not pronounce the hamza.

Concerning them, there is disagreement: Mujahid, al-Hasan and Ibn Abi Najih said: the Sabians are between the Jews and the Magians. Qatadah said: the Sabians are a people who worship the angels, pray towards the qiblah, [and recite the Zabur and pray on Thursday]. al-Suddi said: they are a group of the People of the Book. al-Khalil said: they are a people whose religion resembles the religion of the Christians, except that their qiblah is towards the direction of the south wind facing midday; they claim that they are upon the religion of Nuh.

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds—for them is their reward with their Lord﴾ there are two opinions. One: it was revealed concerning Salman al-Farisi and his companions among the Christians, by whose hands he had become Christian before the mission of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; they had informed him that a prophet would be sent, and that they would believe in him if they lived to see him. This is the opinion of al-Suddi.

The second: it is abrogated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 85]. This is the opinion of Ibn ʿAbbas.

If it is said: why did He say ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾ in the singular, and then say ﴿for them is their reward with their Lord﴾ in the plural? It is said: because the word (man) is singular in form but plural in meaning, so at times it is construed according to its form and at times according to its meaning. The poet said:

Greet Salma for us both, if you pass by her, and say to her: turn back to those who stayed behind.

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 63–64:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We raised the mount (al-Tur) above you﴾. Concerning al-Tur there are three opinions. The first: it is the name of the mountain upon which God spoke to Musa and upon which the Torah was revealed, and no other. This is the narration of Ibn Jurayj from Ibn Abbas.

The second: al-Tur refers specifically to those mountains that bear vegetation, to the exclusion of those that do not. This is the narration of al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas.

The third: al-Tur is the name for every mountain. This is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah, except that Mujahid said: it is the name of every mountain in Syriac (al-Suryaniyya), while Qatadah said: rather, it is an Arabic name. al-Ajjaj said:

*Its wing-tip was near to al-Tur, so that its swoop passed by, as the falcon swoops when the falcon turns back.*

Mujahid said: the mountain was raised above them like a canopy, and it was said to them: "Either you believe, or it will fall upon you." So they believed.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾, there are three interpretations. The first: the "strength" (quwwah) is diligence and striving (al-jidd wa al-ijtihad). This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and al-Suddi.

The second: it means with obedience to God, may He be exalted. This is the view of Abu al-Aliyah and al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

The third: it is acting upon what is in it (al-'amal bima fihi). This is the view of Mujahid.

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 63–64:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We raised the mount (al-Tur) above you﴾. Concerning al-Tur there are three opinions. The first: it is the name of the mountain upon which God spoke to Musa and upon which the Torah was revealed, and no other. This is the narration of Ibn Jurayj from Ibn Abbas.

The second: al-Tur refers specifically to those mountains that bear vegetation, to the exclusion of those that do not. This is the narration of al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas.

The third: al-Tur is the name for every mountain. This is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah, except that Mujahid said: it is the name of every mountain in Syriac (al-Suryaniyya), while Qatadah said: rather, it is an Arabic name. al-Ajjaj said:

The Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 65–66:

The words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed concerning the Sabbath﴾. Regarding their transgression on the Sabbath there are two opinions: (p-١٣٥)

The first: they took the fish on it by way of considering it lawful (istihlal, regarding something as permissible), and this is the saying of al-Hasan.

The second: they held the fish back on the day of the Sabbath and took them on the day of Sunday, and the Sabbath is the known day.

Concerning the naming of it by this name there are four sayings. The first: al-sabt is a name for a portion of time, so that day was named after it, and this is the saying of al-Zajjaj.

The second: it was named this because the creation of everything ceased (sabata khalq kull shay'), meaning it was brought to an end and completed, and this is the saying of Abu 'Ubayda.

The third: it was named this because the Jews rested (yasbitun) on it, meaning they ceased their work on it.

The fourth: the origin of sabt is stillness and calm in comfort and ease, and for this reason the sleeper is called masbut, because of his rest and the stillness of his body, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿And We made your sleep a rest﴾. So the day was named after it because of the Jews' rest on it.

Regarding the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So We said to them, "Be apes, despised"﴾ there are two opinions. The first: they were transformed into apes, and they became, because of their transgression on the Sabbath, in the form of the apes that had been created before, during the six days.

Ibn 'Abbas said: no transformed being (maskh) ever lived beyond three days, and it neither ate nor drank.

The second, which is the saying of Mujahid: they were not transformed into apes, but it is a parable (mathal) that Allah struck for them, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿The likeness of the donkey that carries books﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 5].

Regarding His words, Exalted: ﴿despised (khasi'in)﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: khasi' means distanced and driven away, and from it comes the saying "khasa'ta al-kalb" (you drove the dog away), when you distance it and drive it off. (p-١٣٦)

The second: its meaning is humbled and abased, and this is the saying of Mujahid.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: khasi'an means humiliated (dhalil).

His words, Exalted: ﴿So We made it an exemplary punishment for what was before it and what was after it﴾. Concerning what was made an exemplary punishment there are six sayings. The first: it is the punishment.

The second: it is the fish.

The third: it is the town whose people transgressed.

The fourth: they are the nation that transgressed, and they are the people of Ayla.

The fifth: they are those who were transformed into apes.

The sixth: they are the apes, transformed in their (human) forms.

Regarding His words, Exalted: ﴿exemplary punishment (nakal)﴾ there are three interpretations. The first: it is a punishment, and this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is a lesson by which whoever sees it is deterred (yunakkal).

The third: nakal is being made notorious through disgrace.

Regarding His words, Exalted: ﴿for what was before it and what was after it﴾ there are five interpretations. The first: what was before it and what was after it of the towns, and this is the narration of Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: what was before it means those after them among the nations, and what was after it means those who remained with them, and this is the narration of al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: what was before it means what was below it (min duniha), and what was after it means those who come after them among the nations, and this is the saying of al-Suddi.

The fourth: what was before it means the sins of the people, and what was after it means the fish that they took, and this is the saying of Qatadah.

The fifth: what was before it means what had passed of their wrongdoings, and what was after it means their wrongdoings by which they were destroyed, and this is the saying of Mujahid. (p-١٣٧)

The Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 65–66:

The words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And you certainly knew those among you who transgressed concerning the Sabbath﴾. Regarding their transgression on the Sabbath there are two opinions: (p-١٣٥)

The first: they took the fish on it by way of considering it lawful (istihlal, regarding something as permissible), and this is the saying of al-Hasan.

The second: they held the fish back on the day of the Sabbath and took them on the day of Sunday, and the Sabbath is the known day.

Concerning the naming of it by this name there are four sayings. The first: al-sabt is a name for a portion of time, so that day was named after it, and this is the saying of al-Zajjaj.

The second: it was named this because the creation of everything ceased (sabata khalq kull shay'), meaning it was brought to an end and completed, and this is the saying of Abu 'Ubayda.

The third: it was named this because the Jews rested (yasbitun) on it, meaning they ceased their work on it.

The fourth: the origin of sabt is stillness and calm in comfort and ease, and for this reason the sleeper is called masbut, because of his rest and the stillness of his body, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿And We made your sleep a rest﴾. So the day was named after it because of the Jews' rest on it.

Regarding the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So We said to them, "Be apes, despised"﴾ there are two opinions. The first: they were transformed into apes, and they became, because of their transgression on the Sabbath, in the form of the apes that had been created before, during the six days.

Ibn 'Abbas said: no transformed being (maskh) ever lived beyond three days, and it neither ate nor drank.

The second, which is the saying of Mujahid: they were not transformed into apes, but it is a parable (mathal) that Allah struck for them, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿The likeness of the donkey that carries books﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 5].

Regarding His words, Exalted: ﴿despised (khasi'in)﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: khasi' means distanced and driven away, and from it comes the saying "khasa'ta al-kalb" (you drove the dog away), when you distance it and drive it off. (p-١٣٦)

The second: its meaning is humbled and abased, and this is the saying of Mujahid.

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: khasi'an means humiliated (dhalil).

His words, Exalted: ﴿So We made it an exemplary punishment for what was before it and what was after it﴾. Concerning what was made an exemplary punishment there are six sayings. The first: it is the punishment.

The second: it is the fish.

The third: it is the town whose people transgressed.

The fourth: they are the nation that transgressed, and they are the people of Ayla.

The fifth: they are those who were transformed into apes.

The sixth: they are the apes, transformed in their (human) forms.

Regarding His words, Exalted: ﴿exemplary punishment (nakal)﴾ there are three interpretations. The first: it is a punishment, and this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is a lesson by which whoever sees it is deterred (yunakkal).

The third: nakal is being made notorious through disgrace.

Regarding His words, Exalted: ﴿for what was before it and what was after it﴾ there are five interpretations. The first: what was before it and what was after it of the towns, and this is the narration of Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: what was before it means those after them among the nations, and what was after it means those who remained with them, and this is the narration of al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: what was before it means what was below it (min duniha), and what was after it means those who come after them among the nations, and this is the saying of al-Suddi.

The fourth: what was before it means the sins of the people, and what was after it means the fish that they took, and this is the saying of Qatadah.

The fifth: what was before it means what had passed of their wrongdoings, and what was after it means their wrongdoings by which they were destroyed, and this is the saying of Mujahid. (p-١٣٧)

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun*) on Surah 2, verse 67:**

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when Moses said to his people, "Indeed, Allah commands you to slaughter a cow"﴾. The reason for Moses' command to his people was what the exegetes (al-Mufassirun, the scholars of tafsir, or Qur'anic exegesis) mentioned: that a man among the Children of Israel was wealthy and had no child, and he had a relative who would inherit from him. The relative grew impatient for his death, so he killed him secretly and threw him at the place of the al-Asbat, and he accused one of them of the killing. They brought the matter before Moses, and he said, "Who among you has knowledge of this?" They said, "You are the Prophet of Allah, and you know more than us." So he said, "Indeed, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commands you to slaughter a cow." When they heard this, and there was no apparent answer in it to what they had asked about, ﴿they said, "Do you make a mockery of us?"﴾ And al-Huzu' (mockery) means play and ridicule.

The rajaz poet says:

*Umm Taysala has mocked me, saying: "I see him destitute, having nothing at all."*

﴿He said, "I seek refuge in Allah from being among the ignorant."﴾ Because deviating from the answer of a seeker of guidance into mockery is ignorance, Moses sought refuge from it, since it is a quality that is negated in the Prophets. And He commanded the slaughter of a cow specifically, and not something else, (God knows best) because it was of the same kind as the calf they had worshipped, so that the reverence they had felt for it would be diminished in their eyes, and so that, by their compliance, it would be known that the attachment to its worship that was in their souls had disappeared.

The word *baqarah* (cow) is a name for the female, while *thawr* is for the male, like *naqah* and *jamal*, and *imra'ah* and *rajul*, so its feminine form is without its own word-form.

The name *baqarah* is derived from splitting, from their saying *baqara batnahu* when he split his belly, because it splits the earth in ploughing.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 68–71:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is."﴾ Al-Hasan narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, had they taken any cow and slaughtered it, it would have sufficed them. But they made it difficult, so God made it difficult for them." ﴿He said, "Indeed, He says it is a cow neither old (fari') nor virgin (bikr).﴾" Regarding al-Fari' (old) there are two interpretations. The first: it is the large, decrepit one, and this is the view of the majority.

The rajaz poet said:

"Grey has touched my temples, and my head has become white, like litters in which are men who are feeble (furrad)."

By his saying furrad, he means "aged" (harmá).

The second: al-Fari' is the one that has borne many births, so that her belly has become wide for that, because the meaning of fari' in the language is "wide." This is the view of some later scholars, and they cited the words of the rajaz poet:

"O many a one with rancor against me, who has periods like the periods of a menstruating woman."

Al-Bikr (virgin) is the young one that has not conceived. Bikr applies to females of animals and of the sons of Adam as long as the male has not mounted her; it is with a kasra on the ba'. As for al-Bakr with a fatha on the ba', it means a young camel.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿neither old nor virgin, but between that (awan bayna dhalik)﴾. Al-'Awan is the middle-aged one that has given birth to one or two litters. ﴿Between that﴾ means between the young and the old, and she is at her strongest and best condition as a cow. The poet said:

"They went forth upon him between a noble virgin and a middle-aged one like the cloud, of middle age."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "Indeed, He says it is a cow, yellow (safra')﴾. It is related from al-Hasan al-Basri that by His saying safra' is meant black, intensely black, just as the Arabs say "a yellow she-camel" meaning a black one. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Those are my horses from it and those are my mounts; they are yellow, and their offspring are like raisins."

And the rajaz poet said:

"And yellow ones, not yellowish, but rather black like dates."

But the rest of the exegetes said: it is yellow in color, from the well-known yellowness, and this is more sound, because it is the apparent meaning, and because He said: ﴿bright in its color (faqi' lawnuha)﴾, and faqi' is among the attributes of yellowness; blackness is not described by that. One says: "intensely black (aswad halik)," "deep red (ahmar qani)," "pure white (abyad nasi')," "verdant green (akhdar nadir)," and "bright yellow (asfar faqi')."

Then, regarding what is meant by the yellowness, there are two views. The first: its horn and hoof are yellow; this is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The second: its whole color is yellow; this is the view of Mujahid.

And regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿bright in its color﴾ there are three interpretations. The first: it is intensely yellow; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan. The second: it is purely yellow; this is the view of Qutrub. The third: it is clear; this is the view of Abu al-'Aliyah and Qatadah.

﴿gladdening the beholders (tasurru al-nazirin)﴾: in it there are two aspects. The first: it pleases the beholders with its yellowness, so it pleases with gladness, which is what the heart is affected by, and joy, which is what the eye rejoices in. And His saying ﴿gladdening the beholders﴾ may carry two meanings. The first: by the beauty of its color, so it is ... due to its yellowness.

The second: the goodliness of its appearance (husn samtiha). It is described with this so that it becomes an additional condition in its description, beyond what was mentioned earlier of its yellowness. Thus the cow on the first view has one attribute, and on the second view has two attributes.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is."﴾ They asked a third question, and they did not comply with the command after the second clarification. Ibn Jurayj narrated from Qatadah that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "They were commanded with the least cow, but when they made things hard for themselves, God made it hard for them. By God, had they not made the exception, it would never have been made clear to them until the end of time." That is, had they not said, ﴿and indeed, if God wills, we will be guided﴾, they would never have been guided to it.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿He said, "Indeed, He says it is a cow, not broken to labor (la dhalul)"﴾, meaning labor has not made her submissive.

﴿that plows the earth (tuthir al-ard)﴾: ithara means scattering a thing, that is, she is not one that plows the earth for sowing, nor is she irrigated for crops.

[It was also said: "yuthir" is a new (resumptive) verb, and the meaning is the obligation of plowing for her, and that she used to plow and not irrigate.] But this view is nothing; rather, all of that is negated from her.

﴿sound, with no mark on her (musallamah la shiyata fiha)﴾: regarding this there are four interpretations. The first: sound of defects; this is the view of Qatadah and Abu al-'Aliyah. The second: free of labor. The third: free of usurpation and theft, so that she is lawful. The fourth: free of ... And regarding (shiyah) there are three aspects. The first: there is no particular mark on her, related from al-Suddi. The second: there is no color in her that differs from her own color, of black or white. The third: it is the pied (wadah), which is a combination of colors of black and white.

Its root is from the embroidering (washy) of cloth, which is the beautifying of its flaws with varied colors, and from this the informer before a ruler is called "washi" (a tale-bearer), because he embellishes his lie before him until he accepts it from him.

﴿They said, "Now you have brought the truth."﴾ Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: "Now you have made the truth clear"; this is the view of Qatadah. The second: its meaning is that when he clarified it for them they said, "This is the cow of so-and-so; now you have brought the truth concerning it." This is the view of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

And regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they slaughtered her, though they had nearly not done it (wa ma kadu yafalun)﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: they nearly did not do it because of the high price of her, for they bought her at the price of her hide filled with gold from the property of the slain man; this is what Ibn 'Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b related. And it was said: at ten times her weight.

The second: they nearly did not do it out of fear of disgrace upon themselves regarding identifying the killer; this is the view of Wahb. 'Ikrimah said: her price was only three dinars.

And it was said: the cow was a wild one.
