"Grey has touched my temples, and my head has become white, like litters in which are men who are feeble (furrad)."

By his saying furrad, he means "aged" (harmá).

The second: al-Fari' is the one that has borne many births, so that her belly has become wide for that, because the meaning of fari' in the language is "wide." This is the view of some later scholars, and they cited the words of the rajaz poet:

"O many a one with rancor against me, who has periods like the periods of a menstruating woman."

Al-Bikr (virgin) is the young one that has not conceived. Bikr applies to females of animals and of the sons of Adam as long as the male has not mounted her; it is with a kasra on the ba'. As for al-Bakr with a fatha on the ba', it means a young camel.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿neither old nor virgin, but between that (awan bayna dhalik)﴾. Al-'Awan is the middle-aged one that has given birth to one or two litters. ﴿Between that﴾ means between the young and the old, and she is at her strongest and best condition as a cow. The poet said:

"They went forth upon him between a noble virgin and a middle-aged one like the cloud, of middle age."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said, "Indeed, He says it is a cow, yellow (safra')﴾. It is related from al-Hasan al-Basri that by His saying safra' is meant black, intensely black, just as the Arabs say "a yellow she-camel" meaning a black one. From this is the saying of the poet:

"Those are my horses from it and those are my mounts; they are yellow, and their offspring are like raisins."

And the rajaz poet said:

"And yellow ones, not yellowish, but rather black like dates."

But the rest of the exegetes said: it is yellow in color, from the well-known yellowness, and this is more sound, because it is the apparent meaning, and because He said: ﴿bright in its color (faqi' lawnuha)﴾, and faqi' is among the attributes of yellowness; blackness is not described by that. One says: "intensely black (aswad halik)," "deep red (ahmar qani)," "pure white (abyad nasi')," "verdant green (akhdar nadir)," and "bright yellow (asfar faqi')."

Then, regarding what is meant by the yellowness, there are two views. The first: its horn and hoof are yellow; this is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The second: its whole color is yellow; this is the view of Mujahid.

And regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿bright in its color﴾ there are three interpretations. The first: it is intensely yellow; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan. The second: it is purely yellow; this is the view of Qutrub. The third: it is clear; this is the view of Abu al-'Aliyah and Qatadah.

﴿gladdening the beholders (tasurru al-nazirin)﴾: in it there are two aspects. The first: it pleases the beholders with its yellowness, so it pleases with gladness, which is what the heart is affected by, and joy, which is what the eye rejoices in. And His saying ﴿gladdening the beholders﴾ may carry two meanings. The first: by the beauty of its color, so it is ... due to its yellowness.

The second: the goodliness of its appearance (husn samtiha). It is described with this so that it becomes an additional condition in its description, beyond what was mentioned earlier of its yellowness. Thus the cow on the first view has one attribute, and on the second view has two attributes.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said, "Call upon your Lord for us to make clear to us what it is."﴾ They asked a third question, and they did not comply with the command after the second clarification. Ibn Jurayj narrated from Qatadah that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "They were commanded with the least cow, but when they made things hard for themselves, God made it hard for them. By God, had they not made the exception, it would never have been made clear to them until the end of time." That is, had they not said, ﴿and indeed, if God wills, we will be guided﴾, they would never have been guided to it.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿He said, "Indeed, He says it is a cow, not broken to labor (la dhalul)"﴾, meaning labor has not made her submissive.

﴿that plows the earth (tuthir al-ard)﴾: ithara means scattering a thing, that is, she is not one that plows the earth for sowing, nor is she irrigated for crops.

[It was also said: "yuthir" is a new (resumptive) verb, and the meaning is the obligation of plowing for her, and that she used to plow and not irrigate.] But this view is nothing; rather, all of that is negated from her.

﴿sound, with no mark on her (musallamah la shiyata fiha)﴾: regarding this there are four interpretations. The first: sound of defects; this is the view of Qatadah and Abu al-'Aliyah. The second: free of labor. The third: free of usurpation and theft, so that she is lawful. The fourth: free of ... And regarding (shiyah) there are three aspects. The first: there is no particular mark on her, related from al-Suddi. The second: there is no color in her that differs from her own color, of black or white. The third: it is the pied (wadah), which is a combination of colors of black and white.

Its root is from the embroidering (washy) of cloth, which is the beautifying of its flaws with varied colors, and from this the informer before a ruler is called "washi" (a tale-bearer), because he embellishes his lie before him until he accepts it from him.

﴿They said, "Now you have brought the truth."﴾ Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: "Now you have made the truth clear"; this is the view of Qatadah. The second: its meaning is that when he clarified it for them they said, "This is the cow of so-and-so; now you have brought the truth concerning it." This is the view of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

And regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So they slaughtered her, though they had nearly not done it (wa ma kadu yafalun)﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: they nearly did not do it because of the high price of her, for they bought her at the price of her hide filled with gold from the property of the slain man; this is what Ibn 'Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b related. And it was said: at ten times her weight.

The second: they nearly did not do it out of fear of disgrace upon themselves regarding identifying the killer; this is the view of Wahb. 'Ikrimah said: her price was only three dinars.

And it was said: the cow was a wild one.

He said, may He be exalted and glorified: **﴿And when you killed a soul and disputed over it﴾**. This means: who killed the Israelite? He was killed by his nephew. There are two opinions about the reason for his killing. The first is that it was for a beautiful daughter of his whom the nephew wished to marry.

The second is that it was to seek his inheritance, and he claimed that the man had been killed by one of the tribes (al-Asbat).

Regarding His words, **﴿disputed over it﴾**, there are three interpretations. The first is that *al-darʼ* (الدَّرْءَ) means crookedness (al-iʻwijaj), and from this is the poet's saying:

*"I withheld from them the crookedness of enemies, and they treated madness with madness."*

That is, the crookedness of the enemies.

The second, which is the best known, is that *al-darʼ* means repelling (al-mudafaʻa), and its meaning is: "you pushed one another away regarding the killing." From this is the saying of Ruʼbah ibn al-Ajjaj:

*"I overtook her before every proud warrior, by pushing away from me the arrogance of every haughty one."*

The third is that it means they differed and disputed. This was said by al-Suddi. It was also said that although this verse comes later in the recitation, it comes earlier in the sequence of address, before His words: **﴿And when Moses said to his people, "Indeed, God commands you..."﴾**, because they were commanded to slaughter it after the killing, and they differed about who had killed him.

His words, may He be exalted: **﴿And God will bring out what you were concealing﴾**, meaning: God will manifest what you were secretly doing of the killing. At this point the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If one of you were to work inside a solid rock with no door, God would bring out his deed."

His words, may He be exalted: **﴿So We said, "Strike him with part of it."﴾** The scholars differed about the part of the cow with which the slain man was struck, in five opinions:

The first is that he was struck with the thigh of the cow. This is the view of Mujahid, Ikrimah and Qatadah.

The second is that he was struck with the piece between the two shoulders. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The third is that he was struck with one of its bones. This is the view of Abu al-ʻAliyah.

The fourth is that he was struck with its ear. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

The fifth is that he was struck with the tip of its tail (ʻajb al-dhanab), which is the part the earth does not consume. This is the view of al-Farraʼ.

*Al-baʻd* (الْبَعْضُ) means less than half.

**﴿Thus God brings the dead to life﴾**, meaning: when the slain man was struck with part of the cow, God brought him back to life. His name was ʻAmil, and he said, "My nephew killed me." Then he died again. His nephews said, "By God, we did not kill him." Thus they denied the truth after witnessing it.

Al-Farraʼ said: there is an omission in the speech, and its implied meaning is: "So We said: strike him with part of it, so that he might live." (p-١٤٤)

They struck him, and he came to life.

**Thus God brings the dead to life.** By this He indicated the resurrection and the raising up. The cause of his revival was made to be striking him with a dead thing that has no life in it, so that no one with doubts would suppose that life had passed to him from what he was struck with. This removes doubt and strengthens the proof.

Regarding His words, **﴿Thus God brings the dead to life﴾**, there are two interpretations. The first is that it is a report of Moses' words to his people. The second is that it is an address from God to the polytheists of Quraysh.

**﴿So that you may understand﴾**: regarding this there are two interpretations. The first is "so that you may act" (taʻmalun). The second is "so that you may take heed" (taʻtabirun).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 74:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then your hearts hardened﴾, scholars differed over who is referred to by the hardening, on two views. The first: the nephews of the dead man, when they denied his killing after they had heard it from him when God revived him. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that it refers to all of the Children of Israel. Whoever holds this says: "after that" means after all His signs which He showed to Musa.

As for the hardening of their hearts, there are two meanings: the first is their hardness, so that they do not soften. (p-145)

The second is their harshness, so that they show no compassion.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿after that﴾, there are two meanings: the first is after the reviving of the dead, and this address is directed to their community as a whole.

The second is after the speech of the slain man, and the address is directed to the nephews.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿so they are like stones, or even harder in hardness﴾ means the hearts that hardened.

The scholars differed about the meaning of (aw) ("or") in this place and in similar ones, such as His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and he was two bow-lengths away, or nearer﴾ [al-Najm: 9], into five opinions. The first: it is an expression of ambiguity toward the addressees, though God is All-Knowing; that is, it is that, as Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali said:

I love Muhammad with an intense love, and 'Abbas, and Hamza, or 'Ali. And if their love is guidance, I am rightly guided; and I am not mistaken if it is error.

Without doubt, Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali was not doubtful about his love for them, but he left it ambiguous to the one he was addressing. It was said to Abu al-Aswad when he said that: "Are you doubtful?" He said: "Certainly not." Then he cited the saying of Exalted God: ﴿And indeed we or you are upon guidance, or in clear error﴾ [Saba': 24], and said: "Was the one who reported this a doubter?"

The second: that "or" here means "and," and its sense is: "so it is like stones and harder in hardness." A similar usage is the verse of Jarir:

He came to the caliphate, or it was for him a decree, just as his Lord came to Musa at an appointed measure.

The third: that "or" in this place means "rather," so that it reads: "rather harder in hardness," as He said, Exalted is He: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand, or they increase﴾ [al-Saffat: 147], meaning: "rather they increase."

The fourth: that its meaning is permission, and the sense is: if you liken them to stones, they are like them; and if you liken them to something harder, they are like it.

The fifth: "so they are like stones, or harder in hardness, in your estimation."

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed among stones is that from which rivers burst forth﴾, meaning that among stones is that which is more beneficial than your hard hearts, since rivers burst forth from them.

Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed among them is that which falls down out of fear of God﴾. They differed about the pronoun in (minha) ("among them"), to what does it refer? On two views. The first: it refers to the hearts, not to the stones, so the meaning of the statement is: "And indeed among hearts is that which submits out of fear of God." This was mentioned by Ibn Bahr.

The second view: it refers to the stones, since they are the nearest mentioned noun.

Those who held this view differed about these stones on two views. The first: that they are the hail falling from the clouds; this is a view held alone by some of the theologians.

The second, which is the view of the majority of the exegetes: that they are the solid stones of the mountains, since they are more firm in hardness.

Those who held this view differed on two views. The first: that it is the mountain which God made crumble when He spoke to Musa.

The second: that it is general, covering all mountains.

Those who held this view differed about the interpretation of their falling, on four opinions. The first: the falling of what falls out of fear of God, the Qur'an was revealed concerning this.

The second: ... ... ... The third: that whoever magnifies the command of God appears as if he were falling humbly, as Jarir said: (p-147)

When the news of al-Zubayr arrived, the walls of Madina humbled themselves, and the lofty mountains.

The fourth: that God gave some mountains knowledge, so it understood the obedience to God and obeyed Him, like what is narrated concerning the trunk of the palm tree on which the Prophet (ﷺ) used to lean, and when he moved away from it, it wailed. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed a stone used to greet me in the Jahiliyya; indeed I recognize it now." The meaning of the statement is: indeed among the mountains is that which, if the Qur'an were revealed upon it, would fall down out of fear of God, in humility and submission.

**The Qur'anic verse:** ﴿And there was a group of them who used to hear the words of Allah, then they would distort them﴾. There are two views about this:

The first: they are the scholars of the Jews, and what they distort is the Torah. They make the lawful unlawful and the unlawful lawful, following their own desires and aiding those who take bribes from them. This is the view of Mujahid and al-Suddi.

The second: they are the group whom Musa (Moses) chose from among his people. They heard the words of Allah but did not comply with His command, and they distorted the statement when reporting to their people. This is the view of al-Rabi' ibn Anas and Ibn Ishaq.

Regarding the words of Allah that they heard, there are two views. The first: it is the Torah, which the scholars of the Jews knew. The second: it is the revelation which they used to hear, just as the prophets hear it.

Regarding His words: ﴿after they had understood it, while they knew﴾, there are two meanings. The first: after they had heard it, while they knew that they were distorting it. The second: after they had understood it, while they knew the punishment that comes with distorting it.

**The Qur'anic verse:** ﴿And when some of them meet with others﴾. There are two views concerning them. The first: they are the Jews, who, when they were alone with the hypocrites, were told by the hypocrites: "Are you telling the Muslims what Allah has opened up to you?"

The second: they are the Jews, and some of them said to others: ﴿Do you tell them what Allah has opened up to you?﴾ Regarding this there are four opinions:

The first: "what Allah has opened up to you" means what I remind you of by Allah. This was related by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas.

The second: "what Allah has sent down to you in the Torah, concerning the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his being sent," ﴿so that they may argue with you about it before your Lord﴾. This was related by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn Abbas, and it is the view of Abu al-'Aliyya and Qatada.

The third: they meant the statement of the Jews of Bani Qurayza, when the Prophet (ﷺ) likened them to being brothers of the apes; they said, "Who told you this?" This happened when he sent 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah ennoble his face, to them. This is the view of Mujahid.

The fourth: some Jews had embraced Islam, then became hypocrites, and they would tell the Arab Muslims what their forefathers had been punished with. Then some of them said to others: "Do you tell them what Allah has opened up to you of the punishment?" This is the view of al-Suddi.

Regarding ﴿opened up﴾, there are two meanings. The first: what Allah has taught you. The second: what Allah has decreed. Among the Arabs, "fath" (opening) means judgment and ruling, and from this is the poet's saying:

*Unquestionably, convey to the Bani 'Usum a messenger, that I am independent of your judge (fattah).*

The judge is called "al-fattah," and from this is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord, judge between us and our people in truth﴾ [al-A'raf: 89].

Regarding His words: ﴿so that they may argue with you about it before your Lord﴾, there are three meanings. The first: ﴿so that they may argue with you about it before your Lord﴾, where the mention of the Book is omitted for brevity. The second: ﴿so that they may argue with you about it before your Lord﴾, so that the proof against you becomes manifest to Him, and they become more deserving of Allah than you. This is the view of al-Hasan. The third: ﴿so that they may argue with you about it before your Lord﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, as the Exalted said: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, you will dispute﴾ [az-Zumar: 31].

Regarding ﴿opened up﴾, there are two meanings. The first: what Allah has taught you. The second: what Allah has decreed. Among the Arabs, "fath" (opening) means judgment and ruling, and from this is the poet's saying:

*Unquestionably, convey to the Bani 'Usum a messenger, that I am independent of your judge (fattah).*

The judge is called "al-fattah," and from this is the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord, judge between us and our people in truth﴾ [al-A'raf: 89].

Regarding His words: ﴿so that they may argue with you about it before your Lord﴾, there are three meanings. The first: ﴿so that they may argue with you about it before your Lord﴾, where the mention of the Book is omitted for brevity. The second: ﴿so that they may argue with you about it before your Lord﴾, so that the proof against you becomes manifest to Him, and they become more deserving of Allah than you. This is the view of al-Hasan. The third: ﴿so that they may argue with you about it before your Lord﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, as the Exalted said: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection, before your Lord, you will dispute﴾ [az-Zumar: 31].

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 78–79:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And among them are unlettered ones (ummiyyun)﴾ have two interpretations. The first: the ummi (unlettered) is the one who neither writes nor reads. This is the view of Mujahid, and it is the most apparent interpretation of it. (p-150)

The second: the ummiyyun are a people who did not believe in a messenger whom Allah had sent, nor in a book which Allah had revealed, but who wrote a book with their own hands, and the ignorant among them said to their people: "This is from Allah." This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

Regarding the naming of the one who does not write as ummi, there are two views. The first: it is derived from the ummah (community), meaning according to the original state in which the community is, because he remains in his natural condition of not writing. From this is the verse of al-A'sha:

"And indeed Mu'awiyah, the most noble, handsome of faces, tall of stature (ummam)."

The second: it is derived from the umm (mother). Regarding its derivation from umm, there are two explanations. The first: it is derived from it, because he remains as his mother bore him, in that he does not write.

The second: he is attributed to his mother, because writing belongs to men and not to women, so a man who does not write is attributed to his mother, due to her ignorance of writing, rather than to his father.

Regarding the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They know not the Book, except wishful fancies (amani)﴾ there are four interpretations. The first: "except amani" means: except lies. This was said by Ibn Abbas and Mujahid. The poet said:

"But that which was between you two was only the amani of what met neither sky nor earth."

The second: "except amani" means that they wish from Allah what is not theirs. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: "except amani" means merely recitation without understanding. This was said by al-Farra' and al-Kisa'i, and from it is the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Except when he wishes, Satan casts into his wish﴾ [Surah al-Hajj: 52], meaning Satan casts into his desire. Ka'b ibn Malik said:

"He wished for the Book of Allah at the first of his night, and at its end he met the death-fate of the decrees."

The fourth: amani means estimation. This was related by Ibn Bahr, who recited the words of the poet:

"And do not say of a thing, 'I will surely do it,' until what the one who estimates for you has estimated becomes clear."

("Illa") in this place has the meaning of ("lakin", but), and this, according to them, is an exceptive of the disconnected type (istithna' munqati'). (p-151)

From it is the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption﴾ [al-Nisa': 157]. al-Nabigha said:

"I swore an oath not subject to qualification, and there is no knowledge except good assumption regarding a companion."

﴿And they are only assuming (in yazunnun)﴾ has two aspects. The first: they lie, said by Mujahid. The second: they speak falsely, said by the Basrans.

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So woe to those who write the Book with their own hands﴾ — regarding al-wayl (woe) there are six sayings. The first: it is punishment, said by Ibn Abbas. The second: it is condemnation, the view of al-Asma'i, and from it is the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And woe to you for what you describe﴾ [al-Anbiya': 18]. The poet said:

"Meanness clothed an arrow with greenness on its skins, so woe to the arrow from its green garments."

The third: it is grief, said by al-Mufaddal. The fourth: it is disgrace and humiliation. The fifth: that al-wayl is a valley in Hell, and this is the view of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri. The sixth: that it is a mountain in the Fire, and this is the view of Uthman ibn Affan.

﴿Who write the Book with their own hands﴾, i.e., they alter what is in the Book concerning the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his description.

Regarding the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿with their own hands﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: by this He intended to confirm the attribution, even though writing is only done by the hand, as in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿for what I created with My two hands﴾. The second: the meaning of ﴿with their own hands﴾ is from their own selves, said by Ibn al-Sarraj. (p-152)

Regarding the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿that they may purchase with it a little price﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: that they might take with it the goods of this world, because it is of short duration, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: the enjoyment of this world is little﴾. This is the view of Abu al-Aliyah.

The second: it is little because it is unlawful.

﴿And woe to them for what they earn﴾ has two aspects. The first: from their distortion of their Books. The second: from the days of their sins.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 80:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they said, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days."﴾ The difference between al-lams (touching) and al-massu (contact) is that al-lams carries a sense of perception.

Regarding "the numbered days" there are two opinions. The first: they are forty days. This is the view of Qatadah, al-Suddi, Ikrimah, and Abu al-Aliyah, and al-Dahhak narrated it from Ibn Abbas. Those who hold this view differed over the reason for specifying forty: some of them said, "Because it is the number of days during which they worshipped the calf."

Ibn Abbas said: The Jews claim that they found written in the Torah that the distance between the two edges of Hell is a journey of forty years, and they cover the journey of each year in one day. So when the journey ends, the punishment is over and the Fire perishes. This is the view of those who specified "the numbered days" as forty.

The second opinion: the numbered days during which the Fire will touch them are seven days, because they claimed that the age of the world is seven thousand years, and that they would be punished one day for every thousand years. This is the view of Mujahid, and it is the narration of Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn Abbas.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 81–82:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Yes, whoever earns an evil deed﴾. As for (bala) "yes," it is the answer to a negation, and as for (na'am) "yes," it is the answer to an affirmation. Al-Farra' said: If a man says to his companion, "You have no claim against me," and the other replies, "Na'am" (yes), that is confirmation that he owes nothing. But if he says "bala" (yes, indeed), that is a rejection of his statement, and its implied meaning is: "Yes, you do have a claim against me."

As for His saying: ﴿whoever earns an evil deed﴾, the scholars differed regarding the meaning of "evil deed" here, in two views. One of them: it is shirk (polytheism), and this is the view of Mujahid.

The second: it is the sins for which Allah, Exalted is He, has promised the Fire, and this is the view of al-Suddi.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and his sin has encompassed him﴾, there are two interpretations. One of them: he died in it (in that state), and this is the view of Ibn Jubayr.

The second: it has blocked all the paths to him, and this is the view of Ibn al-Sarraj.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 83:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when We took the covenant of the Children of Israel: "Worship none but Allah"﴾, meaning in the Torah, concerning the coming of Muhammad (ﷺ). It is also said: the first covenant was when they were brought forth from the loins of Adam. ﴿And speak to the people good words﴾. As for the one who recites ḥasanan (good), it means a true statement concerning the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ). As for the one who recites ḥusnan with a raised vowel (ḥusnun), meaning: speak good to all people, that is, deal with people with good character.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 84–86:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when We took your covenant: that you shall not shed your blood, nor expel yourselves from your homes⦾﴾. As for "nafs" (self, soul), it is derived from "nafasah" (preciousness), which is nobility; so the self of a person is the most precious of what is in him. As for "diyar" (homes), it is the dwelling in which there are structures for residence, as opposed to a place of passing through. Al-Khalil said: every place in which a people settles is their "dar" (home), even if there are no structures in it.

If it is said: Does anyone shed his own blood or expel himself from his home? There are two views on this: (p-155)

One of them: its meaning is that some of you do not kill others among you, nor expel them from their homes. This is the view of Qatadah and Abu al-'Aliyah.

The second: it refers to the retaliation (qisas) by which they are made to answer for those they killed.

There is also a third view: that His saying "anfusakum" (your selves) means "ikhwanakum" (your brethren), so they are like one soul.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then you back one another against them in sin and aggression﴾. It means: you help one another. "Ithm" (sin) is the act for which one deserves blame. Regarding "'udwan" (aggression) there are two views: one of them is that it is transgressing the truth; the second is that it is excessiveness in wrongdoing.

﴿And if they come to you as captives, you ransom them﴾. Hamzah read "asra" (captives). Regarding the difference between "asra" and "usara" there are two views: one of them is that "asra" is the plural of "asir," and "usara" is the plural of "asra." The second is that "al-asra" are those who are in one's hand even if they are not bound, and this is the view of Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'. "Al-usara" are those who are in bonds.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 87:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We gave Moses the Book﴾, meaning the Torah (al-Tawrah).

﴿And We sent after him a succession of messengers﴾. Al-taqfiyah (the act of following up) means ittiba' (to follow), and its meaning here is "and We made to follow." It is said: istaqfaytuhu (I made him follow), when you come up behind him. The rhyme of a poem (qafiyah) was named qafiyah because it comes after (khalfahu) the verse.

﴿And We gave Jesus, son of Mary, the clear signs﴾. There are three opinions regarding the "clear signs":

The first: that the clear signs are the proofs (al-hujaj).

The second: that they are the Gospel (al-Injil).

The third, which is the view of Ibn 'Abbas: that the clear signs given to Jesus were the raising of the dead, and his fashioning from clay the likeness of a bird, which then became a bird by the permission of God, and the healing of illnesses.

﴿And We supported him with the Holy Spirit (ruh al-qudus)﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations:

The first: that the Holy Spirit is the Name by which Jesus raised the dead. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that it is the Gospel, which He called a spirit, just as God called the Qur'an a spirit in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Thus We have revealed to you a spirit of Our command﴾.

The third, which is the most apparent: that it is Gabriel, peace be upon him. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Rabi', al-Suddi and al-Dahhak.

They differed concerning the naming of Gabriel as the Holy Spirit, in three opinions:

The first: that he was called a spirit because he stands in the position of spirits to bodies, giving life by what he brings of the clear signs from God, the Mighty and Majestic.

The second: that he was called a spirit because the quality dominating his body is spirituality (al-ruhaniyyah), owing to its subtlety. The same applies to all the angels, but Gabriel is singled out for it as an honour.

The third: that he was called a spirit because God, the Exalted, brought into being for him a spirit from Himself without birth.

As for al-quds (holiness), there are three opinions concerning it: The first: it is God, the Exalted, and for this reason Jesus, peace be upon him, was called the Holy Spirit, because God the Exalted brought him into being without a father. This is the view of al-Hasan, al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd.

Ibn Zayd said: al-quds and al-quddus are one and the same.

The second: it is purity (al-tuhr), as if by it He indicated purification from sins.

The third: that al-quds is blessing (al-barakah), which is the view of al-Suddi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 88:

Regarding His saying, ﴿And they say, "Our hearts are covered."﴾ there are two interpretations (ta'wil). The first: it means they are in coverings and veils, so they do not understand. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Suddi.

The second: it means they are receptacles (awiyah) for knowledge. This is the view of ʿAtiyyah, and a report from al-Dahhak from Ibn ʿAbbas.

﴿Nay, Allah has cursed them for their disbelief.﴾ Al-laʿn means expulsion and distancing. From it is the verse of al-Shammakh:

"I startled the sandgrouse with it, and drove away from it the place of the wolf, like the accursed man."

The sense of the speech is: the standing place of the accursed wolf, like the man.

Regarding His saying, ﴿So little is it that they believe.﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: its meaning is "few of them are those who believe." This is the view of Qatadah, because those among the polytheists who believed were more numerous than those among the People of the Book who believed.

The second: its meaning is "they believe only in a little of what is in their hands." This is related from Qatadah.

Here, the word ﻣﺎ (ma) is a silah (a particle inserted for tawkid, emphasis), as Muhalhil said:

"Even if he came to Abanayn proposing to her, the nose of the one who dyes would have been stained with blood." (p-158)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 89:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when there came to them a Book from Allah﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿confirming what they already have﴾, there are two interpretations (p-159):

One: it confirms what is in the Torah and the Gospel of the reports contained in them.

The second: it confirms that the Torah and the Gospel are from Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿And previously they had been seeking victory over those who disbelieved﴾, meaning they were seeking victory (yastanṣirūn). Ibn 'Abbas said: The Jews used to seek victory over the Aws and the Khazraj through the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) before his mission. When Allah sent him from among the Arabs, they disbelieved in him. Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Bishr ibn al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur said to them: Did you not used to inform us that he would be sent? Salam ibn Mishkam said: He has not brought us anything we recognize, and he is not the one we used to mention to you. So Allah, Exalted, revealed that.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 90:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Wretched is that for which they have sold themselves﴾ — "ishtaraw" (they bought) here means "baa'u" (they sold).

﴿that they disbelieve in what Allah has sent down, out of insolence﴾ — meaning out of envy. This is what Qatadah, al-Suddi and Abu al-'Aliyah said, and they are the Jews.

Al-baghy (insolence) is the intense seeking of superiority over others, and its root meaning is seeking; for this reason a fornicating woman is called baghiyy (baghiyyah), because she seeks fornication.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so they incurred wrath upon wrath﴾, there are three opinions:
The first: the first wrath was for their disbelief in Jesus, and the second wrath was for their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ). This is the view of al-Hasan, Ikrimah, al-Sha'bi, Qatadah and Abu al-'Aliyah.

The second: it refers to their earlier disbelief in their saying, "'Uzayr is the son of Allah," and their saying, "The hand of Allah is chained," and their altering of the Book of Allah, and then their disbelief in Muhammad.

The third: since wrath was constantly upon them, this was an emphasis (tawkid).

﴿And for the disbelievers is a humiliating punishment﴾ — "al-muhin" means "al-mudhill" (the one who humiliates).

Punishment is of two kinds: the humiliating kind is the punishment of the disbelievers, because it does not expiate their sins.

The second is non-humiliating, which is that in which there is expiation (tamhis) of its recipient, such as the cutting off of the hand of a thief from among the Muslims, and the prescribed punishment (hadd) for an adulterer.

And when it is said to them, "Believe in what Allah has sent down," they say, "We believe in what was sent down to us" — meaning the Torah — "and they reject what comes after it" — meaning what is after it.

"And it is the truth" — meaning the Qur'an — "confirming what is with them" — meaning the Torah, because the Books of Allah the Exalted confirm one another.

"Say, 'Why then did you kill the prophets of Allah before?'" Its meaning is: "Why did you kill?" So He expressed the past action with the future form (al-mustaqbal). This is permissible in what has the status of a descriptive (ṣifah), as in His saying, "And they followed what the devils recited" (tatlū), meaning what they recited (talat). The poet said:

"Indeed I come to you with thanks for what has passed of the matter, and with approval of what would be in tomorrow."

He means what will be in tomorrow.

It was also said that its meaning is: "Why do you consent to the killing of the prophets of Allah, if you are believers?"

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Take what We have given you with strength﴾, meaning with earnestness and diligence.

﴿And listen﴾. There are two ta'wil (interpretations, meanings) of this:

The first: meaning, act upon what you have heard.

The second: meaning, accept what you have heard, as it is said, "God heard the one who praised Him" (sami'a Allahu liman hamidah), i.e., God accepted his praise. And the rajaz poet said:

"Hearing, obedience, and submission are better, and more beneficial for the Banu Tamim."

﴿They said, "We hear and we disobey"﴾. There are two ta'wil of this:

The first: they said that literally, and its meaning is: "We have heard your words, and we have disobeyed your command."

The second: they did not say it, but they did what indicated it, so the action on their part took the place of the saying, as the poet said:

"The pool was full and said, 'Enough!' Slowly, slowly, you have filled my belly."

﴿And they were made to drink the calf into their hearts because of their disbelief﴾. There are two ta'wil of this:

The first: Musa burned the calf, scattered it in water, and no one who loved the calf drank it without the residue of gold appearing on his lips. This is the view of al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj.

The second: they were made to drink the love of the calf into their hearts. It is said: "his heart was made to drink the love of such-and-such." Zuhayr said:

"I sobered from it after an inward love, and love is a disease that makes its way into your heart." (p-162)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 94–96:

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Say: If the Last Abode with Allah is specifically yours, to the exclusion of the people, then wish for death, if you are truthful.﴾ He means the Jews, who claim that Paradise is exclusively theirs to the exclusion of other people. Regarding this (the phrase "to the exclusion of the people") there are two views:

The first: to the exclusion of all people.

The second: to the exclusion of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his Companions who believed in him. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him).

It was said: ﴿then wish for death, if you are truthful﴾ because whoever believes that he is among the people of Paradise, death is more beloved to him than life, due to what he will attain of the blessings of Paradise and what will be removed from him of the harms of this world. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "If the Jews were to wish for death, they would die, and they would see their place in the Fire."

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿But they will never wish for it, because of what their hands have sent forward﴾, as a confirmation of their lying. Regarding their refraining from displaying a wish (for death) there are two views:

The first: they knew that if they wished for death, they would die, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said, and therefore they did not wish for it. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: Allah turned them away from displaying the wish, so that this would be a sign for His Prophet (ﷺ).

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And you will surely find them the most covetous of people for life﴾, meaning the Jews.

﴿And of those who associate partners (with Allah)﴾, meaning the Magians (Majus), because the Magians are the ones of whom one of them loves that he be granted a life of a thousand years. Their love of life reached the point that they made their greeting "Live a thousand years" (ʿish alf sana), out of covetousness for life. So these, who say "the Paradise is exclusively theirs," are more covetous of life than all people, and more than these (the Jews).

﴿And he is not one to remove him from the punishment﴾, i.e., one who would keep him far from the punishment ﴿by being granted long life﴾, because if he were granted long life he would not wish for death, since the length of life would not have repelled from him the punishment of Allah for his sins.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 2, verses 97–98:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel, indeed it is he who brought it down upon your heart by the permission of Allah﴾. The occasion of revelation of this verse is that Ibn Suriya and a group of the Jews of Fadak, when the Prophet (ﷺ) came to Madinah, asked him, saying: "O Muhammad, how is your sleep? For we have been told about the sleep of the Prophet who will come at the end of time." He said: "My eyes sleep, but my heart is awake." They said: "You have spoken truly, O Muhammad. Then tell us about the child: is it from the man or from the woman?" He said: "As for the bones, the sinews and the veins, they are from the man; and as for the flesh, the blood, the nail and the hair, they are from the woman." They said: "You have spoken truly, O Muhammad. Then what is the matter with the child that resembles its paternal uncles, having none of the resemblance of its maternal uncles, or resembles its maternal uncles, having none of the resemblance of its paternal uncles?" He said: "Whichever of the two fluids prevails, the resemblance is to it." They said: "You have spoken truly, O Muhammad. Then tell us about your Lord: what is He?" So Allah revealed (p-163)

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ [Al-Ikhlas, verse 1] to the end of the surah. Ibn Suriya said to him: "There is one characteristic: if you say it, I will believe in you and follow you. Which angel comes to you with what Allah says?" He said: "Gabriel." He said: "That is our enemy. He descends with fighting, hardship and war, while Mika'il descends with glad tidings and ease. If it were Mika'il who came to you, we would have believed in you." Then Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, said at that point: "I bear witness that whoever is an enemy to Gabriel, indeed he is an enemy to Mika'il." Then Allah, may He be exalted, revealed this verse.

As for Jibril and Mika'il, they are two names: one of them is ʿAbd Allah (the servant of Allah) and the other is ʿUbayd Allah (the slave of Allah), because "Iyl" is Allah, and "Jabr" is servant, and "Mika" is slave. So Jibril is ʿAbd Allah and Mika'il is ʿUbayd Allah. This is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas, and none of the mufassirin (commentators of the Qur'an) opposes it.

If it is said: Why did He say: ﴿Whoever is an enemy to Allah and His angels and His messengers and Gabriel and Mikal, then indeed Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾, when Gabriel and Mika'il are already included in the generality of the angels, why were they singled out for mention? The answer to this has two parts. The first: they were singled out for mention to honour them and distinguish them.

The second: when the Jews said, "Gabriel is our enemy, and Mika'il is our ally," they were singled out for mention because the Jews claimed that they are not enemies of Allah and His angels, since Gabriel and Mika'il are specified from among the angels. So they were named explicitly to refute what they interpreted as a particularization. Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿then indeed Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers﴾, and He did not say "to them," because it is possible that they may turn away from enmity through faith. (p-164)

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 2, verses 99–103:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And they followed what the devils recited over the kingdom of Solomon﴾. The people of tafsir (Qur'anic exegesis) differed about the cause of this, on two views.

The first: the devils used to eavesdrop on the heavens and extract sorcery (*sihr*, magic). God informed Solomon son of David of this, so he extracted it from their hands and buried it beneath his throne. The jinn could not get near the throne. After Solomon's death, mankind said: "The knowledge with which Solomon subjected the devils and the winds is beneath his throne." So they dug it up and said: "He was a sorcerer and was not a prophet." They learned it and taught it. God then revealed the innocence of Solomon through this verse.

The second: Asaf ibn Barkhiya, who was the scribe of Solomon, colluded with a group of devils over a book they had written as sorcery and buried beneath the throne of Solomon. They then extracted it after his death and said: "This is the sorcery of Solomon." God cleared him of their saying, so He said: ﴿Solomon did not disbelieve﴾. They did not attribute disbelief (*kufr*) to him, but they attributed sorcery to him. Yet since sorcery is disbelief, they became like one who attributed disbelief to him.

He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿But the devils disbelieved﴾. Concerning this there are two views:
The first: they disbelieved by what they attributed to Solomon of sorcery.
The second: they disbelieved by what they extracted of sorcery.

﴿They taught people sorcery﴾. Concerning this there are two views:
The first: they cast it into their hearts, so they learned it.
The second: they guided them to extracting it from beneath the throne, so they learned it.

﴿And what was sent down upon the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut﴾. Concerning *ma* (what) here there are two views:
The first: it means *alladhi* (that which), and its implied sense is: "That which was sent down upon the two angels."
The second: it is negative in meaning, and its implied sense is: "Nothing was sent down upon the two angels."

Concerning "the two angels" there are two readings (*qira'at*, recited variants):
One: with a kasra on the lam, meaning they were two of the kings of Babylon and its non-Arab (*'ulujuha*) rulers, Harut and Marut. This is the view of Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali.
The second reading: with a fatha on the lam, meaning from the angels.

Concerning this there are two views:
The first: the sorcerers of the Jews claimed that God sent down sorcery through the tongue of Gabriel and Michael to Solomon son of David. God refuted them in this. In the speech there is a transposition, and its implied sense is: "Solomon did not disbelieve, and nothing was sent down upon the two angels, but the devils disbelieved, teaching people sorcery at Babylon, Harut and Marut, who were two men at Babylon."

The second: Harut and Marut were two angels whom God, may He be exalted and glorified, sent down to the earth. The cause of this was that when God informed the angels of the disobediences of the children of Adam, they wondered at their disobedience despite His abundant blessings upon them. God, may He be exalted, said to them: "Indeed, if you were in their place you would do the same as their deeds." They said: "Glory be to You, it is not fitting for us." So God commanded them to choose two angels to descend to the earth. They chose Harut and Marut, and they were sent down to the earth. He made lawful for them everything, on condition that they should not associate anything with God, nor steal, nor commit adultery, nor drink wine, nor kill a soul which God has forbidden except by right. A woman appeared to them, and they were judging between people. She was disputing with her husband, and her name in Arabic was al-Zuhra, and in Persian was Fandarikht. She captivated them, and they sought her, but she refused them unless they worshipped an idol and drank wine. So they drank wine, worshipped the idol, had intercourse with her, and killed a passerby who had passed by them, fearing that he would make their affair known. She taught them the word which, when a speaker spoke it, he would ascend to the heaven. So she spoke it and ascended. Then she forgot what she had spoken, by which, had she spoken it again, she would have descended, so she was transformed into a star. Ka'b said: "By God, they had not finished their evening of that day on which they descended, until they had completed all that they had been forbidden from, so the angels marvelled at that."

Then Harut and Marut were not able to ascend to the heaven, so they used to teach sorcery.

It is related from al-Rabi' that their descent was in the time of Idris.

As for sorcery (*sihr*), people have differed about its meaning. A group said: the sorcerer is able to transform the essences (*a'yan*) by his sorcery, so he turns a man into a donkey, and creates essences and bodies.

Others said: sorcery is deception and appearances which the sorcerer produces, so it is imagined to him that something is other than what it is, like one who sees a mirage from afar and imagines it to be water, or the sailors of a swiftly moving ship who imagine that the trees and mountains they see are moving along with them.

Hisham ibn Urwa related from his father, from Aisha, may God be pleased with her, who said: "A Jew from the Jews of Banu Zuraiq, called Labid ibn al-A'sam, bewitched the Messenger of God (ﷺ), until the Messenger of God (ﷺ) imagined that he was doing a thing when he had not done it."

They said: if it were within the power of the sorcerer to create bodies and change essences from what they are in their forms, there would be no distinction between falsehood and truth, and it would be permissible for all bodies to be among what the sorcerers had bewitched, so their essences would be changed. God, may He be exalted, has described the sorcerers of Pharaoh: ﴿Then their ropes and their staffs were imagined to him, by their sorcery, to be moving﴾.

Others said, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i: the sorcerer may whisper by his sorcery and thus cause sickness, and perhaps kill, because imagining is the beginning of whispering, whispering is the beginning of sickness, and sickness is the beginning of perishing.

As for the land at Babylon, there are three sayings (*aqawil*) about it:
One: it is Kufa and its surroundings, and it was so named because tongues were confused (*tabalbalat*) there. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud.
The second: it is from Nusaybin to Ras al-'Ayn. This is the view of Qatada.
The third: it is the mountain of Nahawand.

And it is a [fatr] of the earth.

﴿And they do not teach anyone until they say: "We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve"﴾ by what you learn of our sorcery.

﴿So they learn from the two what they use to cause separation between a man and his wife﴾. Concerning the intended meaning of "from them" (*minhuma*) there are three aspects:
One: it means from Harut and Marut.
The second: from sorcery and disbelief.
The third: from the devils and the two angels, so they learn sorcery from the devils, and from the two angels what they use to cause separation between a man and his wife.

﴿And they cannot harm anyone with it﴾, meaning the sorcery.

﴿except by God's permission﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:
One: it means by God's command.
The second: by God's knowledge.

﴿And they learn what harms them and does not benefit them﴾, meaning what harms them in the Hereafter and does not benefit them in this world.

﴿And they certainly knew that whoever purchases it﴾, meaning the sorcery by which they cause separation between a man and his wife,

﴿has no share (*khalaq*) in the Hereafter﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations:
One: *khalaq* means portion, and this is the view of Mujahid and al-Suddi.
The second: *khalaq* means direction, and this is the view of Qatada.
The third: *khalaq* means religion, and this is the view of al-Hasan.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And wretched is what they sold themselves for, if only they knew﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:
One: meaning, wretched is what they sold their souls for, of sorcery and disbelief, in teaching it and practising it.
The second: from their attribution of sorcery to Solomon and their inciting to falsehood.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, do not say, "Raina" (Ra'ina)﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: its meaning is "Do not say [it]."

.. This is the view of ʿAṭāʾ.

The second: it means "Arinā samʿaka" (give us your attention), i.e., listen to us and we will listen to you. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid.

They differed as to why the Muslims were forbidden from this, according to three opinions. The first: it was a word that the Jews used to say to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in a manner of mockery and abuse, as they said: ﴿We have heard and disobeyed, and [say], "Hear, may you not hear," and "Raʿina," distorting with their tongues﴾. So the Muslims were forbidden from saying it. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās and Qatādah.

The second: the one who said it was a particular man from among the Jews, called Rifāʿah ibn Zayd, and so the Muslims were forbidden from it. This is the view of al-Suddī.

The third: it was a word that the Anṣār used to say in the Jahiliyyah, and Allah forbade them from it in Islam. (p. 171)

As for His saying ﴿and say, "Unẓurnā" (Look upon us)﴾, there are three interpretations. The first: its meaning is "Make us understand and clarify to us." This is the view of Mujāhid.

The second: its meaning is "Grant us respite (amhilnā)."

The third: its meaning is "Turn toward us and look at us."

﴿And listen﴾: meaning, to what you are commanded.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 106–107:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whatever a verse We abrogate⁠—﴾. Regarding the meaning of its "abrogation" (naskh, lit. cancellation or replacement) there are three interpretations. The first: it is its removal (qabd), which is the view of al-Suddi.

The second: it is its replacement (tabdil), which is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The third: it is the retention of its written form while its ruling is changed, which is the view of Ibn Mas'ud.

﴿Or cause you to forget it⁠﴾ (aw nunsiha). Concerning this there are two readings. One of them is this (nunsiha), and the second is (aw nansa'ha). As for the one who reads (aw nansaha), there are four interpretations of it:

The first: that it means "or We withhold it" (aw numsikuha). It has been mentioned that in the codex of Abdullah ibn Mas'ud it was: "Whatever verse We withhold, or abrogate it, We bring a better than it or the like of it." And that is because the Prophet ﷺ used to recite a verse and then forget it, and it was lifted up. Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (p-172) used to read: "Whatever verse We abrogate or cause you to forget," in the sense of address to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, so its implied meaning is: "or you, O Muhammad, forget." Al-Qasim ibn Rabi'ah said to Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas: "Verily Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib reads: ﴿or cause it to be forgotten⁠﴾," so Sa'd said: "The Qur'an was not revealed to Ibn al-Musayyib, nor to the family of al-Musayyib. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿We shall make you recite, so you will not forget⁠﴾ [al-A'la: 6] and ﴿Remember your Lord when you forget⁠﴾ [al-Kahf: 24]." This is the meaning of the view of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: that this means abandonment, from the saying of the Exalted: ﴿They forgot Allah, so He forgot them⁠﴾, i.e., they abandoned Him, so He abandoned them. Thus the sense of the statement becomes: ﴿Whatever a verse We abrogate⁠﴾, meaning We lift it and replace it, ﴿or cause you to forget it⁠﴾, i.e., We leave it and do not replace it or abrogate it. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and al-Suddi.

The third: that His saying ﴿Whatever a verse We abrogate or cause you to forget⁠﴾ refers to the abrogating and the abrogated. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

The fourth: that the meaning of "nunsiha" is "We erase it." This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

As for the one who reads (aw nansa'uha), its meaning is "We postpone it," from the expression "nasa'tu hadha al-amr" when you delay it, and from this is their saying "bi'tu bi-nasa'" meaning "by deferment." This is the view of Ata' and Ibn Abi Najih.

﴿We bring a better than it or the like of it⁠﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. One: i.e., better for you in benefit and more lenient toward you; this is the view of Ibn Abbas. The second: that the meaning of "better" (khayr) than it is lighter than it, by way of concession in it; this is the sense of the view of Qatadah.

Thus the interpretation of the verse is: whatever ruling of a verse We alter, so We replace it, or We leave it so We do not replace it, We bring you, O believers, a ruling better than it, either by lightening in the immediate, like what occurred in the abrogation of the night prayer (qiyam al-layl) as a relief, or by benefit through abundance of reward in the hereafter, like what occurred in the abrogation of fasting certain numbered days by the month of Ramadan.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿or the like of it⁠﴾, meaning the like of its ruling in lightness and heaviness, reward and recompense, like what occurred in the abrogation of facing Bayt al-Maqdis by facing the Ka'bah, and that (p-173) is similar to it in hardship and reward. ﴿Do you not know that Allah is over all things capable?⁠﴾ ﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth?⁠﴾

If it is said: Was the Prophet ﷺ unaware that Allah is over all things capable, and that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth? It is said: concerning this there are three answers. The first: that His saying "Do you not know" (alam ta'lam) means "Have you been informed" (a-'alimta).

The second: that it is in the form of affirmation (taqrir), not in the form of a question (istifham). As Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when Allah says, "O Jesus son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah'?"⁠﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 116]; it is in the form of affirmation, not in the form of a question.

The third: that this address is to the Prophet ﷺ, but what is intended is his community (ummah). Do you not see that after this He said: ﴿And you have no protector or helper besides Allah⁠﴾?

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 108–110:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Many of the People of the Book wish they could turn you back to disbelief after your belief﴾. The occasion of its revelation: it is narrated that a group of Jews, among them Finhas and Zayd ibn Qays, invited Hudhayfah and Ammar to their religion and said: "We are more rightly guided in the way than you are."

(p-174)

Ammar said to them: "And how would the breaking of the covenant be regarded by you?" They said: "Severely." Ammar said: "Indeed, I have pledged to my Lord that I will never disbelieve in Muhammad (ﷺ), nor follow any religion other than his." The Jews said: "As for Ammar, he has apostatized and strayed from the right path. And what about you, O Hudhayfah?" Hudhayfah said: "Allah is my Lord, Muhammad (ﷺ) is my Prophet, the Qur'an is my guide. I obey my Lord, I follow the example of my Messenger, and I act by the Book of my Lord."

They said: "By the God of Moses, your hearts have been saturated with love of Muhammad (ﷺ)." So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed this verse.

﴿After the truth has become clear to them﴾: that is, after it has become clear to the Jews that Muhammad (ﷺ) is a truthful Prophet and that Islam is the true religion.

﴿So pardon and overlook﴾: by his saying "pardon," he means: leave the Jews alone, and overlook what they say. ﴿Until Allah brings His command﴾: that is, what He has permitted regarding the Banu Qurayzah, of killing and captivity, and regarding the Banu al-Nadir, of expulsion and exile.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 111–113:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who prevents the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned in them?﴾ As for "mosques" (masajid), they are places of worship (ʿibadat). Regarding what is meant by them here, there are two opinions. The first: what is attributed to worship among the houses of Allah the Exalted, using the word in its literal sense. (p-175)

The second: that every place on earth where worship is established, whether among the houses of Allah or others, is a mosque, based on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "The earth has been made for me a mosque."

Regarding "those who prevent the mosques of Allah from having His name mentioned in them," there are four opinions. The first: they are Bukhtnasr (Nebuchadnezzar) and his companions from the Magians, who destroyed Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). This is the view of Qatada.

The second: they are the Christians who helped Bukhtnasr in its destruction. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The third: they are the polytheists of Quraysh, who prevented the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the Sacred Mosque in the year of al-Hudaybiyya. This is the view of Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

The fourth: it is general, applying to every polytheist who prevents access to any mosque.

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and strives for their ruin﴾, there are two interpretations. The first: by preventing the mention of Allah in them. The second: by demolishing them.

﴿Those would not have entered them except in fear.﴾ In this there are two interpretations. The first: fearful of paying the jizya (poll tax); this is the view of al-Suddi. The second: fearful of terror, so that if they were to gain power over them they would be punished; this is the view of Qatada.

**Qur'an 2:114: "For them in this world is disgrace."** There are two interpretations of this:

First: it refers to the killing of the combatant (al-harbi) and the poll-tax (jizya) of the protected non-Muslim (al-dhimmi).

Second: it refers to the conquest of their cities: ʿAmūriyya, Qusṭanṭiniyya (Constantinople), and Rūmiyya. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbās.

**"And for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment."** It is the most severe of all punishments, because they are more wrongdoing than every wrongdoer.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 115:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west; so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾. The interpreters (ahl al-ta'wil) differed regarding its interpretation and its occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), into seven opinions:

The first: its occasion was that "the Prophet ﷺ, after his migration, prayed facing Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) for sixteen months, or seventeen months, until the Jews said: 'Muhammad and his companions did not know where their qibla was until we guided them.' So Allah the Exalted commanded them to face the Ka'bah, and the Jews spoke out, so Allah the Exalted revealed this verse." This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: this verse was revealed before the facing of the qibla was made obligatory, and it permitted them to direct their prayers wherever they wished from the regions of the east and the west. This is the view of Qatadah and Ibn Zayd.

The third: it was revealed concerning voluntary prayer (salat al-tatawwu') for the traveller, wherever he is facing, and for the one in fear, wherever he is able, whether east or west. This is the view of Ibn 'Umar. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from him that he said: When this verse was revealed, ﴿so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾, [it meant] that you pray wherever your mount turns you during travel, as a voluntary prayer: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ, when he returned from Makkah, would pray on his mount in voluntary prayer, gesturing with his head towards Madinah."

The fourth: it was revealed concerning those for whom the qibla was obscure, who did not know its direction, so they prayed towards different directions. (p-177)

'Asim ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amir ibn Rabi'ah, from his father, who said: "We were with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on a dark night, and we halted at a station, and a man began taking stones and building a mosque in which to pray. When we woke in the morning, we found that we had prayed towards other than the qibla. So we said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we prayed all this night towards other than the qibla.' So Allah the Exalted revealed this verse."

The fifth: it was revealed concerning the Negus (al-Najashi). Abu Qatadah narrated that "the Prophet ﷺ said: (Your brother al-Najashi has died, so pray over him.) They said: 'Shall we pray over a man who is not a Muslim?' He said: Then this was revealed: ﴿And among the People of the Book are those who believe in Allah and in what has been revealed to you and what has been revealed to them, humbly submitting to Allah﴾ [Surat Al 'Imran: 199] (p-178). They said: 'He did not pray towards the qibla,' so Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿To Allah belong the east and the west; so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾."

The sixth: its occasion of revelation was that "when Allah the Exalted revealed His saying: ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾, they said: 'To where?' So this was revealed: ﴿so wherever you turn, there is the Face of Allah﴾" [al-Baqarah: 115].

The seventh: its meaning is that wherever you are, from east or west, there is a qibla for you that you face, meaning a direction towards the Ka'bah. This is the view of Mujahid.

From this difference regarding His saying ﴿there is the Face of Allah﴾ arise two interpretations:

One: its meaning is "there is the qibla of Allah."

The second: "there is Allah the Exalted," and "the Face" is an expression for Him, as He said: ﴿And there remains the Face of your Lord﴾ [al-Rahman: 27].

As for "thumma" (ثَمَّ), it is a word used to indicate a place: if it is near, one says "hunaa Zayd" (here is Zayd), and if it is far, one says "hunaka Zayd" (there is Zayd).

**His saying, ﴿And they say, "God has taken a son."﴾** There are two opinions regarding this:

**The first:** They are the Christians in their saying, "The Messiah is the son of God."

**The second:** They are the polytheist Arabs in their saying, "The angels are the daughters of God."

**﴿Glory be to Him! Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 118:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who do not know say, "Why does Allah not speak to us or a sign come to us?"﴾ Regarding them there are three opinions. The first: they are the Christians; this is the view of Mujahid.

The second: they are the Jews; this is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The third: they are the polytheists of the Arabs; this is the view of Qatadah and al-Suddi.

His saying, ﴿Why does Allah not speak to us?﴾ means: "Would that Allah spoke to us" (halla, a particle of urging or reproach). It is like the saying of al-Ashhab ibn Ramliyya:

"You count the slaughter of the she-camels the best of your glory, O Banu Dawtara, rather than [the] hidden [warrior] who is covered [in armor]."

Here "law la" is in the sense of "hal la" (why not), i.e., "Why do you not count the hidden [warrior] who is covered [in armor]?"

﴿Likewise said those before them, the like of their saying﴾. Regarding them there are two opinions. The first: they are the Jews; this is the view of Mujahid.

The second: they are the Jews and the Christians; this is the view of Qatadah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Their hearts are alike﴾ means in disbelief. There are two interpretations concerning it. The first: the hearts of the Jews resemble the hearts of the Christians; this is the view of Mujahid.

The second: the hearts of the polytheists of the Arabs resemble the hearts of the Jews and the Christians; this is the view of Qatadah.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 119:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾. He means Muhammad, whom He sent with the religion of truth.

﴿A bringer of good tidings and a warner﴾: that is, a bringer of good tidings of Paradise to whoever obeys, and a warner of the Fire to whoever disobeys.

﴿And you will not be questioned about the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾: that is, you will not be held accountable for the disbelief of those who disbelieve after the good tidings and the warning. Some of the people of Medina recited it: ﴿wa la tasal﴾ (and do not ask), with a fathah on the ta' and a jazm on the lam. It is mentioned that the occasion of its revelation is what Musa ibn Ubayd narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "I wish I knew what my two parents did," and then Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿Indeed, We have sent you with the truth as a bringer of good tidings and a warner, and you will not be questioned about the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 120–121:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book recite it as it should be recited﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

One of them: they are the believers in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and "the Book" is the Qur'an. This is the view of Qatadah.

The second: they are the scholars of the Jews, and "the Book" is the Torah. This is the view of Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

﴿recite it as it should be recited﴾ has two interpretations. One of them: they read it as it should be read.

The second: they follow it as it should be followed, so they make lawful what it makes lawful and forbid what it forbids. This is the view of the majority (al-Jumhur).

﴿It is they who believe in it﴾, meaning in Muhammad (ﷺ), because whoever reads either of the two Books believes in him, due to what both contain of the obligation to follow him.

[p. 183]

Allah's words: ﴿And when Abraham was tested by his Lord with certain words, and he fulfilled them﴾. There is an omitted element in this verse, and its implied meaning is: "Remember when..." *ibtala* means *ikhtabara*, he tested. *Ibrahim* in Syriac means "compassionate father." Regarding the words with which Allah the Mighty and Majestic tested him, there are eight opinions.

The first: they are the laws of Islam. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Allah did not test anyone with them and have him fulfil all of them except Ibrahim. He was tested with Islam and completed it, so Allah wrote freedom from disbelief for him, and said: ﴿And Abraham who fulfilled [his covenant]﴾ [al-Najm 53:37]." He said: "They are thirty portions: ten of them are in Surah Bara'ah (al-Tawbah): ﴿The repentant, the worshippers, the praisers, the travellers, the bowers, the prostrators﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:112]."

[p. 184] ... And ten are in al-Ahzab: ﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women, the devoutly obedient men and devoutly obedient women, the truthful men and truthful women, the patient men and patient women, the humble men and humble women, the charitable men and charitable women, the fasting men and fasting women, the men who guard their private parts and the women who guard them, and the men who remember Allah much and the women who remember Allah—Allah has prepared for them forgiveness and a great reward﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:35]. And ten are in Surah al-Mu'minun: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded. They who are during their prayer humbly submissive. And they who turn away from ill speech. And they who are payers of zakah. And they who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands possess, for indeed, they are not to be blamed. But whoever seeks beyond that, then it is those who are the transgressors. And they who are to their trusts and their promises attentive. And they who strictly maintain their prayers. Those are the inheritors who will inherit al-Firdaws; they will abide therein eternally﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:1–11]. And in Surah Sa'ala sa'il, from: ﴿Except the observers of prayer, who are constant in their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'arij 70:22–23], to: ﴿And they who strictly maintain their prayers﴾ [al-Ma'arij 70:34].

The second opinion: they are characteristics from the sunan of Islam, five on the head and five on the body. Ibn 'Abbas related the five on the head: trimming the moustache, rinsing the mouth, inhaling water into the nose, using the miswak, and parting the hair.

And on the body: trimming the nails, shaving the pubic hair, circumcision, plucking the armpit hair, and washing away traces of urine and feces with water.

This is the opinion of Qatadah.

The third opinion: they are ten characteristics, six pertaining to a person and four pertaining to the rites (mashair). Those pertaining to a person are: shaving the pubic hair, circumcision, plucking the armpit hair, trimming the nails, trimming the moustache, and the ghusl on Friday.

Those pertaining to the rites are: the tawaf, the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah, the stoning of the pillars (ramy al-jimar), and the ifadah.

al-Hasan related this from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth opinion: Allah the Exalted said to Ibrahim: "I am going to test you, O Ibrahim." He said: "Will You make me an imam for the people?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And from my offspring?" He said: "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers." He said: "Will You make the House a place of return for the people?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And a place of security?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And will You make us submitting to You and from our descendants a community submitting to You?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And show us our rites and accept our repentance?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And will You make this city secure?" He said: "Yes."

[p. 185] He said: "And will You provide its people with fruits, those who believe?" He said: "Yes." These are the words with which Allah tested Ibrahim. This is the opinion of Mujahid.

The fifth: they are specifically the rites of the Hajj. This is the opinion of Qatadah.

The sixth opinion: they are the six traits: the stars, the moon, the sun, the fire, the migration (hijrah), and circumcision, with which he was tested and he was patient with them. This is the opinion of al-Hasan.

The seventh opinion: what Sahl ibn Mu'adh ibn Anas related from his mother, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: 'Shall I not inform you why Allah named Ibrahim His khalil, the one who fulfilled? Because he used to say whenever he woke in the morning and whenever he retired in the evening: Glory be to Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning, and to Him is praise in the heavens and the earth, and at night and when you are at noon.'"

The eighth opinion: what al-Qasim ibn Muhammad related from Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "﴿And Abraham who fulfilled﴾ — he said: 'Do you know what he fulfilled?' They said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'He fulfilled the work of a day with four rak'ahs during the day.'"

﴿He said: "Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people"﴾: that is, one who is sought after and followed. From this comes the term imam of the worshippers, who is the one followed in the prayer.

﴿He said: "And from my descendants?"﴾ This admits of two interpretations. The first: he hoped for the imamate for his descendants, so he asked Allah the Exalted for this on their behalf.

The second: he said this as an inquiry about their condition, whether they would be people of obedience so that they would become imams. So Allah the Exalted informed him that among them there would be a disobedient one and a wrongdoer who does not deserve the imamate, so He said: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾.

Regarding this covenant there are seven interpretations. The first: it is prophethood. This is the opinion of al-Suddi.

The second: it is the imamate. This is the opinion of Mujahid.

The third: it is faith. This is the opinion of Qatadah.

The fourth: it is mercy. This is the opinion of 'Ata'.

The fifth: it is the religion of Allah. This is the opinion of al-Dahhak.

The sixth: it is the reward and recompense.

The seventh: there is no covenant for you over a wrongdoer that you should obey him in his wrongdoing. This is the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿And when We made the House a place of return for the people and a place of security, and [said], "Take from the station of Abraham a place of prayer."﴾ [p. 186]

Allah's words: ﴿And when We made the House a place of return for the people﴾. There are two opinions regarding this. The first: a gathering place for people to assemble at it for the Hajj and the 'Umrah.

The second: a place of return, from the saying of them: "The cause has returned (thabat) when it came back (raja'at)."

The poet said:

A place of return for the tribes of every kind, to which the swift she-camels and the fast mounts long to go.

Regarding their returning to it, there are two aspects. The first: they return to it time after time.

The second: in each of the two rites, the Hajj and the 'Umrah, they return to it from the non-sacred state (hill) to the sacred precinct (haram), because joining between the non-sacred and the sacred in each of the two rites is a required condition.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And a place of security﴾. There are two opinions regarding this. The first: because of its security during the Jahiliyyah from the raids of the Arabs, based on His saying: ﴿and He gave them security from fear﴾ [Quraysh 106:4]. The second: because of the security it gives to wrongdoers from the establishment of prescribed punishments upon them, until they leave it.

﴿And take from the station of Abraham a place of prayer﴾. Hammad related from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: 'I said: O Messenger of Allah, if only you would take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer.' So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And take from the station of Abraham a place of prayer﴾." [He read it with a kasrah on the kha'] from the phrase "wa-ttakhidhu," in the form of a command. Some people of Madinah read "wa-ttakhadhu" with a fathah on the kha', in the form of a report.

[p. 187] The exegetes differed about this station, which they were commanded to take as a place of prayer, into four opinions. The first: it is the entire Hajj. This is the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is 'Arafat, Muzdalifah, and the pillars (jimar). This is the opinion of 'Ata' and al-Sha'bi.

The third: it is the entire sacred precinct. This is the opinion of Mujahid.

The fourth: it is the stone in the Mosque, which is his well-known station, and this is the most correct.

Regarding His saying: ﴿a place of prayer﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: a place of supplication in which one supplicates. This is the opinion of Mujahid.

The second: a place of prayer where one prays nearby. This is the opinion of Qatadah, and it is the more apparent of the two interpretations.
