﴿And when We made the House a place of return for the people and a place of security, and [said], "Take from the station of Abraham a place of prayer."﴾ [p. 186]

Allah's words: ﴿And when We made the House a place of return for the people﴾. There are two opinions regarding this. The first: a gathering place for people to assemble at it for the Hajj and the 'Umrah.

The second: a place of return, from the saying of them: "The cause has returned (thabat) when it came back (raja'at)."

The poet said:

A place of return for the tribes of every kind, to which the swift she-camels and the fast mounts long to go.

Regarding their returning to it, there are two aspects. The first: they return to it time after time.

The second: in each of the two rites, the Hajj and the 'Umrah, they return to it from the non-sacred state (hill) to the sacred precinct (haram), because joining between the non-sacred and the sacred in each of the two rites is a required condition.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And a place of security﴾. There are two opinions regarding this. The first: because of its security during the Jahiliyyah from the raids of the Arabs, based on His saying: ﴿and He gave them security from fear﴾ [Quraysh 106:4]. The second: because of the security it gives to wrongdoers from the establishment of prescribed punishments upon them, until they leave it.

﴿And take from the station of Abraham a place of prayer﴾. Hammad related from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: 'I said: O Messenger of Allah, if only you would take the station of Abraham as a place of prayer.' So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And take from the station of Abraham a place of prayer﴾." [He read it with a kasrah on the kha'] from the phrase "wa-ttakhidhu," in the form of a command. Some people of Madinah read "wa-ttakhadhu" with a fathah on the kha', in the form of a report.

[p. 187] The exegetes differed about this station, which they were commanded to take as a place of prayer, into four opinions. The first: it is the entire Hajj. This is the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is 'Arafat, Muzdalifah, and the pillars (jimar). This is the opinion of 'Ata' and al-Sha'bi.

The third: it is the entire sacred precinct. This is the opinion of Mujahid.

The fourth: it is the stone in the Mosque, which is his well-known station, and this is the most correct.

Regarding His saying: ﴿a place of prayer﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: a place of supplication in which one supplicates. This is the opinion of Mujahid.

The second: a place of prayer where one prays nearby. This is the opinion of Qatadah, and it is the more apparent of the two interpretations.

[p. 183]

Allah's words: ﴿And when Abraham was tested by his Lord with certain words, and he fulfilled them﴾. There is an omitted element in this verse, and its implied meaning is: "Remember when..." *ibtala* means *ikhtabara*, he tested. *Ibrahim* in Syriac means "compassionate father." Regarding the words with which Allah the Mighty and Majestic tested him, there are eight opinions.

The first: they are the laws of Islam. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Allah did not test anyone with them and have him fulfil all of them except Ibrahim. He was tested with Islam and completed it, so Allah wrote freedom from disbelief for him, and said: ﴿And Abraham who fulfilled [his covenant]﴾ [al-Najm 53:37]." He said: "They are thirty portions: ten of them are in Surah Bara'ah (al-Tawbah): ﴿The repentant, the worshippers, the praisers, the travellers, the bowers, the prostrators﴾ [al-Tawbah 9:112]."

[p. 184] ... And ten are in al-Ahzab: ﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and Muslim women, the believing men and believing women, the devoutly obedient men and devoutly obedient women, the truthful men and truthful women, the patient men and patient women, the humble men and humble women, the charitable men and charitable women, the fasting men and fasting women, the men who guard their private parts and the women who guard them, and the men who remember Allah much and the women who remember Allah—Allah has prepared for them forgiveness and a great reward﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:35]. And ten are in Surah al-Mu'minun: ﴿Certainly the believers have succeeded. They who are during their prayer humbly submissive. And they who turn away from ill speech. And they who are payers of zakah. And they who guard their private parts, except from their wives or what their right hands possess, for indeed, they are not to be blamed. But whoever seeks beyond that, then it is those who are the transgressors. And they who are to their trusts and their promises attentive. And they who strictly maintain their prayers. Those are the inheritors who will inherit al-Firdaws; they will abide therein eternally﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:1–11]. And in Surah Sa'ala sa'il, from: ﴿Except the observers of prayer, who are constant in their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'arij 70:22–23], to: ﴿And they who strictly maintain their prayers﴾ [al-Ma'arij 70:34].

The second opinion: they are characteristics from the sunan of Islam, five on the head and five on the body. Ibn 'Abbas related the five on the head: trimming the moustache, rinsing the mouth, inhaling water into the nose, using the miswak, and parting the hair.

And on the body: trimming the nails, shaving the pubic hair, circumcision, plucking the armpit hair, and washing away traces of urine and feces with water.

This is the opinion of Qatadah.

The third opinion: they are ten characteristics, six pertaining to a person and four pertaining to the rites (mashair). Those pertaining to a person are: shaving the pubic hair, circumcision, plucking the armpit hair, trimming the nails, trimming the moustache, and the ghusl on Friday.

Those pertaining to the rites are: the tawaf, the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwah, the stoning of the pillars (ramy al-jimar), and the ifadah.

al-Hasan related this from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth opinion: Allah the Exalted said to Ibrahim: "I am going to test you, O Ibrahim." He said: "Will You make me an imam for the people?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And from my offspring?" He said: "My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers." He said: "Will You make the House a place of return for the people?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And a place of security?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And will You make us submitting to You and from our descendants a community submitting to You?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And show us our rites and accept our repentance?" He said: "Yes." He said: "And will You make this city secure?" He said: "Yes."

[p. 185] He said: "And will You provide its people with fruits, those who believe?" He said: "Yes." These are the words with which Allah tested Ibrahim. This is the opinion of Mujahid.

The fifth: they are specifically the rites of the Hajj. This is the opinion of Qatadah.

The sixth opinion: they are the six traits: the stars, the moon, the sun, the fire, the migration (hijrah), and circumcision, with which he was tested and he was patient with them. This is the opinion of al-Hasan.

The seventh opinion: what Sahl ibn Mu'adh ibn Anas related from his mother, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: 'Shall I not inform you why Allah named Ibrahim His khalil, the one who fulfilled? Because he used to say whenever he woke in the morning and whenever he retired in the evening: Glory be to Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning, and to Him is praise in the heavens and the earth, and at night and when you are at noon.'"

The eighth opinion: what al-Qasim ibn Muhammad related from Abu Umamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "﴿And Abraham who fulfilled﴾ — he said: 'Do you know what he fulfilled?' They said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'He fulfilled the work of a day with four rak'ahs during the day.'"

﴿He said: "Indeed, I will make you an imam for the people"﴾: that is, one who is sought after and followed. From this comes the term imam of the worshippers, who is the one followed in the prayer.

﴿He said: "And from my descendants?"﴾ This admits of two interpretations. The first: he hoped for the imamate for his descendants, so he asked Allah the Exalted for this on their behalf.

The second: he said this as an inquiry about their condition, whether they would be people of obedience so that they would become imams. So Allah the Exalted informed him that among them there would be a disobedient one and a wrongdoer who does not deserve the imamate, so He said: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾.

Regarding this covenant there are seven interpretations. The first: it is prophethood. This is the opinion of al-Suddi.

The second: it is the imamate. This is the opinion of Mujahid.

The third: it is faith. This is the opinion of Qatadah.

The fourth: it is mercy. This is the opinion of 'Ata'.

The fifth: it is the religion of Allah. This is the opinion of al-Dahhak.

The sixth: it is the reward and recompense.

The seventh: there is no covenant for you over a wrongdoer that you should obey him in his wrongdoing. This is the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 125–128:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We charged Ibrahim and Isma'il﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: that is, We commanded them. The second: that is, We revealed to Ibrahim and Isma'il.

﴿That purify My House﴾. Concerning this there are three aspects. The first: from idols. The second: from disbelievers. The third: from impurities.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿My House﴾ refers to the Sacred House (al-Bayt al-Haram).

If it is said: there was no house to be purified in the time of Ibrahim before the House was built. It is answered: there are two responses to this. The first: its meaning is: We charged Ibrahim and Isma'il that they build My House pure. This is the view of al-Suddi. The second: its meaning is: purify the place of the House.

﴿For those who circumambulate﴾. Concerning them there are two interpretations. The first: they are the strangers who come to the House from afar. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The second: they are those who circle around the House. This is the view of Ata'.

﴿And those who stay devoted﴾. Concerning them there are four interpretations. The first: they are the people of the Sacred City (ahl al-balad al-haram). This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah. The second: they are those who observe i'tikaf (retreat in the mosque). This is the view of Mujahid. The third: they are those who pray. This is the view of Ibn Abbas. The fourth: they are those who dwell near the Sacred House without circumambulation, without i'tikaf, and without prayer. This is the view of Ata'.

﴿And those who bow and prostrate﴾. He means the people of prayer, because prayer comprises bowing and prostration.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when Ibrahim said: My Lord, make this city secure﴾, meaning Makkah, ﴿and provide its people with fruits﴾, so that security and abundance are combined for its people, and they live in ease and plenty of provision.

﴿Whoever among them believes in Allah﴾. Concerning this there are two aspects. The first: this is part of Ibrahim's speech, connected to his request that He make it a secure city and provide its people who believe in Him with fruits, because Allah the Exalted had informed him with His saying: ﴿My covenant does not reach the wrongdoers﴾ that among them there would be a wrongdoer who deserves punishment rather than reward; so he did not ask for the people of disobedience as he asked for the people of obedience. The second aspect: his request was general and unrestricted, and Allah the Exalted restricted the granting to whoever among them believes in Allah and the Last Day. Then He resumed informing about the state of the disbelievers, saying: ﴿And whoever disbelieves, I will grant him enjoyment for a little﴾, meaning in this world.

﴿Then I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire﴾, meaning for his sins if he dies upon his disbelief.

Scholars differed concerning Makkah: did it become a secure sanctuary through the supplication of Ibrahim, or was it already so? There are two views. The first: it had always been a sanctuary free from tyrants and oppressors, and from earth-subsidence and earthquakes; and Ibrahim only asked his Lord to make it secure from barrenness and famine, and to provide its people with fruits. This is based on the narration of Sa'id ibn al-Maqburi, who said: I heard Abu Shurayh al-Khuza'i say: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ conquered Makkah, the Khuza'ah killed a man from Hudhayl. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood up delivering a sermon and said: (O people, Allah the Exalted made Makkah sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth, so it is sacred until the Day of Resurrection. It is not lawful for a person who believes in Allah and the Last Day to shed blood in it or to cut down a tree in it. It was not lawful for anyone before me, and it was not made lawful for me except for this hour, in anger against its people. Now it has returned to its former state of sanctity as it was yesterday. Let the one who is present inform the one who is absent.) So if anyone says: the Messenger of Allah killed in it, say: Allah the Exalted made it lawful for His Messenger, and He did not make it lawful for you."

The second: Makkah was lawful before the supplication of Ibrahim, like other lands, and by his supplication it became a secure sanctuary, and by his declaring it sacred it became forbidden, just as Madinah became forbidden by the declaration of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ after having been lawful. This is based on the narration of Ash'ab, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (Indeed Ibrahim was the servant and friend of Allah, and I am His servant and messenger. Indeed Ibrahim made Makkah sacred, and I have made Madinah sacred between its two lava plains: its trees and its game are protected, no weapon for fighting may be carried in it, and no tree may be cut from it for fodder.)

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when Ibrahim raised the foundations of the House, and Isma'il﴾. The first whom Allah the Exalted guided to the place of the House was Ibrahim, and he was the first to build it together with Isma'il, and the first to perform its pilgrimage. Before that, people used to pray facing it without knowing its exact place.

The foundations (al-qawa'id) of the House: its singular is qa'idah, and it is like the base for what is above it.

﴿Our Lord, accept from us﴾. The meaning: they both say, "Our Lord, accept from us," as the Exalted said: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾, ﴿Peace be upon you﴾, meaning they say: "Peace be upon you." It is thus in the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "And when Ibrahim and Isma'il raised the foundations of the House, saying: Our Lord, accept from us."

The interpretation of (Isma'il): "Hear, O Allah," because "Il" in Syriac is Allah. When Ibrahim supplicated to his Lord, he said: "Hear, O Il." When He answered him and granted him the child he had asked for, he named him by what he had supplicated.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Our Lord, and make us two submitting to You﴾, in the dual form. ʿAwf al-A'rabi recited: "Muslimayn laka" in the plural form.

It is said: no prophet supplicated except for himself and his nation, except Ibrahim, for he supplicated, along with his supplication for himself and his nation, for this nation in His saying: ﴿And from our descendants a Muslim nation to You﴾. The Muslim is one who submits to the command of Allah and humbles himself before Him, and in religion he is one who accepts the commands of Allah, secretly and openly.

﴿And show us our rites﴾, meaning: make known to us our rites. Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: they are the rites and landmarks of the Hajj. This is the view of Qatadah and al-Suddi. The second: they are the rites of the sacrifices which are offered to Allah the Mighty and Majestic. This is the view of Mujahid and Ata'.

The word al-manasik is the plural of mansak. Scholars differed about why it is called a mansak, on two grounds. The first: because it is habitual and people repeatedly go to it for Hajj and 'Umrah, from their saying: "So-and-so has a mansak" when he has a place he frequents for good or evil; thus the rites of Hajj were called so because they are habitually performed. The second: nusuk is the worship of Allah the Exalted, and for this reason the ascetic is called nasik for worshipping his Lord; so these were called manasik because they are acts of worship.

﴿Then I will compel him to the punishment of the Fire﴾, meaning for his sins if he dies upon his disbelief.

Scholars differed concerning Makkah: did it become a secure sanctuary through the supplication of Ibrahim, or was it already so? There are two views. The first: it had always been a sanctuary free from tyrants and oppressors, and from earth-subsidence and earthquakes; and Ibrahim only asked his Lord to make it secure from barrenness and famine, and to provide its people with fruits. This is based on the narration of Sa'id ibn al-Maqburi, who said: I heard Abu Shurayh al-Khuza'i say: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ conquered Makkah, the Khuza'ah killed a man from Hudhayl. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood up delivering a sermon and said: (O people, Allah the Exalted made Makkah sacred on the day He created the heavens and the earth, so it is sacred until the Day of Resurrection. It is not lawful for a person who believes in Allah and the Last Day to shed blood in it or to cut down a tree in it. It was not lawful for anyone before me, and it was not made lawful for me except for this hour, in anger against its people. Now it has returned to its former state of sanctity as it was yesterday. Let the one who is present inform the one who is absent.) So if anyone says: the Messenger of Allah killed in it, say: Allah the Exalted made it lawful for His Messenger, and He did not make it lawful for you."

The second: Makkah was lawful before the supplication of Ibrahim, like other lands, and by his supplication it became a secure sanctuary, and by his declaring it sacred it became forbidden, just as Madinah became forbidden by the declaration of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ after having been lawful. This is based on the narration of Ash'ab, from Nafi', from Ibn Umar, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: (Indeed Ibrahim was the servant and friend of Allah, and I am His servant and messenger. Indeed Ibrahim made Makkah sacred, and I have made Madinah sacred between its two lava plains: its trees and its game are protected, no weapon for fighting may be carried in it, and no tree may be cut from it for fodder.)

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when Ibrahim raised the foundations of the House, and Isma'il﴾. The first whom Allah the Exalted guided to the place of the House was Ibrahim, and he was the first to build it together with Isma'il, and the first to perform its pilgrimage. Before that, people used to pray facing it without knowing its exact place.

The foundations (al-qawa'id) of the House: its singular is qa'idah, and it is like the base for what is above it.

﴿Our Lord, accept from us﴾. The second: nusuk is the worship of Allah the Exalted, and for this reason the ascetic is called nasik for worshipping his Lord; so these were called manasik because they are acts of worship.

﴿And those who bow and prostrate﴾. He means the people of prayer, because prayer comprises bowing and prostration.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 129:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Our Lord, and send among them﴾, meaning among this community, ﴿a messenger from among them﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ). It is said that in the recitation of Ubayy ibn Ka'b it reads: "Our Lord, and send among their last ones a messenger from among them." Khalid ibn Ma'dan has narrated: "A group of the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: (p-192) 'O Messenger of Allah, inform us about yourself.' He said: 'Yes, I am the answer to the prayer of Ibrahim and the glad tidings of Isa.'"

﴿who will recite to them Your verses﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: he will recite to them Your proof. The second: he will explain to them Your religion.

﴿and teach them the Book﴾, meaning the Qur'an.

﴿and the wisdom﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: it is the Sunnah, and this is the saying of Qatadah. The second: it is knowledge of the religion, understanding of it, and following it, and this is the saying of Ibn Zayd.

﴿and purify them﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: its meaning is that he will cleanse them from associating others with Allah and from worshipping idols. The second: he will purify them through His religion when they follow it, so they will be pure in the sight of Allah.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 130–132:

The Most High said: ﴿And who turns away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself﴾. In this there are three interpretations: (p-193)

The first: that it means he has made a fool of himself, i.e., he did to himself of foolishness what made him a fool. This is the view of al-Akhfash.

The second: that it carries the meaning of "foolish in himself," so the preposition was dropped, as in the words of the Most High: ﴿And do not determine the resolve of marriage﴾, i.e., "upon the resolve of marriage." This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The third: that it carries the meaning of "destroyed himself and ruined it." This is the view of Abu 'Ubayda.

Al-Mubarrad and Tha'lab said: safiha, with a kasra on the fa', is transitive, while safuha, with a damma on the fa', is not transitive.

﴿And We certainly chose him in this world﴾, i.e., We selected him. His wording is derived from al-safwa (the choice part of something), so the meaning is: We selected him in this world for the messengership.

﴿And indeed, in the Hereafter, he is among the righteous﴾, for himself, in saving it from ruin.

The Most High said: ﴿And Abraham instructed his sons with it﴾. The pronoun refers back to the religion, because of the preceding words: ﴿And who turns away from the religion of Abraham﴾. Wassa (to enjoin repeatedly) is more emphatic than awsa (to enjoin), because awsa may have been said once, whereas wassa cannot occur except repeatedly.

﴿And Jacob [did likewise]: "O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you the religion, so do not die except while you are Muslims."﴾ The meaning is that Abraham instructed, then after him Jacob instructed his sons, and both of them said: ﴿O my sons, indeed Allah has chosen for you the religion﴾, meaning He chose for you the religion, i.e., Islam, ﴿so do not die except while you are Muslims﴾. If it is asked: how can they be forbidden from death when it is not their act, since they are only made to die? It is answered: this is understood in the breadth of the language, because the prohibition is directed at abandoning Islam, not at death; its meaning is: hold fast to Islam and do not depart from it until death.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 133–135:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they said: "Be Jews or Christians, you will be guided."﴾ Meaning: the Jews said, "Be Jews, you will be guided," and the Christians said, "Be Christians, you will be guided." So God, the Exalted, refuted them, and said: ﴿Say: "Rather, [follow] the creed (millah) of Ibrahim, a ḥanīf."﴾ There is an omission in the speech, which allows two interpretations:

The first: the omitted part is "Rather, we follow the creed of Ibrahim." For this reason, *millata* came in the accusative case.

The second: the omitted part is "Rather, we are guided by the creed of Ibrahim." When the preposition was omitted, *millata* became accusative.

The *millah* is the religion. It is derived from *al-imlā'* (dictation), that is, what they dictate from their books.

As for *al-ḥanīf*, there are four interpretations:
First: it means the sincere one (al-mukhlis). This is the view of al-Suddi.
Second: it means the follower (al-muttabi'). This is the view of Mujahid.
Third: it means the pilgrim (al-ḥājj). This is the view of Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan.
Fourth: it means the upright (al-mustaqim).

Regarding the root meaning of *al-ḥanīf* in the language, there are two views:
The first: it means inclination. The meaning is that Ibrahim inclined (ḥanafa) toward the religion of God, which is Islam, and so he was called *ḥanīf*. It is said that a man is called *aḥnaf* (knock-kneed) because each of his feet leans toward the other.

The second view: its origin is uprightness (al-istiqamah). Thus the religion of Ibrahim was called *al-Ḥanīfiyyah* because of its uprightness. It is also said of a man *aḥnaf*, as an omen against inclination (taṭayyur min al-mayl) and an optimistic sign of uprightness (tafā'ul bil-istiqamah), just as the one bitten by a snake is called *salīm* (the safe one), and a deadly land is called *mafāzah* (the place of safety).

﴿If they believe in the like of what you believe in, then they have been guided.﴾ If it is asked: Is there a like of faith that is not faith? It is answered: The meaning of the speech is: If they believe as you believe, and affirm as you affirm, then they have been guided. This is the meaning of the qira'a (variant recitation), even though it differs from the mushaf (the written codex).

﴿But if they turn away, then they are only in shiqaq (opposition).﴾ That is, in hostility and enmity. The root of shiqaq is distance, from the saying: "So-and-so has taken a shiqq (side), and so-and-so has taken another shiqq," when they separate from one another.

Likewise, it is said of one who leaves the community: "He has split the staff of the Muslims," because of his distance from them.

﴿The sibgha (dye) of Allah. And who is better than Allah in sibgha?﴾ Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: its meaning is the religion of Allah. This is the view of Qatada.

The reason for this is that the Christians used to dip their children in water that they had, and they would say, "This is a purification for them, like circumcision." So Allah the Exalted refuted this by saying: ﴿The sibgha of Allah﴾, i.e., the sibgha of Allah is the best sibgha, and it is Islam.

The second: that the sibgha of Allah is the creation of Allah. This is the view of Mujahid.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 142–143:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾. "Al-sufaha'" (the foolish): its singular is safih, and the safih is one who is light of forbearance (khafif al-hilm), from their saying: a safih garment is one that is loosely woven (khafif al-naskh), and a safih spear is one whose piercing is swift.

Regarding who is meant by "the foolish" here, there are three opinions. The first: the Jews; this is the view of Mujahid.

The second: the hypocrites; this is the view of al-Suddi.

The third: the disbelievers of Quraysh; al-Zajjaj related this.

﴿What turned them away from their qiblah which they had been facing﴾, meaning: what turned them away from their qiblah which they had been facing, which is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), where the Messenger of Allah ﷺ faced while in Makkah, after his migration to Madinah, for sixteen months according to the narration of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib; and according to the narration of Mu'adh ibn Jabal, thirteen months; and according to the narration of Anas ibn Malik, nine or ten months. Then the qiblah of Bayt al-Maqdis was abrogated (naskh) by facing the Ka'bah, while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in Madinah, during the Zuhr prayer, and he had prayed two rak'ahs facing toward Bayt al-Maqdis, then he turned his face toward the Ka'bah. This is the saying of Anas ibn Malik. al-Bara' ibn 'Azib said: "We were in the 'Asr prayer at Quba', when a man passed by the people of the mosque while they were bowing in the second rak'ah, and said: 'I bear witness that I prayed with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ facing Makkah.' So they turned around as they were, facing the House." The qiblah of everything is what faces its front.

The scholars differed over whether the Messenger of Allah ﷺ's facing Bayt al-Maqdis was by his own opinion and effort (ra'y and ijtihad), or was by the command of Allah exalted, based on His saying: ﴿And We did not make the qiblah which you had been facing except that We might make evident who follows the Messenger﴾. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj.

The second opinion: that he faced it by his own opinion and effort. This is the view of al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah, Abu al-'Aliyah, and al-Rabi'.

They differed regarding the reason for his choosing Bayt al-Maqdis, according to two opinions. One: that he chose Bayt al-Maqdis in order to win over the People of the Book; this is the view of Abu Ja'far al-Tabari.

The second: because the Arabs performed Hajj to the House without being accustomed to Bayt al-Maqdis, so Allah loved to test them with what they were not accustomed to, that He might know who follows from among those who turn back on their heels; this is the view of Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ faced the Ka'bah, Ibn 'Abbas said: "Rifa'ah ibn Qays, Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, al-Rabi' and Kinanah ibn Abi al-Huqayq came and said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: 'What turned you away from your qiblah which you had been facing, while you claim that you are upon the religion and creed of Ibrahim? Return to your qiblah which you had been facing, and we will follow you and believe you.'

They only wanted to seduce him away from his religion. So Allah exalted revealed: ﴿The foolish among the people will say: What turned them away from their qiblah which they had been facing? Say: To Allah belong the east and the west; He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾." Meaning: wherever Allah exalted has commanded that one face, from east or west.

Al-sirat: the path; al-mustaqim: the level.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾. In it there are three interpretations. The first: it means "best" (khiyaran), from their saying: "So-and-so is of middle lineage among his people," when they intend by it one elevated in lineage; and from it is the saying of Zuhayr:

*They are a middle (wasat) whose judgment Allah is pleased with, when one of the great calamities descends upon the honored one.*

The second: that wasat is from moderation (tawassut) in affairs, because the Muslims took a middle course in religion: they are neither people of excess in it, nor people of negligence in it, unlike the Jews who altered the Book of Allah, killed their prophets, and lied against their Lord. So Allah exalted described them as a middle, because the most beloved of affairs to Him are the most moderate of them.

The third: by wasat is meant "just" ('adl), because justice is a middle between excess and deficiency. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Prophet ﷺ regarding His saying exalted: ﴿And thus We made you a middle nation﴾ that it means "just" ('adl).

﴿That you may be witnesses over the people﴾. In it there are three interpretations. The first: that you may bear witness against the People of the Book, by the Messenger's delivery to them of the message of their Lord.

The second: that you may bear witness against the earlier nations, by their prophets' delivery to them of the message of their Lord. This is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ, that the earlier nations will say to them: "How do you bear witness against us when you did not witness us?" They will say: "The Prophet of Allah informed us of what was revealed to him of the Book of Allah."

The third: that the meaning of His saying: ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾ is that you may be proving (muhtajjin) against all the nations, so testimony is expressed as argument. This is an opinion related by al-Zajjaj.

﴿And the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾. In it there are three interpretations. The first: the Messenger will be a witness over his ummah that he has conveyed to them the message of his Lord.

The second: that the meaning of that is that he will be a witness for them through their faith, and "over them" (alayhim) is in the sense of "for them" (lahum). The third: that the meaning of His saying: ﴿And the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾ is that he will be proving (muhtajjan).

﴿And We did not make the qiblah which you had been facing﴾, i.e., Bayt al-Maqdis, ﴿except that We might make evident who follows the Messenger from who turns back on his heels﴾. If it is said: Allah knows things before they occur, so how is the changing of the qiblah made a means to His knowledge? It is said: In His saying ﴿except that We might know (li-na'lam)﴾ there are four interpretations. The first: it means "except that My Messenger, My party, and My allies might know," because it is characteristic of the Arabs to attribute what the followers of a leader do to him, as they say: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab conquered the plains of Iraq and collected its taxes."

The second: that His saying exalted ﴿except that We might know﴾ means "except that We might see," and the Arabs sometimes place knowledge in the place of sight and sight in the place of knowledge, as He exalted said: ﴿Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the companions of the elephant?﴾ [al-Fil: 1], meaning: "Have you not known?"

The third: His saying exalted ﴿except that We might know﴾ means "except that you might know that We know," because the hypocrites were in doubt about Allah's knowledge of things before they occurred.

The fourth: that His saying ﴿except that We might know﴾ means "except that We might distinguish the people of certainty from the people of doubt"; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying exalted: ﴿who follows the Messenger﴾, meaning in what he commanded of facing the Ka'bah, ﴿from who turns back on his heels﴾, meaning: from who apostatizes from his religion, because the apostate returns and turns back from what he was upon; so He likened him to one who turns back on his heels, because when the qiblah was changed, some of the Muslims apostatized, some became hypocrites, the Jews said: "Muhammad has longed for the land of his father," and Quraysh said: "Muhammad has come to know that we are upon guidance and he will follow us."

Then He exalted said: ﴿And indeed it was difficult except for those whom Allah guided﴾. In it there are three interpretations. The first: its meaning is that turning away from Bayt al-Maqdis toward the Ka'bah, and changing toward it, was indeed difficult; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatadah.

The second: that the "difficult thing" is the qiblah itself which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to face from Bayt al-Maqdis before the change; this is the view of Abu al-'Aliyah al-Riyahi.

The third: that the "difficult thing" is the prayer which they had prayed toward the first qiblah; this is the view of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

Then He exalted said: ﴿And Allah would not have caused your faith to be lost﴾, meaning your prayers toward Bayt al-Maqdis. He called the prayer "faith" because it comprises intention, speech, and action. The cause of this was that when the Muslims were turned from facing Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ka'bah, they said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "What of those of our brothers who have died?" So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿And Allah would not have caused your faith to be lost﴾. If it is said: They asked him about the prayer of others, and he answered them about the state of their own prayer? It is said: Because the people feared that their prayers toward Bayt al-Maqdis would be nullified for those who had died and for those who remained, so he answered them with what indicated both matters. Moreover, some people have narrated that they said: "How will our prayer toward Bayt al-Maqdis be lost?" and Allah exalted revealed that.

﴿Indeed Allah is to the people Kind (la-ra'uf), Merciful﴾. Ra'fah (kindness) is stronger than rahmah (mercy). Abu 'Umar 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' said: ra'fah is more than rahmah.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 144:

His words, exalted is He: ﴿We have certainly seen the turning of your face toward the heaven﴾. This verse was revealed earlier than His words: ﴿The foolish among the people will say﴾. In His words ﴿the turning of your face toward the heaven﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: its meaning is the turning of your face toward the sky; this is the view of al-Tabari. The second: its meaning is the turning of your eyes in gazing toward the sky; this is the view of al-Zajjaj.

﴿So We will surely turn you to a qiblah that you will be pleased with﴾, meaning the Ka'bah. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was pleased with it, chose it, and asked [his Lord] that he be turned toward it.

Scholars differed on the reason for his choosing this, according to two views. The first: opposing the Jews and disliking to resemble them, because they said: "Does he follow our qiblah and oppose us in our religion?" This was the view of Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.

The second: that he chose it because it was the qiblah of his father Ibrahim (Abraham); this was the view of Ibn Abbas.

If it is said: Was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) displeased with Bayt al-Maqdis being his qiblah, such that He said to him concerning the Ka'bah: ﴿So We will surely turn you to a qiblah that you will be pleased with﴾? It is said: It is not permissible that the Messenger of Allah be displeased with Bayt al-Maqdis when Allah commanded him with it, because the prophets are obligated to be pleased with the commands of Allah, exalted is He. But the meaning of "you will be pleased with" is: you will love it and desire it. He loved it, along with what we have mentioned of the first two views, because of what it contained of the gathering together of his people and their hastening to answer him. It is also possible that His words "you will be pleased with" are to be taken literally, meaning: you will be pleased with what results from it of gathering and quickness of response. Then He, exalted is He, answered his desire and commanded him with his request, saying: ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾, that is, turn your face in prayer toward the Sacred Mosque, that is, toward the Sacred Mosque, as al-Hudhali said:

"Indeed, the difficulty with her is a disease that mixes into her, so her direction is a gaze of the two eyes, exhausted."

That is, toward her. The word shatr (direction) is one of the words with opposite meanings: one says shatara ila kadha when one turns toward something, and shatara 'an kadha when one moves away from it and turns aside from it. The shatr of a thing is its half. As for the shatir (one who deviates) among men, it is because he has taken a course other than the straight one.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿the Sacred Mosque﴾, by which is meant the Ka'bah, because it is within it, so it is referred to by it.

The people of knowledge differed concerning the place toward which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to turn his face. 'Abdullah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As said concerning ﴿So We will surely turn you to a qiblah that you will be pleased with﴾: He said: opposite the spout (mizab) of the Ka'bah.

And 'Abdullah ibn Abbas said: the whole House, and the qiblah of the House is the door.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾, meaning toward the Sacred Mosque as well, as an emphasis of the first command, because its generality requires it. But by the emphasis he intended the possibility of specification. Then he made the first command addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and the second addressed to all people. Both commands are general concerning the Prophet (ﷺ) and all his community. But he differentiated between the two commands so as to prevent any change in the command regarding what is commanded, and so that each of them would continue to apply in its generality.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed, those who were given the Book﴾, meaning the Jews and the Christians.

﴿certainly know that it is the truth from their Lord﴾, meaning the change of the qiblah from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ka'bah.

﴿And Allah is not unaware of what they do﴾, of engaging in misleading the Muslims from their religion through that.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 145:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And even if you were to bring those who were given the Scripture every sign, they would not follow your qibla﴾ — meaning, facing the Ka'bah.

﴿Nor are you one who will follow their qibla﴾ — meaning, facing Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), after your qibla had been changed to the Ka'bah.

﴿Nor are some of them followers of the qibla of others﴾ — meaning, the Jews do not follow the Christians in the qibla; they differ regarding it, though they are united in their opposition to the Prophet ﷺ.

﴿And if you were to follow their desires﴾ — meaning, regarding the qibla.

﴿After the knowledge has come to you﴾ — meaning, regarding its change from Bayt al-Maqdis to the Ka'bah.

﴿Indeed, you would then be among the wrongdoers﴾. It is not permissible that the Prophet would do that which would make him a wrongdoer.

In this address there are two aspects. The first: this is a description that is negated of the Prophet, and He only intended by it to explain its ruling, had it been the case.

The second aspect: this is an address to the Prophet, but what is meant by it is his community (ummah).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 146–147:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Those to whom We have given the Book﴾ means the Jews and the Christians, who were given the Torah and the Injil (Gospel).

﴿They recognise it as they recognise their own sons﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: they recognise that the changing of the qibla from Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) to the Ka'ba is true, just as they recognise their sons.

The second: they recognise the Messenger and the truth of his message, just as they recognise their sons.

﴿And indeed a group of them﴾ means their scholars and elite. (p-205)

﴿conceal the truth﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: the truth is facing the Ka'ba (in prayer).

The second: the truth is Muhammad (ﷺ), and this is the view of Mujahid and Qatada.

﴿while they know﴾ may have two meanings. The first: they know that he is a truth to be followed.

The second: they know the punishment deserved for it.

﴿The truth is from your Lord﴾ means facing the Ka'ba, not what the witnesses from their qibla have informed you of.

﴿So do not be among the doubters﴾, that is, among the skeptics. It is said: "Fulan mara fi kadha" when certainty presents itself to him once and doubt another time, so he pushes one against the other.

If it is said: Was he doubting when he was forbidden from it? It is said: although this is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), what is meant is others from his community.

And for every one there is a direction toward which he turns; that is, for every community of the various religions there is a direction toward which it turns.

On this there are two opinions. The first: it is the qibla which they face. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ata' and al-Suddi.

The second: it means the prayer which they perform. This is the view of Qatada.

Regarding His saying, ﴿He is the one who turns it﴾, there are two opinions. The first: the people of each direction are those who turn to it and face it.

The second: that for the people of each direction, it is God Most High who turns them toward it and commands them to face it. It has been read as "He is its Master" (mawlaha), and this is a good reading which supports the second of the two opinions.

﴿So race to the good works﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: its meaning is, hasten to the righteous deeds. This is the view of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

The second: its meaning is, do not be overcome regarding your qibla by what the Jews say, namely that if you follow their qibla, they will follow you. This is the view of Qatada.

﴿Wherever you are, God will bring you all together﴾: to God is your return, all of you, meaning on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Indeed God is over all things Competent﴾: meaning, He is able to restore you to Him alive after death and decay.

Then Allah reinforced His command regarding facing the Ka'bah, because of what the polytheists had said and the support the hypocrites had given them, by repeating it. He said: ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and indeed it is the truth from your Lord. And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾, to clarify it for His Prophet and to turn him away from being deceived by the statement of the Jews that they would follow him if he returned.

﴿And Allah is not unaware of what you do﴾ may have two meanings. The first: that He says this to encourage them toward good. (p-207)

The second: as a warning against opposition.

Then Allah, exalted is He, repeated the affirmation of His command, so that there would be removed from their hearts what they had regarded as grave, namely their being turned to something other than what they were accustomed to. So He said: ﴿And from wherever you set out, turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque; and wherever you are, turn your faces toward it﴾. Each of the three commands conveyed a new benefit, although they are equal in binding the ruling. As for the first command, it serves to abrogate what came before it. As for the second command, it serves, by the saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿and indeed it is the truth from your Lord﴾, to show that it is not followed by any abrogation.

As for the third command, it serves to show that there is no argument against them in it, by His saying: ﴿so that people will have no argument against you﴾. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿except those of them who have wronged﴾. He does not mean that they have an argument against you.

Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: the meaning is, "But those who have wronged may argue against you with baseless proofs." The name "argument" may be applied to what is invalid of them, because they set them up in their reliance upon them in the place of what is sound, until their corruption becomes evident to one who knows, while remaining hidden from one who is ignorant, as Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Their argument is futile in the sight of their Lord﴾. So He called it an argument and made it futile in the sight of Allah.

The second opinion: the meaning is, "So that people will have no argument against you after those who have wronged," so that "except" (illa) carries the meaning of "after" (ba'da), as was said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed﴾ [An-Nisa': 22], meaning "after what has already passed."

And as was said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will not taste death therein except the first death﴾ [Ad-Dukhan: 56], meaning "after the first death."

By "those who have wronged" he meant the Quraysh and the Jews: the Quraysh, because of their saying when he faced the Ka'bah, "He knows that we are upon guidance," and the Jews, because of their saying, "If he turns back from it, we will follow him."

﴿So do not fear them, but fear Me﴾ in opposition, ﴿and that I may complete My favor upon you﴾. This may have two meanings. The first: in what We guided you to regarding the qiblah. The second: what I have prepared for you of the reward for obedience. (p-208)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 151–152:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿As We have sent among you﴾, meaning from among the Arabs, ﴿a Messenger from yourselves﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿reciting to you Our verses﴾, meaning the Qur'an.

﴿And purifies you﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: meaning He purifies you from polytheism (shirk).

The second: that He commands you to do that by which you become pure (azkiya') in the sight of God.

﴿And teaches you the Book﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: it is the Qur'an.

The second: the informing about what is in the earlier books of the accounts of the past generations.

﴿And the wisdom﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: it is the Sunnah (the prophetic custom and practice).

The second: the admonitions of the Qur'an.

﴿And teaches you what you did not know﴾, meaning the rulings of the religion and the affairs of this world.

﴿So remember Me, and I will remember you﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: remember Me with gratitude, and I will remember you with blessing.

The second: remember Me with acceptance, and I will remember you with reward.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 153–154:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, seek help through patience and prayer﴾. As for "patience" here, there are two opinions (p-209):

One of them: steadfastness upon the commands of Allah, Exalted is He.

The second: fasting, intended for the sake of Allah, Exalted is He.

As for "seeking help through prayer," it admits of two meanings. One of them: seeking help through its reward.

The second: seeking help through what is recited in the prayer, so that through it the excellence of obedience becomes known, and it becomes a help in carrying out the commands.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not say of those who are killed in the way of Allah, "They are dead." Rather, they are alive, but you do not perceive﴾. The reason for this is that they used to say of the slain of Badr and Uhud, "So-and-so has died, so-and-so has died." Then the verse was revealed, and there are two interpretations of it. One of them: they are not dead, even though their bodies are the bodies of the dead; rather, with Allah they are alive in their souls, with bodies that are given comfort.

The second: they are not dead in misguidance; rather, they are alive in obedience and guidance, as Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Is one who was dead and We gave him life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people like one who is in darkness and cannot emerge from it?﴾ [al-An'am: 122]. So He made the misguided one dead and the guided one alive.

It may also admit a third interpretation: that they are not dead, by the cutting off of remembrance with Allah being sustained and the reward being established.

And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger, and loss of wealth, lives and crops. The "you" here means the people of Makkah, because of what came before: the Prophet (ﷺ) had supplicated that God make it upon them years like the years of Yusuf, when they suffered drought for seven years. So God, answering His Prophet's supplication, said: ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger﴾. "Fear" means terror in battle, and "hunger" means famine through drought.

﴿And loss of wealth﴾ admits of two meanings:

The first: its loss through destroying calamities.

The second: an increase in expenditure during drought.

﴿And lives﴾ means the loss of lives through killing and death.

﴿And crops﴾ means scarcity of plants and the rising of blessings away.

﴿And give good tidings to the patient﴾ admits of three meanings. The first: give good tidings of victory to those who are patient in jihad.

The second: give good tidings of reward to those who are patient in obedience.

The third: give good tidings of reward to those who are patient in calamities, and this is most fitting given His saying afterwards: ﴿Who, when a calamity afflicts them, say: "Indeed we belong to God, and indeed to Him we return."﴾ Meaning: when a calamity afflicts them in self, family or wealth, they say, "Indeed we belong to God": that is, our souls, our families and our wealth belong to God, Who does us no wrong in what He does with us. ﴿And indeed to Him we return﴾ means: by resurrection, for the reward of the good-doer and the punishment of the wrongdoer.

Then God said concerning these: ﴿Upon them are blessings from their Lord, and mercy. And those are the guided.﴾ The word ṣalāh (blessing, prayer) is a homonym in meaning: from God it is mercy, from the angels it is seeking forgiveness, and from people it is supplication, as God said: ﴿Indeed God and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet. O you who believe, send blessings upon him and greet him with peace.﴾ And the poet said:

"May a Generous Lord bless Yahya and his companions, and an obeyed intercessor."

His saying, ﴿Upon them are blessings from their Lord﴾, meaning: mercy. He mentioned it in the plural form because some of them follow others.

As for His saying, ﴿And those are the guided﴾, there are two possible meanings: The first: guided to the easing of calamities and lightening of grief. The second: guided to deserving reward and abundant recompense.

﴿Indeed, al-Safa and al-Marwa are among the rites of God﴾. As for al-Safa and al-Marwa, they are the starting point and the endpoint of the sa'y (the ritual running between them).

On this there are two opinions. The first is that al-Safa refers to the white stones and al-Marwa to the black stones.

The derivation of al-Safa comes from the expression "safa yasfu," meaning "it became pure," and it is a plural whose singular is safah.

The second is that al-Safa refers to the hard stones that do not produce anything, while al-Marwa refers to the soft stones. This is the more apparent of the two opinions in lexical usage.

The use of al-Safa in the sense of hard rock is shown by the verse of al-Tirimmah:

"My strength and my height refused that my hoof should ever wear down the hard rock."

The use of al-Marwa in the sense of soft stone is shown by the verse of al-Kumayt:

"He turns the ground with a slender hoof, and when it meets the marw, it crushes."

It is related from Ja'far ibn Muhammad, who said: Adam descended upon al-Safa and Hawwa' (Eve) upon al-Marwa. So al-Safa was named after Adam, the chosen one (al-Mustafa), and al-Marwa was named after the woman.

It is also said that the name al-Safa was given the masculine form because of Isaf, an idol that stood upon it and was masculine in name, while al-Marwa was given the feminine form because of Na'ilah, an idol that stood upon it and was feminine in name.

As for His words ﴿of the rites of God﴾, there are two interpretations. The first: it means of the landmarks of God, which He made markers for His servants. From this is the verse of al-Kumayt:

"We slay them generation after generation; you see them as offerings of sacrifice through which nearness [to God] is sought."

(p-٢١٢)

The second: the word sha'a'ir is the plural of sha'irah, which is a report that God has informed about. It means that God made His servants aware (ish'ar) of the matter of al-Safa and al-Marwa and of the circumambulation between them that is incumbent upon them. This is the view of Mujahid.

Then He said ﴿So whoever performs the hajj to the House or the 'umrah﴾. As for the hajj (the major pilgrimage), there are two opinions. The first: it means intent (al-qasd). The rite was named after it because the House is the object of intent in it. From this is the verse of the poet:

"And I witness from 'Awf many gatherings, who frequent the saffron-clad Zibriqan."

By his words "yahujjun" he means they frequently return to him because of his nobility and leadership. So the hajj was called hajj because the pilgrim comes toward the House, then returns to it for the tawaf al-ifadah (the circumambulation of return), then goes out to Mina and returns to it for the tawaf al-sadr (the farewell circumambulation). Because of the repeated returning to it time after time, he was called hajj (one who returns).

As for the 'umrah (the minor pilgrimage), there are two opinions. The first: it also means intent, and every one who intends something is a mu'tamir (one who makes 'umrah). Al-'Ajjaj said:

"Ibn Ma'mar has indeed campaigned when he set out, a distant campaign from a distant place, and endured."

By his words "when he set out" he means when he intended.

The second opinion: it means visitation. From this is the verse of the poet:

"The soul stirred when their remnant came, and a rider came from Tathlith as a visitor."

That is, a visitor.

Then He said ﴿there is no blame upon him for going around them both﴾. The lifting of blame belongs to the rulings on what is permissible (mubahat), not to obligatory acts (wajibat).

Abu Hanifah held that the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwa is not obligatory as a rite in the hajj and the 'umrah, on two grounds. The first is His words ﴿there is no blame upon him for going around them both﴾, and the lifting of blame belongs to the rulings on what is permissible, not to obligatory acts.

The second is that Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud recited: ﴿there is no blame upon him for going around them both﴾.

Al-Shafi'i, Malik, and the jurists of the two Harams (Makkah and Madinah) held that the sa'y is obligatory in both rites, relying on the implication of the address (fahwa al-khitab) and the explicit text (nass) of the Sunnah. In His words ﴿there is no blame﴾ there is no evidence that it is merely permissible and not obligatory, because it came in response to a specific cause. That cause was that upon al-Safa in the pre-Islamic period there was an idol named Isaf, and upon al-Marwa an idol named Na'ilah. When the pre-Islamic people ran between al-Safa and al-Marwa, they circumambulated around al-Safa and al-Marwa, glorifying Isaf and Na'ilah. When Islam came and the idols were abolished, the Muslims disliked agreeing with the pre-Islamic people in circumambulating around al-Safa and al-Marwa, out of avoidance of what they had been doing in glorifying Isaf and Na'ilah. So God permitted it for them in Islam because the intention had changed, and He said: ﴿there is no blame upon him for going around them both﴾.

As for the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas, ﴿there is no blame upon him for going around them both﴾, it is not a proof for dropping the obligation of the sa'y between them, because the particle "la" (no) is not a superfluous particle (sillah) in speech when it is preceded by a negation. Like His words ﴿What prevented you from prostrating when I commanded you?﴾ [al-A'raf: 12], meaning: what prevented you from prostrating. And as the poet said:

"The Messenger of God did not approve their deed, nor did the two good men, Abu Bakr and 'Umar."

﴿And whoever volunteers good﴾. There are three opinions about it. The first: whoever volunteers by performing the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwa. This is the view of those who dropped the obligation of the sa'y.

The second: whoever volunteers with an addition beyond what is obligatory. This is the view of those who made the sa'y obligatory.

The third: whoever volunteers with the hajj and the 'umrah after performing their obligatory forms.

(p-٢١٤)

﴿Indeed God is Appreciative, All-Knowing﴾. It admits of two interpretations. The first: He is Appreciative of the deed and All-Knowing of the intention. The second: He is Appreciative of the little and All-Knowing of the reward.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 159–162:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what We have sent down﴾. It is said: they are the leaders of the Jews, Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, Ka'b ibn Asad, Ibn Suriya, and Zayd ibn al-Tabut. They are the ones who concealed what Allah had sent down.

﴿of the clear proofs (al-bayyinat) and the guidance (al-huda)﴾. Concerning this there are two views. The first: the clear proofs are the evidences indicating the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), and the guidance is the command to follow him.

The second: the clear proofs and the guidance are one and the same, and combining them is for emphasis. That is what made clear his prophethood and guided to following him.

﴿after We have made it clear for the people in the Book﴾ meaning the Qur'an.

﴿Those are cursed by Allah, and cursed by the cursers﴾. Concerning them there are four views. The first: they are everything on earth of animals and inanimate things, except the two weighty ones (al-thaqalan), mankind and jinn. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and al-Bara' ibn Azib. (p-215)

The second: "the cursers" are two persons who curse each other; the curse falls upon the one who deserves it of them both, and if neither deserves it, the curse returns upon the Jews. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud.

The third: they are the beasts; when the earth dries up, the beasts say, "This is because of the sinners of the children of Adam." This is the view of Mujahid and Ikrimah.

The fourth: they are the believers among mankind and jinn, and the angels curse whoever disbelieves in Allah and the Last Day. This is the view of al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

﴿Except those who repent﴾, meaning by embracing Islam from their disbelief, ﴿and make amends﴾. This may bear two meanings. The first: the amendment of their inner selves and their deeds.

The second: they amend their people by guiding them to Islam.

(And make clear) meaning what is in the Torah concerning the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the obligation to follow him. ﴿Those, I accept their repentance﴾. Repentance from the servants is giving up sin, and repentance from Allah, exalted is He, is His acceptance of it from His servants.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers﴾. He conditioned death upon disbelief only because its ruling becomes fixed by dying upon it, and it is lifted by repenting from it.

﴿Upon them is the curse of Allah﴾. The curse from the servants is expulsion, and from Allah, exalted is He, it is punishment.

﴿and of the angels and mankind, all together﴾. Al-Hasan al-Basri read (wal-mala'ikati wan-nasi ajma'una) with the nominative case, and its interpretation: their recompense is that Allah curses them, the angels curse them, and mankind all curses them.

If it is said: all of mankind does not curse them, since their own people do not curse them, the answer to this has two parts. The first: the curse from most people is attributed to all people, so the ruling of the majority prevails over the minority.

The second: the intended meaning is the Day of Resurrection, when their own people curse them along with all of mankind, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿On the Day of Resurrection some of you will disavow others and some of you will curse others﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 25]. Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Abiding therein; their punishment will not be lightened for them﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations: (p-216)

The first: it will not be lightened by reduction or rest.

The second: it will not be lightened by patience with it or endurance of it.

﴿Nor will they be reprieved﴾. This may bear two meanings. The first: they will not be delayed from it or given respite.

The second: Allah, exalted and majestic is He, will not look upon them so as to have mercy on them.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 163:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And your God is one God﴾. By this he intended two matters.

The first: the God of all creation is one, not as the idol-worshippers among the Arabs and others have claimed, that every people has a god other than the god of those who are other than them.

The second: that God, although He is God to all creation, is one, having no second and no like.

Then He affirmed this with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There is no god but He﴾. Then He described Himself, saying: ﴿The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾, encouraging worship of Him and urging obedience to Him.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 164:

Then he pointed to what He reminded them of regarding His oneness and His power, by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth and the alternation of the night and the day﴾. The sign in the heaven is its being raised without pillars beneath it and without supports above it, and then what is in it of the sun, the moon, and the moving stars.

The sign in the earth is its seas, its rivers, its minerals, its trees, its plains, and its mountains.

The sign in the alternation of the night and the day is their alternating, by the advance of one of them and the retreat of the other. The night advances from a place not known, and the day retreats to a place not known. This is their alternation.

Then He said: ﴿And the ship that runs in the sea with what benefits people﴾. Al-fulk (الفلك) means ships; the singular and plural share one form, and it may be treated as masculine or feminine.

The sign in it is in two respects: first, its staying afloat while carrying its load; second, its reaching its destination.

Then Almighty God said: ﴿And what Allah sends down from the sky of water﴾, meaning by it the rain sent down from it, which comes usually when needed and stops when people are free of need for it, and that is among His signs.

Then Almighty God said: ﴿and gives life thereby to the earth after its death﴾. Its being given life by it may be in two respects: first, what its rivers and springs flow with; second, what grows from it of its trees and crops. Both of these are a cause of the life of creatures, both speaking and dumb.

Then Almighty God said: ﴿and He scattered therein every kind of moving creature﴾, meaning all the animals that He brought into being in it. He named it (dābba, moving creature) because of its crawling upon it. The sign in it, together with the manifestation of the power to create it, is in three respects: first, the diversity of its creation; second, the difference of its natures; third, His inspiring it with the ways of its welfare.

Then Almighty God said: ﴿and the turning of the winds﴾. The sign in it is in two respects: first, the variation of their blowing, in the shift of the north wind to the south, and the east wind to the west, so that no cause is known for their shifting, nor a direction for their turning away.

Second, what He placed in their variation of favour that benefits, and of vengeance that harms.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Shurayh, who said: No wind ever blew except for the sickness of a healthy person or the healing of a sick one. The word al-riyah (الرياح) is the plural of rih (ريح), and its origin is arwah (أرواح).

Abu Mu'adh related that in the codex of Hafsa there was: "and the turning of the winds (الأرواح)." Ibn Abbas said: the wind was so named because it gives rest (turiha) hour after hour.

Dhu al-Rumma said:

When the winds blow from the direction where are the traces of Mayy, its blowing stirs my longing.

Then Almighty God said: ﴿and the clouds made subservient between the sky and the earth﴾. Al-musakhkhar means the made docile. The sign in it is in three respects: first, the beginning of its formation and the end of its dispersal; second, its remaining between the sky and the earth without pillars or supports; third, its subjection and its being sent wherever Allah, Mighty and Majestic, wills.

This verse has gathered from His signs, which point to His oneness and His power, what has become a guide for people of intellect and a leader to the truth.

Thus Allah did not limit us to mere information until He joined it with reflection and consideration.

Then He informed that, alongside these dazzling signs for people of intellect, ﴿And among the people are those who take, besides Allah, equals﴾. The andad (equals) are likenesses, singular nidd, and what is meant by them are the idols which they took as gods and worshipped as they worship Allah the Exalted, despite their incapacity relative to the power of Allah in His signs that point to His oneness.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They love them as they love Allah﴾, meaning that they, despite the incapacity of the idols, love them as they love Allah despite His power.

﴿But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah﴾, meaning more than the love of the people of idols for their idols. Its meaning is that the sincere ones devoted to Allah the Exalted are the true lovers.

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed﴾. There are two opinions concerning them. One: that those who were followed are the leaders and chiefs, who disowned those who followed them in disbelief. This is the view of ʿAṭāʾ.

The second: that they are the devils, who disowned humankind. This is the view of al-Suddi.

﴿And they see the punishment﴾, meaning by it the followed and the followers.

Regarding their seeing the punishment there are two possible meanings. One: their certainty of it at the moment of direct witnessing in the world.

The second: that the command concerning their punishment (is given) at the time of the gathering and questioning in the Hereafter.

﴿And their bonds are cut off from them﴾. In this there are five interpretations. One: that the "asbab" (bonds) are their connections in the world. This is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: the dwellings they had in the world. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: that they are the kinship ties (arham). This is a narration of Ibn Juraij from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The fourth: that they are the deeds they used to do in the world. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The fifth: that they are the covenants and alliances that existed between them in the world.

﴿And those who followed said: If only we had a return, we would disown them as they have disowned us﴾. He means by this that the followers said to the followed: If only we had a return, i.e., a return to the world, we would disown you there just as you disowned us in the Hereafter.

﴿Thus Allah shows them their deeds as regrets upon them﴾. He means the followed and the followers. The ḥasrah (regret) is the intensity of remorse over a grief that has passed.

Regarding ﴿their deeds as regrets upon them﴾ there are two meanings. One: their righteousness, which was nullified by their disbelief, since the disbeliever is not rewarded along with his disbelief.

The second: what their lifespans were diminished by through acts of disobedience, in that they were not directed toward obedience to Allah.

﴿And they will not be out of the Fire﴾. By this He means two things. One: the impossibility of a return.

Regarding ﴿their deeds as regrets upon them﴾ there are two meanings. One: their righteousness, which was nullified by their disbelief, since the disbeliever is not rewarded along with his disbelief.

The second: what their lifespans were diminished by through acts of disobedience, in that they were not directed toward obedience to Allah.

﴿And they will not be out of the Fire﴾. By this He means two things. One: the impossibility of a return. 

The second: their eternal abiding in the Fire.

Then He informed that, alongside these dazzling signs for people of intellect, ﴿And among the people are those who take, besides Allah, equals﴾. The andad (equals) are likenesses, singular nidd, and what is meant by them are the idols which they took as gods and worshipped as they worship Allah the Exalted, despite their incapacity relative to the power of Allah in His signs that point to His oneness.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They love them as they love Allah﴾, meaning that they, despite the incapacity of the idols, love them as they love Allah despite His power.

﴿But those who believe are stronger in love for Allah﴾, meaning more than the love of the people of idols for their idols. Its meaning is that the sincere ones devoted to Allah the Exalted are the true lovers.

The saying of the Exalted: ﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed﴾. There are two opinions concerning them. One: that those who were followed are the leaders and chiefs, who disowned those who followed them in disbelief. This is the view of ʿAṭāʾ.

The second: that they are the devils, who disowned humankind. This is the view of al-Suddi.

﴿And they see the punishment﴾, meaning by it the followed and the followers.

Regarding their seeing the punishment there are two possible meanings. One: their certainty of it at the moment of direct witnessing in the world.

The second: that the command concerning their punishment (is given) at the time of the gathering and questioning in the Hereafter.

﴿And their bonds are cut off from them﴾. In this there are five interpretations. One: that the "asbab" (bonds) are their connections in the world. This is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: the dwellings they had in the world. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: that they are the kinship ties (arham). This is a narration of Ibn Juraij from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The fourth: that they are the deeds they used to do in the world. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The fifth: that they are the covenants and alliances that existed between them in the world.

﴿And those who followed said: If only we had a return, we would disown them as they have disowned us﴾. He means by this that the followers said to the followed: If only we had a return, i.e., a return to the world, we would disown you there just as you disowned us in the Hereafter.

﴿Thus Allah shows them their deeds as regrets upon them﴾. He means the followed and the followers. The ḥasrah (regret) is the intensity of remorse over a grief that has passed.

Regarding ﴿their deeds as regrets upon them﴾ there are two meanings. One: their righteousness, which was nullified by their disbelief, since the disbeliever is not rewarded along with his disbelief.

The second: what their lifespans were diminished by through acts of disobedience, in that they were not directed toward obedience to Allah.

﴿And they will not be out of the Fire﴾. By this He means two things. One: the impossibility of a return. 

The second: their eternal abiding in the Fire.

O mankind, eat of what is on the earth, lawful and good (﴿يا أيُّها النّاسُ كُلُوا مِمّا في الأرْضِ حَلالا طَيِّبًا﴾). It was said: it was revealed concerning Thaqif, Khuza'ah and Banu Mudlij, regarding what they had forbidden to themselves of livestock and crops, so God Most High permitted them to eat it and made it lawful and good for them.

﴿And do not follow the steps of Satan﴾ (﴿وَلا تَتَّبِعُوا خُطُواتِ الشَّيْطانِ﴾). The word (khutuwat, "steps") is the plural of (khutwah, "step"). The exegetes differed concerning what is meant by it, in four opinions:

First: the steps of Satan are his deeds. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

Second: they are his sins. This is the view of Mujahid.

Third: they are his obedience (to him). This is the view of al-Suddi.

Fourth: they are vows made in disobedience.

﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾ (﴿إنَّهُ لَكم عَدُوٌّ مُبِينٌ﴾), i.e., one whose enmity is evident.

﴿He only commands you to evil and immorality﴾ (﴿إنَّما يَأْمُرُكم بِالسُّوءِ والفَحْشاءِ﴾). Al-Suddi said: "evil" (al-su') in this place means the disobediences of God; it was called evil because it harms its doer through its bad consequences.

As for "immorality" (al-fahsha') here, there are three opinions: First: fornication (al-zina). Second: sins. Third: everything for which there is a prescribed punishment (hadd); it was so named for the grossness of the act and the ugliness of what is heard about it.

﴿And that you say about God what you do not know﴾ (﴿وَأنْ تَقُولُوا عَلى اللَّهِ ما لا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾). Concerning this there are two opinions: First, that you forbid for yourselves what God has not forbidden for you. Second, that you make for Him a partner.

(p-221)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 170–171:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Follow what Allah has sent down,"﴾ meaning: in permitting what they had forbidden of the cattle, the baḥīrah, the sā'ibah, the waṣīlah and the ḥām. ﴿They say, "Rather, we follow what we found our fathers upon."﴾ meaning: in their prohibition of those things upon themselves.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the example of those who disbelieve is like that of one who shouts to that which hears nothing except a call and an outcry﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: the example of the disbeliever in what he is admonished with is like the beast that is called to with a shout; it hears the sound but does not understand its meaning. This is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid.

The second: the example of the disbeliever in his calling upon his gods that he worships besides Allah is like the shepherd of a beast who hears its voice but does not understand it. This is the saying of Ibn Zayd.

﴿Deaf, dumb, blind; so they do not reason﴾. That is: deaf to the admonition, so they do not hear it; dumb to the truth, so they do not mention it; blind to right guidance, so they do not see it; therefore they do not reason it, because when they do not act upon what they hear, say and see, they are in the position of one who has lost hearing, speech and sight.

The Arabs say of one who hears what he does not act upon: "ṣamm" (deaf).

The poet said:

؎ ... ... ... ∗∗∗ deaf to what displeases him, though he hears (well)
