Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 172–173:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, He has forbidden you only carrion, blood⁠﴾ (p-222) — Allah, Exalted is He, informed of what He forbade after His saying: ﴿Eat of the good things We have provided you⁠﴾, so that it would indicate the restriction of the prohibition from the generality of the permission. So He said: ﴿Indeed, He has forbidden you carrion⁠﴾, which is that whose soul has departed without slaughter (dhakat).

(And blood) is that which flows from the animal by slaughter or by wound.

﴿And the flesh of swine⁠﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: the prohibition is confined to its flesh alone, not to other parts, restricting itself to the text. This is the view of Dawud ibn Ali.

The second: the prohibition is general to the whole of the swine, and the mention of the flesh is an indication of all of it, because it is its main part. This is the view of the majority (al-Jumhur).

﴿And that over which has been invoked [the name] of other than Allah⁠﴾. By his saying "uhilla" (was invoked) he means: dhubiha (was slaughtered). The slaughter was called ihlal only because, when they wanted to slaughter what they had offered to their idols, they mentioned the name of their idols at it and raised their voices with it. So every slaughterer who raised his voice with the naming, or did not raise it, was called "muhill," just as the state of ihram was called ihlal because of their raising their voices at it with the talbiyah, until it became its name even if no voice was raised at it.

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿other than Allah⁠﴾, there are two interpretations. The first: what was slaughtered for other than Allah, namely idols. This is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: what had the name of other than Allah mentioned over it. This is the view of Ata' and al-Rabi'.

﴿But whoever is compelled [by necessity], neither desiring nor transgressing, then there is no sin upon him⁠﴾. Idturra is formed (ifta'ala) from ad-darurah (necessity). Regarding it there are two opinions. The first: its meaning is: whoever is compelled to eat it, there is no sin upon him. This is the view of Mujahid.

The second: whoever is in need of eating it due to a necessity that compels him out of fear for his self, there is no sin upon him. This is the view of the majority.

Regarding His saying: ﴿neither desiring nor transgressing⁠﴾, there are three opinions. The first: neither rebelling against the Imam nor transgressing against the community by corrupting their unity; so the rebel against the Imam and his community is included, and the transgressor (al-'adi) is the highway robber. This is the meaning of the saying of Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. (p-223)

The second: neither desiring in eating it beyond his need, nor transgressing, meaning exceeding the limit in eating it while he finds other food. This is the view of Qatadah, al-Hasan, Ikrimah, al-Rabi', and Ibn Zayd.

The third: neither desiring in eating it for lust and pleasure, nor transgressing by pursuing eating to the point of satiety. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The root of al-baghy in the language is: seeking corruption. It is said: "baghat al-mar'ah tabghi bighaan" when the woman committed fornication.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And do not compel your slave girls to prostitution, if they desire chastity⁠﴾ [al-Nur: 33]. Sometimes al-baghy is used in seeking what is not corruption. The Arabs say: "The man went out in search of (bighaa') his camels," meaning in seeking them. From this is the saying of the poet:

Let not the seeking (bighaa') of good be prevented from you by the tying of amulets,
Indeed the ill-omened are like the auspicious days, and the auspicious are like the ill-omened.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 174–176:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who conceal what Allah has revealed of the Book﴾ means the scholars of the Jews concealed what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, had revealed in the Torah about the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the authenticity of his message.

﴿and exchange it for a small price﴾ means accepting bribes in return for concealing his message and altering his description. He called it "small" because of its brief duration and its evil consequence.

It is said: it is because what they used to take as bribes was small.

﴿They consume nothing into their bellies except the Fire﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: it means that it is unlawful, and Allah will punish them with the Fire because of it, so what they consume becomes fire. Thus He named it at present by what it will become in the end, as the poet said:

"And the mother of Simak, do not grieve, for death is what the mother bears."

﴿And Allah will not speak to them on the Day of Resurrection﴾. In this there are three opinions: (p-224)

The first: its meaning is that He will be angry with them, from the saying of people: "So-and-so does not speak to so-and-so" when he is angry with him.

The second: He will not send the angels to them with greetings.

The third: its meaning is that He will not make them hear His speech.

﴿Nor will He purify them﴾. In this there are two views. The first: it means He will not correct their wicked deeds.

The second: He will not praise them, and whoever Allah does not praise is punished. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾, meaning painful and agonizing.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those are the ones who have purchased error at the price of guidance﴾, meaning those scholars of the Jews mentioned earlier bought disbelief in exchange for faith, ﴿and punishment in exchange for forgiveness﴾, meaning the Fire in exchange for Paradise.

﴿How patient they are for the Fire!﴾ In this there are four opinions. The first: its meaning is "how bold they are toward the Fire," and this is the saying of Abu Salih.

The second: "how patient they are upon a deed that leads them to the Fire."

The third: its meaning is "how long will He keep them in the Fire," from the saying of people: "How patient is so-and-so in prison," meaning how long he is kept in it.

The fourth: in the sense of "what has made them patient for the Fire?"

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 177:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward the east or the west﴾ — the verse — has two interpretations. The first: its meaning is that righteousness is not the prayer alone, but rather righteousness is faith together with the performance of the obligations which Allah has prescribed. This was after the Hijrah to Madinah and the establishment of the obligations and the limits (ḥudūd). This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid.

The second: what is meant by this is the Jews and the Christians, because the Jews turn toward the west and the Christians turn toward the east in prayer, and they consider that to be righteousness. So Allah, mighty and majestic, informed them that this alone is not righteousness, until they believe in Allah and His Messenger and do what He mentioned. This is the view of Qatadah and al-Rabi'.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿But righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allah﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: its meaning is "but the one of righteousness is he who believes in Allah." The second: its meaning is "but righteousness is the righteousness of one who believes in Allah," meaning the affirmation of His oneness and the confirmation of His messengers. Al-Zajjaj related both of them.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and the Last Day﴾ means belief in the Resurrection and the recompense.

﴿and the angels﴾ means in what they were commanded with, from recording the deeds and carrying out the recompense.

﴿and the Book﴾ means the Qur'an, and what it includes of facing the Ka'bah, and that there is no qiblah other than it.

﴿and the prophets﴾ means belief in all the prophets, and that one does not believe in some of them and disbelieve in others.

﴿and gives wealth, in spite of love for it﴾ means in spite of love for wealth.

Ibn Mas'ud said: that one is healthy and miserly, hoping for long life and fearing poverty.

Al-Sha'bi used to narrate from Fatimah bint Qays that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Indeed, in wealth there is a right beyond zakat," and he recited this verse: ﴿It is not righteousness that you turn your faces toward...﴾ to its end. (p-226) Al-Sha'bi and al-Suddi went to the obligation of that on the basis of this report. It was related from the Prophet ﷺ that he was asked: "Which charity is the best?" He said: "Striving on behalf of a relative who is hostile (al-kāshiḥ)." The majority went to the view that there is no right in wealth beyond zakat, and that this is to be understood as referring to zakat or to voluntary charity chosen freely.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and gives wealth, in spite of love for it, to the near relatives﴾ intends the relatives of a man from both sides, through his parents. If this is understood as referring to zakat, two conditions are observed regarding them: the first: poverty; the second: the cessation of the obligation of maintenance.

If this is understood as referring to voluntary charity, neither of the two is considered, and it is permissible both with wealth and poverty, and with the obligation of maintenance or its cessation, because in giving to them while wealthy there is the maintenance of a righteous kinship tie. (p-227)

﴿and the orphans﴾ — they are those in whom two conditions are combined: minority and the absence of a father. Regarding the consideration of poverty for them there are two views, like the relatives.

﴿and the needy﴾ — they are those who lack the sufficient amount for subsistence. Regarding the consideration of their being Muslim there are two views.

﴿and the wayfarer﴾ — they are the poor travellers.

﴿and those who ask﴾ — they are those whom poverty has compelled to beg.

﴿and for the freeing of slaves﴾ — regarding them there are two views: the first: they are slaves who are to be freed, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him. The second: they are mukatabs (slaves under a contract of manumission) who are assisted in their contract with what they owe, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah.

﴿and establishes prayer﴾ means toward the Ka'bah, with its conditions and at its times.

﴿and gives zakat﴾ means to its rightful recipients when it becomes due.

﴿and those who fulfill their promise when they promise﴾ — this is in two respects: the first: the vows which are between him and Allah, the Exalted; the second: the contracts which are between him and the people, and both of them obligate him to fulfil them.

﴿and the patient in poverty and adversity﴾ — Ibn Mas'ud said: "poverty" (al-ba'sā') is poverty, and "adversity" (al-ḍarrā') is sickness.

﴿and in time of battle﴾ — that is, during fighting.

Regarding all of this there are two views: the first: that it is specific to the prophets, peace be upon them, because no one other than them is able to carry out all of this with its conditions. The second: that it is general, applying to all people, since the speech is addressed generally and the address is universal.

﴿Those are the ones who have been true﴾ — regarding this there are two interpretations: (p-228)

The first: their intentions corresponded to their deeds.

The second: their words agreed with their actions.

﴿And those are the righteous﴾ — regarding this there are two interpretations: the first: that their inner selves oppose their outward conduct. The second: that people praise them for what is not in them.

The commentary of Abu al-Hasan al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun) on verses 178–179 of Surah al-Baqarah

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿O you who have believed, retribution is prescribed for you concerning the slain﴾. The meaning of His saying ﴿prescribed for you﴾ is: obligated upon you. From this is the saying of Nabigha Banu Ja'da:

*O daughter of my paternal uncle, the Book of God has driven me away from you, so will I forbid what God has done?*

And the saying of Umar ibn Abi Rabi'a:

*Killing and fighting have been prescribed for us, and for the wanton women the trailing of their skirts.*

Qisas (retaliation, the requital of an act with its like) is derived from qassa al-athar, "tracing the footprints."

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿The free for the free, the slave for the slave, and the female for the female﴾. The people of ta'wil (interpretation) differed about this in four opinions.

The first: it was revealed concerning a people of the Arabs who were mighty and powerful, who would not kill a slave of theirs except a master, nor a woman of theirs except a man, out of arrogance in their strength and vanity in their might. So this verse was revealed concerning them. This is the view of al-Shafi'i and Qatada.

The second: it was revealed concerning two parties who had fought one another in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and a number of men, women and slaves were killed from both parties. So this verse was revealed concerning them, and the Messenger of God ﷺ made the blood money of a man equal to the blood money of a man, the blood money of a woman equal to the blood money of a woman, and the blood money of a slave equal to the blood money of a slave, and then reconciled them. This is the view of al-Suddi and Abu Malik.

The third: that this is a command from God, Exalted and Majestic, to offset the blood money of the killer who is subject to retaliation against the blood money of the slain whose kin is seeking retaliation, and to take the surplus after the offsetting. This is the view of Ali, who used to say in interpreting the verse: Whichever free man kills a slave, he is liable to qawad (retaliation), and if the masters of the slave wish to kill the free man, they may kill him and offset the price of the slave against the blood money of the free man, and pay to the heirs of the free man the remainder of his blood money. And whichever slave kills a free man, he is liable to qawad, and if the heirs of the free man wish, they may kill the slave and offset the price of the slave against the blood money of the free man, and take the remainder of the free man's blood money. And whichever man kills a woman, he is liable to qawad, and if the heirs of the woman wish, they may kill him and pay the remainder of the blood money to the heirs of the man. And whichever woman kills a man, she is liable to qawad, and if the heirs of the man wish, they may kill her and take half the blood money.

The fourth: God, Exalted and Majestic, prescribed by this verse at the beginning of Islam that a man be killed for a man, a woman for a woman, and a slave for a slave. Then His saying in Surah al-Ma'idah abrogated that (naskh, abrogation): ﴿And We prescribed for them therein that the life is for the life﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45]. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿But whoever is pardoned by his brother in any respect, then pursuit should be made in a reasonable manner, and payment made to him with good conduct﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions.

The first: whoever is pardoned by the victim's heir from retaliation against him, then there is pursuit in a reasonable manner, which is that the heir seeks the blood money in a reasonable way, and the killer pays the blood money with good conduct. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.

The second: the meaning of His saying ﴿whoever is pardoned by his brother in any respect﴾ is "whoever is left with a surplus." This is the interpretation of those who claim that the verse was revealed concerning two parties who were at the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and from both parties some were slain, so they offset the blood money of the slain against one another. Whoever is left with a remainder, let him pursue it in a reasonable manner, and let the one who owes the surplus repay it with good conduct. The meaning of ﴿whoever is pardoned by his brother in any respect﴾ is: whoever has a surplus due to him from his brother who is the killer. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The third: this is to be understood in light of Ali's (may God be pleased with him) interpretation of the beginning of the verse, concerning retaliation between man and woman, free and slave, and the payment of the surplus of blood money between them.

Then, concerning "pursuit in a reasonable manner" and "payment to him with good conduct," there are two possibilities mentioned by al-Zajjaj. The first: that "pursuit in a reasonable manner" refers to the heir of the slain, that he should demand the blood money in a reasonable way, and "payment" refers to the killer, that he should pay the blood money with good conduct. The second: that both refer to the killer, that he should pay the blood money in a reasonable and good manner.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿That is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy﴾, meaning the option of the heir between retaliation and blood money. Qatada said: The People of the Torah used to say, "It is only retaliation or pardon, with no compensation between them," and the People of the Gospel used to say, "It is only compensation or pardon, with no retaliation between them." So this community was given retaliation, pardon and blood money, whichever they choose, which was made lawful for them and was not for any community before them. This is His saying, Exalted: ﴿That is an alleviation from your Lord and a mercy﴾.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿And whoever transgresses after that, for him is a painful punishment﴾, meaning whoever kills after having taken the blood money, for him is a painful punishment. Concerning this there are four interpretations.

The first: the painful punishment is that he be killed in retaliation. This is the view of Ikrimah, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak.

The second: the painful punishment is that the ruler kills him as an absolute requirement, with no pardon. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj, and it is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ used to say: "I will not pardon a man who kills after taking the blood money."

The third: the painful punishment is the punishment of the ruler (sultan).

The fourth: the painful punishment is the reclaiming of the blood money from him, and there is no retaliation against him. This is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri.

His saying, Exalted: ﴿And in retaliation there is life for you﴾. Concerning this there are two views.

The first: when the wrongdoer who transgresses remembers it, he refrains from killing, and so there is life. This is the view of Mujahid and Qatada.

The second: that the prescription of retaliation upon the killer, and the abandonment of transgression onto one who is not a killer, is a life for souls, because when the killer knows that his own soul will be taken for the soul he killed, he refrains from killing, and so there is life: either he is not killed in retaliation, or the victim is not killed unjustly.

The two meanings are close, but the second is more general, and it is the meaning of the saying of al-Suddi.

His saying, Exalted: ﴿O people of understanding﴾, meaning O people of intellects, because life in retaliation is understood through reflection.

His saying, Exalted: ﴿That you may be God-fearing﴾. Ibn Zayd said: That you may be mindful, lest you kill him and be killed for him.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 180–182:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿It has been prescribed for you, when death approaches any of you﴾, meaning: it has been made obligatory upon you. His saying ﴿when [death] approaches﴾ does not intend the mention of the bequest at the moment death arrives, because the dying person is occupied with other matters. Rather, the gift is to be made by what precedes the arrival of death through bequest. Then He, exalted, said: ﴿if he leaves behind wealth, [a bequest] to parents and close relatives﴾. The "wealth" (khayr) here means property, according to the consensus. Mujahid said: "Khayr in the whole Qur'an means property."

﴿And indeed he is, in his love of wealth (khayr), intense﴾ [al-Adiyat: 8], meaning property. ﴿Indeed, I have preferred the love of wealth (khayr) over the remembrance of my Lord﴾ [Sad: 32]. ﴿So write them [a contract of emancipation], if you know in them any good (khayr)﴾ [al-Nur: 33]. And Shu'ayb said: ﴿Indeed, I see you in prosperity (khayr)﴾ [Hud: 84], meaning wealth and property.

The scholars differed regarding whether the ruling of this verse remains in effect. The majority of the Successors and jurists held that acting upon it was obligatory before the prescription of inheritance, lest a man place his property with distant people seeking reputation and show. When the verse of inheritance was revealed, specifying the entitled heirs and determining what they deserve, the obligation of bequest was abrogated by it, and the Sunnah forbade bequest to heirs. Others said: its ruling was established regarding bequest to parents and close relatives as a binding right; when the verses of inheritance were revealed and the inheritance of the two parents was prescribed, the bequest to parents and to every heir was abrogated by it, and the obligation of bequest to close relatives who do not inherit remained in its state. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatadah, Tawus, and Jabir ibn Zayd.

If one bequeaths a third of his property to someone other than his relatives, those who hold this view differ regarding the ruling on his bequest, in three positions. The first: that one-third of the third is returned to his relatives, and two-thirds of the third go to the one to whom he bequeathed it. This is the view of Qatadah.

The second: that two-thirds of the third are returned to his relatives, and one-third of the third goes to the one to whom he bequeathed it. This is the view of Jabir ibn Zayd.

The third: that he returns the whole third to his relatives. This is the view of Tawus.

They differed regarding the amount of property from which one is obligated to bequeath, in three opinions. The first: it is one thousand dirhams, interpreting His saying ﴿if he leaves behind wealth (khayr)﴾ as meaning that wealth (khayr) is one thousand dirhams. This is the view of Ali.

The second: from one thousand dirhams down to five hundred dirhams. This is the view of Ibrahim al-Nakha'i.

The third: that it is not limited, and that bequest is obligatory on little property and much. This is the view of al-Zuhri.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿according to what is reasonable, as a duty upon the God-fearing﴾. His saying "according to what is reasonable" may bear two meanings: (p-233)

The first: with the moderate justice that involves neither deficiency nor excess.

The second: "according to what is reasonable" means from his property, not from what is unknown.

His saying, exalted: ﴿as a duty upon the God-fearing﴾ means: by piety, from the heirs, that they not be wasteful, and from the relatives, that they not be stingy. Ibn Mas'ud said: "The nearest first, then the nearest," meaning the most needy first, then the most needy.

The limit beyond which there is no extravagance is one-third, due to the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "A third, and a third is much." Al-Hasan narrated that Abu Bakr and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, bequeathed a fifth and said: "Let him bequeath with what Allah has approved for Himself, a fifth." He used to say: "A fifth is reasonable, a quarter is effort, and a third is the most that judges permit."

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿So whoever alters it after he has heard it﴾, meaning: whoever changes the bequest after he has heard it. The word is masculine although the bequest (wasiyyah) is feminine, because it refers to the statement of the testator, and his statement is masculine.

﴿Indeed, its sin is upon those who alter it﴾, meaning those who hear it and divert it from its rightful recipient, either by inclination or betrayal. The deceased has the reward of his intention and the reward of his bequest, even if it is changed after him.

His saying, exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾, meaning: All-Hearing of the words of the testator, All-Knowing of the action of the executor.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿But whoever fears from a testator partiality (janaf) or sin and brings about reconciliation among them﴾. The exegetes differed in the interpretation of this, in five opinions. The first: its interpretation is: whoever attends a sick person who is making a bequest as he approaches death, and fears that he will err in his bequest, doing what is not his right, or that he will deliberately act unjustly in it, commanding what is not his to command, there is no blame upon the one who attends and hears that from him, if he brings about reconciliation between him and his heirs by ordering him to justice in his bequest. This is the view of Mujahid.

The second: its interpretation is: whoever fears from the executors of the deceased partiality (janaf) in his bequest, and reconciles between his heirs and those to whom he bequeathed, regarding what was bequeathed to them, until he returns the bequest to justice, there is no sin upon him. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Qatadah.

The third: its interpretation is: whoever fears from a testator partiality or sin in his gift to his heirs at the approach of his term, so that he gives some and not others, there is no sin upon him in reconciling among his heirs concerning that. This is the view of Ata.

The fourth: its interpretation is: whoever fears from a testator partiality, or sin, in a bequest to someone other than his heirs, by which its benefit returns to his heirs, and reconciles among his heirs, there is no sin upon him. This is the view of Tawus.

The fifth: its interpretation is: whoever fears from a testator, for his parents and relatives, partiality toward some of them over others, and reconciles between the parents and the relatives, there is no sin upon him. This is the view of al-Suddi.

Regarding His saying, ﴿partiality (janaf) or sin﴾, there are two interpretations: The first: that janaf is error and sin is deliberate wrong. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The second: that janaf is inclination, and sin is that he has sinned by favoring some of them over others. This is the view of Ata and Ibn Zayd.

Janaf in the language of the Arabs is injustice and deviation from the truth, and from it is the saying of the poet:

؎ They are the patrons, yet they have been unjust (janafu) toward us, and we are indeed visitors to their meeting.

The first: its interpretation is: whoever attends a sick person who is making a bequest as he approaches death, and fears that he will err in his bequest, doing what is not his right, or that he will deliberately act unjustly in it, commanding what is not his to command, there is no blame upon the one who attends and hears that from him, if he brings about reconciliation between him and his heirs by ordering him to justice in his bequest. This is the view of Mujahid.

The second: its interpretation is: whoever fears from the executors of the deceased partiality (janaf) in his bequest, and reconciles between his heirs and those to whom he bequeathed, regarding what was bequeathed to them, until he returns the bequest to justice, there is no sin upon him. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Qatadah.

The third: its interpretation is: whoever fears from a testator partiality or sin in his gift to his heirs at the approach of his term, so that he gives some and not others, there is no sin upon him in reconciling among his heirs concerning that. This is the view of Ata.

The fourth: its interpretation is: whoever fears from a testator partiality, or sin, in a bequest to someone other than his heirs, by which its benefit returns to his heirs, and reconciles among his heirs, there is no sin upon him. This is the view of Tawus.

The fifth: its interpretation is: whoever fears from a testator, for his parents and relatives, partiality toward some of them over others, and reconciles between the parents and the relatives, there is no sin upon him. This is the view of al-Suddi.

Regarding His saying, ﴿partiality (janaf) or sin﴾, there are two interpretations: The first: that janaf is error and sin is deliberate wrong. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The second: that janaf is inclination, and sin is that he has sinned by favoring some of them over others. This is the view of Ata and Ibn Zayd.

Janaf in the language of the Arabs is injustice and deviation from the truth, and from it is the saying of the poet:

؎ They are the patrons, yet they have been unjust (janafu) toward us, and we are indeed visitors to their meeting.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 180–182:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿It has been prescribed for you, when death approaches any of you﴾, meaning: it has been made obligatory upon you. His saying ﴿when [death] approaches﴾ does not intend the mention of the bequest at the moment death arrives, because the dying person is occupied with other matters. Rather, the gift is to be made by what precedes the arrival of death through bequest. Then He, exalted, said: ﴿if he leaves behind wealth, [a bequest] to parents and close relatives﴾. The "wealth" (khayr) here means property, according to the consensus. Mujahid said: "Khayr in the whole Qur'an means property."

﴿And indeed he is, in his love of wealth (khayr), intense﴾ [al-Adiyat: 8], meaning property. ﴿Indeed, I have preferred the love of wealth (khayr) over the remembrance of my Lord﴾ [Sad: 32]. ﴿So write them [a contract of emancipation], if you know in them any good (khayr)﴾ [al-Nur: 33]. And Shu'ayb said: ﴿Indeed, I see you in prosperity (khayr)﴾ [Hud: 84], meaning wealth and property.

The scholars differed regarding whether the ruling of this verse remains in effect. The majority of the Successors and jurists held that acting upon it was obligatory before the prescription of inheritance, lest a man place his property with distant people seeking reputation and show. When the verse of inheritance was revealed, specifying the entitled heirs and determining what they deserve, the obligation of bequest was abrogated by it, and the Sunnah forbade bequest to heirs. Others said: its ruling was established regarding bequest to parents and close relatives as a binding right; when the verses of inheritance were revealed and the inheritance of the two parents was prescribed, the bequest to parents and to every heir was abrogated by it, and the obligation of bequest to close relatives who do not inherit remained in its state. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatadah, Tawus, and Jabir ibn Zayd.

If one bequeaths a third of his property to someone other than his relatives, those who hold this view differ regarding the ruling on his bequest, in three positions. The first: that one-third of the third is returned to his relatives, and two-thirds of the third go to the one to whom he bequeathed it. This is the view of Qatadah.

The second: that two-thirds of the third are returned to his relatives, and one-third of the third goes to the one to whom he bequeathed it. This is the view of Jabir ibn Zayd.

The third: that he returns the whole third to his relatives. This is the view of Tawus.

They differed regarding the amount of property from which one is obligated to bequeath, in three opinions. The first: it is one thousand dirhams, interpreting His saying ﴿if he leaves behind wealth (khayr)﴾ as meaning that wealth (khayr) is one thousand dirhams. This is the view of Ali.

The second: from one thousand dirhams down to five hundred dirhams. This is the view of Ibrahim al-Nakha'i.

The third: that it is not limited, and that bequest is obligatory on little property and much. This is the view of al-Zuhri.

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿according to what is reasonable, as a duty upon the God-fearing﴾. His saying "according to what is reasonable" may bear two meanings: (p-233)

The first: with the moderate justice that involves neither deficiency nor excess.

The second: "according to what is reasonable" means from his property, not from what is unknown.

His saying, exalted: ﴿as a duty upon the God-fearing﴾ means: by piety, from the heirs, that they not be wasteful, and from the relatives, that they not be stingy. Ibn Mas'ud said: "The nearest first, then the nearest," meaning the most needy first, then the most needy.

The limit beyond which there is no extravagance is one-third, due to the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "A third, and a third is much." Al-Hasan narrated that Abu Bakr and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, bequeathed a fifth and said: "Let him bequeath with what Allah has approved for Himself, a fifth." He used to say: "A fifth is reasonable, a quarter is effort, and a third is the most that judges permit."

Then He, exalted, said: ﴿So whoever alters it after he has heard it﴾, meaning: whoever changes the bequest after he has heard it. The word is masculine although the bequest (wasiyyah) is feminine, because it refers to the statement of the testator, and his statement is masculine.

His saying, exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾, meaning: All-Hearing of the words of the testator, All-Knowing of the action of the executor.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 183–184:

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿O you who have believed, fasting has been prescribed for you﴾ means: fasting has been made obligatory upon you. Ṣiyām (fasting) in every sense means abstaining from something. From His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I have vowed to the Most Merciful a fast﴾, meaning silence, because it is abstention from speech. A Bedouin censured a people and said: "They fast from what is good and they speak excessively of indecencies." Its origin is taken from the fasting of horses, which is their refraining from running and from fodder. Al-Nābigha al-Dhubyānī said:

؎ Some horses are fasting, and others not fasting, beneath the dust, while others chew the bits.

For this reason it is said of the one standing at midday: "The day has fasted," because the sun delays in it from moving, so it becomes, through its delay, like one who refrains from it. The poet said:

؎ So leave her, and draw away your worry with a swift she-camel, when the day fasts and the heat wave blazes.

However, in the Sharia, fasting is only abstention from the prohibited things of fasting during its time. Thus He made fasting one of the most emphatic of worships and the most binding of its obligations, to the extent that it is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah, mighty and majestic, says: every deed of the son of Adam is for himself except fasting, for it is for Me and I will reward it. And the odour from the mouth of the fasting person is more fragrant to Allah than the scent of musk." The reason fasting is specifically attributed to Him, although all worships are for Him, is due to two matters by which fasting is distinguished from the rest of the worships:

The first: fasting is a restraint from the pleasures of the self and its desires, which the other worships do not restrain.

The second: fasting is a secret between the servant and his Lord, which appears to none but Him. Therefore it became specially His. The other worships are apparent, and one may do them out of pretence and show, so fasting is more особенно (more specifically) His than others.

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿as it was prescribed for those before you﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions: The first: they are the Christians; this is the saying of al-Shaʿbī, al-Rabīʿ and Asbāṭ.

The second: they are the People of the Book; this is the saying of Mujāhid.

The third: they are all people; this is the saying of Qatādah.

They differed concerning the point of comparison between our fasting and the fasting of those before us, on two views. The first: the comparison is in the ruling of fasting and its description, not in its number, because the Jews fast from ʿAtama (night prayer) to ʿAtama and do not eat anything after sleep. The Muslims were upon that at the beginning of Islam, not eating anything after sleep, until what befell ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb and Abū Qays ibn Ṣirma occurred, so Allah, exalted is He, permitted them eating and drinking. This is the saying of al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The difference between our fasting and the fasting of the People of the Book is the pre-dawn meal (suḥūr)." The second view: the comparison is in the number of fasting days, and concerning this there are two sayings. The first: that Allah had prescribed for the Christians the fasting of thirty days as He prescribed it for us, so it sometimes fell in the summer heat, so they moved it to the season between winter and summer, then they atoned for it by fasting twenty additional days, to be a purification of their sins and an expiation for their alteration. This is the saying of al-Shaʿbī.

The second: they are the Jews, who were required to fast three days from every Ashura and three days of every month, and they remained upon that for seventeen months until it was abrogated by the fasting of Ramadan. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The first thing abrogated was the matter of the qibla and the first fasting."

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that you may become righteous﴾, there are two sayings: The first: so that you may guard against what has been forbidden to you during fasting, from eating food, drinking drink, and intercourse with women; this is the saying of Abū Jaʿfar al-Ṭabarī.

The second: its meaning is that fasting is a means that leads its doer to the fear of Allah, because of what it contains of subduing the self, breaking desire, and removing arrogance; this is the meaning of the saying of al-Zajjāj.

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿for a certain number of days﴾. Concerning this there are two sayings: The first: they are the days of the month of Ramadan that He later explained; this is the saying of Ibn Abī Layla and the majority of the exegetes.

The second: they are the fasting of three days of every month, which were obligatory before the fasting of the month of Ramadan, then were abrogated by it; this is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah and ʿAṭāʾ, and they are the white days (al-ayyām al-bīḍ) of every month. Concerning them there are two aspects: The first: that it is the twelfth and what follows it. The second aspect: that they are the thirteenth and what follows it, and this is the more apparent of the two aspects, because the days of the month are divided among the Arabs into ten parts, each part of which is three days, and each has a specific name. The first of them is three ghurar, then three shuhab, then three buhar, then three ʿushar, then three bīḍ, then three durac. The durac is the blackness of the front of a sheep and the whiteness of its rear, so these three were called durac because the moon sets in their first part, so their night becomes durac due to the blackness of its beginning and the whiteness of its end. Then three khunas, because the moon recedes (yakhnis) in them, i.e. delays. Then three duhum, and it is said: ḥanādis due to their darkness. Then three fuḥum, because the moon blackens (yatafaḥḥam) in them, i.e. rises at the end of the night. Then three rādd, and they are the last of the month, taken from al-radda, which is to hasten the movement of its legs until it places them where its hands were.

Abū Zayd and Ibn al-Aʿrābī have related that they assigned to the moon in each night of the ten nights a name, and they said: "A night ʿatama, Suhaylah; its people alighted at Rumaylah." And "the son of two nights: a story of Mayn, false and manifest"; Ibn al-Aʿrābī narrated it as "kadhib wa Mayn" (a lie and Mayn). And "the son of three: little tarrying." And "the son of four: ʿatamat rubaʿ, neither hungry nor nursing." And "the son of five: a talk and companionship." And "the son of six: travel and spend the night." And "the son of seven: the nocturnal walk of the hyena." And "the son of eight: a moon bright and lit." And "the son of nine: the thong of the sandal has snapped." And in the narration other than Abū Zayd: "in it the jiz' is gathered." And "the son of ten: a third of the month", related from Abū Zayd and others, and no separate name was assigned to it for what exceeds ten.

They differed concerning when the crescent (hilāl) becomes a moon (qamar). A group said: it is called hilāl for two nights, then after that it is called qamar. Others said: it is called hilāl up to three, then after that it is called qamar. Others said: it is called hilāl until it becomes ḥajjar, and its ḥajjar is that it encircles itself with a fine line; this is the saying of al-Aṣmaʿī. Others said: it is called hilāl until its light overpowers the blackness of the night; when its light overpowers, it is called qamar, and this does not occur except on the seventh night.

[Then we returned to the exegesis of what remains of the verse.] His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever among you is ill or on a journey﴾, meaning: an ill person who, with his illness, is not able to fast, or one on a journey for whom fasting is burdensome during his travel.

﴿then an equal number of other days﴾. Concerning this there are two sayings: The first: that with the existence of travel, he is obliged to make up the fast, whether he fasted during his journey or broke it; this is the saying of Dāwūd al-Ẓāhirī.

The second: that in the speech there is an omitted element, its estimation being: "and he broke the fast, then an equal number of other days." If he fasted during his illness or journey, he does not need to make it up, because breaking the fast on account of them is a concession, not an obligation; this is the saying of al-Shāfiʿī, Mālik, Abū Ḥanīfah and the majority of jurists.

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿And for those who are able to fast, there is a ransom: the feeding of a poor person﴾. Thus most readers recited it. Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujāhid recited: ﴿And for those who are able to fast (yuṭīqūnahu), there is a ransom﴾. Its interpretation: and for those who are charged with it, but cannot fast due to their inability to do so, like the aged man and the aged woman, the pregnant and the nursing woman: a ransom of feeding a poor person, and there is no making up upon them because of their inability.

On the well-known reading, there are two interpretations: The first: that it came at the beginning of Islam, when Allah, exalted is He, gave those among all people who were able to fast the choice between fasting without ransom, and breaking the fast and paying a ransom of feeding a poor person for each day. Then this was abrogated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾. It was said: rather it was abrogated by His saying: ﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾. This is the saying of Ibn ʿUmar, ʿIkrimah, al-Shaʿbī, al-Zuhrī, ʿAlqamah and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

The second: that its ruling remains valid, and the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and for those who are able to fast﴾ is: they used to be able to fast in their youth, and when they became old and were unable to fast due to their old age, they should break the fast. This is the saying of Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab and al-Suddī.

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever volunteers good, it is better for him﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations: The first: whoever volunteers by feeding more than one poor person, it is better for him; this is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujāhid, Ṭāwūs and al-Suddī.

The second: whoever volunteers by fasting along with the ransom, it is better for him; this is the saying of al-Zuhrī and the narration of Ibn Jurayj from Mujāhid.

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾. It admits two interpretations: The first: fasting while travelling is better than breaking it and making it up afterward. The second: fasting is better and more rewarded for one who is able, than paying the expiation for one who breaks it due to inability.

﴿if you only knew﴾ admits two meanings: The first: if you know what I have legislated for you and clarified of your religion. The second: if you know the excellence of your deeds and the reward of your actions.

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿And for those who are able to fast, there is a ransom: the feeding of a poor person﴾. Thus most readers recited it. Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujāhid recited: ﴿And for those who are able to fast (yuṭīqūnahu), there is a ransom﴾. Its interpretation: and for those who are charged with it, but cannot fast due to their inability to do so, like the aged man and the aged woman, the pregnant and the nursing woman: a ransom of feeding a poor person, and there is no making up upon them because of their inability.

On the well-known reading, there are two interpretations: The first: that it came at the beginning of Islam, when Allah, exalted is He, gave those among all people who were able to fast the choice between fasting without ransom, and breaking the fast and paying a ransom of feeding a poor person for each day. Then this was abrogated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾. It was said: rather it was abrogated by His saying: ﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾. This is the saying of Ibn ʿUmar, ʿIkrimah, al-Shaʿbī, al-Zuhrī, ʿAlqamah and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

The second: that its ruling remains valid, and the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and for those who are able to fast﴾ is: they used to be able to fast in their youth, and when they became old and were unable to fast due to their old age, they should break the fast. This is the saying of Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab and al-Suddī.

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿So whoever volunteers good, it is better for him﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations: The first: whoever volunteers by feeding more than one poor person, it is better for him; this is the saying of Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujāhid, Ṭāwūs and al-Suddī.

The second: whoever volunteers by fasting along with the ransom, it is better for him; this is the saying of al-Zuhrī and the narration of Ibn Jurayj from Mujāhid.

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿And that you fast is better for you﴾. It admits two interpretations: The first: fasting while travelling is better than breaking it and making it up afterward. The second: fasting is better and more rewarded for one who is able, than paying the expiation for one who breaks it due to inability.

﴿if you only knew﴾ admits two meanings: The first: if you know what I have legislated for you and clarified of your religion. The second: if you know the excellence of your deeds and the reward of your actions.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 185:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿The month of Ramadan in which the Qur'an was sent down﴾. As for "the month" (al-shahr), it is derived from "fame" (al-shuhra). From this comes the saying: "So-and-so unsheathed his sword" (shahara sayfahu), meaning he drew it out. As for Ramadan, some lexicographers claim it was named for the intensity of the heat found in it, to the point that the weaning camels' young were scorched (tarmadu) in it, just as the month of Hajj was named Dhu al-Hijjah. In the Jahiliyyah, the month of Ramadan was called Natiq.

As for Mujahid, he disliked that it be said "Ramadan," and said: "Perhaps it is among the names of Allah, Mighty and Majestic."

As for the sending down of the Qur'an, there are two opinions. The first: Allah, Exalted, sent the Qur'an down all at once from the Preserved Tablet to the lowest heaven in the month of Ramadan, on the Night of Decree (laylat al-qadr) within it. Then He sent it down upon His Prophet ﷺ over the course He willed for its revelation to him.

Abu Muslim narrated from Wathilah, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "The scrolls of Ibrahim were sent down on the first night of Ramadan, the Torah was sent down six nights after Ramadan had passed, the Gospel was sent down thirteen nights after Ramadan had passed, and the Qur'an was sent down on the twenty-fourth of Ramadan."

The second: it means that the Qur'an was sent down concerning the obligation of fasting it, and this is the view of Mujahid.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿a guidance for mankind﴾, meaning guidance for people.

﴿And clear proofs of the guidance and the criterion﴾, that is, clear proofs concerning the lawful and the unlawful, and a criterion between truth and falsehood.

﴿So whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast it﴾. The month is never absent from anyone. Regarding its interpretation there are three views. The first: whoever witnesses the beginning of the month while he is resident, it is obligatory upon him to fast it to its end, and he has no right to break his fast during the remainder of it. This is the view of Ali, Ibn Abbas, and al-Suddi.

The second: whoever of you witnesses the month, let him fast what of it he witnesses while he is resident, excluding what he did not witness while traveling. This is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and al-Hasan al-Basri.

The third: whoever witnesses it as an adult, sane, and legally responsible, let him fast it, and the obligation of fasting the rest of it does not lapse if he becomes insane during it. This is the view of Abu Hanifa and his two companions.

﴿And whoever is ill or on a journey, then a number of other days﴾. He repeated the mention of breaking the fast due to illness and travel, although it had been mentioned shortly before, because it was abrogated in the ruling of that verse, so he repeated it, lest the abrogated ruling be joined with the abrogating one. Its implied meaning is: whoever is ill or on a journey during the month of Ramadan and breaks his fast, then for him is the same number of days of what he broke, to make them up afterward.

They differed regarding the illness which permits breaking the fast during Ramadan, on three views. The first: any illness with which one is unable to pray standing; this is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri. The second: an illness in which, most likely, fasting would greatly increase its severity beyond what is bearable; this is the view of al-Shafi'i. The third: any illness to which the name "illness" applies; this is the view of Ibn Sirin.

As for travel, they differed concerning it on three views. The first: whatever a journey applies to, whether long or short; this is the view of Dawud. The second: a distance of three days' march; this is the view of Abu Hanifa.

They differed regarding whether breaking the fast during travel is obligatory on two views: the first, that it is obligatory, the view of Ibn Abbas; the second, that it is permissible, the view of the majority.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿Allah intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾. Ibn Abbas said: "Ease is breaking the fast, and hardship is fasting during travel." Similar was narrated from Mujahid and Qatadah.

﴿And that you complete the number﴾, meaning the number of what you broke the fast of, and in the month of Ramadan by making it up at another time.

﴿And that you glorify Allah for having guided you﴾. It was said: this refers to the takbir of breaking the fast from the beginning of the month.

His saying, ﴿for having guided you﴾, meaning to the fasting of the month of Ramadan, and it may be that it refers to the general guidance He gave us to His religion.

﴿So that you may be thankful﴾. This admits of two meanings: the first, that you give thanks for His guidance to you; the second, for what He has bestowed upon you of the reward of obedience to Him. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on surah 2, verse 186:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near﴾. The people of ta'wil (interpretation) differed regarding the occasion of revelation (*sabab al-nuzul*) of this verse, in four opinions. The first: it was revealed concerning a questioner who asked the Prophet ﷺ, saying: "O Muhammad, is our Lord near so that we may confide to Him, or far so that we must call out to Him?" So this verse was revealed. This is the saying of al-Hasan al-Basri.

The second: it was revealed concerning a people who asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ at what hour they should call upon Allah. This is the saying of 'Ata' and al-Suddi.

The third: it was revealed in answer to a people who said: "How should we call upon Him?" This is the saying of Qatada.

The fourth: it was revealed concerning a people when His saying, may He be exalted, was revealed: ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾, and they said: "To where should we call Him?" This is the saying of Mujahid. (p-243)

Regarding His saying, ﴿near﴾, there are two interpretations. One: nearness of response. The other: nearness to hearing the supplication.

Regarding His saying, ﴿I respond to the invocation of the supplicant when he calls upon Me﴾, there are two interpretations. One: its meaning is, "I hear the supplication of the one who calls upon Me," and He expressed hearing by response, because hearing is the precursor of response.

The second: He intended responding to the supplicant with what he asks. The supplicant's request is either in accordance with the public good (*maslaha*) or contrary to it. If it is contrary to the public good, responding to it is not permissible. If it is in accordance with the public good, the supplicant's condition is one of two: either he has fulfilled the conditions of the request, or he is deficient in them. If he has fulfilled them, his response is permissible, and regarding whether it is obligatory there are two opinions. One: it is obligatory, because it runs in the manner of the reward for deeds, since supplication is an act of worship whose reward is response. The second: it is not obligatory, because it is a desire and a request, so responding to it becomes an act of bounty.

If he is deficient in the conditions of the request, his response is not granted, and regarding its permissibility there are two opinions. One: it is not permissible; this is the saying of those who made it obligatory when its conditions are fulfilled. The second: it is permissible; this is the saying of those who did not make it obligatory when its conditions are fulfilled.

Regarding His saying, ﴿So let them respond to Me﴾, there are four interpretations. One: the *istijaba* (responding) means *ijaba* (answering); one says "istajabtu lahu" meaning "ajabtuhu." This is the saying of Abu 'Ubayda, and he recited the verse of Ka'b ibn Sa'd al-Ghanawi:

Many a caller called: "O you who answers my call!" but no answerer answered him at that time.

That is, he did not answer him.

The second: *istijaba* is seeking agreement with answering. This is the saying of Tha'lab. (p-244)

The third: its meaning is "so let them respond to Me with obedience."

The fourth: "so let them respond to Me," meaning, "so let them call upon Me."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 187:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is made lawful for you on the night of the fast to go in unto your wives﴾. Ibn Mas'ud used to recite both (al-rafath) and (al-rufuth), and it means intercourse in his statement. Its origin is obscene speech, as al-Ajjaj said:

﴿... ... ... ∗∗∗ ...from idle talk and obscene speech﴾

It is used as a euphemism for intercourse, because when it is mentioned in a place other than its proper place it becomes vulgarity.

And in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are a garment for you and you are a garment for them﴾, there are three interpretations. The first: they are like a garment, since each of the two spouses reaches the other, and covers himself with the other as with a worn garment, as al-Nabigha al-Ja'di said:

؎ When the clamor bent her side, ∗∗∗ she bent upon him and became a garment.

The second: they are a garment, meaning a source of tranquility (sakan), in accordance with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We made the night a garment﴾ [al-Naba' 10], that is, a tranquility. This is the view of Mujahid, Qatadah and al-Suddi. (p-245)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves﴾. The cause of this betrayal by which the people were betraying themselves was two things. The first: approaching the women. The second: eating and drinking. This is because Allah, exalted is He, had permitted at the beginning of Islam eating, drinking and intercourse during the night of the fast before a person sleeps, and forbade them to him after he sleeps, until 'Umar ibn al-Khattab came one night in the month of Ramadan, desiring his wife. She said to him: "I have already slept," and he thought she was making an excuse to him, so he had intercourse with her. Abu Qays ibn Sirmah also came, having been working on a land of his, and he wanted to eat, so his wife said to him: "We will prepare something for you." His eyes overcame him, then she brought the food to him, but he did not eat from it. When he woke in the morning he was exhausted.

'Umar and Abu Qays informed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of what had happened from both of them, so Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Allah knew that you were betraying yourselves﴾ ﴿so He turned to you and pardoned you﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: the pardon of their sins. The second: the pardon regarding the prohibition of that after sleep.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So now, associate with them (bashiruhunna)﴾, meaning intercourse, because the origin of mubasharah is the joining of skin to skin. And this was from Him an explanation of what had occurred in the intercourse of 'Umar.

And in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And seek what Allah has prescribed for you﴾ there are three views. The first: seeking offspring; this is the view of Mujahid, Ikrimah and al-Suddi. The second: the Night of Power (laylat al-qadr); this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, who used to recite: ﴿And seek what Allah has prescribed for you﴾. The third: what Allah, exalted is He, has made lawful for you and permitted; this is the view of Qatadah.

Then He, exalted is He, said regarding what had occurred with Abu Qays ibn Sirmah: ﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread at dawn﴾ (p-246). There has been disagreement about what is meant by the white thread and the black thread, according to three opinions. The first: what Sahl ibn Sa'd narrated, who said: "When the verse ﴿And eat and drink until the white thread becomes distinct to you from the black thread﴾ was revealed, some men who wished to fast would tie a white thread and a black thread to their feet, and would continue eating until they could see both of them distinctly. Then Allah, exalted is He, revealed afterwards ﴿of dawn﴾, and they knew that it means night and day."

The second opinion: that by the white thread He means the light of day, which is the second dawn, and by the black thread the blackness of the night before the second dawn.

Al-Sha'bi narrated from 'Adi ibn Hatim that he took two threads, a white and a black, and placed them under his pillow, and he would observe them during his fast. Then he informed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he said: "Indeed you have a wide pillow; it is only the whiteness of the day and the blackness of the night." It was called a thread because the first appearance of whiteness extends like a thread. The poet said:

؎ The white thread is the light of the morning breaking forth, ∗∗∗ and the black thread is the color of the night, concealed.

In their speech, "thread" is an expression for a color.

The third: what is related from Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, that the white thread is the light of the sun; a similar view is related from 'Ali and Ibn Mas'ud.

Zirr ibn Hubaysh narrated from Hudhayfah, who said: "The Prophet ﷺ used to take the pre-dawn meal (tasahhur) while I could see the places of the arrows." He said: "I said: after the dawn?" He said: "It is the dawn, except that the sun has not risen." This view is one on which consensus has been established against it. Sawadah ibn Handhalah narrated from Samurah ibn Jundub who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Let not the adhan of Bilal nor the elongated dawn prevent you from your pre-dawn meal, but rather the dawn that spreads across the horizon." Al-Harith ibn 'Abd al-Rahman narrated from Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Thawban (p-247)

who said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Dawn is of two kinds: that which is like the tail of a wolf does not make anything unlawful, but as for the spreading one that covers the horizon, it makes prayer lawful and makes food unlawful."

As for "fajr" (dawn), it is a verbal noun from their saying: "fajara al-ma'" (the water gushed forth), when it flowed and burst out. Therefore the first gleam of the sun's light at its rising is called "fajr," because its light bursts forth. Thus the time of the fast, in which eating and drinking are agreed to be forbidden and permitted outside of it, is what lies between the rising of the second dawn and the setting of the sun.

'Ata' narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "The greatest of fasting people in reward are those closest to them in breaking the fast at night and day." ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾, meaning by it the setting of the sun.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not associate with them while you are devoting yourselves to worship in the mosques﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: by mubasharah is meant intercourse; this is the view of most scholars. (p-248)

The second: what is less than intercourse, such as touching and kissing; this was said by Ibn Zayd and Malik.

﴿These are the limits of Allah﴾, that is, what He has forbidden. Regarding calling them "the limits of Allah," there are two aspects. The first: because Allah, exalted is He, defined them by mention and explanation. The second: because of what He has made obligatory in most of the prohibited matters of the limits.

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Thus Allah makes clear His signs to the people﴾ has two interpretations. The first: by His signs He means the markers of His acts of worship. The second: that by the signs here He means the obligations and rulings.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 188:

﴿And do not consume one another's wealth by false means﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: by usurpation and injustice.

The second: by gambling and amusements (al-malahi).

﴿And present it to the rulers﴾ is derived from idla' al-dalw (lowering the bucket), when you send it down.

It may also bear a second meaning: "and present your case with it before the judge," from their saying: "he presented his proof (adla bi-hujjatihi)" when he set it forth.

Concerning this "wealth" there are two opinions. The first: that it refers to deposits and to whatever other property no evidence can establish, such that if one denies it, he is judged to be a denier concerning it.

The second: that it refers to the wealth of orphans, over which he is entrusted (mu'taman).

﴿So that you may consume a portion of the wealth of people through sin﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: "so that you may consume some of the wealth of people through sin," where "some" is expressed by "a portion" (fariq).

The second: by inversion of order (al-taqdim wa al-ta'khir), its sense being: "so that you may consume the wealth of a portion of people through sin."

Concerning "its consuming" (akluhu) there are three possibilities. The first: by denial (al-judud).

The second: by false testimony (shahadat al-zur).

The third: by bribing the judges (rishwat al-hukkam).

﴿While you know﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: "while you know that it belongs to people."

The second: "while you know that it is sin."

Muqatil said: this verse was revealed concerning Imru' al-Qays al-Kindi and 'Abdan ibn Rabi'ah al-Hadrami, who disputed over a piece of land in which 'Abdan was the wrongdoer and Imru' al-Qays the wronged. He wished to swear an oath, so this verse was revealed, and he refrained from the oath.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 189:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the new moons﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Tha'labah ibn Ghanamah, who were both from the Ansar, asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about the increase and waxing of the new moons, so this verse was revealed." The name of the crescent (hilal) is derived from the people's istihlal, that is, raising their voices when they sight it. Al-mawaqit (the appointed times) are the measures of times for their debts and their Hajj. By "al-ahilla" (the new moons) he means their months. The crescent is sometimes referred to as the month because it revolves within it. The poet said:

"Two brothers from Najd, in certainty, and the month is like the paring of a fingernail
until it became complete in its roundness
in four [nights] it grew beyond ten."

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is not righteousness that you enter the houses from their backs, but righteousness is [in] one who fears Allah. And enter the houses through their doors﴾. Concerning this there are six opinions:

The first: the occasion of its revelation is what Dawud related from Qays ibn Jubayr: "The people, when they entered the state of ihram, would not enter a garden through its gate. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered a house, and there was a man from the Ansar called Rifa'ah ibn Ayyub. He came and climbed over the wall to the Messenger of Allah. When he [the Prophet] came out through the door of the house, Rifa'ah came out. The Messenger of Allah said: 'What made you do that?' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I saw you come out of it, so I came out of it.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I am a man of Ahmas.' He said: 'If you are of Ahmas, then our religion is one,' so Allah, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿It is not righteousness...﴾, the verse." This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Qatadah and Ata'. As for his saying "Ahmas", it means from Quraysh. They were called al-Hums (the Hums) because they were zealous (tahammasu) in their religion, that is, they were strict. Al-hamasah means severity. Al-Ajjaj said:

"And how many hard, rugged sand-hills we have crossed"

that is, severe.

The second opinion: "the houses" means women. They were called houses because of seeking shelter in them, just as one seeks shelter in houses. The meaning is: do not approach women from the back where it is not permitted, and approach them from the front where it is permitted. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: it concerns the nasi' (intercalation) and the delay of the Hajj through it, when they would make a permitted month forbidden by delaying the Hajj, and a forbidden month permitted by delaying the Hajj beyond it. The mention of houses and entering them from their backs is then an example of opposing what is obligatory concerning the Hajj and its months. Opposition is coming to a matter from behind it; "khalf" and "zahr" in the speech of the Arabs are the same. This was related by Ibn Bahr.

The fourth: a man, when he went out for his need and returned without success, would not enter through his door, but would enter from behind it, out of superstitious fear of failure. So Allah commanded them to come to their houses through their doors.

The fifth: its meaning is that righteousness is not that you seek good from other than its people and come to it from other than its door. This is the view of Abu Ubaydah.

The sixth: it is a parable that Allah, mighty and majestic, struck for them, that they should come to righteousness from its proper direction, and not come to it from other than its proper direction.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 190–193:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you﴾. There are two opinions regarding this verse.

The first: it is the first verse revealed in Medina concerning fighting the polytheists. The Muslims were commanded in it to fight those among the polytheists who fought them, and to refrain from those who refrained from them. Then it was abrogated (naskh) by Surat Bara'a (al-Tawba). This is the view of al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd.

The second: it remains operative in its ruling (muhkam). In it they were commanded to fight all the polytheists, and the transgression (i'tida') they were forbidden from is the killing of women and children. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, and Mujahid.

Regarding Allah's words ﴿and do not transgress﴾ there are three opinions. The first: transgression is fighting those who do not fight. The second: it is killing women and children. The third: it is fighting for other than the religion.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And kill them wherever you encounter them﴾, meaning wherever you gain mastery over them, ﴿and expel them from where they expelled you﴾, meaning from Mecca.

﴿And fitnah is worse than killing﴾. By fitnah is meant disbelief (kufr), according to all scholars. Disbelief was called fitnah because it leads to destruction, just as fitnah does.

﴿And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram until they fight you there. But if they fight you, then kill them﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: this ruling is abrogated, because Allah the Exalted had forbidden fighting the people of the Sacred Precinct (ahl al-Haram) unless they initiated the fighting, and then this was abrogated by His words: ﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾. This is the view of Qatadah.

The second opinion: it is muhkam, and it is not permissible for us to begin fighting the people of the Sacred Precinct unless they initiate the fighting. This is the view of Mujahid.
