This is the view of Qatadah.

The second opinion: it is muhkam, and it is not permissible for us to begin fighting the people of the Sacred Precinct unless they initiate the fighting. This is the view of Mujahid.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 190–193:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And fight in the way of Allah those who fight you﴾. There are two opinions regarding this verse.

The first: it is the first verse revealed in Medina concerning fighting the polytheists. The Muslims were commanded in it to fight those among the polytheists who fought them, and to refrain from those who refrained from them. Then it was abrogated (naskh) by Surat Bara'a (al-Tawba). This is the view of al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd.

The second: it remains operative in its ruling (muhkam). In it they were commanded to fight all the polytheists, and the transgression (i'tida') they were forbidden from is the killing of women and children. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, and Mujahid.

Regarding Allah's words ﴿and do not transgress﴾ there are three opinions. The first: transgression is fighting those who do not fight. The second: it is killing women and children. The third: it is fighting for other than the religion.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And kill them wherever you encounter them﴾, meaning wherever you gain mastery over them, ﴿and expel them from where they expelled you﴾, meaning from Mecca.

﴿And fitnah is worse than killing﴾. By fitnah is meant disbelief (kufr), according to all scholars. Disbelief was called fitnah because it leads to destruction, just as fitnah does.

﴿And do not fight them at al-Masjid al-Haram until they fight you there. But if they fight you, then kill them﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: this ruling is abrogated, because Allah the Exalted had forbidden fighting the people of the Sacred Precinct (ahl al-Haram) unless they initiated the fighting, and then this was abrogated by His words: ﴿And fight them until there is no fitnah﴾. This is the view of Qatadah.

The second opinion: it is muhkam, and it is not permissible for us to begin fighting the people of the Sacred Precinct unless they initiate the fighting. This is the view of Mujahid.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 194:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month﴾. Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are two opinions.

The first: that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had entered the state of ihram for the 'umrah in Dhu al-Qa'dah in the sixth year (of the Hijrah), but the polytheists prevented him from the House. So he made a treaty with them that he would perform it in the following year. He then removed his ihram and returned. Then he performed the 'umrah as a making-up (qada') in Dhu al-Qa'dah of the seventh year, and Quraysh vacated Makkah for him until he had completed his 'umrah.

Then the revelation came: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month﴾, meaning: the Dhu al-Qa'dah in which he made up the 'umrah in its year, which is one of the sacred months, is (equal) to the sacred month in which they prevented you, which was Dhu al-Qa'dah of the previous year. Dhu al-Qa'dah was so named because the Arabs would sit (qu'ud) in it, refraining from fighting, on account of its sanctity.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And the sacred things are subject to retaliation﴾, because Quraysh boasted over the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when they prevented him, so Allah, mighty and majestic, exacted retribution on his behalf. This is the view of Qatadah and al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

The second opinion: that the occasion of its revelation was that the polytheists of the Arabs said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Have you been forbidden, O Muhammad, from fighting us in the sacred month?" He said: "Yes." So they intended to fight him in the sacred month, and Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: ﴿The sacred month for the sacred month, and the sacred things are subject to retaliation﴾. That is, if they violate the sanctity of the sacred month by fighting you in it, then you may violate its sanctity against them in the same way as they violated it against you. This is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri.(p-253)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 195:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And spend in the way of Allah﴾, meaning jihad (striving in the cause of God).

﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾. Regarding the particle bi (بِ, "with") there are two opinions. The first: it is superfluous (zaʾida), and its implied sense is: "and do not throw your hands into destruction."

The second opinion: it is not superfluous, meaning: "and do not throw yourselves, with your own hands, into destruction." Al-tahlukah (التَّهْلُكَة, destruction) and al-halak (الهَلاك, perishing) are the same.

Regarding ﴿and do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾ there are six interpretations:

The first: that you abandon spending in the way of Allah, the Exalted, and thus perish through sin. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and Hudhayfah.

The second: meaning, do not go out without provisions, and thus perish through weakness. This is the view of Zayd ibn Aslam.

The third: meaning, despair of forgiveness when committing sins, so that you do not repent. This is the view of al-Baraʾ ibn ʿAzib.

The fourth: that you abandon jihad in the way of Allah, and thus perish. This is the view of Abu Ayyub al-Ansari.

The fifth: that it is rushing headlong into battle without inflicting harm on the enemy. This is the view of Abu al-Qasim al-Balkhi.

The sixth: that it is general and encompasses all of that together. This is the view of Abu Jaʿfar al-Tabari.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And do good; indeed, Allah loves those who do good﴾. Concerning it there are three interpretations:

The first: that it refers to excellence in performing the obligatory duties. This is the view of some of the Companions.

The second: and think well of divine decree (al-qadar). This is the view of ʿIkrimah.

The third: return good to those who have nothing in their hand. This is the view of Zayd ibn Aslam.(p-254)

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 196:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And complete the Hajj and the ʿUmrah for Allah﴾. Ibn Masʿud, as ʿAlqamah narrated from him, read: "And complete the Hajj and the ʿUmrah for the House (al-Bayt)." The scholars differed concerning the interpretation of completing them, in five opinions:

The first: it means, complete the Hajj with its rites (manasik) and its sunnahs, and complete the ʿUmrah with its limits and its sunnah. This is the view of Mujahid and ʿAlqamah ibn Qays.

The second: completing them means that you enter into ihram for both from the dwelling-place of your family (duwayrat ahlika). This is the view of ʿAli, Tawus, and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The third: completing the ʿUmrah means performing it outside the sacred months, and completing the Hajj means performing all its rites so that no expiatory sacrifice (dam) becomes obligatory for making up a deficiency. This is the view of Qatadah.

The fourth: that you set out from your family's dwelling-place for the sake of both, not intending anything else, such as trade or profit. This is the view of Sufyan al-Thawri.

The fifth: that completing them is obligatory upon entering into them. This is the view of al-Shaʿbi, Abu Burdah, Ibn Zayd, and Masruq.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿But if you are prevented, then what is feasible of the hady (sacrificial offering)﴾. Regarding this ihsar (being prevented from completing the rites), there are two opinions. The first: it is any restraint, whether from an enemy, illness, or some other excuse. This is the view of Mujahid, Qatadah, ʿAta', and Abu Hanifah. (p-255)

The second: it is ihsar only by an enemy, not by illness. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, Anas ibn Malik, and al-Shafiʿi.

Regarding ﴿what is feasible of the hady﴾ there are two opinions. The first: it is a sheep (shah). This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, al-Suddi, ʿAlqamah, ʿAta', and most of the jurists.

The second: it is a camel (badanah). This is the view of ʿUmar, ʿAisha, Mujahid, Tawus, and ʿUrwah, and they understood it to include whatever is feasible of young and mature camels.

Regarding the etymology of hady, there are two opinions. The first: it is derived from hadiyyah (gift). The second: it is derived from their saying "hadaytuhu hadyan," when I led him to the path of right guidance (sabil al-rashad).

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿And do not shave your heads until the hady reaches its place of sacrifice (mahill)﴾. Regarding the place of sacrifice for the one who is prevented, there are three opinions. The first: it is wherever he was prevented, whether in the non-sacred area (hill) or in the sacred area (haram). This is the view of Ibn ʿUmar, al-Miswar ibn Makhramah, and Harun ibn al-Hakam, and al-Shafiʿi said likewise.

The second opinion: it is the haram. This is the view of ʿAli, Ibn Masʿud, and Mujahid, and Abu Hanifah said likewise.

The third opinion: its place of sacrifice is that he exits from his ihram, beginning his rite, while remaining in ihram until the ihsar is lifted. It is not permissible for the muhrim to exit from ihram due to ihsar after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). If his ihram was for ʿUmrah, it does not lapse; if it was for Hajj, he makes it up by a later performance (qada') after exiting from it. This is related from Ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAisha, and Malik said likewise.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿So whoever among you is ill, or has an injury to his head, then an expiation (fidyah) of fasting, or charity, or a sacrifice﴾. Its meaning: if he shaves, then this is obligatory upon him. (p-256)

As for fasting, there are two opinions. The first: fasting three days. This is the view of Mujahid, ʿAlqamah, Ibrahim, and al-Rabiʿ, and al-Shafiʿi said likewise.

The second opinion: fasting ten days, like the fasting of the mutamattiʿ (one who combines ʿUmrah and Hajj). This is the view of al-Hasan and ʿIkrimah.

As for charity, there are two opinions. The first: six needy persons, which is the view of those who obligate three days of fasting. The second: feeding ten needy persons, which is the view of those who obligate ten days of fasting.

As for the sacrifice, it is a sheep.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿But when you are secure﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: from your fear. The second: from your illness.

﴿Then whoever enjoys (tamattaʿa) the ʿUmrah until the Hajj, then what is feasible of the hady﴾. The scholars differed concerning this mutamattiʿ in three opinions. The first: he is the one prevented from Hajj who was released from it by ihsar, then returned to his land as a mutamattiʿ after his release. When he performs his Hajj in the following year, he becomes a mutamattiʿ by having a release between the two ihrams. This is the view of al-Zubayr.

The second: it is the one who converted his Hajj into ʿUmrah (faskh), and enjoyed the ʿUmrah after annulling his Hajj. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The third: it is the one who came to the haram as a muʿtamir in the months of Hajj, then stayed in Makkah until he entered ihram from it for Hajj in the same year. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar, Mujahid, ʿAta', and al-Shafiʿi.

Regarding ﴿what is feasible of the hady﴾, the two opinions we have mentioned apply.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿So whoever does not find (a hady), then fasting three days during the Hajj﴾. The scholars differed about its time during Hajj, in two opinions: (p-257)

The first: after entering ihram and before the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). This is the view of ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, Tawus, al-Suddi, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, ʿAta', and al-Shafiʿi in his new opinion (qawl jadid).

The second: they are the days of tashriq. This is the view of ʿAisha, ʿUrwah, Ibn ʿUmar in the narration of Salim from him, and al-Shafiʿi in his old opinion (qawl qadim).

They differed about the permissibility of performing them before entering ihram for Hajj, in two opinions. The first: it is not permissible. This is the view of Ibn ʿUmar and Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: it is permissible.

Those who held that it is permissible differed about the time of performing them before Hajj, in two opinions. The first: the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah, and it is not permissible before them. This is the view of Mujahid and ʿAta'. The second: during the months of Hajj, and it is not permissible before them. This is the view of Tawus.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿And seven when you return﴾. Regarding its time there are two opinions. The first: when you return from your Hajj on your route. This is the view of Mujahid. The second: when you return to your families in your cities. This is the view of ʿAta', Qatadah, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, and al-Rabiʿ.

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿Those are ten complete﴾. Concerning this there are four interpretations. The first: they are ten complete in reward, like one who offered a hady. This is the view of al-Hasan. The second: they are ten that complete for you the reward of one who remained in his ihram, did not exit from it, and did not perform tamattuʿ. The third: it is expressed in the form of a report, but its meaning is that of a command, i.e., "those are ten, so complete their fasting and do not break it during them." The fourth: it is an emphasis in speech. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas. (p-258)

Then He, Exalted, said: ﴿That is for one whose family are not present at the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram)﴾. Concerning those who are "present" (hadirin) there are four opinions. The first: they are the people of the haram. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and Tawus.

The second: they are those between Makkah and the miqat (boundaries of ihram). This is the view of Makhul and ʿAta'.

The third: they are the people of the haram and those whose dwelling is near it, like the people of ʿArafah and al-Raji'. This is the view of al-Zuhri and Malik.

The fourth: they are those who are at a distance in which prayer is not shortened (qasr). This is the view of al-Shafiʿi.

The Exalted said: ﴿The Hajj is in well-known months﴾. The scholars differed over its interpretation (ta'wil) in three opinions. The first is that they are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah and the whole of Dhu al-Hijjah. This is the view of Qatadah, Tawus and Mujahid, from Ibn Umar, and it is the position of Malik.

The second is that they are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah and the first ten days of Dhu al-Hijjah. This is the view of Abu Hanifah.

The third is that they are Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah and ten nights of Dhu al-Hijjah, up to the break of dawn on the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, al-Suddi, Nafi', from Ibn Umar, Ata', al-Dahhak and al-Shafi'i.

Then He said: ﴿Whoever undertakes the obligation of Hajj therein﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first is that it is the entering into the state of consecration (ihram) by pronouncing the talbiyah. This is the view of Umar, Mujahid and Tawus. (p-259)

The second is that it is the ihram itself. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Ata' and al-Shafi'i.

﴿No obscenity (rafath)﴾: regarding this there are three interpretations. The first is that it is sexual intercourse. This is the view of Ibn Umar, al-Hasan, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ikrimah, Qatadah and al-Zuhri.

The second is that it is intercourse, or approaching it by means of a promise of it or by playful talk. This is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri.

The third is that it is using foul speech to a woman in conversation, such as saying, "When we come out of the state of ihram we will do such-and-such to you," explicitly. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Tawus.

﴿Nor wickedness (fusuq)﴾: regarding this there are five interpretations. The first is doing what is forbidden during ihram, such as killing game, shaving hair, and clipping nails. This is the view of Abd Allah ibn Umar.

The second is cursing (sibab). This is the view of Ata' and al-Suddi.

The third is slaughtering for idols. This is the view of Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd.

The fourth is mutual insulting by nicknames. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

The fifth is all acts of disobedience. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Tawus.

﴿Nor disputing (jidal) during Hajj﴾: regarding this there are six interpretations. The first is that a man argues with his companion, meaning that he disobeys him. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Mujahid.

The second is cursing (sibab). This is the view of Ibn Umar and Qatadah.

The third is quarrelling and disagreeing about who has the better Hajj. This is the view of Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

The fourth is the disagreement that used to occur among them on the day on which their Hajj took place. This is the view of al-Qasim ibn Muhammad. (p-260)

The fifth is their disagreement over the standing places of Hajj, as to who is correctly standing at the place of Ibrahim. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

The sixth is that its meaning is: no disputing during its time, because of its being fixed, and the abolition of the intercalation (nasi') of the month which they used to practise every year. Thus they would perform Hajj sometimes in Dhu al-Qa'dah and sometimes in Safar. This is the view of Abu Ja'far al-Tabari.

Regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿And take provision, for the best provision is piety (taqwa)﴾, there are two interpretations. The first: take provision of righteous deeds, for the best provision is piety.

The second: it was revealed concerning a people from the people of Yemen who used to perform Hajj without taking provisions, saying, "We are those who rely upon God (mutawakkilun)." So this was revealed about them: ﴿And take provision﴾, meaning of food.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 198:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas narrated, he said: Dhu al-Majaz and ʿUkaz were two marketplaces for the people in the Jahiliyyah. When Islam came, they abandoned that, until this was revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾. Ibn al-Zubayr used to recite, in the verse on the times of the Hajj: ﴿Then when you pour forth from ʿArafat﴾.

Regarding it (the word ifadah, "pouring forth") there are three opinions. The first: its meaning is "when you return from where you began."

The second: that al-Ifadah (pouring forth) is the pushing off in a mass, like the overflowing of a vessel when it is full.

The third: that al-Ifadah is hastening from one place to another.

Regarding ʿArafat (ʿArafat) there are two opinions. The first: that it is the plural of ʿArafah. The second: that it is a single proper noun, even though it is in the form of the plural.

This is the saying of al-Zajjaj. (p-261)

They differed about naming the place ʿArafah, in four opinions. The first: that Adam recognized Eve there (ʿarafa fihi Hawwa, "recognized") after they had been sent down from the Garden.

The second: that Ibrahim recognized the place at the time of the vision, because of what had preceded for him in the description.

The third: that Jibril made the Prophets recognize their rites there.

The fourth: that it was named so because of the height of the people in it, and the Arabs call whatever is elevated ʿArafah and ʿArafat, and from this the crest of the rooster (ʿurf al-dik) is named, because of its height.

﴿So remember Allah at the Sacred Monument﴾. Al-Mashʿar is the landmark; it was so named because supplication is made at it, and staying there is among the landmarks of the Hajj. The boundary of al-Mashʿar is what lies between Mina and Muzdalifah, from the limit where the two defiles of ʿArafah open out to Muhassar. The two defiles of ʿArafah are not part of al-Mashʿar.

"His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾ — concerning this there are two views.

The first: it was revealed concerning the Quraysh, who were called al-Hums (the staunch ones). In their pilgrimage they would not leave the Sacred Precinct (al-Haram); they would stand at Muzdalifah and say: "We are the people of God, so we do not leave the Sanctuary of God." The rest of the Arabs would stand at Arafat, which is the station of Ibrahim, peace be upon him. So God Exalted revealed: ﴿Then depart from where the people depart﴾, meaning all the Arabs. This is the view of ʿAʾishah, ʿUrwah, Mujahid, and Qatadah.

The second view: it is a command to all creation, from the Quraysh and others, that they depart from where the people depart, and by "the people" is meant Ibrahim. The term "the people" may be used to refer to a single person, as God Exalted said: ﴿Those to whom the people said, "Indeed the people have gathered against you"﴾ [Al ʿImran: 173], while the speaker was one man, namely Nuʿaym ibn Masʿud al-Ashjaʿi. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And seek forgiveness of God; indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, there are two interpretations. The first: seek forgiveness from God for your sins. The second: seek forgiveness from Him for your opposition regarding the time and the departure (ifadah)."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 200–202:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when you have completed your rites (manasikakum)﴾. As for al-manasik (the rites), they are the acts of worship (al-mutaʿabbadat), and there are two interpretations regarding them here:

The first: they are the sacrificial animals (al-dhaba'ih). This is the saying of Mujahid.

The second: they are what they were commanded to do in the Hajj. This is the saying of al-Hasan al-Basri.

And regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then remember Allah﴾, there are two interpretations:

The first: this remembrance is the takbir (saying "Allahu akbar") during the days of Mina.

The second: it is everything that is prescribed of supplications (al-ad'iyah) in all the places of the Hajj.

And regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿as you remember your fathers, or with a more intense remembrance﴾, there are three interpretations:

The first: in the Jahiliyyah, when they finished their Hajj, they would sit in Mina in circles and boast of the virtues of their forefathers. So Allah, exalted is His remembrance, revealed: ﴿Then remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with a more intense remembrance﴾. This is the saying of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: its meaning is, "Remember Allah as you remember your fathers, the way young children remember their fathers when they say: 'Abah, ummah (Father, mother!)'." This is the saying of Ata' and al-Dahhak.

The third: they used to make supplication, and one of them would say: "O Allah, indeed my father was one of great bowls, great domes, and abundant wealth, so give me the like of what You gave him," and he would mention none but his father. So they were commanded to remember Allah, as they remember their fathers, or with a more intense remembrance. This is the saying of al-Suddi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among them is he who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good"﴾. Regarding it there are four interpretations: (p-263)

The first: that "good" (hasanah) is well-being in this world and the Hereafter. This is the saying of Qatadah.

The second: that it is the blessings of this world and the blessings of the Hereafter. This is the saying of the majority of the people of knowledge.

The third: that the good in this world is knowledge and worship, and in the Hereafter it is Paradise. This is the saying of al-Hasan and al-Thawri.

The fourth: that the good in this world is wealth, and in the Hereafter it is Paradise. This is the saying of Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 200–202:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when you have completed your rites (manasikakum)﴾. As for al-manasik (the rites), they are the acts of worship (al-mutaʿabbadat), and there are two interpretations regarding them here:

The first: they are the sacrificial animals (al-dhaba'ih). This is the saying of Mujahid.

The second: they are what they were commanded to do in the Hajj. This is the saying of al-Hasan al-Basri.

The third: they used to make supplication, and one of them would say: "O Allah, indeed my father was one of great bowls, great domes, and abundant wealth, so give me the like of what You gave him," and he would mention none but his father. So they were commanded to remember Allah, as they remember their fathers, or with a more intense remembrance. This is the saying of al-Suddi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among them is he who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good"﴾. Regarding it there are four interpretations: (p-263)

The first: that "good" (hasanah) is well-being in this world and the Hereafter. This is the saying of Qatadah.

The second: that it is the blessings of this world and the blessings of the Hereafter. This is the saying of the majority of the people of knowledge.

The fourth: that the good in this world is wealth, and in the Hereafter it is Paradise. This is the saying of Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 200–202:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when you have completed your rites (manasikakum)﴾. As for al-manasik (the rites), they are the acts of worship (al-mutaʿabbadat), and there are two interpretations regarding them here:

The first: they are the sacrificial animals (al-dhaba'ih). This is the saying of Mujahid.

The second: they are what they were commanded to do in the Hajj. This is the saying of al-Hasan al-Basri.

And regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿then remember Allah﴾, there are two interpretations:

The first: this remembrance is the takbir (saying "Allahu akbar") during the days of Mina.

The second: it is everything that is prescribed of supplications (al-ad'iyah) in all the places of the Hajj.

And regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿as you remember your fathers, or with a more intense remembrance﴾, there are three interpretations:

The first: in the Jahiliyyah, when they finished their Hajj, they would sit in Mina in circles and boast of the virtues of their forefathers. So Allah, exalted is His remembrance, revealed: ﴿Then remember Allah as you remember your fathers, or with a more intense remembrance﴾. This is the saying of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: its meaning is, "Remember Allah as you remember your fathers, the way young children remember their fathers when they say: 'Abah, ummah (Father, mother!)'." This is the saying of Ata' and al-Dahhak.

The third: they used to make supplication, and one of them would say: "O Allah, indeed my father was one of great bowls, great domes, and abundant wealth, so give me the like of what You gave him," and he would mention none but his father. So they were commanded to remember Allah, as they remember their fathers, or with a more intense remembrance. This is the saying of al-Suddi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among them is he who says, "Our Lord, give us in this world good and in the Hereafter good"﴾. Regarding it there are four interpretations: (p-263)

The first: that "good" (hasanah) is well-being in this world and the Hereafter. This is the saying of Qatadah.

The second: that it is the blessings of this world and the blessings of the Hereafter. This is the saying of the majority of the people of knowledge.

The third: that the good in this world is knowledge and worship, and in the Hereafter it is Paradise. This is the saying of al-Hasan and al-Thawri.

The fourth: that the good in this world is wealth, and in the Hereafter it is Paradise. This is the saying of Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 203:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And remember Allah during the appointed days﴾. They are the days of Mina, according to the opinion of all the exegetes (mufassirun), although some jurists (fuqaha') differed by associating some of them with the known days (al-ayyam al-ma'lumat).

﴿Then whoever hastens in two days, there is no sin upon him﴾, meaning he hastens the first departure (al-nafr al-awwal) on the second day of the days of Mina.

﴿And whoever delays﴾, meaning until the second departure (al-nafr al-thani), which is the third day of the days of Mina.

﴿There is no sin upon him﴾. Regarding the sin here, there are five interpretations. The first: whoever hastens, there is no sin upon him for his hastening, and whoever delays, there is no sin upon him for his delaying. This is the saying of 'Ata'.

The second: whoever hastens in two days, he is forgiven and there is no sin upon him, and whoever delays, he is forgiven and there is no sin upon him. This is the saying of Ibn Mas'ud.

The third: there is no sin upon him, if he is mindful of God (ittaqa) in what remains of his life. This is the saying of Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Suddi.

The fourth: there is no sin upon him, if he is mindful of God in hunting game on the third day, until they may leave the state of ihram during the days of tashriq. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

The fifth: there is no sin upon him, if he is mindful of God in avoiding what he has been forbidden from, so that his past sins are forgiven him. This is the saying of Qatadah.

As for the meaning of remembering Allah, may He be exalted, during the appointed days, it is the takbir (proclaiming Allahu akbar) during them after the obligatory prayers. Opinions differ on this in four schools of thought. The first: it is takbir from after the dawn prayer on the Day of 'Arafah until after the 'asr prayer on the last of the days of tashriq. This is the saying of 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and among the jurists, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad said the same.

The second: it is takbir from the dawn prayer on the Day of 'Arafah until the 'asr prayer on the Day of Sacrifice (yawm al-nahr). This is the saying of Ibn Mas'ud, and among the jurists, Abu Hanifah said the same.

The third: it is takbir from after the noon prayer on the Day of Sacrifice until after the 'asr prayer on the last of the days of tashriq. This is the saying of Zayd ibn Thabit.

The fourth: it is takbir from after the noon prayer on the Day of Sacrifice until the last prayer of dawn on the last of the days of tashriq. This is the saying of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar, and among the jurists, al-Shafi'i said the same.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 2, verses 204–207**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among the people is one whose speech about the worldly life pleases you﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: it means [his speech is pleasing] in beauty and goodness.

The second: [it means it pleases you] because of his love for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his desire for his religion.

﴿And he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: he says, "O Allah, bear witness for me concerning this," while his inner self is contrary to it.

The second: its meaning is: and in his heart is that which Allah witnesses to be contrary to it.

The third: its meaning is: and he seeks Allah's witness to the truth of what is in his heart, while he knows that it is contrary to it.

In the recitation (qira'a, a established reading of the Qur'an) of Ibn Mas'ud, it is: ﴿And he calls Allah to witness what is in his heart﴾. ﴿Yet he is the most stubborn of opponents﴾. Al-alladd (the most stubborn) among men is the one who is very intense in disputing. Regarding al-khisam (the disputing) there are two opinions. The first: that it is a verbal noun (masdar), and this is the opinion of al-Khalil. The second: that it is the plural of khasim (opponent), and this is the opinion of al-Zajjaj.

Regarding the interpretation of ﴿the most stubborn of opponents﴾ here, there are four aspects. The first: that he is one full of disputation, and this is the opinion of Ibn Abbas. The second: meaning that he does not act straightforwardly in dispute, but is crooked in it, and this is the opinion of Mujahid and al-Suddi. The third: meaning that he is a liar, in the opinion of al-Hasan al-Basri. The fourth: that he is severely hardened in disobedience to Allah, and this is the opinion of Qatada.

Ibn Abi Mulaykah narrated from Aisha that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The most hateful of men to Allah, the Exalted, is the most stubborn disputer (al-alladd al-khasim)."

Regarding whom this verse and what follows was directed at, there are two opinions. The first: that it is a description of the hypocrite (munafiq), and this is the opinion of Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan. The second: that it was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq, and this is the opinion of al-Suddi.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when he turns away, he strives in the land﴾. Regarding his saying "turns away" (tawalla) there are two interpretations. The first: it means he became angry, related by al-Naqqash. The second: it means he departed, and this is the apparent opinion of al-Hasan.

Regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿to cause corruption therein﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: he causes corruption in it by obstruction (sadd, hindering [people from the path of Allah]). The second: by disbelief.

﴿And to destroy the crops and the offspring﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: by captivity and killing. The second: by misguidance which leads to captivity and killing.

﴿And Allah does not love corruption﴾. Its meaning: He does not love those who spread corruption.

Some of them said: He does not praise corruption nor commend it. It was also said: He does not love that it be a religion and a law. It may also mean: He does not love acting upon corruption.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," pride in sin seizes him﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: its meaning is that pride calls him to commit sin. The second: its meaning is that when it is said to him, "Fear Allah," his self is too proud to accept it, because of the sin that prevents him from it.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among the people is one who sells himself seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾. "Yashri nafsahu" means he sells his self, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and they sold him for a paltry price﴾ [Yusuf: 20], meaning they sold him. (p-٢٦٧) Al-Hasan al-Basri said: the deed for which he sold himself is jihad in the way of Allah.

There is disagreement about who this verse was revealed concerning, with two opinions. The first: it was revealed concerning a man who enjoined what is right and forbade what is wrong, and was killed. This is the opinion of Ali, Umar, and Ibn Abbas. The second: that it was revealed concerning Suhayb ibn Sinan, who bought himself from the polytheists with all his wealth and joined the Muslims. This is the opinion of Ikrima.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 208–209:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who have believed, enter into peace (al-silm) completely﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and al-Kisa'i read "al-sallm" with a fatha on the sin, while the rest read it with a kasra. The scholars of language differed regarding the fatha and the kasra, in two ways. The first: they are two dialects, each of which is used in the place of the other.

The second: their meanings differ. The distinction between them is that al-silm with a kasra means Islam, and al-salm with a fatha means peaceful reconciliation (al-musalamah), from His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾ [al-Anfal: 61]. Regarding the meaning of "entering into peace," there are two interpretations. The first: entering into Islam; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Dahhak.

The second: its meaning is enter into obedience; this is the view of al-Rabi' and Qatadah.

Regarding His saying ﴿completely (kaffah)﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: it refers to ﴿those who have believed﴾, that they should all enter into peace together.

The second: it refers to peace (al-silm), that they should enter into all of it.

﴿And do not follow the footsteps (khutuwat) of Satan﴾: meaning his traces. (p-268)

﴿Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: he is clear in himself (mubin li-nafsihi).

The other: he is clear through his enmity (mubin bi-'udwanihi).

They differed regarding by what his enmity was made clear, according to two views. The first: by his refusal to prostrate to Adam.

The second: by his saying: ﴿I will surely seize his descendants, except a few﴾ [al-Isra': 62]. They also differed regarding who was commanded to enter into peace completely, according to three opinions. The first: that those commanded are the Muslims, and entering into peace means acting upon all the laws of Islam; this is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: that it was revealed concerning the People of the Book, who believed in the prophets who came before, so they were commanded to enter into Islam; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak.

The third: that it was revealed concerning Tha'labah, 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, Ibn Yamin, Asad, Usayd (the two sons of Ka'b), Sa'id ibn 'Amr, and Qays ibn Zayd, all of them from the Jews, who said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "On the Day of Sabbath we used to honor it and refrain from work in it, and the Torah is the Book of Allah, the Exalted, so let us fast our days and stand in prayer through the nights." So this verse was revealed; this is the view of 'Ikrimah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you slip (zalaltum)﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: its meaning is you disobeyed.

The second: its meaning is you disbelieved.

The third: if you go astray; this is the view of al-Suddi.

﴿After the clear proofs (al-bayyinat) have come to you﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations. The first: they are the proofs and evidences of Allah.

The second: Muhammad; this is the view of al-Suddi.

The third: the Qur'an; this is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

The fourth: Islam.

﴿Then know that Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾: meaning, Mighty in Himself, Wise in His action.

The first: that those commanded are the Muslims, and entering into peace means acting upon all the laws of Islam; this is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: that it was revealed concerning the People of the Book, who believed in the prophets who came before, so they were commanded to enter into Islam; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak.

The third: that it was revealed concerning Tha'labah, 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, Ibn Yamin, Asad, Usayd (the two sons of Ka'b), Sa'id ibn 'Amr, and Qays ibn Zayd, all of them from the Jews, who said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "On the Day of Sabbath we used to honor it and refrain from work in it, and the Torah is the Book of Allah, the Exalted, so let us fast our days and stand in prayer through the nights." So this verse was revealed; this is the view of 'Ikrimah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you slip (zalaltum)﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: its meaning is you disobeyed.

The second: its meaning is you disbelieved.

The third: if you go astray; this is the view of al-Suddi.

﴿After the clear proofs (al-bayyinat) have come to you﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations. The first: they are the proofs and evidences of Allah.

The second: Muhammad; this is the view of al-Suddi.

The third: the Qur'an; this is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

The fourth: Islam.

﴿Then know that Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾: meaning, Mighty in Himself, Wise in His action.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 210:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they await only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds, and the angels?﴾ Qatadah recited: "fi zilal al-ghamam" (in the shades of the clouds). There are two interpretations of it:

One of them: its meaning is "Only that Allah should bring to them canopies of clouds, and the angels."

The second: "Only that Allah should come to them in canopies of clouds."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 211–212:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Ask the Children of Israel how many clear signs We gave them﴾. The question is not asked in the sense of seeking information, but in the sense of rebuke (tawbikh).

Regarding the intended meaning of His asking the Children of Israel, there are three opinions. The first: their prophets. The second: their scholars ('ulama'). The third: all of them.

The clear signs (al-ayat al-bayyinat) are: the splitting of the sea (falq al-bahr), the shading clouds (al-zulal min al-ghamam), and other things.(p-270)

﴿And whoever substitutes the blessing of God after it has come to him﴾ means: the blessing of God, namely His Messenger ﷺ. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The worldly life has been made attractive to those who disbelieved﴾ — regarding the worldly life and its being made attractive to them, there are three opinions. The first: Satan made it attractive to them, and this is the saying of al-Hasan (al-Basri). The second: those among mankind and jinn who led them astray made it attractive to them, and this is the saying of some of the theologians (mutakallimun). The third: that God, exalted is He, made it attractive to them through the desires (al-shahawat) which He created for them.

﴿And they mock those who believed﴾ because they imagined that they were upon the truth; so this is their mockery of the weak among the Muslims.

Regarding who does this, there are two opinions. One: they are the scholars of the Jews. The second: the polytheists of the Arabs.

﴿But those who feared God will be above them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ meaning: they will be above the disbelievers in this world.

﴿And God provides for whom He wills without account﴾. If it is said: how does He provide for whom He wills without account, when He, exalted is He, has said: ﴿a gift from your Lord, an account﴾ [al-Naba' 36]? In this regard there are six answers. The first: the diminishing is without account, while the recompense is by account. The second: without account due to the vastness of His dominion, which does not diminish by giving, and so cannot be measured by reckoning. The third: their sufficiency is without account and without constriction. The fourth: it is perpetual, not ending, so it does not become countable; this is the saying of al-Hasan. The fifth: provision in this world is without account, because it encompasses the believer and the disbeliever alike; He does not provide the believer according to the measure of his faith, nor the disbeliever according to the measure of his disbelief. The sixth: He provides the believers in the Hereafter, and He does not call them to account for it nor bestow it upon them as a favour.(p-271)

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 2, verse 213:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Mankind was one community﴾. Regarding His words ﴿one community﴾ there are five opinions:

First: They were upon disbelief. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan.

Second: They were upon the truth. This is the view of Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

Third: Adam was upon the truth and was an imam (leader) for his offspring, so God sent the Prophets among his descendants. This is the view of Mujahid.

Fourth: They were ten groups between Adam and Noah, upon a shari'ah (divine law, a way of guidance) of truth, and then they differed. This is the view of Ikrimah.

Fifth: He intended all of mankind being one community upon one religion on the day God brought forth the descendants of Adam from his loins, presented them to Adam, and they acknowledged servanthood and Islam. Then they differed after that.

Ubayy ibn Ka'b used to recite: "Mankind was one community, then God sent the Prophets as bearers of good news and warners." This is the view of al-Rabi' and Ibn Zayd.

Regarding His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And none differed concerning it﴾ there are two opinions: one of them is concerning the truth; the other is concerning the Book, which is the Torah.

﴿Except those who were given it﴾ means the Jews.

﴿After clear proofs had come to them﴾ means the proofs and evidences. ﴿Out of envy among themselves﴾ is a verbal noun from the saying of the speaker: "So-and-so transgressed against so-and-so" (baghā fulān 'alā fulān), when he wronged him.

﴿Then God guided those who believed to the truth concerning that over which they differed, by His permission﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions:

First: It means Friday (al-Jumu'ah, the congregational prayer), because the People of the Book differed about it and went astray from it. The Jews made it Saturday, and the Christians made it Sunday, so God guided those who believed to what they differed about of the truth by His permission. That is, God guided those who believed to it. This is the view of Abu Hurayrah.

Second: They differed about the prayer. Some of them prayed toward the east and some toward Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), so God guided us to the qiblah (direction of prayer). This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Third: They differed about the revealed Books, so some of them disbelieved in the Book of others, and God guided us to affirm all of them.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 214–215:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: Whatever wealth you spend, let it be for the parents and the near relatives, the orphans, the needy and the wayfarer.﴾ Regarding this verse there are two opinions.

The first: that it was revealed before the verse of zakat (obligatory alms), concerning the obligation of spending on one's family and giving charity, and that it was then abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by later revelation) by the verse of zakat. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The second: that the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked him about their wealth, where they should place it, and so Allah revealed this verse. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 214–215:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: Whatever wealth you spend, let it be for the parents and the near relatives, the orphans, the needy and the wayfarer.﴾ Regarding this verse there are two opinions.

The first: that it was revealed before the verse of zakat (obligatory alms), concerning the obligation of spending on one's family and giving charity, and that it was then abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by later revelation) by the verse of zakat. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The second: that the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked him about their wealth, where they should place it, and so Allah revealed this verse. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 216:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you﴾, meaning it has been made obligatory (furida).

Regarding its obligation there are three opinions:

The first: that it is incumbent upon the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The second: that it is an address to every single person among all of mankind, for all time, until there rises up to it those among them who are sufficient for it. This is the view of the jurists (fuqaha') and the scholars ('ulama').

The third: that it is obligatory upon every Muslim individually (fard 'ayn) for all time. This is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And it is hateful to you﴾. Al-kurh, with a dammah, is bringing hardship upon oneself without anyone compelling one to it. Al-karh, with a fathah, is bringing hardship upon oneself by another's compelling one to it.

Then there are two views on this: the first is that there is an elision in it, and its estimate is: "and it is something that is a burden (dhu kurh) to you." This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The second is that its meaning is "and it is disliked by you" (makruh lakum), and the estimated word is placed in the position of the one that is supplied.

Then regarding its being a kurh (burden), there are two interpretations: the first is that it is a burden for you before the command to worship (al-ta'abbud), but after it, it is not.

The second: it is a burden for you in your natures, before the obligation and after it.

It is only admissible in the sense of worship (al-ta'abbud).

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿But it may be that you hate a thing and it is good for you, and it may be that you love a thing and it is bad for you﴾. Regarding "it may be" ('asa) here there are two views: the first is that it is the hope of one who is apprehensive, along with the presence of doubt.

The second is that it means "qad" (indeed).

Al-Asamm said: ﴿It may be that you hate a thing﴾ — from fighting — ﴿and it is good for you﴾, meaning in this world through victory and spoils, and in the Hereafter through reward and recompense. ﴿And it may be that you love a thing﴾, meaning from abandoning and refraining, ﴿and it is bad for you﴾, meaning in this world through your being overcome, and in the Hereafter through the diminishing of your rewards.

﴿And Allah knows﴾ what contains your benefit, ﴿and you do not know﴾.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 217–218:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the sacred month, about fighting in it. Say: Fighting in it is a great (sin)﴾. The occasion of the revelation of this verse was that ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh set out by the command of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with seven men of his companions: Abu Hudhayfa ibn ʿUtba ibn Rabiʿa, ʿUkkasha ibn Mihsan, ʿUtba ibn Ghazwan, Suhayl ibn al-Bayda, Khalid ibn al-Bukayr, Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, Waqid ibn ʿAbd Allah, and ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh was their commander. Saʿd and ʿUtba lagged behind the group to look for a camel of theirs that had strayed, and they met ʿAmr ibn al-Hadrami, and Waqid ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Tamimi shot him with an arrow and killed him, and they took ʿUthman ibn ʿAbd Allah and al-Hakam ibn Kaysan as captives, and the caravan was seized as booty. This happened on the last night of Jumada al-Akhira or the first night of Rajab. Quraysh reproached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) for this, and when ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh arrived, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) blamed him, and the Muslims blamed him too, until Allah revealed this verse concerning it.

They differed about those who asked about this, on two views. One: they were the polytheists, to reproach the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with it, and they considered fighting him in it lawful; this is the view of the majority.

The second: they were the Muslims, who asked about fighting in the sacred month in order to know its ruling.

Allah informed them that barring from the way of Allah, expelling its people from it (the Sacred Mosque), and fitna (disbelief/persecution) are greater than killing in the sacred month and in the Sacred Precinct. This is the view of Qatada.

They differed regarding whether the prohibition of fighting in the sacred months has been abrogated (naskh) or not. Al-Zuhri said: it has been abrogated by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And fight the polytheists all together as they fight you all together﴾. ʿAta said: its ruling is firm, and the prohibition of fighting in it remains, not abrogated. The first view is more sound, because of what the reports have widely transmitted from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): that he fought the Hawazin at Hunayn and the Thaqif at al-Ta'if, and sent Abu al-ʿAs to Awtas to fight those polytheists there in some of the sacred months; and the Pledge of Ridwan was made for fighting Quraysh in Dhu al-Qaʿda.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever of you turns back from his religion﴾, i.e., returns, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿So they went back, retracing their footsteps﴾ [al-Kahf: 64], i.e., they returned. From this it is said: so-and-so recovered (istaradda) his right.

﴿and dies while he is a disbeliever, those—their deeds have become void﴾, i.e., have been nullified. The root of ḥubūṭ is corruption, so deeds that are nullified are said to have become ḥabiṭat, because of their corruption.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and those who emigrated﴾, to the end of the verse.

The occasion of its revelation: some of the Muslims said about ʿAbd Allah ibn Jahsh and those with him: if they did not commit a sin in their journey, then there is no reward in it. So Allah, Exalted is He, revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who believed﴾, meaning in Allah and His Messenger, ﴿and those who emigrated﴾, meaning from dwelling among the polytheists in their cities. For this reason the emigrants among the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were called muhajirun, because they abandoned their houses and dwellings out of aversion to humiliation by the polytheists and their authority. (﴿and strove﴾), meaning fought. The root of mujahada is mufaʿala, from their saying: jahida kadha, when it troubled and burdened him; if the action is between two, each of whom faces hardship and difficulty from the other, it is said: so-and-so jahada so-and-so.

As for ﴿in the way of Allah﴾, it means the path of Allah, and His path is His religion.

If it is said: how then did He say, ﴿those hope for the mercy of Allah﴾, when the mercy of Allah is due to the believers? There are two answers to this. One: since they did not know their state in the future, it was permissible for them to hope for mercy, fearing that something might happen in their future affairs that would make them no longer deserving of it. The second answer: they hoped for mercy only because they were not certain of it, by fulfilling everything that Allah, Exalted is He, had made obligatory upon them.

He said, may He be exalted: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling﴾, the verse. That is, your companions ask you, O Muhammad, about wine and gambling and drinking them. This is the first verse revealed concerning them.

Khamr (wine) is everything that veils the intellect and covers it, from their saying "I covered the vessel" (khammartu al-inā' idhā ghaṭṭaytahu, "I covered the vessel when you cover it"). It is also said: "He is in the khumār and ghumār of the people," meaning he has entered among them and concealed himself among them. From this comes the khimār of a woman, because it covers her. From it is also said: "He walks to you in khamar," meaning secretly. Al-'Ajjāj said:

In the glittering of the eagles, he does not come in khamar,
He directs the earth and drives the trees.

By his saying "he does not come in khamar," he means he does not come secretly, but openly, with banners and armies.

As for maysir, it is gambling, from the speaker's saying: "This thing came to me easily (yasara li hādhā al-shay' yasran wa maysiran)." So the yāsir is the player with the arrows (al-qidāḥ), then the gambler was also called yāsir and yasar, as the poet said:

So I spent the night like a yasar gabīn (a loser),
Turning over after the arrows were drawn.

﴿Say: In them is great sin and benefits﴾. Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read (... kathīr) with the letter thāʼ.

Regarding their sin there are two interpretations. The first: the drinker of wine becomes intoxicated and harms people, and the sin of gambling is that a man gambles and thus withholds the right and wrongs others. This is the saying of al-Suddī.

The second: the sin of wine is the loss of the intellect of its drinker when he becomes intoxicated, until knowledge of his Creator is lost to him (p-277)

from him.

The sin of gambling is the preoccupation it causes from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer, and the arising of enmity and hatred, as Allah, exalted, described: ﴿Satan only wants to cast enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling, and to turn you away from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 90]. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbās.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and benefits for people﴾, the benefits of wine are its price and the profit of its trade, and the pleasure they obtain by drinking it, as Ḥassān ibn Thābit said:

We drink it, and it leaves us kings,
And lions whom the encounter does not repel.

And as another said:

When I drink, then indeed I am
Lord of al-Khawarnaq and al-Sadīr,
And when I become sober, then indeed I am
Lord of al-Shuwayhah and the camel.

As for the benefits of gambling, there are two sayings. The first: acquiring wealth without toil.

The second: what they obtain of the shares of the slaughtered camel. That is because they used to draw lots (yatayāsarūn) over the camel, and when a man among them prevailed over his companions, they slaughtered it, then divided it into tenths according to the number of arrows. About this A'shā Banī Thaʻlabah says:

And a camel of gambling, to which I called for generosity,
The middle of a barren land whose shade was light.

This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbās, Mujāhid and al-Suddī.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And their sin is greater than their benefit﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: their sin after the prohibition is greater than their benefit after the prohibition, and this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbās. (p-278)

The second: both before the prohibition, meaning the sin that arises from their causes, is greater than their benefit. This is the saying of Sa'īd ibn Jubayr.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus﴾, there are six interpretations. The first: what exceeds the family's needs. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbās.

The second: that it is the moderate middle in spending, as long as it is not extravagance or stinginess. This is the saying of al-Ḥasan.

The fourth: that al-'afw is that what they bring of little or much be taken from them. This is a saying also related from Ibn 'Abbās.

The fifth: that it is charity from surplus wealth (ʿan ẓahr ghinā). This is the saying of Mujāhid.

The sixth: that it is the obligatory charity (al-ṣadaqah al-mafrūḍah). This is also related from Mujāhid.

They differed regarding this spending which is al-'afw, whether it was abrogated (nusikhat). Ibn 'Abbās said: it was abrogated by zakāt.

Mujāhid said: it remains in force.

They differed regarding this verse: was the prohibition of wine by it or by something else? A group of the people of reasoning (ahl al-naẓar) said: wine was prohibited by this verse.

Qatādah said, and most of the scholars hold to it: it was prohibited by the verse of al-Mā'idah.

'Abd al-Wahhāb related from 'Awf, from Abū al-Qalūṣ Zayd ibn 'Alī, who said: "Allah, exalted and majestic, revealed three verses concerning wine. The first thing Allah, exalted, revealed was: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin and benefits for people, and their sin is greater than their benefit﴾, (p-279) So some Muslims drank it, or whoever Allah willed among them, until two men drank it and entered into the prayer, and began saying words that 'Awf did not understand. Then Allah, exalted, revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not approach the prayer while you are intoxicated until you know what you say﴾. So whoever among them had drunk it, abstained from it at the time of prayer, until a man, according to what Abū al-Qalūṣ claimed, drank it and began to lament over the slain of Badr, and he said:

Umm Bakr greets with safety,
But is there any safety for me after my people?
Leave me, let me drink in the morning with Bakr,
For I have seen death has reported about Hishām.
And would that al-Mughīrah, if they had ransomed him
With a thousand men or livestock.
And many in the well of the well of Badr,
Of the shīzā (bowls) covered with fat.
And many in the well of the well of Badr,
Of the youths and the noble garments.

He said: When this reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he came in alarm, dragging his cloak from the alarm until he reached him. When the man saw him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) raised something that was in his hand to strike him, the man said: "I seek refuge in Allah from the anger of Allah and the anger of His Messenger; I will never eat it again." So Allah revealed concerning its prohibition: ﴿O you who believe, wine, gambling, idols and divining arrows are only an abomination﴾ up to His saying: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 90–91]. They said: "We have desisted."»

Mūsā related from 'Amr, from Asbāṭ, from al-Suddī, who said: This verse was revealed: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In them is great sin﴾, and they continued to drink it, until 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn 'Awf prepared food and invited people from the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), among them 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. They drank until they became intoxicated. The prayer came, and 'Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah be pleased with him, led them and recited: ﴿Say: O disbelievers﴾ [al-Kāfirūn: 1], but he did not complete it correctly. So Allah, exalted, revealed, sternly regarding wine: ﴿O you who believe, do not approach the prayer﴾ up to His saying: ﴿what you say﴾. Then it was permitted for them to drink it from the dawn prayer until the day rose or reached midday, then they would stand for the noon prayer while sober. Then they did not drink it until they prayed the 'Atamah (night prayer), then they drank it until midnight, and they slept and got up for the dawn prayer while it was morning. They continued in this manner, drinking it, until Sa'd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ prepared food and invited (p-280)

people from the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), among them a man from the Anṣār. He prepared for them the head of a camel, then invited them to it. When they ate and drank wine, they became intoxicated and began talking. Sa'd said something, and the Anṣārī became angry, lifted the jaw of the camel and broke Sa'd's nose. Then Allah, exalted, revealed the abrogation (naskh) of wine and its prohibition, saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, wine, gambling, idols and divining arrows are only an abomination﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 90] up to His saying: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They ask you about orphans. Say: Setting things right for them is best﴾. The exegetes said: When the sūrah of Banī Isrā'īl was revealed, and His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner﴾, and in sūrat al-Nisā': ﴿Indeed, those who consume the property of orphans unjustly consume only fire in their bellies﴾, the Muslims scrupled to mix their food with the food of those orphans who were with them, and they would separate their food from their food and their drink from their drink, until perhaps their food spoiled. This was hard on them, so they complained of that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Allah, exalted, revealed: ﴿And if you mix with them, then they are your brothers﴾, meaning in food, drink, dwelling, riding an animal, and employing a slave. Al-Sha'bī said: Whoever mixes with an orphan, let him be generous to him, and whoever mixes by eating, let him not do so.

﴿And Allah knows the corrupter from the reformer﴾. Ibn Zayd said: Allah knows when you mix your property with his property, whether you intend to set right his property or to corrupt his property unjustly.

﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have burdened you﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: He would have made it harder for you. This is the saying of al-Suddī.

The second: He would have made what you took from the property of orphans a ruin (mūbiqan). This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbās.

﴿Indeed Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾, meaning: Mighty in His authority and power over causing hardship, Wise in what He does in His management and in His leaving off causing hardship.

He said, may He be exalted: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling﴾, the verse. That is, your companions ask you, O Muhammad, about wine and gambling and drinking them. This is the first verse revealed concerning them.

Khamr (wine) is everything that veils the intellect and covers it, from their saying "I covered the vessel" (khammartu al-inā' idhā ghaṭṭaytahu, "I covered the vessel when you cover it"). It is also said: "He is in the khumār and ghumār of the people," meaning he has entered among them and concealed himself among them. From this comes the khimār of a woman, because it covers her. From it is also said: "He walks to you in khamar," meaning secretly. Al-'Ajjāj said:

In the glittering of the eagles, he does not come in khamar,
He directs the earth and drives the trees.

By his saying "he does not come in khamar," he means he does not come secretly, but openly, with banners and armies.

As for maysir, it is gambling, from the speaker's saying: "This thing came to me easily (yasara li hādhā al-shay' yasran wa maysiran)." So the yāsir is the player with the arrows (al-qidāḥ), then the gambler was also called yāsir and yasar, as the poet said:

So I spent the night like a yasar gabīn (a loser),
Turning over after the arrows were drawn.

﴿Say: In them is great sin and benefits﴾. Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read (... kathīr) with the letter thāʼ.

Regarding their sin there are two interpretations. The first: the drinker of wine becomes intoxicated and harms people, and the sin of gambling is that a man gambles and thus withholds the right and wrongs others. This is the saying of al-Suddī.

The second: the sin of wine is the loss of the intellect of its drinker when he becomes intoxicated, until knowledge of his Creator is lost to him (p-277)

from him.

The sin of gambling is the preoccupation it causes from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer, and the arising of enmity and hatred, as Allah, exalted, described: ﴿Satan only wants to cast enmity and hatred among you through wine and gambling, and to turn you away from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 90]. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbās.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and benefits for people﴾, the benefits of wine are its price and the profit of its trade, and the pleasure they obtain by drinking it, as Ḥassān ibn Thābit said:

We drink it, and it leaves us kings,
And lions whom the encounter does not repel.

And as another said:

When I drink, then indeed I am
Lord of al-Khawarnaq and al-Sadīr,
And when I become sober, then indeed I am
Lord of al-Shuwayhah and the camel.

As for the benefits of gambling, there are two sayings. The first: acquiring wealth without toil.

The second: what they obtain of the shares of the slaughtered camel. That is because they used to draw lots (yatayāsarūn) over the camel, and when a man among them prevailed over his companions, they slaughtered it, then divided it into tenths according to the number of arrows. About this A'shā Banī Thaʻlabah says:

And a camel of gambling, to which I called for generosity,
The middle of a barren land whose shade was light.

This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbās, Mujāhid and al-Suddī.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And their sin is greater than their benefit﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: their sin after the prohibition is greater than their benefit after the prohibition, and this is the saying of Ibn 'Abbās. (p-278)

The second: both before the prohibition, meaning the sin that arises from their causes, is greater than their benefit. This is the saying of Sa'īd ibn Jubayr.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they ask you what they should spend. Say: the surplus﴾, there are six interpretations. The first: what exceeds the family's needs. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbās.

The second: that it is the moderate middle in spending, as long as it is not extravagance or stinginess. This is the saying of al-Ḥasan.

The fourth: that al-'afw is that what they bring of little or much be taken from them. This is a saying also related from Ibn 'Abbās.

The fifth: that it is charity from surplus wealth (ʿan ẓahr ghinā). This is the saying of Mujāhid.

The sixth: that it is the obligatory charity (al-ṣadaqah al-mafrūḍah). This is also related from Mujāhid.

They differed regarding this spending which is al-'afw, whether it was abrogated (nusikhat). Ibn 'Abbās said: it was abrogated by zakāt.

Mujāhid said: it remains in force.

They differed regarding this verse: was the prohibition of wine by it or by something else? A group of the people of reasoning (ahl al-naẓar) said: wine was prohibited by this verse.

Qatādah said, and most of the scholars hold to it: it was prohibited by the verse of al-Mā'idah.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 221:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not marry polytheistic women until they believe﴾. The scholars differed concerning it in three opinions:

The first: that it applies to all polytheistic women, both the People of the Book (kitabiyyat) and those who are not of the People of the Book, and that its ruling has not been abrogated (mansukh). Therefore it is not permissible for a Muslim man to marry a polytheistic woman, ever. It is mentioned that Talhah ibn Ubayd Allah married a Jewish woman, and Hudhayfah married a Christian woman, so ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab became exceedingly angry, to the point that he almost seized them. They said: "We will divorce them, O Commander of the Believers, so do not be angry." He said: "If their divorce is permitted, then their marriage is (also) permitted. Rather, let them take from you a small, humiliating stone (ṣaghara qamʾa)."

The second: that it was revealed with reference to the polytheistic women of the Arabs and whoever adopts the religion of the People of the Book, and that it is firmly established, nothing of it having been abrogated. This is the view of Qatadah and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The third: that it is general to all polytheistic women, and that from among them the People of the Book have been abrogated by His saying, may He be exalted, in al-Ma'idah: ﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Book before you﴾. Al-Saltu ibn Bahram reported from Sufyan who said: Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman married a Jewish woman, so ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab wrote to him: "Release her." He wrote back: "Do you claim that she is forbidden, so that I should release her?" He said: "I do not claim that she is forbidden, but I fear that you will shun the believing women among them."

The meaning of "nikah" here is marriage (al-tazwij), which is its literal sense in the language, though it is also used figuratively for intercourse (al-wat'). Al-Aʿsha said:

"And do not approach a neighbouring woman, for her secret is forbidden to you, so marry, or abstain."

That is: so marry, or remain chaste.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And a believing slave-woman is better than a polytheist woman﴾. That is: the marriage to a believing slave-woman is better than the marriage to a polytheistic free woman, other than the People of the Book, even if her lineage is noble and her origin honourable. Al-Suddi said: This verse was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Rawahah, who had a black slave-woman. He slapped her in anger, then regretted it, so he came to the Prophet ﷺ and informed him. He said: "What is she, O ʿAbd Allah?" He said: "She fasts, prays, performs wudu well, and bears witness to the two testimonies." The Messenger of Allah said: "She is a believer." Ibn Rawahah said: "I will certainly free her and marry her," and he did so. Some Muslims criticised him for this, so Allah revealed this.

﴿And even if she pleases you﴾, that is: her beauty, her lineage, and her wealth.

﴿And do not marry polytheistic men until they believe﴾. This is on its generality by consensus (ijma'): it is not permissible for a Muslim woman to marry a polytheist, ever.

Al-Hasan reported from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "We marry the women of the People of the Book, but they do not marry our women." In this is evidence that the guardians (awliya') of a woman have more right to marry her than the woman herself.

His statement, Exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about menstruation. Say: it is an injury﴾. Al-Suddi said: The questioner was Thabit ibn al-Dahdah al-Ansari. The Arabs and the Muslims in the early days of Islam used to avoid living with menstruating women, eating with them, and drinking with them. So they asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and this verse was revealed. This is also the view of Qatadah.

Mujahid said: They used to keep away from menstruating women in the vagina, and would have intercourse with them in their anus during their menses. So this verse was revealed. The "injury" (al-adha) is that which harms, namely the foul smell, the burden (sin), and the impurity.

﴿So keep away from women during menstruation﴾. The scholars differed about what is meant by "keeping away" (al-i'tizal), and there are three opinions. The first: one should avoid all contact with her body by touching her with any part of one's body. This is the view of Ubaydah al-Salmani.

The second: what lies between the navel and the knee. This is the view of Shurayh.

The third: the private part (al-farj). This is the view of Aishah, Maymunah, Hafsah, and the majority of the exegetes.

Then He said: ﴿And do not approach them until they are purified﴾. Here there are two recitations (qira'ah, a canonical mode of reciting the Qur'an). The first is with light emphasis and a damma on the ha', which is the recitation of the majority. Its meaning is when the blood has stopped. This is the view of Mujahid and Ikrimah.

The second is with shadda (emphasis) and a fatha on the ha', recited by Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Asim, and in the transmission of Abu Bakr from him. Its meaning is until she performs ghusl (the full bath).

Then He said: ﴿And when they have purified themselves﴾, meaning with water. There are three opinions: The first: its meaning is when they have performed ghusl. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, and al-Hasan.

The second: wudu' (ablution). This is the view of Mujahid and Tawus.

The third: washing the private part.

Regarding His statement: ﴿So come to them as Allah has commanded you﴾, there are four interpretations. The first: the front passage (al-qubul) which He forbade during menstruation. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The second: ﴿come to them from the place of their purity, not from the place of their menstruation﴾. This is the view of Ikrimah and Qatadah.

The third: ﴿come to the women from the lawful means of marriage, not from the means of immorality﴾. This is the view of Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah.

The fourth: ﴿from where Allah has made lawful for you﴾, so do not approach them while in ihram (the sacred state of pilgrimage), nor while fasting, nor while in i'tikaf (seclusion in the mosque). This is the view of al-Asamm.

﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who repent and loves those who purify themselves﴾. Here there are three interpretations: (p-284)

The first: those who purify themselves with water. This is the view of Ata.

The second: Allah loves those who purify themselves from having intercourse with women in the anus. This is the view of Mujahid.

The third: Allah loves those who purify themselves from sins, by not returning to them after repenting of them. This is also reported from Mujahid.

His statement: ﴿Your women are a tilth for you﴾, that is, a field where your children are sown and the place where your offspring are cultivated. Tilth is a metaphor for marriage. ﴿So come to your tilth﴾, meaning marry the field where your children are sown.

﴿As you wish﴾. Here there are five interpretations. The first: meaning in whatever manner you wish, in various positions. Abdullah ibn Ali narrated that some of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ were sitting one day, and a Jew was near them. Some of them said: "I come to my wife while she lies on her side." Another said: "I come to her while she is standing." Another said: "I come to her while she is on her side." Another said: "I come to her while she is kneeling." The Jew said: "You are nothing but like animals. But we only have intercourse with her in one position." So Allah revealed this verse. This is the view of Ikrimah.

The second: meaning from whatever direction you wish, toward her front passage, or from her back toward her front passage.

Jabir narrated that the Jews said: "The Arabs have intercourse with women from behind, and when they do so the child is born cross-eyed." So Allah refuted their claim and said: ﴿Your women are a tilth for you, so come to your tilth as you wish﴾. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and al-Rabi'.

The third: meaning from wherever you wish. This is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and others.

The fourth: how you wish, whether you practice coitus interruptus (al-'azl) or not. This is the view of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib.

The fifth: wherever you wish, from the front or from the back. This was transmitted by Nafi' from Ibn Umar, and he reported it from others too. (p-285)

Hubaysh ibn Abdullah al-San'ani narrated from Ibn Abbas that some people from Himyar came to the Prophet ﷺ asking him about various matters. A man among them said: "O Messenger of Allah, I am a man who loves women. What is your view on this?" So Allah revealed in Surah al-Baqarah the explanation of what they had asked about. He revealed concerning what the man asked: ﴿Your women are a tilth for you, so come to your tilth as you wish﴾. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Facing or with her back to you, as long as it is in the vagina."

﴿And send forth for yourselves﴾, meaning good deeds. This is the view of al-Suddi.

The second: "send forth for yourselves" the remembrance of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, during intercourse. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The third: the private part (al-farj). This is the view of Aishah, Maymunah, Hafsah, and the majority of the exegetes.

The third: washing the private part.

The second: ﴿come to them from the place of their purity, not from the place of their menstruation﴾. This is the view of Ikrimah and Qatadah.
