Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 255:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah! There is no god but He﴾ — the verse.

It is phrased as a negation, that no god other than Allah may be valid, while its real meaning is the affirmation of one God, who is Allah. Its implied sense is: Allah is the God, to the exclusion of anyone else.

Regarding ﴿al-Hayy (the Living)﴾ there are four interpretations. The first: He named Himself living because He directs affairs to their courses and determines things in their measures; so He is living through determining, not through a life.

The second: He is living with a life which is an attribute of His.

The third: it is one of Allah's names by which He is named, so we say it in submission to His command.

The fourth: the intended meaning of al-Hayy is the Everlasting, as said by al-Suddi, and from it is the verse of Labid:

"When you see me today, having risen safe, I am not more alive than Kilab and Ja'far."

(al-Qayyum) ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab recited it as (al-Qayyam). Regarding it there are six interpretations. The first: the One who maintains the management of His creation, as said by Qatadah.

The second: meaning the One standing over every soul for what it has earned, until He recompenses it for its deed, since He is knowing of it, nothing of it being hidden from Him, as said by al-Hasan.

The third: the meaning of al-Qa'im is existence, which is the saying of Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The fourth: that He is the One who does not cease and is not changed, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The fifth: that He is the Knower of affairs, from the saying of people: "So-and-so stands by this book," meaning he knows it.

The sixth: that it is one of Allah's names, derived from istiqamah (uprightness), as said Umayyah ibn Abi al-Salt:

"The heaven and the stars were not created,
and the sun with the moon that stands with it,
the Guardian, the Self-Subsisting, measured them,
and the Resurrection, the Garden and the Scalding Water,
except for a matter of great importance."

﴿Neither drowsiness nor sleep overtakes Him﴾. Al-sinah is drowsiness by the agreement of all, and nu'as is what is in the head; when it reaches the heart it becomes sleep. Al-Mufaddal distinguished between them, saying: sinah is in the head, nu'as is in the eye, and nawm is in the heart.

What the majority hold, equating sinah with nu'as, is more fitting. ʿAdiy ibn al-Riqa' said:

"A drowsy one whom slumber overcame, so that in his eye sinah flowed, yet he is not asleep."

﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾. Regarding this there are two views. One: what is before them is what preceded their creation, and what is behind them is what follows their death.

The second: what is before them is what they have made apparent, and what is behind them is what they have concealed.

﴿And they encompass nothing of His knowledge except what He wills﴾, that is, of His known things, except that He informs them of it and makes them know it.

﴿His Kursi extends over the heavens and the earth﴾. Concerning the Kursi there are two views. One: it is among the attributes of Allah, Exalted.

The second: it is among the features of His dominion (malakut).

If it is said that it is among the attributes, there are four sayings: (p-325)

The first: it is the knowledge of Allah, said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: it is the power of Allah.

The third: it is the dominion of Allah.

The fourth: it is the management of Allah.

If it is said that it is among the features of His dominion, there are three sayings: The first: it is the Throne ('arsh), said by al-Hasan.

The second: it is a throne below the Throne.

The third: it is a footstool (kursi) beneath the Throne, and the Throne is above the water.

The root of kursi is knowledge, and from it a written sheet containing knowledge is called kurrasah. Abu Dhu'ayb said:

"I have no kursi concerning your affair that I conceal, nor is there any created kursi of the Knower of the Unseen."

The scholars are also called al-karasi, because they are relied upon, just as they are called "the pegs of the earth," because it is through them that the earth is set right. The poet said:

"Around them gather white-faced and noble men, a kursi for the calamities when they befall."

That is, scholars of the events of affairs. These testimonies indicate that the most sound of its interpretations is what Ibn ʿAbbas said, that it is the knowledge of Allah, Exalted.

Ya'qub al-Hadrami recited (wus'u kursiyyihi al-samawatu wal-ardu), with the sin of wus' vowelless and the ʿayn of it dammah, and the heavens and the earth in the nominative as subject and predicate. Regarding its interpretation there are two views: One: its preserving them does not burden Him, according to the majority.

The second: its preserving them is not great to Him, related by Aban ibn Taghlib.

He recited:

"Has Salma's new love departed today from you, and withheld, while bounty had never wearied her?"

They differed over what the pronoun in "its" (hā') refers to, on two views: One: it refers to the name of Allah, the meaning being: the preserving of the heavens and the earth does not burden Allah.

The second: it refers to the Kursi, the meaning being: the preserving of them does not burden the Kursi.

﴿And He is the Most High, the Mighty﴾. Concerning al-ʿAliyy there are two interpretations. One: al-ʿAliyy in might and the power of authority.

The second: al-ʿAliyy above likenesses and equals.

Regarding the difference between al-ʿAliyy and al-ʿAali there are two probable views: One: al-ʿAali is one who exists in a place of height, while al-ʿAliyy is one deserving of height.

The second: al-ʿAali is one who may be shared in his height, while al-ʿAliyy is one who may not be shared in his height. On this second view, it is permissible to describe Allah as al-ʿAliyy but not as al-ʿAali; on the first view, it is permissible to describe Him by both.

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 2, verse 256:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no compulsion in religion﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: this applies to the People of the Book, who are not compelled to adopt the religion if they pay the jizyah (poll tax). This was said by Qatadah.

The second: it was revealed specifically concerning the Ansar. A woman among them would be one whose children did not survive, so she would vow that if a child of hers lived, she would raise him as a Jew, hoping for him a long life. This was before Islam. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ expelled the Banu al-Nadir, there were among them sons of the Ansar. The Ansar said: "How shall we deal with our sons?" So this verse was revealed. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: it was abrogated by the obligation of fighting. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

﴿So whoever disbelieves in al-Taghut﴾. Regarding this there are seven opinions. The first: it is Satan, and this is the view of Umar ibn al-Khattab.

The second: it is the sorcerer, and this is the view of Abu al-'Aliyah.

The third: it is the soothsayer, and this is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The fourth: it is the idols.

The fifth: it is the rebellious ones of mankind and the jinn.

The sixth: it is everyone who transgresses against Allah and is worshipped instead of Him, either by compulsion over those who worship him or by their obedience to him, whether the one worshipped is a human or an idol. This is the view of Abu Ja'far al-Tabari.

The seventh: it is the self (nafs), because of its transgression in what it commands of evil, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, the soul is a persistent commander of evil﴾ [Yusuf: 53]. (p-328)

They differed concerning the word ﴿al-Taghut﴾ on two grounds. One: it is a non-Arabic word that has been Arabicized, and it applies to the singular and the plural. The second: it is an Arabic word derived from al-taghiyah (tyranny, excess), this was said by Ibn Bahr.

﴿And believes in Allah, has grasped the most trustworthy handhold﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations. The first: it is faith in Allah, and this is the view of Mujahid.

The second: it is the Sunnah of the Messenger.

The third: it is success (tawfiq).

The fourth: it is the Qur'an, said by al-Suddi.

﴿There is no breaking for it﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: there is no severance for it, said by al-Suddi.

The second: there is no fracturing for it. The root of fasm is splitting (al-sad').

The Almighty's words: ﴿Allah is the Protector of those who believe﴾ may have two meanings. One is that He takes charge of them with victory. The second is that He takes charge of them with guidance.

﴿He brings them out of darkness into light﴾ has two meanings. The first is that He brings them out of the darkness of misguidance into the light of guidance; this is the view of Qatadah. The second is that He brings them out of the darkness of punishment in the Fire into the light of reward in Paradise.

﴿As for those who disbelieve, their protectors are the false deities (taghut). They bring them out of the light into darkness﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: they bring them out of the light of guidance into the darkness of misguidance. (p-329)

The second: they bring them out of the light of reward into the darkness of punishment in the Fire.

According to a third view, held by the people of inner insights (ashab al-khawatir): they bring them out of the light of truth into the darkness of desire.

If it is asked: how can they bring them out of the light when they never entered it? There are two answers to this. The first is that the verse was revealed concerning people who had apostatised; this is the view of Mujahid. The second is that it was revealed concerning those who had always been disbelievers, and that it is said of them in this way because, had those (leaders) not done this to them, they would have entered (the light). Thus, through what they did, they are in the position of those who have driven them out of it.

There is also a third meaning: they were upon the natural disposition (fitrah) at the time the covenant was taken from them, and when those (leaders) led them to disbelief, they brought them out of the light of their natural disposition.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 258:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Have you not considered the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord⦾﴾ He was Nimrod son of Kan'an, and he was the first to tyrannize over the earth and to claim lordship (al-ruboobiyyah).

﴿Because Allah had given him kingship⦾﴾ There are two opinions concerning this. One: it refers to Nimrod, since when he was given kingship he argued about Allah, exalted is He. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: it refers to Abraham, since when Allah gave him kingship, Nimrod argued with him. This is the view of Abu Hudhayfah.

As for the "argument" (al-muhajjah), there are two possible meanings. One: it is the counter-argument of a proof with its like. The second: it is the objection to a proof with something that nullifies it. (p-330)

﴿When Abraham said, "My Lord is He who gives life and causes death." He said, "I give life and cause death."⦾﴾ He meant that he gives life to whoever is owed death by being released and spared, and causes death by killing without a cause that requires killing. Thus he countered the wording with its like, and he diverted from the difference between the two acts in their causes.

﴿Abraham said, "Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west."⦾﴾ If it is said: Why did Abraham turn away from supporting his first argument to another, and does this not weaken the argument and is it not unbecoming of prophets? There are two answers to this. One: the corruption of his counter-argument had already become evident, so there was no need to support his argument further, and then he followed that with another, as a confirmation of the proof.

The second answer: since in that argument there was a confusion (ishghab) from him through the doubt with which he countered it, Abraham wished to argue against him with something free of confusion, to cut him off and to establish the proof against him. He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west⦾﴾. If it is said: Why did Nimrod not counter him by saying, "Then let your Lord bring it from the west"? There are two answers to this. One: Allah abandoned him by diverting him from this doubt.

The second answer: from what he saw of the signs with him, he knew that he would act, so he feared that he would increase in disgrace.

﴿So the one who disbelieved was confounded⦾﴾ There are two opinions concerning this. One: it means he was bewildered. The second: its meaning is that he was silenced, and this is the view of Abu 'Ubaydah.

It was also read as (fa-baha-ta alladhi kafara) with a fatha on the ba' and the ha', meaning that the king had slandered Abraham with his doubt, i.e., hastened to slander (bu-htan).

﴿And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people⦾﴾ This may have two meanings. One: He does not help them to support wrongdoing. The second: He does not deliver them from the punishment of wrongdoing.

The word "wrongdoing" (al-zulm) here may have two meanings. One: it is disbelief specifically. The second: it is transgression from the truth to falsehood. (p-331)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 259:

﴿Or like the one who passed by a town﴾ Scholars differed about the one who passed by a town, on three opinions. The first: he was ʿUzayr (Ezra), as said by Qatadah.

The second: he was Irmiya (Jeremiah), which is the view of Wahb.

The third: he was al-Khadir (al-Khidr), which is the view of Ibn Ishaq. They also differed about the town, on two views. The first: it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem) when Bukhtansar (Nebuchadnezzar) destroyed it, and this is the view of Wahb, Qatadah, and al-Rabi‘ ibn Anas.

The second: it is the town from which thousands went out fearing death, as said by Ibn Zayd.

﴿while it was fallen down upon its roofs﴾ Regarding khawiyah (fallen down) there are two views. The first: it means ruined, which is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Rabi‘, and al-Dahhak.

The second: it means empty.

The root of khawa' is emptiness. It is said: "The house became khawiyah (empty)" when it was emptied of its people, and khawa' is hunger, because the stomach is empty of food. ﴿upon its roofs﴾: upon its buildings; ʿarsh means building.

﴿He said: How will Allah bring this to life after its death?﴾ Regarding this there are two views. The first: He will rebuild it after its ruin.

The second: He will restore its people after their destruction. (p-332)

﴿So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him up. He said: How long have you remained?﴾ That is, how long did he stay.

﴿He said: I have remained a day or part of a day﴾ Because Allah caused him to die at the beginning of the day and revived him after a hundred years at the end of the day, he said "a day," then he turned and saw the remnant of the sun, so he said: ﴿or part of a day.﴾ ﴿He said: Rather, you have remained a hundred years. Look at your food and your drink; they have not spoiled﴾ Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: its meaning is that they had not changed, from asin water, which is water that has not changed. Ibn Zayd said: The difference between asin and ajin is that ajin is water that has changed yet is still possible to drink, while asin is water that has changed to the point that it cannot be drunk.

The second: its meaning is that the years had not passed over it so that it became changed; this was said by Abu ʿUbayd.

It is said: his food was grape juice, figs, and grapes; he found the juice sweet, and he found the figs and grapes fresh and freshly picked.

If it is asked: How did he know that he had died for a hundred years when his food had not changed? It is answered: He returned to his condition and learned through traces and reports, and he saw the grandchildren of his grandchildren as old men, whereas he had left their fathers as youths, so he knew that he had died for a hundred years.

It is narrated from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah honour his face, that ʿUzayr left his family and left his wife pregnant, and he was fifty years old. Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him up, and he returned to his family while he was fifty years old, and he had a son who was a hundred years old; so his son was fifty years older than him. And this is the one whom Allah made a sign for the people.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And look at the bones, how We raise them﴾ there are two readings. One: nunshiruha with the unpointed ra', read by Ibn Kathir, Nafi‘, and Abu ʿAmr, and its meaning is "We bring them to life." 

Al-nushur is life after death, derived from nashr al-thawb (unfolding of the garment), because the dead person (p-333)

is like one folded up, since he is withheld from action by death; when he is alive and unfolds into activity, it is said: nushira and unshira.

The second reading, read by the rest (nunshizuha) with the pointed z, meaning We raise some of them up upon others. The root of nushuz is elevation, and from it nashz is the name for a raised place of the ground, and from it the nushuz of a woman, due to her rising above obedience to her husband.

It is also said: Allah restored his eyes and returned his sight before reviving his body, so he saw the gathering of his bones and their being clothed with flesh, and he saw how Allah revived his donkey and gathered its bones.

They differed about the one who said to him: How long have you remained? on three views. The first: he was an angel.

The second: he was a prophet.

The third: he was one of the believers who had lived long, who witnessed his death and his revival.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 260:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when Abraham said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead."﴾ The scholars differed over why he asked this, on two views. The first: he saw a carcass being torn apart by beasts of prey, and so he said that. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatadah, and al-Dahhak.

The second: it was due to Nimrod's dispute with him over giving life. This is the view of Ibn Ishaq.

Whichever of the two it was, he wished to know this by direct observation (ʿilm ʿiyan) after knowledge by inference (ʿilm al-istidlal).

For this reason God, may He be exalted, said to him: ﴿"Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but so that my heart may be at rest."﴾ On this there are three interpretations: (p-334)

The first: it means that he wanted his certainty to increase above his existing certainty. This is what al-Hasan, Qatadah, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, and al-Rabiʿ said. It is not permissible that it means "so that my heart may be at rest through knowledge after doubt," because doubt about this would be disbelief, which is not permissible for a prophet.

The second: he meant, "so that my heart may be at rest that You have answered my request and taken me as a friend (khalil), as You promised me." This is the view of Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The third: he did not intend the seeing of the heart, but the seeing of the eye. This is what al-Akhfash said.

Some of those who speak of subtle meanings shied away from this commitment and said: Abraham only meant that he asked his Lord to show him how He gives life to hearts through faith. This interpretation is invalid because of what follows in the explanation.

The alif in His saying ﴿"Have you not believed?"﴾ is not an interrogative alif; it is an alif of affirmation, like the verse of Jarir:

Are you not the best of those who rode the mounts, and the most generous of the people of the world in pouring out wine?

﴿He said, "Then take four birds."﴾ On this there are two sayings: the first: they are the rooster, the peacock, the crow, and the dove. This is what Mujahid said.

The second: four of the "shaqanin" (a kind of bird). This is what Ibn ʿAbbas said.

﴿"Then make them incline toward you"﴾ The majority read the sad with a ḍammah (ṣurhunna). Hamzah alone read it with a kasrah (ṣirhunna). The difference between the ḍammah and the kasrah has been discussed on two views. The first: their meaning is the same while their wording differs. On this view there are four explanations of the interpretation: the first: its meaning is "pluck them, with their feathers and flesh," said by Mujahid.

The second: "cut them up," said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, and al-Hasan.

Al-Dahhak said: in Nabataean it is ṣarta, which means splitting apart.

The third: "gather them to you," said by ʿAta' and Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: "incline them toward you." Ṣawar means inclination, and from it is the poet's description of camels:

They stay, hobbled at the shin, silent, while the south wind makes their noses lean.

The second view: the meanings of the ḍammah and the kasrah differ. On their difference there are two sayings: the first, said by Abu ʿUbayda, is that with the ḍammah the meaning is "gather them," and with the kasrah "cut them up."

The second, said by al-Kisa'i, is that with the ḍammah the meaning is "incline them," and with the kasrah "turn them toward you."

﴿"Then place on every mountain a portion of them"﴾ On this there are four sayings: the first: they were four mountains, said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and Qatadah.

The second: they were seven, said by Ibn Jurayj and al-Suddi.

The third: every mountain, said by Mujahid.

The fourth: he meant the four directions of the world, which are east, west, north, and south, and he represented them by mountains, said by Ibn Bahr.

They differed over whether Abraham cut the birds into pieces which, by that, became dead, or not. On two views: the first: he cut them into pieces which became dead, then called them and they returned living, so that he might see how God gives life to the dead, as he had asked his Lord. This is the view of the majority.

The second: he separated them while alive, then called them, and they answered him and came back to him, reasoning from their return at his call to the return of the dead to life by God's call. It is not valid for Abraham to call the dead to himself. This is said by Ibn Bahr.

The "juz'" (portion) of anything is a part of it, whether it is divisible into equal shares or not, while the "sahm" (share) is that which is divided among all of it into equal parts.

If it is said: how was Abraham answered with the signs of the Hereafter, unlike Moses in His saying ﴿"My Lord, show me Yourself, that I may look upon You"﴾ [al-A'raf: 143]? There are two answers to this: the first: what Moses asked for cannot be valid while the obligation (taklif) remains, whereas what Abraham asked for was specific and valid. (p-336)

The second: circumstances differ, so answering may be better at some times, and refusing at another time in matters for which no permission has been given beforehand.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: God commanded Abraham to do this before a son was born to him, and before the scrolls were sent down to him.

It is related that Abraham slaughtered the four birds and crushed their bodies in a mortar, but not their souls, and made the mixed flesh into ten portions placed on ten mountains. Then he placed their beaks between his fingers, and called them, and they came running; the flesh flew to the flesh, the skin to the skin, and the feathers to the feathers. Some of the jurists among the exegetes went so far as to say, regarding one who bequeaths a portion of his property to a man, that it is a bequest of a tenth, because Abraham placed portions of the birds on ten mountains.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 261:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: it means in jihad (struggle), as said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: it means in all the paths of righteousness.

﴿Is like a grain that grows seven ears, in each ear a hundred grains﴾. Allah struck this as a parable for the fact that spending in the way of Allah is multiplied seven hundredfold. Regarding the multiplication of this in other acts of obedience, there are two views. The first: that a good deed in other than this is multiplied tenfold, as said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: that it may be multiplied seven hundredfold, as said by al-Dahhak.

﴿And Allah multiplies for whom He wills﴾. This admits of two meanings. The first: He multiplies this multiplication for whom He wills.

The second: He multiplies the increase beyond that for whom He wills. (p-337)

﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾. In this there are two views. The first: All-Encompassing, so He is not constrained from increasing, All-Knowing of who deserves it, as said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: All-Encompassing in mercy, so He is not constrained from multiplying, All-Knowing of what was spent.

It may also bear a third interpretation: All-Encompassing in power, All-Knowing of what is in the best interest.

﴿Those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah and then do not follow what they have spent with reminders [of their kindness] or injury, for them is their reward with their Lord, and no fear will there be concerning them, nor will they grieve.﴾ Al-Mann (reminding) in this context is to say, "I did good to you and raised you up," and al-Adha (injury) is to say, "You are always poor, and who has done me a favour through you," which hurts the heart of the one who receives.

﴿For them is their reward with their Lord﴾ means what they deserve, in what He has promised them for their spending.

﴿Nor will there be any fear for them﴾ has two interpretations. The first: they will have no fear of losing the reward. The second: they will have no fear of the terrors of the Hereafter.

﴿Nor will they grieve﴾ admits two meanings. The first: they will not grieve over what they spent. The second: they will not grieve over what they left behind.

It was said that this verse was revealed concerning Uthman ibn Affan (may Allah be pleased with him), regarding what he spent on the Army of Hardship (Jaysh al-'Usra) in the expedition of Tabuk. (p-338)

﴿Kind speech﴾ means good speech in place of al-mann and al-adha. It admits two meanings. The first: that he draws near [to the recipient] if he gives. The second: that he prays for [the recipient] if he refuses.

﴿And forgiveness﴾ has four interpretations. The first: it means pardoning the beggar's harm. The second: by forgiveness is meant safety from sin. The third: that it is abstaining from charity and withholding it, as said by Ibn Bahr. The fourth: that he conceals his poverty and does not expose him by it.

﴿Better than charity followed by injury﴾ admits two meanings for the injury here. The first: that it is al-mann. The second: that it is reproaching for poverty.

His saying ﴿Better than charity followed by injury﴾ also admits two meanings. The first: better than it in giving. The second: better than it in the sight of Allah.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The one who reminds of his giving, Allah will not speak to him on the Day of Resurrection, nor look at him, nor purify him, and for him is a painful punishment."

His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not invalidate your charities with reminders and injury﴾ intends the invalidation of the merit (of charity) without the reward.

It admits a second meaning: the invalidation of its effect in the heart of the giver.

﴿Like one who spends his wealth to be seen by the people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day.﴾ The one who intends by his spending to be seen (riya') is not rewarded, because he did not intend the face of Allah, so he does not deserve its reward. The one who reminds and injures has opposed the one who intends the face of Allah and deserves its reward, even if he repeats his giving and invalidates its merit.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So his example is like a smooth rock with dust upon it.﴾ Al-Safwan is the plural of safwanah (ṣafwānah), and concerning it there are two views. The first: that it is a smooth stone, named so for its smoothness. The second: that it is softer than stones, related by Aban ibn Taghlib.

﴿Then a heavy rain strikes it﴾ is al-wabil, the great rain, heavy in its drops and strong in its impact.

﴿And leaves it bare﴾: al-saldu of stones is that which is hard, and of land is that which does not produce plants, by likeness to a stone that does not produce anything.

﴿They have no power over anything of what they have earned﴾ means of what they spent. He expressed the spending by "earning" because they intended by it gain. So this is set forth as an example for the one who shows off, in the invalidation of his reward, and for the one who reminds and injures, in the invalidation of its merit.

The first: that it is a smooth stone, named so for its smoothness. The second: that it is softer than stones, related by Aban ibn Taghlib.

﴿Then a heavy rain strikes it﴾ is al-wabil, the great rain, heavy in its drops and strong in its impact.

﴿And leaves it bare﴾: al-saldu of stones is that which is hard, and of land is that which does not produce plants, by likeness to a stone that does not produce anything.

﴿They have no power over anything of what they have earned﴾ means of what they spent. He expressed the spending by "earning" because they intended by it gain. So this is set forth as an example for the one who shows off, in the invalidation of his reward, and for the one who reminds and injures, in the invalidation of its merit.

The Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on Surah 2, Verse 265:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the example of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of Allah﴾ may have two meanings. The first: in supporting the people of His religion among the fighters (mujahidun). The second: in aiding the people of His obedience among the Muslims.

﴿And firmly, from their own souls﴾ has four interpretations. The first: firmly from their own souls, through the strength of certainty and the support of the religion, which is the meaning of the saying of al-Sha'bi, Ibn Zayd and al-Suddi. (p. 340)

The second: they make sure (yatathabbatun) where they place their charities, as said by al-Hasan and Mujahid.

The third: it means seeking reward for themselves with Allah, as said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah.

The fourth: training their souls (tawtinan) to remain steadfast in obedience to Allah, as said by some of the theologians (mutakallimun).

﴿Like a garden on a height (rabwah)﴾. Regarding the rabwah there are two views. The first: it is the elevated place of the earth; and it was said: the level place in its height.

The second: everything that is raised above the course of water, as said by al-Yazidi.

﴿Struck by heavy rain (wabil)﴾. Regarding the wabil there are two meanings. The first: intense rain.

The second: abundant, as 'Adi ibn Zayd said:

*Little from me for her, even if she is angry, that I say: "May you be watered, watered with the abundant, flowing rain."*

﴿It yields its produce (ukul) twofold﴾. He specified the rabwah only because its vegetation is finer and its yield greater. Al-A'sha said:

*What garden of the gardens of al-Hazn is lush with pasture, green, upon which a pouring, abundant rain has fallen?*

The ukul, with a dammah, is food, because it is of its nature that it is eaten.

The meaning of ḍi'fayn (twofold) is "two times," because the ḍi'f of a thing is its equal plus an addition to it; and ḍi'fāhu is its two equals plus an addition to it. It was also said: the ḍi'f of a thing is its two equals. The first is the view of the majority (al-jumhur).

﴿But if heavy rain does not strike it, then light rain (tall)﴾. The tall is dew, which is less than rain. The Arabs say: "the tall is one of the two rains," and crops from dew are weaker than crops from rain and yield less. In this there is, though it is little, steadiness and benefit. So by this he intended to strike the example: that abundant righteousness is like the crop of rain, abundant in benefit, and little righteousness is like the crop of dew, little in benefit. And do not abandon little righteousness when you do not do much of it, just as you do not abandon the crop of dew when you cannot produce the crop of rain.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 266:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Would any of you wish to have a garden﴾ — and it is the orchard (al-bustan).

﴿of palm trees and grapevines﴾ — because these are among the finest things to be in it.

﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾ — because the most prized of gardens are those whose water flows.

﴿and old age has overtaken him﴾ — because old age may cause one to forget the youth that was spent in earning it, so he becomes weakest in hope and greatest in regret.

﴿and he has offspring, weak﴾ — because he is most compassionate toward the weak, and his concern for them is greatest.

﴿then it is struck by a fiery whirlwind and burns﴾ — and regarding the whirlwind (al-i'sar) there are two views. The first: it is the scorching wind (al-samum) that kills, related by al-Suddi.

The second: al-i'sar is a wind that blows from the earth up to the sky like a pillar, which the common people call al-zawba'a (dust devil). The poet said:

﴿... ... ... ∗∗∗ if you are a wind, you have met a whirlwind﴾

It was called al-i'sar because it twists like the twisting of a wrung-out garment.

﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you the signs﴾ — this may bear two meanings. The first: He clarifies for you the proofs. The second: He sets forth for you the parables.

﴿so that you may reflect﴾ — this may bear two meanings. The first: that you may take heed, since the one who reflects takes heed. The second: that you may be guided, since guidance is reflection.

They differed concerning this parable which Allah struck regarding the regret over the loss of a blessing: to whom does it refer? There are three opinions. (p-342)

The first: it is a parable for the one who shows off in spending, whose benefit is cut off from him when he is most in need of it, as related by al-Suddi.

The second: it is a parable for one who neglects obedience to Allah for worldly pleasures, and who will attain the supreme regret in the Hereafter, as related by Mujahid.

The third: it is a parable for one whose deed ends in corruption, and this is the view of Ibn Abbas.

﴿O you who believe, spend of the good things you have earned﴾. On this there are four opinions. The first is that it means gold and silver, the view of ʿAlī, peace be upon him. The second is that it means trade, as Mujāhid said. The third is that it means the lawful. The fourth is that it means the best.

﴿And of what We have brought forth for you from the earth﴾ means of the crops and fruits.

Regarding "earnings" (kasb) there are two possible meanings. The first is what comes as newly acquired wealth. The second is what ownership has become settled upon, whether from long ago or recently.

They differed about this spending on two views. The first is that it is the obligatory zakat (almsgiving), as ʿUbaydah al-Salmānī said. The second is that it concerns voluntary charity, as some of the scholars of kalām said.

﴿And do not aim at the bad of it, to spend from it﴾. Tayammum means intending deliberately. Al-Khalīl said: you say amamtuhu when you head toward its front, and yammamtuhu when you deliberately intend it from whatever direction. Others said the two are the same. Al-Khabīth means the inferior of everything. Here there are two views. The first is that they used to bring the shrivelled dates (ḥashaf) and mix them into the dates of charity, so this verse was revealed. This is the view of ʿAlī and al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib. The second is that al-Khabīth means the unlawful, as Ibn Zayd said.

﴿And you would not take it except with closing your eyes to it﴾. On this there are four interpretations. The first: except that you be lenient, the view of al-Barāʾ ibn ʿĀzib. The second: except that you reduce the price, as Ibn ʿAbbās said. The third: except at a loss, so how would you give it in charity? This was said by al-Zajjāj. The fourth: except that you grant yourselves indulgence regarding it, as al-Suddī said. Al-Ṭirimmāḥ said:

No people have tempted us with the inferior, and there are men who, for the sake of the guest, are content with overlooking [faults].

His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿The Shaytān promises you poverty﴾, which is what he frightens you with regarding poverty if you spend or give charity.

﴿And he commands you to indecency﴾. This may have two meanings. The first: to stinginess. The second: to acts of disobedience.

﴿And Allah promises you forgiveness from Him﴾. This may have two meanings. The first: ... for you. The second: pardon for you.

﴿And bounty﴾. This may have two meanings. The first: abundance of provision. The second: multiplication of punishment.

﴿And Allah is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾. It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed the Shaytān has a touch upon the son of Adam, and the angel has a touch. As for the touch of the Shaytān, it is a promise of evil and a denial of the truth. As for the touch of the angel, it is a promise of good and an affirmation of the truth. Whoever finds that, let him know that it is from Allah, and let him praise Allah. And whoever finds the other, let him seek refuge in Allah." Then he recited this verse.

The fifth: correctness (of judgment), as Ibn Abī Najīḥ said from Mujāhid. The sixth: writing, as Mujāhid said. The seventh: intellect, as Zayd ibn Aslam said.

It may also allow an eighth: that wisdom here means the rectitude of religion and the setting right of the worldly life.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 270–271:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿If you disclose your charities, then how excellent they are﴾. He means that there is no disapproval in disclosing them.

﴿And if you conceal them and give them to the poor, it is better for you﴾. Concerning this there are two views. The first: it refers to voluntary charity (sadaqat al-tatawwu'), in which case concealing it is better, because it is further from showing off (riya'). As for obligatory alms (zakat), disclosing them is better, because it is further from suspicion (tuhma). This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Sufyan.

The second: concealing both obligatory and voluntary charity is better. This was said by Yazid ibn Abi Habib, al-Hasan, and Qatada.

﴿And He will remove from you some of your misdeeds﴾. Concerning this there are two views. The first: the word "min" (some of) is superfluous (za'ida), its implied sense being: "and He will remove from you your misdeeds." The second: it is not superfluous, but is used for partition (li-l-tab'id), because obedience removes minor sins (al-saghair) without repentance. Concerning the removal (takfir) of these, there are two views. The first: He conceals them from them. The second: He forgives them for them.

Concerning the removal (takfir) of these, there are two views. The first: He conceals them from them. The second: He forgives them for them.

The Exalted said: ﴿For the poor who have been confined in the way of God﴾. It was said: they are the poor among the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun). Regarding "uhsiru" (have been confined) there are four opinions:

The first: they restrained themselves from earning a livelihood out of fear of the enemy among the disbelievers. This was said by Qatadah and Ibn Zayd.

The second: the disbelievers prevented them by means of fear of them. This was said by al-Suddi.

The third: poverty prevented them from fighting (jihad).

The fourth: their occupation with jihad prevented them from seeking a livelihood.

﴿They are not able to strike about in the land﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions: the first, that it means moving about for business (tasarruf), said by Ibn Zayd.

The second, that it means trade (tijarah), said by Qatadah and al-Suddi.

﴿The ignorant one thinks them wealthy because of their restraint﴾. That is, because of his little experience of them. "Min al-ta'affuf" means from dignified self-restraint, contentment (al-tiqannu, al-iffah, al-qana'ah).

﴿You know them by their mark﴾. Al-simah means the sign. Concerning what is meant here there are two opinions: the first, humility (al-khushu'), said by Mujahid.

The second, poverty, said by al-Suddi.

﴿They do not ask people importunately﴾. Concerning this there are two meanings: the first, that one asks while he has sufficiency. (p-347)

The second, that it is the enveloping of oneself in begging, and from it the name of the blanket (al-lihaf) is derived.

If it is asked: did they ask in a way other than importunately? It is said: No, because they were wealthy through their restraint. Rather, the sense of the statement is: they do not ask, so that their asking would be importunate.

Ibn Abbas said concerning the people of the Suffah (ahl al-Suffah) among the Emigrants: they had no dwellings in Medina and no kin, and they numbered about four hundred.

The Exalted said: ﴿Those who spend their wealth by night and by day, secretly and openly, for them is their reward with their Lord, and no fear shall be upon them, nor shall they grieve﴾. They differed concerning the occasion of its revelation, in three opinions:

The first: it was revealed concerning Ali, may God honor his face. He had four dirhams and spent them on the people of the Suffah: one dirham in the darkness of night, one dirham in the brightness of day, one dirham secretly, and one dirham openly. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: it was revealed concerning the expenditure on horses in the way of God, because they spend by night and by day, secretly and openly. This was said by Abu Dhar and al-Awza'i.

The third: it was revealed concerning everyone who spends his wealth in obedience to God.

And a fourth is possible: that it is specific to the permissibility of benefiting from crops and fruits, because every passerby by night or by day benefits from them, secretly and openly. Thus it is more general, because they are taken without intention and conform to the measure of need.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 275:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Those who consume interest (al-riba)﴾ mean: those who take interest. He expressed taking by consuming, because taking is only intended for consumption. Riba (interest, excess) means increase, from their saying: "rabā al-sawīq yarbū" (the barley-flour rose) when it increased. It is the excess over the amount of the debt in exchange for the term (of repayment).

﴿They will not rise except as one rises whom Satan has driven to madness by his touch﴾ means: from their graves on the Day of Resurrection. In this there are two opinions. The first: they are like the drunkard from wine, who staggers from side to side, and it is attributed to Satan because he obeys him in his intoxication.

The second, said by Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and al-Hasan: they will not rise from their graves on the Day of Resurrection except as one rises whom Satan has driven to madness by his touch, meaning one whom Satan strangles in this world by touch, meaning madness. So that will be on the Day of Resurrection a sign of consuming interest in this world.

They differed concerning the touch of madness: is it by the act of Satan? Some of them said: this is from the act of God, by what He brings about of the overcoming of black bile, so it overpowers him; it is attributed to Satan metaphorically, by way of comparison with what he does of his seduction, which overpowers him.

Others said: rather it is from the act of Satan, by God's empowering him to do so with some people and not others, because this is the apparent meaning of the Qur'an, and there is nothing in reason that prevents it.

﴿That is because they said: "Trade is only like interest."﴾ It was said: it refers to the Thaqif, because they were the most of the Arabs in interest. When they were forbidden from it, they said: "How are we forbidden from interest when it is like trade?" So God, exalted is He, related that about them, then He refuted what they mentioned of the comparison with trade, saying: ﴿But God has permitted trade and forbidden interest.﴾ For al-Shafi'i, concerning His words ﴿But God has permitted trade and forbidden interest﴾, there are three views. The first: that it is of the general (al-'amm) which runs on its generality in the permissibility of every trade and the prohibition of every interest, except what a proof has specified from the prohibition of some trade and the permission of some interest. On this view, it was disputed whether his words are of the generality intended as general, or of the generality intended as particular, on two views. The first: that it is a generality intended as general, even though a proof of specification has entered it.

The second: that it is a generality intended as particular.

In the distinction between the two there are two aspects. The first: that the generality intended as general is that the remainder of the generality after specification is more than the specified part, and the generality intended as particular is that the remainder of it after specification is less than the specified part.

The second distinction: the clarification in what is intended as particular precedes the wording, while what is intended as general comes after the wording and is joined to it. [This] is one of his views. The second view: that it is the mujmal (unspecified, ambiguous) which cannot be used to make a trade lawful or unlawful unless it is joined by a clarification from the Sunnah of the Messenger, even though it indicates the permissibility of trades in general, not in detail.

This is the difference between the general and the mujmal: the general indicates the permissibility of trades in general and does not indicate their permissibility in detail until a clarification is joined to it.

On this view, it is mujmal, and it was disputed whether its ambiguity is due to a contradiction within it or to the conflict of other things with it, on two aspects. The first: that when what is in the verse of permitting trade and forbidding interest, which is a trade, conflicted, it became mujmal by this conflict, and its ambiguity was from itself.

The second: that its ambiguity is by other than itself, because the Sunnah forbade some trades and permitted some trades, so it became mujmal by the Sunnah.

And when its ambiguity is established, it was disputed concerning it: is it ambiguity in meaning without wording, because the wording of "trade" is known in the language, and the Law only made the meaning and ruling ambiguous when it permitted some trade and forbade some trade?

The second aspect: that the ambiguity is in its wording and its meaning, because when it turned "trade" away from its unrestricted sense to what was established in the Law, the wording and the meaning are both open to multiple interpretations. This is the explanation of the second view.

The third view: that it falls under both the general and the mujmal, so it is a generality into which specification has entered, and a mujmal which has been followed by explanation, because its wording admits generality and its meaning admits ambiguity, so the wording is a generality into which specification has entered, and the meaning is mujmal which has been followed by explanation.

The second aspect: its generality is in the first part of the verse, from His words ﴿God has permitted trade and forbidden interest﴾, and its ambiguity is in the last part, from His words ﴿and forbidden interest﴾. So its first part is a general into which specification has entered, and its last part is mujmal which has been followed by explanation.

The third aspect: the wording was mujmal, and when the Messenger explained it, it became general. So it falls within the mujmal before the explanation and within the generality after the explanation.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So whoever has received an admonition from his Lord and desists﴾. Concerning the admonition there are two aspects. The first: the prohibition. The second: the warning.

﴿Then what has passed is his﴾. Said by al-Suddi: that is, what he consumed of interest, he is not obliged to return it.

﴿And his affair is up to God﴾ may bear two aspects. The first: concerning the reckoning and the recompense. The second: concerning pardon and punishment.

It was also said there is a third aspect: concerning protection and success. And it was said there is a fourth aspect: his affair is up to God, and the one who is independent in establishing him upon the prohibition or in his transfer to considering it permissible.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 276–277:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Allah deprives usury of blessing﴾. That is, He diminishes it little by little. It is derived from maḥāq al-shahr (the waning of the month), due to the decrease of the crescent in it. Regarding this there are two views:
First: He annihilates it on the Day of Resurrection when one gives charity from it in this world.

Second: He removes blessing from it in this world, along with punishing its taker for it in the Hereafter. (p. 351)

﴿And He causes charities to grow﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations:
First: He multiplies the wealth from which the charity has been given.

Second: He multiplies the reward of the charity and increases it, and this increase is obligatory by promise, not by deed.

﴿And Allah does not love every ungrateful sinner﴾. Regarding kaffār (ungrateful) there are two views:
First: One who conceals the favours of Allah and denies them.

Second: One who frequently commits what makes him a disbeliever.

And regarding athīm (sinner) there are two views:
First: That he is one who plans sin by night (bayyata al-ithm).

Second: One who frequently commits what makes him a sinner.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verses 278–281:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: O you who have believed with your tongues, fear Allah with your hearts. The second: O you who have believed with your hearts, fear Allah in your actions.

﴿And leave what remains of the interest (riba)﴾. Regarding who this verse was revealed about, there are two opinions. The first: it was revealed concerning the Thaqif tribe, who had dealings with Amir and the Banu Makhzum. They brought their dispute to ʿAttab ibn Usayd in Makkah, who was the judge there on behalf of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. They said: "We entered Islam on the condition that what was due to us from interest remains ours, and what was owed by us is waived." So this verse was revealed concerning them, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wrote to them about it. (p-352)

The second: it was revealed concerning a remainder of interest that was owed to al-ʿAbbas, Masʿud, ʿAbd Yalayl and Habib ibn Rabiʿah with the Banu al-Mughirah.

The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And leave what remains of the interest﴾ are understood to mean that whoever engaged in riba before his Islam, and took some of it while in disbelief, and then embraced Islam while some of it remained, then what he had taken before his Islam is pardoned for him and he is not obligated to return it, while what remains of it after his Islam is forbidden for him and it is not lawful for him to take it. As for practicing riba after Islam, it is obligatory to return what he has taken and what remains is cancelled; he returns what he took and what remains is dropped. This is unlike what was taken in disbelief, because Islam erases what came before it.

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿if you are believers﴾ there are two opinions. The first: it means that whoever is a believer, this is his ruling. The second: its meaning is "if you are believers."

The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿But if you do not do it﴾ mean leaving what remains of interest.

﴿then be informed of a war from Allah and His Messenger﴾. Ḥamzah and ʿĀṣim, in the narration of Abu Bakr, recited (fa-ādhanū) with a long vowel, meaning: "then make others aware." The rest recited it with a short vowel, meaning "then you know," and in this there are two opinions. The first: if you do not desist from riba, I will command the Prophet to fight you. The second: if you do not desist from it, then you are the enemies of Allah and His Messenger, meaning His enemies.

﴿And if you repent, you will have your principal﴾, meaning what you have paid, ﴿without wronging or being wronged﴾: you will not wrong by taking increase over your principal, and you will not be wronged by withholding your principal.

The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And if the debtor is in hardship, then let there be postponement until ease﴾. It has been said that in the recitation of Ubayy it is (dhā ʿusrah), which is permissible in Arabic. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: postponement for one in hardship is obligatory in interest-debts specifically, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Shurayh. The second: it is general, and postponement for one in hardship is obligatory in every debt, based on the apparent wording of the verse; this is the view of ʿAtaʾ and al-Ḍaḥḥak. It has also been said that postponement for one in hardship in interest-debts is established by explicit text, and in other debts by analogy (qiyas).

Regarding His saying: ﴿until ease﴾ there are two opinions. The first: it is a noun of place from ease (yusr), meaning he becomes well-off; this is the view of most scholars. The second: until death, as said by Ibrahim al-Nakhaʿi.

﴿And that you give charity is better for you﴾, meaning: giving charity to the one in hardship by forgiving what he owes is better for you than granting him postponement. Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab narrated from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab who said: "The last of the Qur'an to be revealed was the verse on riba, so leave riba and ribyah (doubtful dealings). The Prophet of Allah ﷺ passed away before he explained it."

The words of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾, meaning: fear Him through obedience in what you have been commanded regarding leaving riba and what remains of it.

Regarding ﴿a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾ there are two opinions. The first: meaning to the recompense of Allah. The second: to the dominion of Allah.

﴿Then every soul will be paid in full what it earned﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: the recompense of the deeds it earned. The second: what it earned of reward and punishment.

﴿And they will not be wronged﴾, meaning: not by diminishing what they deserve of reward, nor by increasing punishment beyond what they deserve.

Ibn ʿAbbas narrated that "the last verse revealed to the Prophet ﷺ was this verse." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "He remained for seven nights after it."

The words of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿O you who believe, when you contract a debt for a specified term﴾, to the end of the verse.

Regarding ﴿contract﴾ (tadayantum), there are two interpretations (ta'wil, the scholarly explanation of a verse's meaning). The first: you deal with one another (tajazaytum). The second: you transact (ta'amaltum).

Regarding ﴿write it down﴾ (fa-ktubuhu), there are two opinions. The first: it is a recommendation (nadb, a desirable but not obligatory act), the view of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, al-Hasan, and al-Sha'bi. The second: it is an obligation (fard), the view of al-Rabi' and Ka'b.

﴿Let a scribe write it between you justly.﴾ The justice of the scribe is that he should not add to what is owed to the detriment of the one who owes it, nor reduce from it to the detriment of the one to whom it is owed.

﴿And let no scribe refuse to write as Allah has taught him, so let him write.﴾ Regarding this there are four opinions. The first: it is an obligation upon the community as a whole (fard 'ala al-kifaya, a collective duty, like jihad), the view of Amir. The second: it is obligatory upon him when he is free, also the view of al-Sha'bi. The third: it is a recommendation, the view of Mujahid. The fourth: this ruling is abrogated (mansukh, superseded by a later ruling) by the words of the Exalted: ﴿Let no scribe or witness be harmed﴾, the view of al-Dahhak.

﴿And let the one who has the obligation dictate﴾, meaning to the scribe, and let him acknowledge it in the presence of the witness.

﴿And let him not diminish anything from it﴾, i.e., let him not reduce anything from it.

﴿But if the one who has the obligation is foolish﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations. The first: he is the one ignorant of what is right regarding what he must dictate to the scribe, the view of Mujahid. The second: he is the child and the woman, the view of al-Hasan. The third: he is the one who squanders his wealth and corrupts his religion, which is the meaning of al-Shafi'i's view. The fourth: he is the one who does not know the value of wealth, does not restrain himself from squandering it, and has no desire to increase it.

﴿Or weak﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: he is the stupid, the view of Mujahid and al-Sha'bi. The second: he is the one unable to dictate, either because of a speech impediment or muteness, the view of al-Tabari.

﴿Or unable himself to dictate﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: he is the mute, speechless one, the view of Ibn Abbas. The second: he is the one prevented from dictating, either by imprisonment or by absence. The third: he is the insane.

﴿Then let his guardian dictate justly﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: the guardian of the one who has the obligation, the view of al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd. The second: the guardian of the right, that is, its holder, the view of Ibn Abbas and al-Rabi'.

﴿And call upon two witnesses from among your men﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: from among the people of your religion (i.e., Muslims). The second: from among your free men, the view of Mujahid.

﴿But if there are not two men, then a man and two women﴾, meaning: if the testimony is not from two men, then from one man and two women, ﴿from those you find acceptable as witnesses﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: they are free, Muslim, upright men, the view of the majority (al-Jumhur). The second: they are the upright among the Muslims even if they are slaves, the view of Shurayh, Uthman al-Batti, and Abu Thawr.

﴿So that if one of them errs﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: lest she err, the view of the people of Kufa. The second: out of aversion to her erring, the view of the people of Basra.

Regarding what is meant by it there are two interpretations. The first: that she makes a mistake. The second: that she forgets, the view of Sibawayh.

﴿Then one of them may remind the other﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: she makes her like a male among men, the view of Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna. The second: she reminds her if she forgets, the view of Qatada, al-Suddi, al-Dahhak, and Ibn Zayd.

﴿And let not the witnesses refuse when they are called﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations: [p. 357]

The first: for undertaking the testimony and recording it in the document, the view of Ibn Abbas, Qatada, and al-Rabi'.

The second: for establishing and delivering it before the judge, the view of Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, and Ata'.

The third: that it applies both to undertaking and to delivering, the view of al-Hasan.

They differed regarding it on three opinions. The first: it is a recommendation and not an obligation, the view of Ata' and Atiyya al-Awfi. The second: it is an obligation upon the community as a whole, the view of al-Sha'bi. The third: it is an individual obligation (fard 'ayn), the view of Qatada and al-Rabi'.

﴿And do not be weary of writing it, whether it is small or large, up to its term.﴾ By "small" he does not mean what is trivial and insignificant, like a qirat or a daniq, since such amounts fall outside the familiar custom.

﴿That is more just in the sight of Allah﴾, i.e., more equitable. It is said: aqsata means he acted justly, so he is muqsit (just), as the Exalted said: ﴿And act justly; indeed, Allah loves those who act justly﴾ [al-Hujurat: 9]. And qasata means he acted unjustly, as the Exalted said: ﴿And as for the unjust, they will be fuel for Hell﴾ [al-Jinn: 14].

﴿And more suitable for testimony﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: more correct for it, derived from uprightness (istiqama). The second: more protective of it, derived from qiyam in the sense of preservation.

﴿And more likely to prevent doubt﴾. This may have two meanings. The first: that you not doubt the one who owes a right, that he would deny it. The second: that you not doubt the witness, that he might err.

﴿Except when it is a present trade that you conduct among yourselves﴾. This may have two meanings. The first: "present" (hadira) refers to what is immediately delivered, with no term attached to the goods or the price. The second: it refers to goods that the buyer takes possession of, being movable merchandise.

﴿That you conduct among yourselves﴾. This may have two meanings. The first: you pass it from hand to hand. [p. 358]

The second: you frequently trade it at all times.

﴿Then there is no blame upon you if you do not write it﴾, meaning that you are not commanded to write it, though it is permissible.

﴿And take witnesses when you conduct a sale﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: it is an obligation, the view of al-Dahhak and Dawud ibn 'Ali. The second: it is a recommendation, the view of al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, Malik, and al-Shafi'i.

﴿And let no scribe or witness be harmed﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations. The first: harm consists in the scribe writing what he was not dictated to, or the witness testifying to what he was not asked to testify, the view of Tawus, al-Hasan, and Qatada. The second: harm consists in preventing the scribe from writing or the witness from testifying, the view of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Ata'. The third: harm consists in summoning the scribe and the witness while they are busy and have a valid excuse, the view of Ikrima, al-Dahhak, al-Suddi, and al-Rabi'.

It may admit a fourth interpretation: that the harm lies in the writing and the testimony.

﴿And if you do so, it is indeed a transgression (fusuq) in you﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: fusuq is disobedience, the view of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak. The second: it is lying, the view of Ibn Zayd.

It may admit a third interpretation: that fusuq is sin (ma'tham).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 283:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And if you are on a journey and do not find a scribe, then a pledge taken into possession﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read (fa-rudunun), while the rest read (fa-rihanun). (p-359)

Concerning it there are two opinions. The first: the rudun (plural of rahn) refer to property, while the rihan refers to horses.

The second: rihan is a plural, and rudun is a plural of a plural, like thimar and thamar. This was said by al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'.

Concerning His saying ﴿pledge taken into possession﴾ there are two views. The first: taking possession (al-qabd) is part of completing the pledge, and before possession it is not complete. This was said by al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifa.

The second: because it is one of the requirements of the pledge, and before full possession it is not complete. This was said by Malik.

Travel is not a condition for the validity of a pledge, because "the Prophet (ﷺ) pledged his armour with Abu al-Shahm the Jew in Medina," and that is a place of residence. Nor is the absence of a scribe and witness a condition for it, because it is an addition of security.

﴿But if some of you trust others﴾, meaning without a scribe, witness, or pledge.

﴿then let him who is trusted discharge his trust﴾, meaning in paying what is owed and not delaying it.

﴿and let him fear God, his Lord﴾, in not concealing anything of the truth.

﴿And do not conceal testimony, for whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful﴾. Concerning it there are two interpretations. The first: its meaning is that his heart is corrupt; this was said by al-Suddi. The second: he is one who earns the sin of testimony.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 284–285:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ Regarding the attribution of this to Allah the Exalted, there are two opinions. The first: it is an attribution of ownership (idafat tamlik), its meaning being: Allah owns whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.

The second: its meaning is the governance (tadbir) of whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.

﴿And whether you show what is in your selves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it.﴾ Showing what is in the self means acting upon what one has harboured, and one is held to account for it and called to account over it. As for concealing it, it is what one harbours and what the soul speaks to itself about, without acting upon it.

Concerning what is meant by it, there are two opinions. The first: that what is meant is specifically the concealing of testimony; this was said by Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah and al-Sha'bi.

The second: that it is general, covering everything the soul speaks to itself about of evil, or harbours of disobedience; and this is the view of the majority (al-jumhur).

This verse has been disputed: is its ruling established regarding being held to account for what one harbours and speaks to oneself about, or is it abrogated (mansukh)? There are two opinions. The first: its ruling is established regarding being held to account for what one harbours. Those who held that it is established differed on it in three views. The first: its ruling is established in general for what a person harbours, so He calls to account whom He wills and forgives whom He wills; this was said by Ibn Umar and al-Hasan.

The second: its ruling is established regarding a person being held to account for what he harbours even if he does not do it, except that Allah forgives it for the Muslims, and holds the disbelievers and hypocrites accountable for it; this was said by al-Dahhak and al-Rabi'. (p-361)

And ﴿He forgives whom He wills﴾ is taken to refer to the Muslims, and ﴿and punishes whom He wills﴾ is taken to refer to the disbelievers and hypocrites.

The third: its ruling is established in general regarding the Muslims being held to account for the calamities and matters that befall them in this world which grieve them, and the disbelievers and hypocrites being held to account with the punishment of the Hereafter; this is the view of A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her.

The second opinion: that the ruling of the verse regarding being held to account for what a person harbours and speaks to himself about, even if he does not do it, is abrogated.

Those who said it was abrogated differed as to what abrogated it, in two opinions. The first: it was abrogated by what al-Ala' ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Ya'qub narrated from his father from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "Allah revealed ﴿And whether you show what is in your selves or conceal it, Allah will call you to account for it﴾, and this weighed heavily upon the people. They said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we will be held to account for what we speak to ourselves about; we are ruined.' So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾." This is also the view of Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: it was abrogated by what Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿And whether you show what is in your selves﴾, something entered their hearts from it such as nothing had entered them before. The Prophet ﷺ said: (Say: We hear and we obey and we submit.)

He said: So Allah cast faith into their hearts. He said: Then Allah revealed: ﴿The Messenger believes﴾ up to the end of the verse.

Then he recited: ﴿Our Lord, do not take us to task if we forget or make mistakes﴾, and He, the Exalted, said: 'I have done so.'

﴿Our Lord, and do not place upon us a burden like that which You placed upon those before us﴾, He said: 'I have done so.' ﴿Our Lord, and do not burden us with that which we have no ability to bear﴾, He said: 'I have done so.'

﴿And pardon us, and forgive us, and have mercy upon us. You are our Protector, so give us victory over the disbelieving people﴾, He said: 'I have done so.'"

What I say regarding what a person harbours and speaks to himself about, without doing it, is that he is held to account for the sin of belief (ma'thim al-i'tiqad) and not for the deed, unless his refraining from the deed is out of regret; for regret is repentance which purifies him of the sin of belief.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿The Messenger believes﴾ up to His saying: ﴿and His angels and His books﴾. As for the belief of the Messenger, it is by two matters: bearing the message and conveying it to the community; and as for the belief of the believers, it is by affirmation and action.

﴿Each believes in Allah and His angels and His books and His messengers.﴾ Belief in Allah is by two matters: affirming His oneness (tawhid), and accepting what He sent down to His Messenger.

Regarding belief in the angels there are two aspects: the first: belief that they are the messengers of Allah to His prophets.

The second: belief that each one of them is a watcher (raqib) and a witness (shahid).

(wa kutubihi) is the reading of the majority, and Hamzah read (wa kitabihi). Whoever reads (wa kutubihi), what is meant is all that Allah sent down of them upon His prophets.

Whoever reads (wa kitabihi), there are two aspects: the first: that it refers to the Qur'an specifically.

The second: that it intends the genus, so its meaning is the same as the first, and that it intends all the books, and belief in them and acknowledgment of their descent from Allah upon His prophets.

Regarding the obligation to act upon what is in them where no abrogation has come, there are two opinions. Then, regarding what was previously mentioned of the belief of the Messenger and the believers, although it came in the form of a report, there are two opinions: the first: that what is meant is praising them for what He reported of their belief.

The second: that what is meant is that others follow them.

Then He said, may He be exalted: ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾, meaning in believing in some of them and not others, as the People of the Book did; so equality among them in affirmation is required. As for the obligation of equality in adhering to their laws, there are the two opinions we mentioned earlier. He made this a report of their saying, and what preceded it a report of their state, so as to combine for them speech and action, past and future. (p-363)

﴿And they say: We hear and we obey﴾, i.e., we hear His word and obey His command.

It may also carry a second meaning: that hearing means acceptance, and obeying means action.

﴿Your forgiveness, our Lord﴾, its meaning is: we ask You for Your forgiveness; therefore it came in the accusative.

﴿And to You is the destination﴾, meaning: to Your recompense.

It may also carry a second meaning: he intends by it: to Your meeting, since meeting precedes recompense.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 2, verse 286:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ means its ability (ṭāqah). There are two interpretations of it. First: it is a promise from Allah and His Messenger to the believers, out of His bounty toward His servants, that He will not burden any soul beyond its capacity.

Second: it is an informing from the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers about Allah, in praise of Him, that He does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.

Then He said: ﴿It has what it earned, and it bears what it earned﴾, meaning: it has what it earned of good deeds, and it bears what it earned, meaning of sins.

Regarding kasabat (earned) and iktasabat (earned, with the iktisab form), there are two views. First: their wording differs but their meaning is one. Second: kasabat is used exclusively for good, and iktasabat is used exclusively for evil.

﴿Our Lord, do not impose blame on us if we forget or make mistakes.﴾ Al-Ḥasan said: its meaning is: say, "Our Lord, do not hold us to account."

﴿If we forget﴾: there are two interpretations of it. First: meaning, if we neglect Your command. Second: we abandon, and forgetting here carries the meaning of abandoning, like His saying: ﴿They forgot Allah, so He forgot them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67]. This was said by Qutrub.

﴿Or make mistakes﴾: there are two interpretations of it. First: what they interpreted (as permissible) of sins by way of doubtful matters (shubuhāt). Second: what they committed deliberately of sins which are an error (khaṭa'), contrary to what is correct.

The people of the language have distinguished between akhṭa'a and khaṭi'a. They said: akhṭa'a may occur both with sin and without sin, whereas khaṭi'a occurs only with sin. From this is the saying of the poet:

"The people blame the ruler when they err in what is right, and the guide is not blamed."

﴿Our Lord, and do not lay upon us a burden (iṣr)﴾: there are four interpretations of it. First: iṣr means a covenant we are unable to fulfill, said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatadah.

Second: meaning, do not transform us into apes and swine; this is the saying of 'Ata'.

Third: it is the sin for which there is neither repentance nor expiation; said by Ibn Zayd.

Fourth: iṣr is a great weight; said by Malik and al-Rabi', and al-Nabighah said:

"O preventer of oppression from affecting their nobles, and the bearer of burdens from them after they had been weighed down."

﴿As You laid it upon those before us﴾, meaning the Children of Israel regarding what they bore of killing themselves.

﴿And do not burden us with what we have no ability to bear﴾: there are two sayings. First: what we have no ability to bear of what the Children of Israel were charged with. Second: what we have no ability to bear of punishment.

﴿And pardon us, forgive us, and have mercy on us. You are our Mawla﴾: there are two views. First: our Owner. Second: our Protector and Helper.

﴿So give us victory over the disbelieving people﴾. ʿAṭā' ibn al-Sā'ib narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "When this verse was revealed: ﴿The Messenger believes in what has been sent down to him from his Lord﴾, and when he reached His saying: ﴿Your forgiveness, our Lord﴾, Allah said: I have forgiven you. When he recited: ﴿Our Lord, do not impose blame on us if we forget or make mistakes﴾, Allah said: I will not hold you to account. When he recited: ﴿Our Lord, and do not lay upon us a burden as You laid it upon those before us﴾, Allah said: I will not lay it upon you. When he recited: ﴿And do not burden us with what we have no ability to bear﴾, Allah said: I will not burden you. When he recited: ﴿And pardon us﴾, Allah said: I have pardoned you. When he recited: ﴿And forgive us﴾, Allah said: I have forgiven you. When he recited: ﴿And have mercy on us﴾, Allah said: I have had mercy upon you. When he recited: ﴿So give us victory over the disbelieving people﴾, Allah said: I have given you victory."

Marthad ibn 'Abd Allah narrated from 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir al-Juhani, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Recite these two verses from the end of al-Baqarah, for Allah gave them to me from beneath the Throne." Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The surah in which al-Baqarah is mentioned is the tent-pole of the Qur'an. So learn it, for learning it is a blessing and abandoning it is regret, and the baṭalah cannot master it." It was asked: "Who are the baṭalah?" He said: "The sorcerers."
